# The Mistakes Ledger

**Every mistake made building Constistant and Destrier, recorded so none of them happens twice.**

Compiled from the complete workmen's diary: **71 source files**, **2026-07-01 → 2026-09-02**, **1063 distinct mistakes**.

> This document exists because the team won the STECON Construction Innovation Challenge 4 — and the
> honest reason it won was not that nothing went wrong. It is that almost everything went wrong at
> least once, got written down, and got fixed. What follows is that record, kept complete on purpose:
> nothing here is trimmed for looking bad, because the entries that look worst are the ones with the
> most value left in them.

---

## How to use this document

1. **Before starting a training round, a paid job, or a data migration** — read *The Rules* below. It is two pages and it is the whole document compressed.
2. **When something breaks** — search this file for the symptom before diagnosing. A large share of these mistakes are second and third occurrences of an earlier one.
3. **When you finish a task** — if you hit something not in here, add it. The format is deliberately uniform: what happened, root cause, impact, fix, and the rule it produces.

Each entry is tagged with its severity and its date, and cites the diary file it came from so the full context is one hop away.

---

## The Rules

These are distilled from the 147 entries rated critical. They are ordered by how much damage they prevented, not by how clever they sound.

### Proof, not vibes

**1. “It completed without an error” is not proof that it worked.**
   After every merge, convert, quantize, export, or migration, measure the artifact — diff the weights, count the rows, read the file back. A step that raises no error has proven nothing about its output.

**2. A guard you have never seen fail is not a guard.**
   Before trusting any check, feed it a known-bad input and watch it fail. A check a broken artifact can pass is worse than no check, because it manufactures confidence.

**3. Never call it done until it has run end-to-end on real production input.**
   Absence of errors is not evidence of function. Hand-written fixtures encode your own assumptions and hide exactly the bug the test exists to catch — build fixtures from real data.

**4. A simulator must import the real code path, never re-implement “what it probably does”.**
   Every shortcut in a simulation becomes an overstatement in its results, and someone will act on that number.

**5. Render what the machine actually receives, and look at it with your eyes.**
   Five minutes of crop-and-compare beats an hour of token arithmetic — and has repeatedly saved an entire paid GPU round.

### Nothing may fail quietly

**6. Missing input must never render as zero.**
   Any cost, quantity, or score path must distinguish “measured as zero” from “unknown”, and shout about the second. A silently-zero line item is indistinguishable from a real one on screen.

**7. Warn on what you discard; never drop silently.**
   Unknown enum values, unparsed fields, filtered rows, unrecognised shapes — every one must name what was dropped and why. A parser that returns empty for an unrecognised shape is a data-loss bug.

**8. Any stage that can drop data needs a reconciliation count downstream.**
   Count in versus count consumed, and assert the expected categories are non-empty. A queue that is only counted and never consumed is a data-loss channel disguised as progress.

**9. Never trust a default you did not choose.**
   Print and assert the effective value at startup — tokens per image, sequence length, image size, timeout, decoding params. A library default you did not pick is a silent config bug waiting for its first expensive run.

**10. Treat unexpectedly good news as a symptom.**
   Unexpectedly low memory use, an unexpectedly green cheap gate, a suspiciously perfect score — investigate before celebrating. Every one of these has hidden a real defect here.

### Measure the right thing

**11. Never report a score without its achievable ceiling.**
   Two identical percentages can be opposite problems. A metric whose ceiling is 4% is measuring your annotation, not your model.

**12. Always attach “measured on what?” to any accuracy number.**
   The eval harness must load the exact artifact that ships. If eval and production load different files, the eval number describes a different system.

**13. A format metric is not a quality metric.**
   Valid-JSON can be 100% while semantic accuracy is 0%. Every eval run needs a human eyeball on real predicted output, and the target metric reported separately.

**14. No ground-truth token may appear in a test prompt.**
   And assert that different inputs produce different outputs — identical answers across inputs is the signature of echo, not of skill.

**15. Re-verify train/val split integrity by entity, every single time.**
   Never inherit a previous round’s split on trust. One authority for split assignment per model; a second hardcoded list is a leak waiting to happen.

**16. Test the highest-value case first.**
   If the core capability is still untested after a full cycle, the cycle measured the wrong thing.

### One authority per fact

**17. A schema change is not done until every consumer and its validator change in the same commit.**
   “The validator passes” is meaningless unless you can point at the gate that would have failed before the fix.

**18. When you fix a bug, grep every sibling call site before you close it.**
   The right fix is the one in the shared function, not the one in the file you happened to be reading. A fix applied to one of two twins is a bug waiting for the twin’s turn.

**19. Two copies of a constant will drift. Assume it.**
   Client and server timeouts, duplicated configs, a second hardcoded list — derive them from one source, and assert the relationship between them (e.g. server timeout < client timeout).

**20. Every engineering constant must carry the standard and clause it came from.**
   So a mismatch is visible on inspection instead of discovered years later — and when a constant changes, recompute everything downstream of it in the same pass.

### Irreversible things get a hard stop

**21. An artifact on rented storage is not a backup.**
   Before any instance is stopped or destroyed, list the file at its off-instance destination and confirm it is really there. Test the destination before you need it.

**22. Backup is an unconditional blocking phase, never a reminder or a step inside a skippable pipeline.**
   Before skipping any phase, enumerate everything that phase was carrying.

**23. A warning about irreversible loss must be standalone, in plain language, with the word STOP.**
   Never folded into a to-do list as “will do later”. If the consequence is unrecoverable, refuse to proceed rather than proceed with a note.

**24. Treat a running job as holding a lock on its whole machine and environment.**
   No pip install, no shared interpreter, no side work. Isolate with a venv or wait for the job to exit.

### Size limits from measured reality

**25. Every cap, limit, and length must come from the measured maximum of the real dataset.**
   Never from a sample, a median, or a guess. And truncation must raise a loud error — silent truncation destroys labels without failing.

**26. Never characterise a dataset from one sample.**
   Any claim of the form “the data looks like X” must come from a script that measures every item and reports min/max/count.

**27. Prove the full deployment path on the base model before spending a training round on it.**
   A model you cannot export, load, or serve is worth zero regardless of its scores.

### Learning must become machinery

**28. A failure that recurs is a missing automated gate, not bad luck.**
   The second time a symptom appears, stop fixing the instance and install a permanent pre-run assertion. In this project the same class of bug recurred three times while its lesson sat written in prose.

**29. A lesson recorded but not applied is a lesson not learned.**
   The day you write “X is a problem” in the diary, grep the whole repo for X and fix every occurrence.

**30. Unrun code is unverified code, and it decays.**
   Execute every script at least once against a tiny fixture before trusting it with a paid run. Code that has sat unrun is riskier than code that never existed.

**31. Never write a root cause you have not proven.**
   Prove it by reading the actual code or with a one-line reproduction. If the evidence is not there, write “cause unknown, suspects A or B” — a confident wrong cause sends everyone in the wrong direction.

## T01 — Verification & False Confidence

*Work claimed as done, correct, or verified when it had not actually been checked.*

**83 entries** · 10 critical · 24 high

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-09 · A tool call reported 'rejected' but .gitignore had actually been modified on disk

**What happened.** The attempt to update 8 raw/ patterns in .gitignore came back from the harness as a rejected tool use. During the final verification it turned out the file content really had been changed to the new folder name — the reported outcome did not match the state on disk.

**Root cause.** The harness's rejection signal cannot be trusted as proof that no write occurred; the team's process treated the tool result as authoritative rather than verifying the artifact.

**Impact.** Had the final check not been done, .gitignore would have been left permanently pointing at a folder name that no longer exists, silently un-ignoring a 533 MB data tree.

**Fix.** Verified the file on disk, restored .gitignore to raw/, and confirmed with a repo-wide grep returning 0 hits for the abandoned name.

**→ Rule.** Never treat a tool's 'rejected'/'failed' report as proof that nothing changed — read the artifact back from disk after any failed or rejected write, especially before concluding a rollback is complete.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-09.md` · tooling/trust</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-13 · Wrong dummy grid value 8.5 defended with evidence that was actually a circular reference back to itself

**What happened.** Asked whether dummy grid `3'` should be 7.6 instead of 8.5, Claude answered incorrectly that 8.5 was confirmed — citing a dimension chain on page06 and beam B4X's span on page19 as independent confirmation. The B4X span had `span_source: "grid_table"`, meaning it had been computed backwards from the grid master's own 8.5 value.

**Root cause.** A derived field was counted as independent confirming evidence. The file's own `confidence_flags` already said `uses_dummy_grid_3'_from_page00_master`, and that flag was not checked before treating it as a second source.

**Impact.** A wrong grid value inherited all the way from the t3/t4 rounds propagated into two B4X beam spans (1.5 instead of 0.6), and the wrong answer was defended through two rounds of questioning before the user forced a re-check with the site-plan image.

**Fix.** Checked page A-03 (site plan), which explicitly states the building overhangs grid 3 by 0.60m. Corrected `3'` from 8.5 to 7.6 and both B4X spans from 1.5 to 0.6, with a warning documenting the circular reference.

**→ Rule.** Before counting any value as independent confirming evidence, check its `span_source`/`confidence_flags` — a field derived from the grid master can never confirm the grid master. Make that an explicit written convention in the schema.

<sub>`2026-07-13.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-15 · Columns modelled with beam-style top/bottom rebar, double-counting main bars 4 as 8

**What happened.** `หน้า21_view2_schedule.json` recorded column C1 with `main_bar.top: 4` and `main_bar.bottom: 4`, totalling 8, although the drawing shows a single set of 4 corner bars (4-Ø12mm). A column has no top/bottom face.

**Root cause.** The beam spec structure was reused for columns without checking that the concept transfers. Some files had even papered over the symptom by adding a `total_main_bar_count` field instead of fixing the structure.

**Impact.** 100% over-count of column main rebar wherever it occurred — a direct steel-quantity and cost error. It was found in house 1, house 2 (page29), house 3 (page35), and then in six more fence-column files across houses 1/2/3.

**Fix.** Changed to a single `main_bar: {count: 4}`. Confirmed project-wide on house 2, then on 2026-07-20 a full-project sweep found and fixed six more files with the same bug and confirmed no occurrence remained.

**→ Rule.** Never reuse an element type's spec structure for a different element type without checking the concept transfers. And when a workaround field like `total_main_bar_count` appears, treat it as a report of an unfixed structural bug and sweep the whole project immediately.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-20 · House 3's structural sheets under-extracted by 60% — page32 went from 20 to 32 elements

**What happened.** A full-sheet image check of house 3's pages 31 (S-04) and 32 (S-05) found page32 missing an entire horizontal beam run along row D, a B3X section on row C, three vertical beams, beam B1 at line B', a BX and the S2 marker — 20 elements became 32. Page31 needed 7 separate fixes including mislabels (B3X→B3 in two places, B2→B1, B3→B2) and a wrong grid attachment (D1-C1→D1'-C1').

**Root cause.** The original extraction was not a systematic full-sheet sweep; elements were recorded as encountered, so whole runs were never noticed missing. Marks were also read without checking against the spec's section, which is why several were labelled with the wrong mark.

**Impact.** A 60% element under-count on a primary structural sheet — the worst measured extraction gap in the project, and the piece needed for the B' cascade (beam B1 at line B') was among the missing ones.

**Fix.** Established a calibrated pixel scale (grid centreline x=1434.3px, grid2 x=1707.7px → 78.1 px/m, E y=756) and re-extracted both sheets fully against it.

**→ Rule.** Extract structural plans by systematic sweep against a calibrated scale, not opportunistically. Verify every row and column line has a continuous member run, and validate each mark against the section spec rather than reading the label alone.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-24 · Declared the model 'ready to use' when it still could not read images at all — the project's entire job

**What happened.** On 2026-07-21 the tuned model was reported as ready for use, but the GGUF produced could only read text; the image-reading component (mmproj) had failed to extract. Reading construction drawings is the sole purpose of the project.

**Root cause.** 'Done' was defined by the pipeline completing without error rather than by the deliverable performing its one core function. No end-to-end acceptance test (feed a real drawing, get a real answer) gated the 'ready' claim.

**Impact.** A false 'finished' state — the origin of the team's 'DAY OF SHAME' label, referenced repeatedly across later sessions as the failure mode all later process rules exist to prevent.

**Fix.** A local dry run (Phase 0.3) was added: download the official mmproj, run llama.cpp against a real house01 drawing page, and confirm Thai text/grid/footing labels are read correctly before any 'ready' claim.

**→ Rule.** Never call a deliverable ready until it has been exercised end-to-end on real production input. Absence of errors is not evidence of function.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24(teach mk).md` · verification</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · A main roof ridge was recorded that does not exist, because two sheets appeared to confirm each other while reading two different look-alike lines

**What happened.** S-06 and A-07 were treated as independently confirming a main roof ridge on the 11.4×11.4 mass. The mass is actually a square hip roof with four lines meeting at a single point — no ridge. S-06 had been reading the centre rafter line and A-07 the A-A section line; two different look-alikes that happened to agree.

**Root cause.** Cross-sheet agreement was accepted as verification without checking that both sheets were reading the same physical feature. Two independent misreadings of two different objects landing on the same wrong answer is the strongest possible false confirmation.

**Impact.** A structural member recorded that does not physically exist, with a confidence rating raised by the false corroboration — the most dangerous class of error, since it looks verified.

**Fix.** Both sheets re-read against the actual geometry; the ridge removed. Recorded as a named principle in the diary.

**→ Rule.** Cross-sheet agreement only counts as verification when both sheets are demonstrably reading the same feature. Agreement between two misreadings is not verification — always name the physical object each source is reading before treating them as independent.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · verification/methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · The GGUF sanity check was passable by a completely untuned model

**What happened.** export_gguf.py:107 guarded against silent merge failure by checking the output starts with '{' and contains any of "png"/"views"/"pattern"/"doc_page". It showed a green ✓ on 24 Jul and was believed ever since. But the prompt itself instructs the model to emit "views" and "pattern", so any model that can follow a prompt passes.

**Root cause.** The check tested for tokens that the prompt supplies to the model, not for tokens that only training could produce. It was written without asking 'if the thing were genuinely broken, would this fire?'

**Impact.** Five days of false confidence in the t01 GGUF; the exact failure the guard existed to catch went undetected. t02's stricter guard (comparing real key names) caught the identical bug immediately — the only difference between caught and uncaught was guard quality.

**Fix.** not fixed — Priority 2 for the next session: rewrite the guard to compare real gold key names (png/doc_page/discipline/sheet_code) the way t02's guard does

**→ Rule.** Every guard must be validated against a known-bad input before it is trusted. Never assert on strings that appear in the prompt — only on strings that exist solely in the training targets. A check that cannot fail is worse than no check, because it manufactures confidence.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · verification-gap</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · export_gguf.py's tuned-model sanity gate checked for words the prompt itself supplies, so an untuned model passes

**What happened.** export_gguf.py:107 declared a model 'tuned' if the reply started with { and contained any of "png", "views", "pattern", "doc_page". But the prompt itself instructs the model to emit "views" and "pattern", so any model that follows instructions passes. The gate showed green on 07-24 and was believed ever since.

**Root cause.** The check was written from what a good answer looks like, not from what only a tuned model could produce. The discriminating tokens (png/doc_page) exist only in the ground truth and are never mentioned in the prompt — but an OR over four terms let the prompt-supplied ones satisfy it.

**Impact.** A false green shielded the merge_and_unload silent failure for five days and gave confidence to ship the GGUF into real extraction work. t02's stricter gate (compare actual key names) caught the identical bug immediately — same bug, different gate quality.

**Fix.** Planned free fix: change the gate to compare real ground-truth key names as t02 does, checking only for tokens absent from the prompt.

**→ Rule.** Design every sanity gate by asking 'if the thing were broken, would this catch it?' A check that a broken artifact can pass is worse than no check, because it manufactures confidence.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · verification-design</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-25 · Format checker reported ALL CHECKS PASS while 345 files had a misspelled discipline value

**What happened.** tools/check_format.py returned "ALL CHECKS PASS" across the whole dataset even though 345 files carried `architecture` instead of the spec's `architectural`, plus 16 more out-of-vocabulary values. In total 485 defects across 423 files in all 49 houses were sitting undetected behind a green validator.

**Root cause.** The schema spec was edited 3 times on 08-21 but the validator that enforces it was never updated in the same change. Spec and checker are two separate sources of truth with nothing binding them together, so the checker silently kept validating an obsolete contract.

**Impact.** 485 defects / 423 files / 49 houses shipped as "validated" training data. Every downstream consumer that filters on `discipline` was silently dropping or mis-routing those files. Required a full 485-point repair sweep across 4,366 files.

**Fix.** Added 5 new gates to check_format.py (discipline vocabulary, `source_image`, notes one-off key, structural roof-framing must be `plan`, gridmaster missing 3 arrays) and batch-repaired all 485 points; all 4,366 files re-parsed clean.

**→ Rule.** A schema edit is not done until the validator that enforces it is edited in the same commit. Treat "validator passes" as meaningless unless you can point to the gate that would have failed the specific defect class you are worried about.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · validation-drift</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · sanitize_elements() silently deleted every element with a negative level, wiping ground beams from the BOQ

**What happened.** `sanitize_elements()` in `worker.py` used the regex `_NEG_DIM_KEYS = r"(_mm|_m|_cm)$"` to treat any key ending in a unit suffix as 'garbage' if its value was negative. But negative values are valid for `level_m` (ground beams below datum, written on Thai drawings as "GB1(-0.50)"), `pos_m` (grid lines before origin) and `level_step_mm` (stepped precast slabs for bathrooms). Whole elements were dropped before reaching BOQ, and the warning blamed the model ('generation หลุด') even though the model had answered correctly. Confirmed on real GT: house 07บ้าน_ใหญ่_2ชั้น_01 page 35 lost 3 of 11 elements.

**Root cause.** A blanket denylist regex on key *suffix* rather than an allowlist of dimensions that genuinely cannot be negative. The validator encoded an assumption ('a measurement is never negative') that is false for elevation/offset fields, and the failure was silent-with-wrong-attribution because the warning text blamed model generation instead of the filter.

**Impact.** Ground beams disappeared entirely from BOQ on every affected house — a missing structural element in a real construction quantity takeoff. Also caused misdirected debugging effort, since the warning pointed at the model.

**Fix.** Replaced the suffix denylist with an explicit allowlist of cross-section dimensions that truly cannot be negative (`width|height|thickness|depth|dia|spacing|length|cover`), plus a regression test. Verified by running old and new regex side-by-side: `level_m`/`level_step_mm`/`pos_m` flip from dropped to kept while `width_mm`/`span_length_m`/`dia_mm`/`depth_mm` still drop.

**→ Rule.** Validate data with an allowlist of fields you have positively confirmed a constraint for, never a denylist matched on name patterns. And when a filter discards data, its warning must name the filter as the actor — never blame an upstream component you did not verify.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · data-validation</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-05 · Eleven pages were extracted at low confidence and shipped into the dataset unverified

**What happened.** Eleven pages were flagged as needing someone to zoom into the image and re-verify before real use: page 19 view2 (SI/SO/ST symbol meanings unknown), page 21 (B5/B5X top/bottom rebar split), 11, 14, 05, 06, 09, 35, 36 (possible wire-size mismatch between BTU 12,000 and 18,000), and 51/53 (BOQ row pairing uncertain).

**Root cause.** Extraction proceeded to completion regardless of confidence, with low confidence recorded as metadata rather than acting as a gate. Combined with the absence of a zoom tool, uncertainty was the expected outcome rather than an exception.

**Impact.** Roughly a fifth of the pages in the house carry data that the team itself says should not be used as ground truth yet — but the files sit in the same folder, in the same format, as verified data. The verification pass was still outstanding at the end of the next day.

**Fix.** Not fixed — listed as a pending item on both 2026-07-05 and 2026-07-06.

**→ Rule.** Low-confidence records must be physically separated (a quarantine folder or an explicit status field consumers filter on), not just annotated. Anything below the confidence threshold cannot be allowed to sit in the same directory as accepted ground truth.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-05.md` · unverified-data</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Three of four dummy gridlines were written into the grid master at only 0.5-0.6 confidence and never verified

**What happened.** The new grid master file recorded 4 dummy gridlines. Only 1' was high confidence (0.85, from actually seeing the full-height line on page 06). 3', A' and A'' were entered at 0.5-0.6 confidence, inferred from Gen 2's 'unnamed_extension' notes plus the positions of beams B4X/B3X/B5X — the printed dimension positions are real, but it was never confirmed that an actual beam runs at those positions.

**Root cause.** Low-confidence inferences were promoted into a master reference file that every other page is meant to cite. A master file implies authority, so uncertainty at the source silently becomes certainty at every consumer.

**Impact.** Three gridlines of unverified existence became the canonical grid reference for the whole house, and page 19 view2 in round t2 was then extracted referencing them. Any error propagates to every page that cites the master.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Flagged as needing comparison against the page 19/20 beam plan when those are redone; confidence scores were kept honest in the file rather than inflated.

**→ Rule.** A master/reference file must contain only verified entries. Keep unverified candidates in a separate staging list until confirmed — the moment an inference is written into an authoritative file, its confidence score stops being read by anyone downstream.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · unverified-data</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · A full day of Label Studio work ended with nothing actually imported, published or reviewable

**What happened.** The script, three XML configs and the task JSON (33 elements tasks, 1 material_list, 22 single) were all created and regenerated several times, but the diary records they were 'not yet imported into Label Studio Cloud for real' — no project created, nothing published, no collaborators invited. The receiving-side script label-studio-import-*.js to convert exports back into annotated/*.json does not exist at all.

**Root cause.** The work was built outward from the generator without ever completing one thin end-to-end slice first. Each of the day's five fix rounds was triggered by a failure that a single early end-to-end attempt would have surfaced at once.

**Impact.** A whole day of tooling work produced zero reviewed records. The round trip is not just unfinished but unproven — the export→annotated direction has no code, so it is unknown whether reviewed data can even be got back out.

**Fix.** Not fixed — carried as pending items #1, #8 and #9 (import and confirm, write the import-side script, create and publish the real project).

**→ Rule.** Build one thin end-to-end slice first — one task, imported, reviewed, exported back to disk — before generating dozens of tasks or polishing layout. Until the round trip is proven, none of the generator work is known to be usable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process-failure / unproven-work</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-07 · The 'overhang past the main grid' was assumed to be one thing; it was three unrelated systems

**What happened.** Confusion about dimensions extending past the main grid was resolved by finding they are three genuinely separate systems: 1.50m ground-floor room extension (real dummy grid 3'/A'), 0.60/1.10m tie-beam corner, and 1.30m roof eave. Confidence in dummy grid A'' was lowered — an agent suspects it is not a grid line at all, just a ground-leveling area.

**Root cause.** Several distinct offsets sharing the visual pattern 'a dimension beyond the last grid line' were collapsed into a single explanation because the grid master had no field for what an offset physically is.

**Impact.** A grid master carrying a possibly-fictitious grid line (A'') that would misplace every element referenced against it; repeated confusion across earlier rounds.

**Fix.** Grid master updated to model the three systems separately; confidence raised on 1'/3'/A' and lowered on A''.

**→ Rule.** Do not collapse similar-looking geometry into one explanation — record what each offset physically is, and lower confidence rather than keeping an unverified grid line at full confidence.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-07 · The t3 generator output was declared verified by comparing the UI against the generated task JSON — the same file that carried the bug

**What happened.** After running label-studio-tasks-makham.js on t3, the check performed was 'tested and confirmed page 19 (footing_plan + beam_plan) matched what Makham actually saw in Label Studio'. It passed. The next day a more thorough check found the generator had never been updated for the Gen 4 field shapes, so every beam's grid_ref and every main-rebar value was empty in that same output — the passing check had compared the UI to the broken file and found them consistent with each other.

**Root cause.** Verification methodology compared two artifacts on the same side of the bug (generated JSON ↔ rendered UI) instead of comparing the end of the chain back to its source (raw JSON ↔ rendered UI). Consistency between two downstream artifacts proves nothing about correctness.

**Impact.** A whole day of confidence in the t3 Label Studio pipeline was false. If the t3 task set had already been imported to Label Studio Cloud, annotators would have been labeling beams with no grid reference and no rebar data, with nothing on screen saying data was missing.

**Fix.** Fixed the next day: the generator was taught both the new (grid_ref_start/end/span_length_m, main_bar.top/bottom) and old field shapes, the XML configs gained the matching boxes, and task JSON was regenerated. A three-way source_image / disk / decoded-URL check was added afterwards.

**→ Rule.** Verify against the source, not against an intermediate artifact. 'The UI shows what the file says' is not a test — pick a value you can see on the original drawing and trace it all the way to the screen.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · verification-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-16 · Two adjacent dimensions summed into a single 1.50m overhang that does not exist

**What happened.** On house 2's page06, '0.60' and '0.90' in the row-F dimension chain had been read as a continuous 1.50m overhang. Zooming in showed they are two separate points (0.60 = exterior, 0.90 = interior partition) that merely share a point at gridline F.

**Root cause.** Adjacent numbers in a dimension chain were treated as additive without checking what each one measures to. The same misreading pattern had already produced the wrong `3'` value on house 1.

**Impact.** A fabricated 1.50m strip in the floor plan; the laundry, kitchen, bedroom1 sub-split and bathroom1 all had to be re-scoped, and a whole warning paragraph that concluded 'no dummy grid needed' had to be rewritten as wrong.

**Fix.** Split into `F-F'' x 1-2` (laundry) and `F''-E x 1-2` (kitchen), pinned bedroom1's split to 3' (6.4+1.30=7.7, exact), and rewrote the warning paragraph.

**→ Rule.** Never add adjacent dimension-chain values without confirming what each one terminates at. A shared endpoint makes two dimensions look continuous when they measure different features.

<sub>`2026-07-16.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-20 · A calibrated scale from pages 31/32 reused on page33 without checking page33's own origin

**What happened.** The conclusion that page33's D-C strip has no 1'/3' extension was reached by reusing the calibration from pages 31/32. The user corrected it directly: page33 does have a real 1'/3' extension, and four short beams (D1'-D1, C1'-C1, D3-D3', C3-C3') had to be added.

**Root cause.** A calibration is per-sheet — it depends on that sheet's own origin and scale — but it was carried across sheets as if it were a project constant.

**Impact.** A wrong negative conclusion written into the file's schema_note and warnings, four missing beams, and a correction that required the user to catch it.

**Fix.** Re-checked page33 against its own origin, added the four beams with confidence 1, and fixed the schema_note/warnings that had stated the opposite.

**→ Rule.** Re-derive the pixel scale and origin for every sheet. Never carry a calibration across sheets — and when a conclusion is overturned, fix the notes and warnings that asserted it, not just the data.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Training scripts had never been read line-by-line against the real dataset's actual numbers

**What happened.** The MAX_LENGTH bug had existed since before house 05 was added and survived every prior round, because nobody had ever compared the script's constants against the real measured properties of the dataset.

**Root cause.** Script review consisted of skimming for obvious errors rather than cross-checking each configured limit against a computed statistic of the data it would process.

**Impact.** A latent answer-truncating bug shipped through at least one full paid tuning round undetected.

**Fix.** Made Phase 0.4 a mandatory step: re-read the scripts seriously against real dataset numbers before every rental.

**→ Rule.** Review configuration by computing the corresponding statistic from the real data and comparing, not by reading the number and judging whether it 'looks reasonable'.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24(teach mk).md` · verification</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · House 07 S-04: a position was eyeball-estimated at ~2.00 m when the drawing prints 1.50 m, and a dimension was measured from the wrong grid row

**What happened.** The second CS2's distance from grid 3 had been recorded as an estimated ~2.00 m; the drawing prints 1.50 m. Separately the 1.60 m dimension at bottom right is measured from row B, not row A — which, once corrected, matches S-02's GB1X exactly.

**Root cause.** An estimate was recorded in a field that reads as a measurement, with no marker distinguishing the two. The datum row for a dimension was assumed rather than traced to its extension line.

**Impact.** A 0.50 m position error (33% off) plus a wrong datum row; both feed element positions and grid resolution. The datum error is what had made S-02 and S-04 appear to disagree.

**Fix.** Positions locked using the chains actually printed on the sheet; the corrected datum reconciled S-04 with S-02.

**→ Rule.** Never write an estimate into a measurement field — if the chain isn't printed, mark it unresolved. Always trace a dimension back to its extension line to confirm which grid line is the datum.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Phase 10 'GGUF passed' only tested that it emitted JSON and didn't crash

**What happened.** t01's Phase 10 acceptance test on 25 Jul checked (a) does it answer in JSON — passed, (b) does it hang or crash — passed. It never checked whether the content was correct. The doc even warned 'don't read this as proven complete', but over time everyone remembered only 'Phase 10 passed'.

**Root cause.** Liveness was tested, correctness was not. And the caveat lived in prose next to a pass verdict, so the verdict survived in memory while the caveat did not.

**Impact.** A known-incomplete test hardened into a team belief that the GGUF was validated, which delayed discovery of the merge bug by days.

**Fix.** not fixed — Phase 10 criteria still need a content-correctness gate added

**→ Rule.** A test that only proves the thing runs must be named as such ('smoke test'), never recorded as a pass. Any caveat attached to a pass verdict must be encoded in the verdict itself (FAIL or PARTIAL), because prose caveats evaporate and the verdict does not.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · verification-gap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Phase 10 'GGUF verified' only tested that it emits JSON and does not crash — content was never checked

**What happened.** The 07-25 Phase 10 GGUF test passed on two criteria: output is JSON, and no hang/crash. Whether the content was correct was never tested. The document itself carried the caveat 'don't read this as proven complete', but over time everyone remembered only 'Phase 10 passed'.

**Root cause.** Acceptance criteria measured liveness rather than correctness, and the written caveat eroded because it lived in prose next to a green checkmark instead of in the pass/fail criteria themselves.

**Impact.** A broken artifact carried a 'verified' label for four days and was used for real extraction work on house 01, producing bad data.

**Fix.** Reframed for future rounds: content correctness must be part of the GGUF acceptance test, using ground-truth key comparison.

**→ Rule.** Acceptance criteria must test the capability you need, not that the process ran. And never park a caveat in prose beside a green result — encode it in the pass condition, or it will be forgotten.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · verification-design</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · 'ALL CHECKS PASS' was declared over 11 houses, then an independent audit found ~500 missing ids, a 5-way format split and a content regression underneath it

**What happened.** Round 4 closed with check_format.py reporting ALL CHECKS PASS on all 11 houses and the working copy and raw folder differing in 0 files. Round 5 then ran an independent audit that deliberately ignored that checker and instead compared the JSON type of every key across all 2,366 files — and found ~500 elements with no element_id, house 04's BOQ files under the wrong pattern, the series price table stored 5 different ways, credits pages split across 4 patterns, string/array values where numbers were required, and a real content regression in house 05's price digits. The checker went from 14 to 19 checks as a result.

**Root cause.** The checker can only enforce rules someone already wrote down; a green result was being read as 'the data is correct' when it only ever meant 'the 14 known rules are satisfied'. Type purity and identity were not among the 14.

**Impact.** A whole session closed believing the dataset was clean and locked. Everything found in round 5 would have gone into training labels unnoticed, including wrong price digits that a prior item had recorded as already fixed.

**Fix.** Ran a type-comparison audit independent of the checker; folded the findings back in as 5 new checks (14 → 19)

**→ Rule.** A passing checker is evidence about the checker, not about the data. Any 'locked and verified' claim needs at least one audit built on a different method than the tool that produced the claim.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · verification</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · Wrongly excluded site_plan/side_profile as grid-line sources, reasoning elevations have no grid axis — and made the same class of assumption twice

**What happened.** The t03 pass design initially excluded site_plan and side_profile from the gridline subtask on the reasoning that elevations have no top-down grid axis. Makham produced a real elevation sheet (A-05, รูปด้าน 1/2) printing grid markers 1/2/3 and D/C/B/A with full dimension chains, same as a plan sheet. The exclusion was reverted. Later the same session, the diary notes this was the second time assuming side_profile/elevations were low-value proved wrong — they are the only place z-levels are printed at all.

**Root cause.** A design decision was made from a mental model of what an elevation drawing contains rather than from opening real sheets in the dataset. The same untested assumption then recurred in a different form within one session.

**Impact.** Would have permanently excluded a genuine grid-line source from t03's gridline subtask, and (second occurrence) would have left the entire vertical axis unextractable. Both caught by Makham, not by any check.

**Fix.** Reverted the exclusion; later added z_levels[], dimension_chains[] for the z axis, and unassigned_dimensions[] to the schema §4 after the second occurrence.

**→ Rule.** Never exclude a drawing pattern from a data source based on what you assume it contains — open three real sheets of that pattern first; and when the same assumption class is disproven twice, treat it as a rule ('elevations carry data plans do not'), not two separate corrections.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · wrong-assumption</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-22 · Answered a model-capability question from memory and got it wrong

**What happened.** Makham asked whether Qwen could output pixel positions for beams to cross-check the grid master. The first answer was "not worth it", citing an in-repo paper doc (FLOORPLANVLM.md) that said 300K pixel-aligned samples plus RL were needed. Makham insisted on real web research, which found Qwen3-VL ships native 2D grounding (bbox in a 0-1000 normalized scale) in the base model — no fine-tuning at that scale required.

**Root cause.** A single in-repo research doc was treated as the current state of the art. It compared a different model family and was never re-checked against vendor docs; capability claims about fast-moving VLMs go stale in weeks.

**Impact.** A genuinely viable QA direction (bbox↔gridmaster cross-check) was almost closed off entirely. The correct answer only surfaced because the user pushed back and demanded live research.

**Fix.** Ran real web research, found native grounding + the GroundCount detection-then-VLM pattern, and wrote the corrected finding into tune_ai/t03/research_beam_grounding_vs_gridmaster.md.

**→ Rule.** Never answer a "can model X do Y" question from memory or from one cached in-repo doc. Check the vendor's current model card/docs live before declaring a capability impossible.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-22.md` · wrong-assumption</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · MAX_PIXELS 7,680 + MAX_LENGTH 47,104 written into the training script before the mandatory 5-step VRAM check was run

**What happened.** Both values were changed in train_t03.py and documented as 'ทำจริงแล้ว', cutting free VRAM from 7.5GB to 4.0GB — while the diary itself records the rule that a short 5-step run must confirm the config before any full run, because a previous run OOM'd with 470MB left.

**Root cause.** The change was made on a spreadsheet estimate of peak VRAM (90.9GB), not on a measured run. The estimate was produced by the same reasoning that had already been wrong once about image capacity.

**Impact.** Next full training round can OOM hours in and burn the round's GPU cost, at a moment when only $8.91 credit remains.

**Fix.** not fixed — flagged in the diary as ⚠️ 'ต้องรันทดสอบสั้น 5 step ยืนยันก่อนรันเต็มทุกครั้ง', not yet executed

**→ Rule.** A config edit is not 'done' until the smoke test that validates it has run. Writing the value and validating the value are two separate tasks; only the second one prevents the burn.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · unverified-config-change</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Only footings were scored against a true count — beams and columns shipped with eyeball verification only, yet the summary claims all three work

**What happened.** The results table gives footings 14/14 and 12/12 against real counts, but beams are reported as bare counts ('17 แถบ', '19 แถบ') with no denominator and the note 'คลุมโครงคานเกือบครบ'. Columns are reported as 14 and 13 with no stated truth either (the 13 was later found to contain a duplicate). The day's summary nonetheless states the tool 'มาร์ค เสา/คาน/ฐานราก ได้จริง'.

**Root cause.** Footings are countable discrete icons so a ground truth was easy; beams are variable-length runs with no obvious unit, so no ground truth was established and the gap was filled with visual inspection.

**Impact.** Beam detection accuracy is unknown — which matters most, because beams are the exact subtask (plan_beam 0%) the whole tool was built to help. A tool with unmeasured recall cannot be used as the 'did the AI miss something' cross-check proposed in section 6.2(ข).

**Fix.** not fixed — no beam ground-truth count was produced

**→ Rule.** The subtask you built the tool for is the one that needs a number, not the one that was easy to count. 'เกือบครบ' is not a measurement.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · unmeasured-claim</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · The 08-24 roof_plan→plan fix was incomplete; 7 more files still hid the missing-roof-beam BOQ bug

**What happened.** A fix made the previous day to retag `roof_plan` as `plan` (which closes a bug where roof beams vanish from the BOQ) had only covered part of the dataset. Seven more files still carried the wrong pattern and had to be fixed again the next day.

**Root cause.** The 08-24 pass fixed only the 11 houses being worked on that day rather than sweeping the whole dataset for the same defect class, so the same bug survived in the houses that were not in scope.

**Impact.** Roof beams were silently absent from the BOQ for those 7 files for an extra day; the same work had to be re-done as part of a second, larger sweep.

**Fix.** Retagged the remaining 7 files `roof_plan`→`plan` as part of the 485-point normalization sweep.

**→ Rule.** When you find a defect class, grep the whole dataset for it and fix every instance in that pass. Fixing only the files in front of you guarantees the same bug comes back on the next file you open.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · incomplete-fix</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · A 22px "+" template poisoned the bank and produced 636 phantom footings on a page with none

**What happened.** A harvested template from บ้าน 11 was a 22px "+" crosshair. It matched every line intersection on the drawing, ballooning footing detections to 636 on a page containing no footings at all.

**Root cause.** The harvest step accepted any repeated icon-sized contour, and a crosshair is a universal drawing primitive rather than a distinguishing symbol. There was no minimum-size or distinctiveness gate on templates entering the bank.

**Impact.** Completely corrupted counts on affected pages; would have poisoned every measurement built on the bank if not caught.

**Fix.** Removed the template and added a gate in `load_templates`: skip any template under 28px with a warning.

**→ Rule.** Any template smaller than a few dozen pixels is probably a drawing primitive, not a symbol. Gate template admission on minimum size and distinctiveness, and test every new template against a page that should score zero.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · false-positive</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Two tightly-cropped templates scored garbage as high as real matches, making a threshold impossible

**What happened.** The solid-shaded 31px templates from บ้าน 05/33 scored 0.87–1.00 on genuine matches in their own house but garbage on other houses reached 0.90 — the score ranges overlap, so no threshold can separate them. A per-template table showed those 2 templates alone emitted 224 junk detections while the other 9 emitted zero.

**Root cause.** The templates were cropped tight to the icon, discarding the surrounding white space. Real icons float alone on white; Thai text characters sit crowded together — the surrounding context is the actual discriminator, and cropping it away removed the only signal that separates them.

**Impact.** 224 false detections across the dataset, and an unfixable threshold until the root cause was addressed.

**Fix.** Diagnosed with a per-template score table before changing anything, then fixed at the source: re-cropped with white margin around the icon (68px instead of 31px), removed the duplicate (05/33 are the same symbol with identical scores), and raised FOOTING_THRESH 0.60→0.72.

**→ Rule.** When a threshold cannot separate signal from noise, the template is wrong — do not tune the threshold. Diagnose per-template before touching a global constant, and crop templates with their surrounding context, since context is often the real discriminator.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · false-positive</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Vast.ai credit on record ($8.91) is not enough to finish even one H200 run ($17.45)

**What happened.** The full-resolution training path (MAX_PIXELS 16,384) requires an H200 at $3.293/hr ≈ $17.45 per 3-epoch run, but the account has $8.91 of credit. A run started against that balance would die mid-training.

**Root cause.** The remaining balance was never checked as part of planning a configuration change that requires a more expensive card.

**Impact.** The 16,384 path is completely blocked until money goes in. Had this not been checked first, a run would have been started and killed partway, burning both the spent credit and the time.

**Fix.** Stated as a hard blocker in plain language to Makham immediately rather than filed as a to-do (per the Day of Shame lesson 3). Nothing was rented; no money spent this session.

**→ Rule.** Check the account balance against the full cost of a planned run before proposing the configuration that requires it, and state a funding blocker out loud rather than burying it in a to-do list.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · budget-blocker</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · MAX_PIXELS/MAX_LENGTH raised on an arithmetic estimate with the mandatory TEST_STEPS=5 confirmation not yet run

**What happened.** MAX_PIXELS was raised 5120→7680 and MAX_LENGTH 32768→47104, narrowing the VRAM margin from 7.5 GB to 4.0 GB. The 90.9 GB peak is an arithmetic estimate, not a measured value, and the mandatory TEST_STEPS=5 confirmation run was not performed.

**Root cause.** The confirmation step requires a GPU rental that was not done in this session, so a configuration change shipped ahead of its own verification gate.

**Impact.** If the estimate is wrong, the next full run OOMs — the previous round OOM'd with only 470 MiB free, so a 4.0 GB estimated margin is not comfortable. A failed full run costs the whole rental.

**Fix.** Documented as a mandatory pre-run gate (rule_of_tune Rule 4) with an explicit fallback order: cut gridline images 4→3 first (peak 89.2), then roll MAX_PIXELS back — never lower MAX_LENGTH alone without lowering MAX_PIXELS, which truncates labels mid-JSON (the t01 §0.4 bug class).

**→ Rule.** A memory-bound config change is not done until a short run confirms the peak on real hardware. Ship the change with the fallback order written down, and treat the confirmation run as a blocking gate, not a to-do.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · unverified-change</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-29 · New span-scaling rule shipped into the schema without ever verifying a VLM can measure pixels accurately

**What happened.** A new rule was adopted: unprinted span/dummy dimensions are measured in pixels against two grid lines of known pos_m and converted by proportion, with a new `span_source: scaled_from_grid` enum value. It shipped across the schema, plan template + 4 rendered files, gridline, pass3, _common, and Constistant's schema.js SPAN_SOURCE_VALUES — before anyone measured whether a VLM can read pixel distances accurately at all.

**Root cause.** An appealing mechanism was designed and propagated across 8+ files based on it being conceptually correct, without a cheap feasibility probe first. The prompt even had to be hardened against the model faking measurements by pasting the label without the numbers.

**Impact.** If VLMs cannot measure pixels reliably, the entire enum value, prompt sections, worked examples and cross-repo schema change are wasted, and the model will have been trained to emit confidently-wrong scaled values.

**Fix.** Not validated. Mitigations shipped: prompt forces the pixel numbers into the flag (`scaled_between:1,3 P:380 U:142` — no P/U means it wasn't measured, so `unresolved` is required); `--hide-grid-lines` was added to infer_house_t03.py (eval only) to hide known pos_m on val pages and measure |measured − GT| directly without building a new dataset. Explicitly flagged that GPU round 1 must compare every scaled_from_grid value against GT before anyone trusts it.

**→ Rule.** Probe a new model capability on a handful of examples before propagating a schema change across two repos. Design the falsification test at the same time as the mechanism — and force the model to show its work so a fabricated answer is detectable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · unverified-assumption</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Assumed a dry-run needs no HF token; push_to_hub actually calls init_hf_repo in SFTTrainer.__init__

**What happened.** The dry-run died with 401 in SFTTrainer.__init__ because push_to_hub=True creates the hub repo at construction time, not at the first save_steps. The standing assumption that a dry-run does not need a token was wrong.

**Root cause.** The library performs a network/auth operation earlier in the lifecycle than the mental model assumed.

**Impact.** Without this discovery, a real run launched without HF_TOKEN would have died in the first second — or worse, been assumed safe until hour 15.

**Fix.** Dry-run now disables push automatically; documented that a real run without HF_TOKEN fails instantly rather than late.

**→ Rule.** Verify when a library actually performs auth/network side effects rather than assuming they happen at first use — construction-time side effects are common and change what a dry-run must cover.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · wrong-assumption</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Destrier (t05) is the surviving model but has never been run end-to-end on a real GPU

**What happened.** Destrier is trained, souped and uploaded to HuggingFace, but its only recall measurement is a single ~43% run under forgiving name matching, and the full pipeline has never been executed once on a real GPU.

**Root cause.** Verification was deferred behind the two failed branches; the surviving model inherited the 'good enough for now' status without ever passing a full-pipeline check.

**Impact.** The one model the project is relying on has an unconfirmed, single-sample, leniently-scored accuracy number and unknown end-to-end behaviour. Any downstream planning built on the 43% figure is built on sand.

**Fix.** Not fixed — explicitly recorded as outstanding: 'ยังไม่เคยรันครบทั้งสายพานกับการ์ดจอจริงสักครั้ง'.

**→ Rule.** A model is not validated until it has run the complete production pipeline at least once on real hardware, and its headline metric has been reproduced under strict (not forgiving) matching. State both conditions explicitly whenever quoting the number.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · verification</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · grid_ref was stored in a machine format ({D1D2,4}) that human reviewers could not read

**What happened.** Reviewers were shown grid_ref values in their raw stored form, e.g. `{D1D2,4}`. A formatGridRefDisplay() function was added to render this as `D1 → D2 (length 4 m)`, including dummy grids with a prime (`{A3A'3,1.5}` → `A3 → A'3 (length 1.5 m)`).

**Root cause.** The storage format was designed for the pipeline and reused verbatim in the human review surface, with no separate display representation. Compactness that helps a parser is exactly what blocks a human reader.

**Impact.** Reviewers could not effectively verify the single most important field on beam elements — the grid span. Undetectably wrong grid refs would have passed review.

**Fix.** Added formatGridRefDisplay() in label-studio-tasks-makham.js producing a new grid_ref_display field, rendered as a green hint below the editable grid_ref box. The editable value itself was deliberately left unchanged to avoid confusion between the two.

**→ Rule.** A human review surface needs a human-readable rendering of every machine-format field, shown alongside (never replacing) the editable raw value. If a reviewer cannot read a field at a glance, that field is effectively unreviewed.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · ux-bug / review-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · Atomic beam segments of the same mark were scattered in the review list instead of grouped together

**What happened.** After moving to atomic segments, all segments of one beam mark (e.g. every B5 segment) appeared in the task list in extraction order rather than together, so a reviewer could not compare them. Fixed by stable-sorting items by element_id before writing the task JSON.

**Root cause.** The atomic-segment schema change (a good change) multiplied the number of rows without any corresponding change to how they were presented for review. Ordering was inherited from extraction order, which carries no meaning for a human checking consistency within a mark.

**Impact.** Reviewers could not spot inconsistencies between segments of the same beam — precisely the check atomic segments exist to enable. Required a regeneration and re-import cycle.

**Fix.** Sort the items list by element_id with a stable sort (preserving each segment's original order within the same mark) before writing the task JSON in label-studio-tasks-makham.js.

**→ Rule.** Whenever a schema change multiplies row count, update the review presentation in the same change. Group rows by the key a human reasons about (the mark), and use a stable sort so within-group order still carries its original meaning.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · review-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · A single BOQ PNG actually contains two overlapping sheets, rotated 90° and split left/right

**What happened.** It was confirmed that one BOQ PNG contains 2 overlapping sheets — rotated 90° and split left/right — matching what the agent working on mk_test pages 48-57 had found independently.

**Root cause.** The page→image conversion step assumed one logical sheet per PNG. The source PDF packs two rotated sheets into one page, and nothing in the pipeline detects or splits that.

**Impact.** Any extractor treating one PNG as one sheet reads a jumble of two documents. Two independent workers each had to rediscover this on their own, which is duplicated discovery effort and a sign the finding was not captured anywhere shared.

**Fix.** Recorded as Generation 3.1 point 10, confirming the finding. No automatic split was implemented.

**→ Rule.** Validate the page→image assumption on a sample of every drawing set before extraction begins, and record source-format quirks in the house's own notes immediately so the next worker does not rediscover them. Two people independently finding the same quirk means the first finding was never written where the second could see it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · data-format-surprise</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-08 · A verification script reported all 61 image files missing — the paths were the bug, not the files

**What happened.** The check that every referenced image exists on disk initially failed for all 61 files, because the script fed a git-bash-style /d/... path into native Node.js. After fixing the script to use path.resolve, all 61 files were confirmed present.

**Root cause.** A hardcoded POSIX-style path built for the shell environment was passed to a Windows-native runtime that does not understand it; the script reported a domain failure ('file not found') for what was an environment failure.

**Impact.** A moment of believing the whole image set was missing; a wasted debug cycle on the wrong layer.

**Fix.** Replaced the hardcoded path with path.resolve, then re-ran and confirmed 61/61 present.

**→ Rule.** When a verification script reports that 100% of items fail, suspect the script before the data — and never hardcode a shell-style path into a native runtime on Windows.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-12 · Parallel spread-footing/pile-foundation BOQ sets misdiagnosed as duplicate reprints

**What happened.** While repairing the pile-foundation BOQ agent's unfinished pages, pages 89-90 were judged to be a reprint of pages 77-78 from the spread-footing BOQ because every number matched. A note saying so was written into the JSON file before the error was caught.

**Root cause.** Identical numbers were treated as proof of duplication without checking the sheet header. A house's BOQ genuinely contains two full parallel sets (spread footing and pile foundation, ~23 sheets each), and categories that do not depend on foundation type (electrical, misc) legitimately have identical numbers in both sets.

**Impact.** A wrong note was written into a delivered JSON file and had to be found and corrected before the work was submitted; time lost re-investigating 6 pages.

**Fix.** Investigated the document structure, confirmed the two parallel BOQ sets are real, and corrected the note in the file before submission. On the next house (house 5) the same page pair was handled correctly from the start by adding a `corresponding_sheet_in_other_variant` cross-reference field.

**→ Rule.** Identical numbers across two BOQ sheets are never by themselves evidence of duplication — always read the sheet header (spread footing vs pile foundation) before calling anything a duplicate, and record the relationship with an explicit cross-reference field instead of deleting or flagging.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-14 · Nearly cascaded a guessed grid range onto WC1 without checking its dedicated detail sheet

**What happened.** After adding dummy grid `D'`, the cascade into `หน้า06_floor_plan.json` continued by momentum and almost changed the WC1 bathroom from `C-B` to `D'-C`. Checking `หน้า11_wc1_plan.json` first showed the dedicated enlarged detail explicitly states 'between gridB and gridC'.

**Root cause.** Cascading a grid change is mechanical, and the mechanical pass does not distinguish rooms whose extent is documented on a dedicated detail sheet from rooms inferred from the overview plan.

**Impact.** Caught before submission — no wrong data shipped, but it is the same class of error that did ship elsewhere.

**Fix.** Reverted to `C-B` per the enlarged detail sheet.

**→ Rule.** Before cascading a grid change into any room or element, check whether a dedicated enlarged-detail sheet exists for it — the detail sheet always outranks a cascade inference from the overview plan.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-15 · Two B4X spans reverted to the wrong dummy grid label after being fixed once

**What happened.** Two spans of B4X were found labelled `3'` with mismatching spans (0.6 vs 1.5), even though the grid master already recorded both should be `3''` at 1.5.

**Root cause.** Editing passes over the same file were not checked against the grid master afterwards, so an earlier correct fix was undone by a later edit and nothing detected the regression.

**Impact.** A previously-fixed value silently regressed; caught only because the two spans disagreed with each other.

**Fix.** Confirmed against the grid master (3-3' = 0.6 is genuinely correct) and both spans fixed back.

**→ Rule.** After any editing pass over a plan file, re-validate every span against the grid master. Two occurrences of the same mark with different spans is a regression signal — treat a self-inconsistency as a bug, never as data.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · The pre-flight check passed all 5 of its checks and caught none of the things that actually broke the session

**What happened.** `verify_env.py` checked compute capability, VRAM, Unsloth loading, Triton version and tokenizer download — all passed. The session was then broken by (a) free disk space running out repeatedly, (b) transformers/torch being silently downgraded by an unrelated pip install, and (c) API drift in transformers (`ip.max_pixels` read-only, `SizeDict` not a dict). None of these are in the checklist.

**Root cause.** The pre-flight was written against "is the GPU big enough" rather than against the failure modes that actually occur on rented ephemeral boxes: disk, package version drift, and API compatibility of the exact code paths the training script uses.

**Impact.** Every one of those three failure classes was discovered live on a $1.056/hr machine instead of in a 30-second check.

**Fix.** Environment was repaired reactively (pin transformers==5.5.0, reinstall the cu128 torch build), and verify_env.py was re-run to confirm.

**→ Rule.** A pre-flight must assert the things that have broken before: free disk ≥ pipeline peak, exact pinned versions of transformers/torch (record and re-assert them), and a 1-example dry run through the real code path (image-processor setting included), not just imports.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · The dataset rollup hash came out different from the previously noted number, causing a false data-changed scare — the formula had never been recorded

**What happened.** On re-checking dataset integrity, the 398-image rollup number differed from what had been noted the first time. The difference was because a different formula was used, not because any data changed — but that could not be determined from the record.

**Root cause.** A derived verification number was recorded without recording the method that produced it, making it impossible to reproduce or to distinguish a method change from a data change.

**Impact.** Time lost investigating a suspected data-integrity failure on a round whose whole premise depends on a byte-identical dataset.

**Fix.** The formula is now recorded alongside the number to prevent the same confusion next time.

**→ Rule.** Never record a checksum, hash, or derived metric without the exact command or formula that produced it. An unreproducible verification number is worse than none — it manufactures false alarms.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Nearly 'fixed' eval_fields.py's missing max_seq_length, which would have broken cross-round comparability for no reason

**What happened.** eval_fields.py does not pass max_seq_length, which looks like the same bug fixed elsewhere. It was deliberately left alone: t01 genuinely ran this file and scored 90% JSON valid on a val set containing a 22,515-token gridmaster. If it truncated at 2048 every row would have failed, not 10% of them.

**Root cause.** Pattern-matching a code shape to a known bug without checking the empirical evidence that the path does not actually exhibit it. The near-miss came from treating 'looks like the bug' as 'is the bug'.

**Impact.** Would have altered the shared measurement ruler between rounds, making t01's and t02's numbers incomparable — silently destroying the entire A/B experiment's validity.

**Fix.** Deliberately not changed; reasoning recorded in the diary as proof the path does not truncate.

**→ Rule.** Before fixing a suspected bug in shared measurement code, look for empirical evidence of whether it actually fires. A result that would be impossible if the bug existed is proof it doesn't — and an unnecessary fix to a shared ruler is worse than the bug.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Model support had been evidenced by a merged PR number rather than by the binary actually on the machine

**What happened.** llama.cpp support for Qwen3-VL had been established from PR #16780 (b6887) against the machine's build b10105. Phase 0.5 replaced this with opening the actual binaries: llama.dll contains qwen3vl and qwen3vlmoe, mtmd.dll contains qwen3vl. The same inspection also produced direct evidence for bug 2 — vision_config genuinely has no image_size key.

**Root cause.** A version-number comparison was treated as proof that a specific build contains a specific capability, which it is not — builds can be patched, features reverted, or the variant (qwen3vlmoe vs qwen3vl) absent.

**Impact.** No harm — the binary did contain the support. But the same reasoning would have failed silently if it hadn't, and inspecting the binary directly is what upgraded bug 2 from an inference to direct evidence.

**Fix.** Evidence upgraded to binary-level symbol inspection; config values read from the real preprocessor_config.json rather than from memory.

**→ Rule.** Prove capability against the actual artefact on the actual machine — inspect the binary, read the real config file. A version or PR number is a hypothesis, not evidence.

**Fix.** Not fixed — listed under 'still can't be confirmed'.

**→ Rule.** When a full run succeeds, harvest its peak VRAM/RAM immediately; that is the only moment the real number is free to obtain. A number from a 5-step test is not a capacity figure.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Destroy of the rented GPU instance was requested twice mid-run before results were downloaded — near-miss data loss

**What happened.** During the house 08 inference run, Makham asked twice to destroy the Vast.ai instance while pages were still only on the rented machine's ephemeral disk. Both times the results were re-synced first (Mark-of-Shame discipline), so nothing was lost — but the request came before any confirmation that outputs were safely off the box.

**Root cause.** No automatic 'sync-then-destroy' step existed; the safety depended entirely on the operator remembering to re-sync before acting on a destroy instruction.

**Impact.** None realised — but 19 pages of paid GPU output were twice one command away from being unrecoverable.

**Fix.** Handled manually by re-syncing before each destroy; the instance was confirmed destroyed only after the final download.

**→ Rule.** Make destroy impossible without a sync: wrap teardown in a script that rsyncs results and verifies the local file count first, so the discipline is not a memory test on a tired operator.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-22 · Built a proposal on top of a model capability never verified on the actual fine-tuned adapter

**What happened.** The bbox↔gridmaster QA proposal assumes the t02 LoRA adapter retained the base model's grounding capability and that Unsloth's chat template emits the grounding special tokens correctly. Neither was tested.

**Root cause.** Heavy fine-tuning toward a single output format can cause catastrophic forgetting of unrelated capabilities, and chat templates routinely omit special tokens (<|box_start|> etc.). Both are cheap to probe but were skipped because the proposal was written between GPU rentals.

**Impact.** A whole proposed pipeline stage rests on an untested assumption. If grounding is degraded or the template is wrong, everything built on top is wasted work.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded honestly in the doc with the cheapest next step named: fire one grounding prompt at the already-available page-26 image on the next GPU rental before building anything else.

**→ Rule.** Before designing a pipeline stage on a base-model capability, spend the ~$0.10 probe to confirm the fine-tuned adapter still has it. Name untested assumptions explicitly in the doc instead of burying them.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Advisor's 'just use a bigger Qwen' assumption was already exhausted

**What happened.** The suggestion to increase the model's parameter count (B) was checked: Qwen3.6 ships only 27B and 35B-A3B as downloadable weights, plus a closed Max-Preview available via API only. The project already runs the largest trainable one.

**Root cause.** An assumption that model families offer a continuous size ladder. In practice, the largest tiers are frequently closed-weight, and 'go bigger' means switching to a different family and a different infrastructure scale.

**Impact.** Investigation time only. Had it been acted on blindly, the next step (Qwen3-VL-235B) would have required 8×80GB GPUs, ~770GB total memory, a rewritten distributed training script, and multiples of the current hourly rate.

**Fix.** Enumerated the family's actual downloadable sizes and priced the jump to 235B, reframing it as a budget/scale decision rather than a parameter tweak.

**→ Rule.** Before accepting 'use a bigger model' as an action item, verify which sizes are actually downloadable and trainable — and price the full infrastructure change, not just the hourly GPU rate.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · planning/assumption</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · F2 footing template fired 3 false positives on a beam plan, which contains no footings at all

**What happened.** After adding the F2 template (vertical rectangle), the tool drew 3 red footing boxes on house 12's beam plan — a drawing type that by definition contains no footings.

**Root cause.** A vertical beam passing through a column box produces the same coarse geometry as the F2 icon (vertical rectangle with something in the middle). Template matching sees shape only and cannot use drawing-type semantics to disambiguate.

**Impact.** False positives on a page type where the correct answer is zero — a reviewer trusting the marked image would be actively misled about what is on the drawing.

**Fix.** Rejected the first idea (raise the threshold), which would have dropped genuine F2 footings in the footing plan — moving the problem rather than fixing it. Applied a domain rule instead: a footing candidate whose centre falls inside a detected beam band is discarded. Provably safe because footing plans detect zero beam bands. Result: beam plan 0 footings, footing plan still 12/12.

**→ Rule.** When a detector confuses two classes, prefer a domain constraint that is provably inert on the good case over tightening a threshold, which trades false positives for false negatives instead of eliminating either.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · algorithm/false-positive</sub>

**What happened.** The new tool reports 14/14 and 12/12 footing detection, but both test houses come from the same series (แบบบ้านยิ้มเพื่อประชาชน, BMA). Whether houses from another design office break it is unknown.

**Root cause.** Validation set was whatever data was closest at hand; sample diversity was not part of the acceptance criterion.

**Impact.** The headline accuracy figures may not generalise at all. Unquantified risk if the tool is put into a review workflow.

**Fix.** Not fixed — explicitly declared as unproven in the diary's 'what we do not yet know' section rather than presented as a general result.

**→ Rule.** State the diversity of your validation set alongside every accuracy number. Two samples from the same source is one sample of the source, not two.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · validation-coverage</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Detection tool never tested on cover pages, sections or BOQ tables — could mark them with confident nonsense

**What happened.** The tool has only ever been run on structural plan sheets. Behaviour on cover pages, section drawings and BOQ tables is untested, and the tool has no page-type gate.

**Root cause.** Scope was defined by the pages the tool was built for; no guard was added to refuse page types outside that scope, and the tool always draws boxes and prints counts regardless of what it is fed.

**Impact.** A reviewer running it on the wrong page type would be shown authoritative-looking boxes and counts on a page with nothing to detect — worse than no tool, since it is trusted.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Flagged as 'should be tested before real use'.

**→ Rule.** A detector that is only valid on some input types must either detect and refuse the others, or must not be handed to users until it has been tested on every page type they will feed it.
