**Root cause.** The probe ran only two isolated samples on a fresh process; PyTorch's caching allocator accumulates fragmentation across steps and never shrinks, so real peak exceeds any short probe.

**Impact.** Two of four folds crashed, ~1 hour lost to re-probing and restarting all four, and a partially-trained checkpoint had to be discarded.

**Fix.** Reduced MAX_PIXELS 7680->6912 uniformly across all folds and re-probed with SORT_LONGEST TEST_STEPS=3 on gpu1, confirming peak dropped 91.4->80.6 GB before restarting.

**→ Rule.** A short worst-case probe measures a floor, not the real peak — leave a fragmentation margin (10%+) above any probe result, and re-verify with numbers before believing a memory fix.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · measurement</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · 96–100% JSON-format score hid a model that was answering about a completely different house

**What happened.** t04's evaluation reported 96–100% correctly formatted JSON every time, which read as a healthy model. Only after someone opened the actual answer files by eye did it emerge that feeding in a footing plan produced a roof plan of an entirely different house.

**Root cause.** The eval metric measured output shape (valid JSON with the right fields), not output truth. A model that memorised the answer format and regurgitated training-set answers scores near-perfect on that metric while understanding nothing.

**Impact.** The failure was masked for the whole training round; the team believed the model was working while it was fundamentally blind. Time and money continued to be spent under a false green signal.

**Fix.** Adopted the practice of opening real answer files and reading them, rather than trusting the aggregate score. Recorded as lessons #2 and #3 in the summary.

**→ Rule.** Never judge a model by a structural/format metric alone. Every eval run must include a human eyeball on real predicted outputs — a format score can be 100% while semantic accuracy is 0%.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · The $2 go/no-go gate first returned a false green because the test prompt leaked the answers

**What happened.** The first run of the pre-training gate passed. Investigation showed the test prompt written by Claude included illustrative examples 'เช่น F1, B2, C1, ผ2' — and F1 and ผ2 happened to be actual ground-truth answers. The blind model simply echoed the examples back and the scoring script counted them as correct. On another page the model enumerated B1, B2, B3 … up to B34, and the first three coincidentally matched the answer key.

**Root cause.** Two compounding flaws: (1) the prompt author put concrete examples in a prompt whose purpose is to test whether the model can read, contaminating the test; (2) the scoring script credited any matching token without checking for enumeration or echo patterns, so brute-force sequential guessing scored partial credit.

**Impact.** Nearly burned a full night of GPU rental (~$60–70) on a model that could not see anything at all — an exact repeat of the t04 failure. Caught only because someone questioned a green result.

**Fix.** Rewrote the gate prompt with the examples removed, then re-ran; the model scored 0/3 and the branch was stopped. New rule established: never put values that appear in the answer key into a prompt used for testing.

**→ Rule.** Test prompts must never contain example values drawn from the ground truth, and scoring must reject echo and enumeration patterns. Treat an unexpectedly green result on a cheap gate as suspicious until you have explained why it passed.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · pass3 required exactly one grid_ref per element, so grouped records (count > 1) produced zero anchors

**What happened.** Ground truth aggregates identical items into a single record with a list of refs (e.g. `F1 · count 11 · grid_refs [11 points]`), but the code enforced `len(refs)==1` and skipped anything else — yielding 0 anchors even though CV had found 12 matching points exactly.

**Root cause.** The code was written against the shape produced by the *first* simulation, in which Claude hand-wrote the model answers as one ref per element. That artificial shape never exercised the grouped form that real GT uses.

**Impact.** pass3 found no anchors on pages where perfectly good data existed. More importantly, the bug was completely invisible to the first simulation.

**Fix.** Handled multi-ref records. The bug was only exposed because Makham ordered the second simulation to use the real GT answers instead of Claude-authored ones.

**→ Rule.** Never build a simulation whose inputs you author yourself — hand-written fixtures encode your own assumptions and mask exactly the bugs the simulation exists to find. Feed simulations real ground-truth data.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · A validation gate passed green because the prompt itself contained the ground-truth answer

**What happened.** The first round of gate checks showed green — but only because the prompt had the answer written into it. The evaluation was measuring the prompt, not the model.

**Root cause.** Ground truth leaked into the evaluation prompt. No separation between the data used to construct the prompt and the data used to score the answer.

**Impact.** A false 'model works' signal that would have let a broken model through. Time lost on a measurement that meant nothing.

**Fix.** Identified and documented as a trap in the teaching document.

**→ Rule.** Before trusting any green eval, diff the prompt against the expected answer — if the answer text appears in the prompt, the score is meaningless. Build eval prompts from a separate code path than the scoring data.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · The headline '191/191, 100%' pass3 result was measured on human-vetted pages; automatic CV on an unchecked house failed 5/5

**What happened.** pass3 was validated at 191/191 leave-one-out accuracy — but on 18 pages a human had already eyeballed and confirmed had good anchors. Run against house02 with fully automatic CV on a house never checked before, all 5 structural pages failed: 2 footing pages rejected by the quality gate, 3 beam pages found 0 anchors.

**Root cause.** The validation set was selected for quality, which silently converted the question from 'does pass3 work on real drawings?' to 'does the fit maths work on good anchors?'. The upstream anchor-detection step — the part that actually fails — was excluded from the measurement.

**Impact.** A headline accuracy figure that overstated real-world capability by a wide margin. Would have led to trusting pass3 in production.

**Fix.** Re-measured honestly on unfiltered CV output on a fresh house and recorded the 0/5 result plainly alongside the 191/191.

**→ Rule.** Never validate a pipeline stage on data that was pre-selected as clean by a human — you measure the wrong stage. Always report the end-to-end number on unfiltered input next to any curated-subset number.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Two full extraction rounds were produced but never systematically compared, so repeat-read consistency was never measured

**What happened.** Round t2 was explicitly instructed to read the images fresh and independently and to report where it differed from t1, specifically to see how consistent repeated reads are. A systematic file-by-file t1 vs t2 comparison was never done — only the agents' own summary reports exist.

**Root cause.** The comparison was the measurement that justified doing a second full round, but it was scheduled after the round rather than built into it, and the day's remaining time went to Label Studio tooling instead.

**Impact.** The cost of a whole second extraction round was paid without collecting its main deliverable — a real number for repeat-read agreement. Without it, per-field reliability is unknown and the t1/t2 conflicts (MEP grid, element vs elements) were found by luck rather than by a systematic diff.

**Fix.** Not fixed — listed as 'should do a t1 vs t2 comparison summary for Makham to see the overall quality picture' and 'has not been done yet'.

**→ Rule.** If a round of work exists to produce a measurement, build the measurement into the round's definition of done. A diff between two extraction rounds should be an automated script run at round close, not a summary task that competes with feature work for time.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · measurement-gap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Round 2 (t2) was not an independent re-read: six structural pages were copied verbatim from t1, and agents were handed t1 to diff against

**What happened.** t2 was set up as a second fresh extraction whose stated purpose included measuring how consistent repeated reads are. But pages 18, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 were copied straight from t1/ into t2/ with no re-read, and the agents doing pages 1-17 and 26-37 were explicitly instructed to report where their reading differed from t1 — i.e. they had access to round 1 while producing round 2.

**Root cause.** Speed was prioritised over experimental hygiene, with the justification that those pattern types were 'unaffected by this round's schema update' — true for the schema, but the consistency measurement is about re-read agreement, which a copy trivially and falsely scores at 100%. Nobody separated 'pages that need a schema-driven redo' from 'pages needed as a blind control'.

**Impact.** Any t1-vs-t2 agreement number computed later would be inflated: six pages would show perfect agreement by construction, and the remaining pages' agreement was measured against a round that was not blind. Repeat-read reliability — the number that would justify trusting the extraction pipeline — cannot be derived from this data at all.

**Fix.** not fixed — the copied pages were never re-read independently, and the systematic t1 vs t2 comparison was still listed as pending at end of day

**→ Rule.** If a round is meant to measure consistency, every page in it must be re-read blind. Never copy files into a comparison set, and never show round 1 to the reader producing round 2 — keep a schema-redo pass and a blind-control pass as separate artifacts.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-07 · Gen 1 extraction recorded concrete grade 240 ksc when the drawing says 210 ksc

**What happened.** A conflict pending since July 5 over whether page 18 (S-01 notes) specifies Fc'=210 or 240 kg/cm2. A fresh independent re-read during the t3 round returned a clear 210 ksc, matching Makham's own first-hand read on July 5. Gen 1's 240 was the wrong value.

**Root cause.** The original Gen 1 pass recorded a structural constant from a single unverified read with no second source and no confidence flag, so a misread became a fact in the dataset.

**Impact.** A wrong concrete grade sat in candidate fine-tuning ground truth for two days; propagated into any downstream BOQ/strength assumption drawn from it.

**Fix.** Re-read page 18 fresh; two independent reads agreed on 210 ksc, so Gen 1's 240 was overruled.

**→ Rule.** Any single structural constant that governs the whole house (concrete grade, cover, lap length) needs two independent reads before it is treated as ground truth — one read is a hypothesis, not data.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-11 · Many house-2 BOQ items were recorded at 0.4-0.6 confidence from tiny 90-degree-rotated text

**What happened.** Items in the decoration, paint and sanitary-fixture categories were extracted at confidence 0.4-0.6 because the source text is very small and printed rotated 90 degrees. They are in the dataset and flagged as needing someone to zoom in and verify before serious use as ground truth.

**Root cause.** The extraction reads the page as rendered, with no preprocessing step (rotation, crop, upscale) for regions the source prints sideways at small size.

**Impact.** A block of ground-truth rows that are more likely wrong than right sitting in a dataset destined for fine-tuning, with the verification unscheduled.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as pending review item 2: zoom in and check the low-confidence items.

**→ Rule.** When confidence drops because of how the page is rendered, fix the rendering (rotate/crop/upscale and re-read) rather than shipping a flagged low-confidence row — and never let a flagged row into training data without a scheduled review.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-11.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Local dry run used a 10.8GB stand-in, so it proved 'it runs' but never that it runs usably

**What happened.** Phase 0.3 on 2026-07-24 validated local inference by downloading a small ~10.8GB test model, running llama.cpp against a real drawing page, and declaring 'ผ่าน'. The real artifact turned out to be 21.2GB — roughly double — and on the same 8GB-VRAM laptop it ran at 3.46 token/s, 13-21 minutes per page, with llama.cpp logging 'failed to fit params to free device memory ... abort'.

**Root cause.** The dry run was sized for convenience, not for the artifact it was supposed to represent, and its pass criterion was binary ('does it run?') with no throughput threshold. A 10.8GB model fits VRAM far better than 21.2GB, so the CPU-offload bottleneck could not appear.

**Impact.** The team walked into the 2026-07-29 real run believing local execution was proven, and only then discovered a full house at ~18 min/page is impractical — forcing an unplanned 2-phase classify-then-extract redesign and a mis-set timeout that killed a healthy job.

**Fix.** Not fixed as a process rule; worked around on 2026-07-29 by splitting into a fast classify pass plus selective extraction (extract_house01_local.py).

**→ Rule.** A dry run must use an artifact of the real size on the real hardware, and must assert a usable rate (sec/page), not just absence of a crash.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · The Phase 4 baseline eval was skipped, so the headline '3x better' figure compares against a different run's baseline

**What happened.** Phase 4 (the untuned-baseline measurement) was skipped to save time on the recommendation of the workflow doc. The Phase 7 results were then reported as element recall 28.2% '⬆️⬆️⬆️ from 9.4%' and view exact match '70% ⬆️ from 60%' — numbers that come from the previous training round on different hardware and a different dataset size (226 train vs 315 train).

**Root cause.** A baseline is treated as a cost rather than as the denominator of every claim in the run. Skipping it makes the improvement unmeasurable within the run, so a prior run's numbers get substituted silently.

**Impact.** The central quality claim of the whole tuning cycle rests on a cross-run comparison whose baseline was measured under different conditions — the improvement could be larger or smaller than reported and nothing in this run can tell.

**Fix.** not fixed — Phase 4 remains skipped and the comparison numbers stand as reported.

**→ Rule.** Never skip the baseline in the run whose improvement you intend to quote. A baseline from another run is a different denominator, and mixing them makes every percentage in the report unfalsifiable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24.md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · The A/B parity table compared only explicitly-set values, so an unset default slipped through

**What happened.** A detailed parity table was built to guarantee t01 and t02 differed only in the model. It listed learning rate, batch size, epochs, etc. It could not catch the resize difference because t02 set resize explicitly while t01 set nothing at all — there was no line to compare.

**Root cause.** The comparison was constructed from remembered/intentional choices rather than from the full argument list of every shared function and class. Unset arguments are still variables, and are the easiest to overlook precisely because they are invisible.

**Impact.** Gave false confidence that the experiment was controlled, allowing an invalid conclusion to stand until a separate deep audit found it.

**Fix.** Recorded as Lesson 12 in rule_of_tune.md: an A/B parity table must enumerate every argument passed to every shared function/class, read from source, not from memory of what was changed.

**→ Rule.** Build A/B parity tables by diffing the effective arguments of every shared call (including defaults) read straight from source — never from the list of things you meant to change.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · experiment-validity</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · The t01 model was tried on house 01, which is inside its own training set (62 examples) — results look better than reality

**What happened.** The tuned t01 model was run against house 01 pages. House 01 contributed 62 examples to the training set, so the model has memorised this material. The output is therefore not a measurement of generalisation.

**Root cause.** The most convenient house to hand was used for a quality trial without first checking whether it was held out. Train/test separation was not enforced at the point of running an evaluation.

**Impact.** Caught and flagged in the diary before anyone quoted the numbers as performance — but had the caution not been written, in-sample results would have circulated as capability evidence.

**Fix.** Explicitly labelled as usable as a smoke test only, never as a measure of generalisation.

**→ Rule.** Before quoting any model output as a quality result, check whether the input is in the training set and label it. In-sample output is a smoke test; only held-out data measures capability.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · evaluation-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · A healthy falling loss curve (1.795 → 0.18-0.21) accompanied a model that scored only 20.6% element recall

**What happened.** t02's training loss fell cleanly from 1.795 to ~0.18-0.21 and eval_loss reached 0.2076 — every indicator of successful learning. Phase 7 field-level measurement then showed JSON valid 65%, element recall 20.6%, losing to t01 on every metric.

**Root cause.** Loss measures mathematical closeness to the target token sequence; it does not measure whether rebar numbers or part names were read correctly. Treating it as a quality signal conflates optimisation progress with task performance.

**Impact.** A model that looks trained by every training-time indicator but fails the actual acceptance criterion — the exact trap that makes a premature 'it worked' claim feel justified.

**Fix.** Phase 7 field-by-field measurement is the gate, not loss; recorded as lesson 4 of the old CLAUDE.md and reinforced in rule_of_tune.md.

**→ Rule.** Never conclude anything about model quality from the loss curve. Only a field-level measurement against held-out data decides whether a round succeeded.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28(teach mk).md` · evaluation-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · Two contradictory sets of t01 headline numbers coexist in the same document, and the eval ran on only 20 of 88 val examples

**What happened.** Section 14 (2026-07-21) records t01 as JSON valid 90% / view 60% / element recall 9.4%. The t02 comparison table (2026-07-28) records the same model as JSON valid 90% / view 70% / element recall 28.2%. The document never reconciles the 60-vs-70 and 9.4-vs-28.2 discrepancy, yet 28.2% is the figure quoted throughout as 'the number we trusted'. The eval output shown is also '0/20' and '0/170' — 20 examples out of the 88-line val set.

**Root cause.** Evaluations were run at different times with different --limit values and possibly on different machines, and each run's headline was written into the diary without stating its sample size or superseding the previous one.

**Impact.** A reader (and the team itself) cannot tell which t01 number is authoritative; the recall figure that drove the entire 'Qwen3.6 beats Qwen3-VL' decision differs by 3x between two places in the same document, and may rest on ~23% of the validation set.

**Fix.** Not fixed — both numbers still stand side by side in the merged teaching document with no note explaining the difference.

**→ Rule.** Every recorded metric must carry its sample size and run identity, and a re-measurement must explicitly supersede the old number rather than silently sitting next to it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The one capability the project exists for — rebar extraction — has never been tested

**What happened.** No structural (S-*) page has ever been fully extracted; pages 07-11 were only classified. The prompt's single biggest rule ('always split top/bottom rebar') therefore has no evidence for or against it, after multiple tuning rounds.

**Root cause.** Testing followed page order and convenience rather than starting from the highest-value capability, so the core requirement kept being deferred behind cheaper pages.

**Impact.** After three tuning rounds and days of evaluation the team still cannot say whether the model can do its actual job.

**Fix.** not fixed — no S-* page extracted yet

**→ Rule.** Test the highest-value capability first, on day one, even with a rough harness. A quality programme that has not exercised the primary use case has measured nothing that matters.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Three candidate causes still entangled — none tested one variable at a time

**What happened.** Merge failure, resolution mismatch and quantization damage are all plausible contributors to the quality collapse, and the diary records that none has been tested separately to see which weighs heaviest.

**Root cause.** All three changed between the measured-good configuration (bf16 + unmerged adapter) and the running configuration (merged + Q4_K_M + different image resolution) — they were varied simultaneously, so no single measurement can attribute blame.

**Impact.** No way to prioritise fixes or estimate how much quality each fix would recover; risk of retraining expensively to fix something quantization or a flag would have solved for free.

**Fix.** not fixed — explicitly listed as still to do, one variable at a time

**→ Rule.** Never change more than one variable between a measured-good configuration and a deployed one. When several have already changed, spend the cheap experiments to isolate them before spending money on a fix — attribution first, remediation second.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The trusted 90% / 28.2% numbers were measured on a path that is not the shipped artifact

**What happened.** eval_fields.py runs full bf16 (load_in_4bit=False) with the LoRA adapter attached at runtime and no merge. The artifact actually in use goes through merge (the suspect step) and Q4_K_M compression. The two paths were never compared, yet the eval numbers were quoted as the product's accuracy.

**Root cause.** The evaluation harness was built around the training artifact, and no one asked whether the evaluated object was the same object being deployed.

**Impact.** Months of decisions rested on a number that describes an artifact nobody runs; the shipped GGUF has never had a measured accuracy at all.

**Fix.** Clarified in the diary that 90%/28.2% remain valid for the adapter only, and that the GGUF is unverified. The tuning work itself is intact — the adapter is safe on HuggingFace.

**→ Rule.** Every accuracy number must be labelled with the exact artifact and path it was measured on, and the shipped artifact must be evaluated on its own path before any number is quoted for it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The 'do not switch to Qwen3-VL' verdict may be wrong on the path that actually ships — t02's training resolution matches llama.cpp's runtime exactly

**What happened.** On 2026-07-28 the A/B concluded Qwen3.6 (t01) beats Qwen3-VL (t02) on every metric and recorded 'อย่าเปลี่ยนไปใช้ Qwen3-VL'. The next night it emerged that t02 was trained at ~3,796 visual tokens per image, which is exactly what llama.cpp feeds at inference, while t01 was trained at ~266 — so on the real local deployment path t02 may in fact be the better model.

**Root cause.** The comparison was run on the bf16 + runtime-adapter path (the measurement path), not on the merged/quantized GGUF path (the deployment path), and train/inference token parity was never a comparison criterion.

**Impact.** A recorded, apparently settled model-selection decision is now unreliable — and the alternative it rejected is currently unusable anyway because the same MoE merge bug blocks its GGUF export, so the merge bug now blocks both rounds rather than only t02.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged as 'ยังไม่ได้พิสูจน์' in the open-questions section.

**→ Rule.** Judge candidate models on the path you will actually deploy, and treat train/inference input parity as a first-class comparison variable, not an afterthought.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-04 · eval_fields.py never records WHICH elements were missed — only the count

**What happened.** The evaluation script logs page-level results only (e.g. 'element 9/14') and never writes out which element IDs were missed, even though the data exists in memory at match time (`pmap`/`ge`/`pe`).

**Root cause.** The evaluator was built to produce a headline score, not to support diagnosis; the per-element detail was computed and then discarded.

**Impact.** Recall can be measured but not diagnosed — there is no way to see whether misses cluster on beams, on faint marks, or on a particular pattern. Every improvement attempt is a guess, and a re-run is needed just to get the list.

**Fix.** Not fixed — identified as needing one added logging line (not a logic change, since t02's rules forbid touching measurement logic) followed by a re-run.

**→ Rule.** An evaluator must emit the per-item failure list, not just the score. A number you cannot decompose cannot be improved — log the misses at match time, where the data already exists.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-20 · An earlier eval plan picked houses 01/03/04 — all already in train/val, which would have measured memorization

**What happened.** The draft experiment plan (ทดลองถอดแบบ_01_03_04_workflow.md) selected houses 01/03/04 for a generalization test of t02. A grep against train.jsonl/val.jsonl showed all three were in the training data. Houses 08/09/10/11 were substituted after confirming their absence.

**Root cause.** Eval houses were chosen by convenience (well-understood houses with good ground truth) without a mechanical check against the training manifest. There is no automated guard preventing a train-set house from being used as an eval house.

**Impact.** Caught before any GPU time was spent. Had it run, it would have produced a flattering recall number that measured memorization, and that number would have been written into SUMMARY.md and believed.

**Fix.** Verified absence from train.jsonl/val.jsonl by grep, switched to houses 08/09/10/11, and wrote ทดลองถอดแบบ_08_09_10_11_workflow.md as the pre-flight doc per rule_of_tune §4. The superseded draft was left in place.

**→ Rule.** Every eval run must grep its candidate houses against train.jsonl/val.jsonl before a GPU is rented, and the pre-flight doc must record the check — an eval on training data produces a number that is worse than no number.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · Initial val split was 10:1 — too small to measure anything, especially plan_beam

**What happened.** The dataset was first built with val = house03 only, giving a 10:1 train:val ratio and just 4 plan_beam validation examples. Makham overruled it ("4/1 ดีกว่า").

**Root cause.** The val set was sized by house count convenience rather than by how many examples the *bottleneck subtask* would get. With plan_beam as the whole point of the round, 4 val examples cannot distinguish signal from noise.

**Impact.** Any plan_beam metric off 4 examples would have been statistically meaningless; the round would have produced an unfalsifiable number.

**Fix.** Rebuilt with val = houses 01-05 (all human-reviewed houses) → train 887 / val 229 = 3.87:1, plan_beam val 4→18. Bonus: val became 100% human-reviewed GT while train was pure op04 — a clean measuring stick.

**→ Rule.** Size the val split by the example count of the subtask you are actually trying to improve, not by house count. And prefer putting human-reviewed GT in val so the ruler is clean.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · Controlled base-model comparison cancelled mid-run — no proof fine-tuning caused the improvement

**What happened.** A Qwen3.6 base (untuned) run on the same job set was started to control variables, but cancelled before the first job even completed because Makham had class in the morning and time ran out.

**Root cause.** The controlled baseline was scheduled last, after training and the tuned run, in a time-boxed overnight session. The most scientifically load-bearing measurement got the least slack.

**Impact.** t03's improvement over t02 cannot be attributed to fine-tuning — the comparison chart had to ship with the base column marked "n/a จริงๆ ไม่ใช่ยังไม่วัด". Still outstanding.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Comparison image (เปรียบเทียบผลทูน_t03_2026-08-25.png) explicitly states the causal claim is unproven. Deferred to the next round.

**→ Rule.** Schedule the controlled baseline run *first* or in parallel, not last. A results chart without its control column is a claim you cannot defend.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · The tuned-vs-untuned comparison ended up on 6 of 34 pages after three rounds of scope cuts

**What happened.** Page scope was cut 34 → 22 → 12 on live orders, then Makham cut every page t01 couldn't finish, leaving 6 pages that both variants completed. The headline 'JSON valid 100%' and the tuned-vs-base result rest on those 6.

**Root cause.** Scope was trimmed reactively around whichever pages stalled, so the surviving sample is exactly the set of pages the model found easy — a selection bias, not a random sample.

**Impact.** The tuned-vs-base conclusion is drawn from a self-selected easy subset; 'base is often faster' and the quality read are both on n=6 with the hard pages removed by construction.

**Fix.** not fixed — result was reported as-is with page counts stated

**→ Rule.** When you drop the runs that failed, you are not shortening the eval, you are changing what it measures. Record failures as failures in the comparison table rather than removing the page from the sample.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Documented 'images are not downscaled' based on measuring a single sample

**What happened.** The team had previously recorded as fact that images were not being downscaled. That claim came from measuring one image and generalizing to the whole set. It was wrong for 100% of the dataset.

**Root cause.** Sampling of one, treated as a population measurement, and then written down as an established fact so nobody re-checked it. Identical to lesson #12 in rule_of_tune.md, which the team had already learned once in round t01.

**Impact.** A false 'this is fine' record blocked investigation of the real bottleneck for several training rounds and several hundred dollars of GPU time.

**Fix.** Replaced the sample-based claim with a full-dataset measurement script that enumerates every image size and its token cost.

**→ Rule.** Never write a dataset-wide claim into the record from a single sample. Measure all N, or label the claim explicitly as 'sample of 1, unverified'.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · plan_beam 0% and section 0% look identical on the scoreboard but have opposite causes

**What happened.** Two subtasks both reported 0% recall. Ceiling analysis showed plan_beam has an 88% ceiling (the model genuinely fails) while section has a 4% ceiling on the evaluated house (the metric is impossible). Averaging or summarising them together would have produced the conclusion 'the model reads badly'.

**Root cause.** Identical-looking numbers from different causes were being reported side by side with no ceiling column, so the scoreboard could not distinguish a model failure from a metric failure.

**Impact.** Risk of a wrong project-level conclusion and misdirected spend; also means that after any future fix, section's score cannot indicate whether the fix worked.

**Fix.** Added a ceiling column per subtask to the reporting; classified each 0% by cause (model-broken vs. metric-broken) before deciding where to invest.

**→ Rule.** Always report a metric next to its achievable ceiling. Two zeroes with different ceilings are two different diseases and must never be aggregated into one conclusion.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · The ID-ceiling problem is not section-only — notes can score at most 2%, and every subtask's scoreboard is uncorrected for its ceiling

**What happened.** The measure_id_ceiling.py results show every subtask has a ceiling below 100%: notes 5 readable ids of 272 = 2%, section 37%, schedule 61%, plan_footing 75%, plan_slab 92%, plan_beam 88%. All rounds t01–t03 were scored and compared against a raw 100% scale, so 'plan_footing 33%' was actually 33 of an achievable 75, and notes was effectively unscoreable from the start.

**Root cause.** The evaluation was built to compare element_id strings without anyone auditing what fraction of those ids physically exist on the drawings. section's 0% was loud enough to trigger the audit; the quieter subtasks never were.

**Impact.** Every cross-round comparison in the project's history is against a moving, uncorrected denominator. schedule '0% → 21.9%' and plan_footing '33.3% stuck' both mean something different once the ceiling is applied, and notes has been carried as a subtask that can never pass.

**Fix.** not fixed — a ceiling-adjusted reporting column was proposed (safe, script-only) but not implemented

**→ Rule.** When one metric turns out to measure the impossible, run the same ceiling check across every sibling metric in the same pass — the broken one is rarely alone.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Every round's subtask scoreboard comes from a single evaluation house (บ้าน 08), whose section pages are fences and plumbing

**What happened.** The section ceiling was computed 'เฉพาะบ้าน 08 ที่ใช้วัดผลจริง' — revealing that the numbers steering three training rounds are one-house measurements. House 08 is single-storey and its section sheets are almost all รั้ว/ประตู/ท่อน้ำ details, not beam/column cross-sections, which is why its ceiling collapses to 4% while the corpus-wide ceiling is 37%.

**Root cause.** One house was chosen as the eval set, presumably for speed, and its representativeness was never checked against the corpus before its numbers were used to pick what to fix.

**Impact.** Round-over-round deltas (schedule 0→21.9%, plan_slab 0→20%) are single-sample readings that could move on house choice alone. The most expensive decision of the week — 'plan_beam is the target' — rests on this one house.

**Fix.** not fixed — no multi-house eval set was created

**→ Rule.** Before a number gets to choose what the next $5 round trains on, check how many houses produced it. A one-house scoreboard measures the house as much as the model.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · The GT batch edit nulled some element_ids that are genuinely printed on the drawing

**What happened.** The approved batch edit moved 1,534 section element ids to null based on the PRINTED_ID regex. Long ids that are in fact printed on the drawing — e.g. `เหล็ก WF 150x150x7x10` — were nulled as collateral, and the next dataset rebuild will train them as null.

**Root cause.** A regex heuristic was used to drive a bulk edit of ground truth. It cannot distinguish a long printed specification string from an invented descriptive name.

**Impact.** A subset of genuinely-readable labels will be trained as null, teaching the model to skip values it could have read. Risk was explicitly accepted before the edit.

**Fix.** Risk stated in one line to Makham before execution and accepted (att1235). Recovery is possible per-record because the original name is preserved in `element_name_assigned`; git was clean before the run as a backup, and the script is idempotent (re-run = 0 changes).

**→ Rule.** When a heuristic drives a bulk ground-truth edit: state the error direction before running, keep the original value in a side field so it is reversible per record, ensure the script is idempotent, and start from a clean git state as the backup.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · heuristic-limitation</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · 343 GT section files were rewritten but train/val/test.jsonl were deliberately left stale — the dataset now disagrees with the ground truth

**What happened.** The element_id convention change moved 1,534 elements to element_name_assigned across 343 section files in json_แก้ไขแล้ว/, but build_dataset_t03.py was not re-run, because rebuilding would overwrite the current train/val/test.jsonl that the existing t03 measurements are tied to. The dataset on disk and the GT it came from now describe different things.

**Root cause.** The measurement history is pinned to a dataset file rather than to a dataset version/hash, so keeping comparability and keeping GT-consistency became mutually exclusive.

**Impact.** Any training or evaluation run started before the rebuild will silently use the old invented-name targets, exactly the problem the GT edit was made to remove; the inconsistency is invisible from the .jsonl alone.

**Fix.** not fixed by design — rebuild deferred into the t03b workflow; recorded as a required first step of that round.

**→ Rule.** Version datasets by hash/name so a GT fix does not force a choice between stale data and lost comparability — and mark a stale build loudly, not only in a diary line.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · data-pipeline</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · `infer_house_t04.py --all-val` still read the original contaminated `val.jsonl` instead of the per-fold val file

**What happened.** The eval script was written before k-fold existed, so `--all-val` loaded `val.jsonl` (the 5 contaminated houses) rather than `val_fold{k}.jsonl`.

**Root cause.** A downstream consumer was not updated when the upstream data layout changed from a single split to k-folds; the script had a hardcoded filename with no fold awareness.

**Impact.** Would have produced eval numbers on the known-contaminated split, reproducing exactly the inflated-recall problem the k-fold work had just been done to eliminate.

**Fix.** Worked around by uploading `val_fold0.jsonl` over the name `val.jsonl` on each rented machine after verifying the schema keys matched; the fold0 machine had never had the original val.jsonf so there was no risk of overwriting real data.

**→ Rule.** When a data layout changes (single split → k-fold), grep every consumer for the old hardcoded filename before running any evaluation — an eval script silently reading the wrong file produces confident wrong numbers.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · evaluation-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Falling train_loss and 96-100% valid JSON were read as 'training is healthy, folds converge consistently' while the model was learning nothing but the schema

**What happened.** fold0 finished at train_loss 0.5503 with 'ลดต่อเนื่องตลอด ไม่มีสัญญาณ overfit'; fold2 finished at 0.5590 and was recorded as 'สัญญาณดีว่าทั้ง 4 folds converge สอดคล้องกัน'. Both readings were used as evidence the run was fine. The post-mortem showed the loss was falling because the model was memorising the JSON schema and the answers of houses it had already seen — it could not read the drawings at all (every image collapsed to one 256-token tile). The same misplaced comfort appears again when the 17773>8192 truncation warning was partly waved off with 'loss ที่ลดปกติดีเป็นสัญญาณบวก'.

**Root cause.** train_loss and output-format validity are both blind to a preprocessing bug: a model that memorises schema plus seen answers drives loss down exactly the same way a model that learned to read does. No metric in the loop measured whether the visual input carried information.

**Impact.** Four full trainings were allowed to run to completion, and two were uploaded to HF and sha256-verified, on the strength of metrics that could not have detected the fault. Discovery was delayed until eval on held-out houses.

**Fix.** Not fixed as a metric; replaced by the t05 rule to probe tokens-per-image before training. The false-positive reading is recorded in the root-cause section of the same day's entry.

**→ Rule.** A converging loss curve is not evidence that the model can see. For a vision task, pair the loss with at least one input-side check (tokens per image, or a rendered sample at the resolution the model actually receives) before treating a run as healthy.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · measurement/eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Only aggregate recall numbers were tracked; nobody opened a raw output file until Makham demanded a root cause — the model was answering about a completely different house and sheet

**What happened.** Eval was reported as plan_beam 6/6=0%, plan_footing 1/1=0%. Makham had to order 'หาสาเหตุก่อน มันไม่ควรแย่ขนาดนั้น' before anyone opened an actual output file. Doing so immediately revealed the model was not producing near-miss element ids — it was answering with a plan of a different house and a different sheet entirely (fed a footing plan, it answered with someone else's roof plan). That qualitative fact, invisible in a recall percentage, is what pointed at a perception failure rather than an accuracy failure.

**Root cause.** The eval harness reported a scalar (recall) and the workflow trusted it as the whole picture. A 0% score has many possible causes — near misses, format failure, total blindness — and the scalar cannot distinguish them, so diagnosis stalled at 'the score is bad' until a human forced a look at the raw text.

**Impact.** Root cause of the entire round's failure sat undiagnosed behind a number that had been available for hours; the diagnosis then took only three checks once actual outputs were read.

**Fix.** Root cause found the same session by opening outputs, dumping image tokens from the training log, reading llamafactory's mm_plugin.py source, and resizing a real beam plan to 448×448 to look at it.

**→ Rule.** When a metric reads 0% (or 100%), read the raw output before theorising. A scalar tells you something is wrong; only the artefact tells you what kind of wrong.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · measurement/eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · t04 changed both model and precision at once, making the result uninterpretable

**What happened.** The t04 round varied the model and the precision simultaneously, so when it failed there was no way to attribute the failure to either variable.

**Root cause.** No experimental discipline of holding all but one variable fixed between rounds.

**Impact.** A failed round produced no usable signal about which change caused the failure.

**Fix.** For this round the dataset content was made byte-identical across both arms deliberately, so any difference could only come from the model.

**→ Rule.** Change exactly one variable per expensive run and freeze everything else — identical data across arms is what makes the comparison mean anything.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · experiment-design</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · The headline 11.8% strict recall badly understated real reading ability due to naming-convention mismatches

**What happened.** Strict recall used exact string tuple equality with no normalization. The model read the footing page 100% correctly by position but scored 1/6 because it wrote mark ids as printed on the drawing ("F4,C1") while the GT convention splits them ("F4" + "C1"). Dummy grid lines were also named differently (1.5B vs 1'), and the footing page has no grid_ref_start/end at all.

**Root cause.** A single strict metric designed for cross-round comparability was being read as a measure of capability.

**Impact.** Reading '11.8%' alone would have concluded the model can barely read drawings, when it read the entire footing page perfectly — a potentially major wrong strategic call.

**Fix.** Added mark_base (88.2%) and position+mark_base (43.5%) metrics, and wrote an explicit interpretation summary so nobody reads the strict number alone.

**→ Rule.** Never report a single strict metric as the capability number — pair every strict score with a convention-forgiving metric and a per-item breakdown, and state which one reflects real ability.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · The hand-made answer key for the benchmark house contained two errors, caught only by the adjudicator

**What happened.** The op04 ground truth for บ้านไทยพอเพียง3 was built by two independent readers per page using different methods. The adjudicator, zooming into the images, found two disagreements were real errors in the key: a dummy gridline named 4' instead of 3', and the wrong y-orientation for beam B0.

**Root cause.** Reading a construction drawing by eye is error-prone even for a careful reader; a single-reader key would have shipped both errors silently.

**Impact.** Two of 34 ground-truth items would have been wrong, corrupting the first real recall measurement of destrier — the number the whole round is judged by.

**Fix.** two-independent-readers-plus-adjudicator process; the adjudicator zoomed and corrected both, then the whole key was re-checked once more against the images

**→ Rule.** A hand-made evaluation key needs at least two independent readers and an adjudicator — the key is measurement apparatus, and an error in it is indistinguishable from a model error.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · evaluation</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Nearly reused t04's data fold for a different model — caught by Makham, not by the process

**What happened.** There was a plan to use t04's fold for training; Makham himself caught that this was wrong, with a confirming table of numbers.

**Root cause.** Fold/split provenance was not tracked per model, so reusing another model's fold looked like a reasonable shortcut. It was only stopped by a human noticing, with no automated guard.

**Impact.** Would have contaminated train/val separation and produced misleading evaluation numbers. Caught before use.

**Fix.** Avoided; documented as section 5 of the teaching document with a confirming numeric table.

**→ Rule.** Folds are model-specific artifacts — record which model each fold belongs to and never reuse one across runs. A human catch is luck; add the provenance field.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · The $2 gate's scoring script counted brute-force mark enumeration (B1…B34) as correct answers

**What happened.** Besides the leaked-example problem, the blind t44 model passed one gate page by simply listing marks in sequence — B1, B2, B3 … up to B34 — and the first three happened to match the ground truth. The scoring script counted those as hits, so a model that could not see the drawing at all scored as reading it.

**Root cause.** The gate metric was recall-only: it checked whether GT marks appeared somewhere in the answer, with no precision penalty and no cap on how many candidates the model could emit. Any model that spams a dense enumeration of a predictable naming space (B1..Bn, C1..Cn) scores non-zero by construction.

**Impact.** Combined with the leaked-example bug this produced a false green on the go/no-go gate; acting on it would have burned the full $60–70 training run on a blind model, repeating t04 exactly.

**Fix.** The diary records the prompt-leak rule ('ห้ามใส่ตัวอย่างที่อยู่ในเฉลย ลงไปใน prompt ที่ใช้ทดสอบ') but records no precision/over-generation penalty in the scorer — the enumeration hole is described, not closed. Not fixed.

**→ Rule.** A recall-only score is gameable by guessing everything. Any gate metric must penalise over-generation (precision, or a hard cap on emitted items) or a model that outputs the whole naming space always passes.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Baseline numbers were measured under a possibly wrong image resolution

**What happened.** The pre-tuning baseline (JSON valid 0/20, elements 0/170) was likely run at the default 16,384-token resolution rather than the intended 5,120, because of the silent SizeDict bug.

**Root cause.** The baseline was measured before the configuration bug was found; there was no assertion that the eval ran under the same settings as the later post-tuning eval.

**Impact.** The before/after comparison is not strictly apples-to-apples. It happened to be harmless here only because 0% is the floor — under any non-zero baseline the whole comparison would have been invalid.

**Fix.** Noted the caveat in the diary and reasoned that 0% is the worst possible result either way; the setting was fixed before the tuned-model eval.

**→ Rule.** Baseline and post-training evals must run under identical, asserted configuration — log and compare the effective settings in both runs, not just the scores.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Headline quality numbers (0%→90%) measured on only 20 of the 88 validation examples

**What happened.** Both the baseline and the post-tune evaluation were run with `--limit 20`, so the whole result table (JSON valid 18/20, view exact 12/20, elements 16/170) rests on a 20-example subset of the 88-example val set. The numbers are reported and celebrated without noting the sample size caveat.

**Root cause.** `--limit 20` was used to save GPU time/money during debugging and then never removed for the real measurement run — the debug setting became the reported result.

**Impact.** One example flipping moves JSON-valid by 5 percentage points; the 90% and 60% figures carry wide error bars that were never stated, and they are now the reference for judging the next tuning round.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the instance was destroyed before a full-val run was done.

**→ Rule.** Debug with `--limit`, but the number you write into the results table must come from a full validation pass; state the sample size next to every reported percentage.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Validation set drawn entirely from a single house (house03) — generalization across houses never measured

**What happened.** Train = houses 01/02/04 (226 examples), val = house03 only (88 examples). Every quality number reported is therefore a measurement against one house's drawing style/draftsman conventions.

**Root cause.** Split was made by house for convenience (clean no-leakage split), but with only 4 houses available a single held-out house is both the entire val set and a single sample of "drawing style".

**Impact.** The 90%/60%/9.4% numbers may not transfer to a fifth house; a low element recall could be house03-specific rather than a general model weakness, which would mislead the next tuning round's priorities.

**Fix.** Not fixed — noted only as "the model never sees this set while being taught".

**→ Rule.** With few source documents, rotate the held-out house (cross-validation) or hold out pages from several houses, otherwise a per-house quirk is indistinguishable from a model weakness.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21(teach mk).md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · "element_id 100%" reported as a quality result, but it is circular if elements are matched by element_id

**What happened.** The results table reports "Field exact-match (for matched elements): element_id 100%, element_type 87.5%, count 100%". If the matcher pairs predicted and ground-truth elements *by* element_id, then element_id exact-match is 100% by construction and measures nothing.

**Root cause.** Per-field accuracy was computed over the subset of elements that survived matching, without stating the matching key — so a tautological field was published alongside genuine ones, over only 16 items.

**Impact.** A meaningless 100% sits in the headline results table and inflates the apparent quality of a model whose real weakness (9.4% recall) is elsewhere; risks the next round optimizing against a metric that cannot move.

**Fix.** Not fixed — reported as-is.

**→ Rule.** Never report exact-match on the field used as the matching key, and always state the matching rule and the n next to conditional metrics (here n=16).

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · t01 and t02 headline numbers were measured on different rented machines with possibly different library versions

**What happened.** t01's 90% / 28.2% were measured on 07-24 on one rented box; t02's numbers on 07-28 on another. After discovering that a library version change had already broken code that day, the comparability of the two measurements became doubtful and a Phase 7.5 re-measurement of t01 on the same machine was required.

**Root cause.** No environment fingerprint (library versions, image pipeline config) was captured alongside the metric, so two numbers from two boxes could not be shown to be comparable.

**Impact.** Extra work and extra GPU time to reload the full 70GB t01 base model on the t02 box purely to re-verify a number that had already been measured.

**Fix.** Ran Phase 7.5 — re-evaluated t01's adapter on the same machine that had just evaluated t02.

**→ Rule.** Store the environment fingerprint with every metric, and evaluate all arms of a comparison on one machine in one session; a number without its measurement conditions cannot be compared to anything.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · The model was judged on page types the pipeline already discards

**What happened.** Pages 03/04/05 are index / notes / material_list / site_plan — patterns that KEEP_PATTERNS filters out of the real pipeline. Most of the night's damning quality assessment was measured on work the model will never be asked to do.

**Root cause.** Extraction ran in page order rather than in relevance order, so the evaluation sample was determined by page numbering, not by what the system actually consumes.

**Impact.** The quality verdict is biased and partly unfair; time was spent grading output that has no downstream consumer, while the pages that matter went ungraded.

**Fix.** partially — the caveat is documented; the next run should extract kept-pattern pages first

**→ Rule.** Evaluate on the distribution the system actually serves. Order any diagnostic run by relevance to the real pipeline, not by file/page order, or you will spend your measurement budget on data you filter away.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · The 'results are damn awful' verdict was nearly taken at face value — the root cause was only found by cataloguing what worked

**What happened.** Makham's reaction to the output was a blanket 'the results are damn awful'. The diary deliberately stops to list what the model does well (มอก. numbers 8/8, floor levels 7/8, rooms 8/8, sheet notes 6/6) before diagnosing, noting explicitly that this has to be said 'otherwise the diagnosis goes wrong'. The decisive clue — hard content right, easy format wrong, which is unnatural for a genuinely tuned model — is only visible once the successes are counted.

**Root cause.** An aggregate quality judgement ('mostly wrong') destroys the error-shape signal. Had the run been scored as a single pass/fail percentage, the format-vs-content asymmetry that pointed at the silent merge failure would have been invisible.

**Impact.** A near-miss on the biggest finding of the project so far. Acting on 'the model is bad' would have led to retraining, prompt rewrites, or renting a GPU — all of which would have reproduced the same output, since the suspected artifact may contain no tuning at all.

**Fix.** avoided — the diary forced a per-item what-worked/what-broke table before drawing any conclusion

**→ Rule.** Never diagnose from an aggregate score. Split every eval into what the model got right and what it got wrong, and read the *shape* of the split: an unnatural pattern (easy things wrong, hard things right) is a cause signal that a single percentage erases.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Every page the model has ever been run on in real use was its own training data — no held-out page has been tested

**What happened.** Pages 03-06, the only full extractions produced, are train.jsonl lines 3-6 — pages the model saw with their answer key three times during training. The entire 'is it usable' judgement, good and bad, was formed on memorised examples; not one unseen page has been extracted end-to-end.

**Root cause.** House 01 was chosen for the first production run because it was convenient and had gold available — which is exactly what makes it training data. Nobody separated 'a page I can score against gold' from 'a page the model has not memorised'.

**Impact.** The unusable-output verdict is measured on the model's best case; real unseen pages can only be worse. Conversely the successes (มอก. 8/8, rooms 8/8) may be recall of training data rather than capability, so both halves of the assessment are unreliable as a generalisation estimate.

**Fix.** not fixed — no held-out extraction was run; the run was halted pending the LoRA test

**→ Rule.** Keep at least one house (or a fixed page set) permanently out of training and run every production sanity check against it. A quality number measured on training data answers a different question from the one being asked — and here it accidentally became the key diagnostic only because the failure was in format, not content.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Model was judged on pages (index/notes/material_list/site_plan) that KEEP_PATTERNS already excludes

**What happened.** The harsh 07-29 verdict was formed largely on pages 03/04/05, whose patterns the current plan filters out of extraction entirely — the model would never be asked to do that work in production.

**Root cause.** The evaluation set was whatever ran first, not a set drawn from the production scope. Nobody checked the tested pages against KEEP_PATTERNS before drawing conclusions.

**Impact.** Risk of condemning (or retraining) the model based on a task it is not used for, while the task that matters remained untested.

**Fix.** Caveat recorded explicitly in the diary before any decision was made on the results.

**→ Rule.** Draw the evaluation set from the production scope filter. Judging a model on inputs your pipeline discards produces a verdict you cannot act on.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Judged the model for emitting zero confidence fields that the prompt and dataset had deliberately stripped out

**What happened.** Section 2.จ of the 2026-07-29 review lists 'ชั้นความมั่นใจหายทั้งหมด' as a defect: confidence_score and confidence_flags appeared 0 times in 6 files. But Appendix B records that confidence was deliberately cut from PROMPT_SHORT during prompt design ('confidence/price-table/specs join ... ตัดออกทั้งหมดเพราะ dataset ไม่มีให้สอนอยู่แล้ว') — the model was never asked for them and never trained on them.

**Root cause.** The evaluation compared model output against the human ground-truth schema, which contains confidence fields, while the model was trained and prompted against a deliberately reduced schema that does not. The two schemas were never reconciled before the comparison.

**Impact.** A self-inflicted gap was logged as a model failure in the defect list, inflating the apparent badness of the run and pointing diagnosis at the model instead of at the prompt/dataset scope decision.

**Fix.** Not fixed — still listed as a model defect in the diary; nobody has decided whether to add confidence back to the dataset+prompt or to drop it from the ground-truth comparison.

**→ Rule.** When scoring against ground truth, first subtract every field you deliberately removed from the prompt or training data — otherwise you audit your own scope decisions as model errors.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · The t02 generalization test was never completed — houses 10/11 never started, house 08 never reached its cap

**What happened.** The planned 4-house generalization test (08/09/10/11) ended with 25 pages of house 08 and 6 structural plan pages of house 09. Houses 10 and 11 were never started at all, and house 08 covered only 25 of its 63 pages. The pending list still records both across 08-20 and 08-21.

**Root cause.** Cascading causes: two bad rentals, a 30x price misread, unmeasured per-page timing, the undiagnosed repetition loop making dense pages hit the token cap, and a 1am deadline. Each shaved scope until the experiment no longer answered its own question.

**Impact.** The 11% element recall figure — now the project's headline model-quality number driving the entire t03 redesign and the 25-30 house dataset target — rests on a fraction of the planned sample from effectively one and a half houses.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recorded across both days' pending lists.

**→ Rule.** When scope is cut below the point where an experiment answers its question, label the resulting number as provisional wherever it is quoted — a headline metric derived from 1.5 of 4 planned houses must carry its sample size everywhere it appears.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · The human ground truth itself could not be fully placed on the drawing (45/48 and 52/53)

**What happened.** When the GT-vs-AI overlays were rendered for house 09, the human-reviewed ground truth resolved 45 of 48 beams on one page and 52 of 53 on another — not 100%. The measuring stick used to score the model has its own small gap, which was noted in passing and not investigated.

**Root cause.** Some ground-truth elements carry grid refs that cannot be resolved against the grid master (missing/ambiguous refs), the same class of gap as the หน้า28 calibration failure — but here in the human data, not the printed sheet.

**Impact.** Every recall number computed against this ground truth carries an unquantified few-percent floor; the 3 unplaceable GT beams are silently excluded from any overlay-based comparison.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded only as the overlay counts in the diary.

**→ Rule.** Audit the ground truth before using it as a ruler: report GT-resolvable rate alongside model recall, otherwise the model is being scored against an incomplete reference without anyone knowing by how much.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Evaluation compares element IDs with exact string equality — whitespace and case cause false misses

**What happened.** The scoring line is `hit = len(set(gt_ids) & set(pred_ids))`, a literal string intersection. A prediction of `"B1 "` does not match a ground truth of `"B1"`.

**Root cause.** The scorer was written as a set intersection without a normalisation step, on the assumption that both sides emit identically formatted strings.

**Impact.** Every recall number in every round is potentially understated by an unknown amount from trailing spaces and case differences alone — the team currently cannot say how much of any 0% is this.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Listed as proposed fix #2 (strip whitespace and normalise case before comparing); flagged as safe to do immediately since it touches only the scoring script, not the ground truth.

**→ Rule.** Any string-equality scorer must normalise (trim, casefold, collapse internal whitespace) before comparing, and should log near-miss pairs so formatting failures are visible rather than silently scored as zero.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · HoughCircles section-label detection scored a perfect 5/5 on one house and collapsed to 3/20 and 0/18 on others

**What happened.** An attempt to find section labels by detecting the circles drawn around names like (B1)(B2) gave a flawless 5/5 with no false positives on house 17, then 3/20 on house 12 and 0/18 on house 01.

**Root cause.** Section sheets are drawn differently by each design office — house 17 circles the label, house 01 prints 'B1 1:20' with an underline and no circle at all. Structural plans use far more stable symbols than section detail sheets do.

**Impact.** Effort spent on an approach that cannot generalise. Had house 17 been the only test, the technique would have been reported as working and possibly built on.

**Fix.** Tested on three houses before drawing any conclusion; recorded the negative result explicitly so nobody retries it.

**→ Rule.** A computer-vision technique that scores perfectly on one document is unvalidated. Test on at least three sources from different origins before reporting it as working — and write the failed attempts down so they are not repeated.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Non-Qwen model search returned InternVL3, which uses a Qwen backbone anyway

**What happened.** Tasked with finding a 100–200B vision model outside the Qwen family, InternVL3-78B and InternVL3.5-241B initially looked like valid candidates until inspection showed they use Qwen2.5/Qwen3 as their language backbone.

**Root cause.** Model families were being filtered by brand name rather than by architecture lineage; a different publisher does not mean a different base model.

**Impact.** Candidates that fail the actual requirement (architectural diversity from Qwen) were carried through part of the evaluation before being caught.

**Fix.** Filter criterion restated as backbone lineage, not brand. Of 8–10 models checked, only GLM-4.6V and Llama-4-Scout survived, and neither has verified Thai reading quality.

**→ Rule.** When the requirement is architectural diversity, verify the backbone in the model card/config — brand names hide shared foundations.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · vendor/evaluation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · The 10-model alternative-VLM survey ranked candidates on spec sheets — only 1 of 10 had any real benchmark score

**What happened.** Models were shortlisted and eliminated on parameter count, licence text and framework support. The OmniDocBench leaderboard was only consulted at the end, and it turned out InternVL3-78B was the single model out of all ten with a real measured document-understanding score (83.76).

**Root cause.** The screening criteria were the easy-to-read ones (B count, licence, 'can Unsloth train it'). Measured document-reading performance — the one thing the project actually needs — was not a screening column at all.

**Impact.** Hours spent evaluating and writing up models whose capability on this task was never established; Pixtral-Large in particular got a deep capability write-up before its licence disqualified it in one line. The survey's own conclusion ('nothing has all three') may be wrong in either direction because capability was never in the comparison.

**Fix.** partially fixed — OmniDocBench was found and noted late, raising confidence in InternVL3-78B slightly

**→ Rule.** Put the hardest-to-fake criterion first in the screen. Licence and parameter count are free to read, which is exactly why they should not be what a survey sorts on.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · research-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Rebar-dot counting scored 1/5, but the test measured the hand-made crops, not the idea

**What happened.** Rebar-dot counting inside hand-cropped section boxes scored 1/5. The crops were eyeballed by hand and at least one clearly missed its box, so the score measures the quality of the crops rather than the viability of the method.

**Root cause.** The experiment's input (the crops) was produced manually and unverified, so the measurement conflated two variables — crop quality and detection quality — with no way to separate them.

**Impact.** A potentially viable idea nearly got recorded as disproven on the strength of an invalid test.

**Fix.** Left explicitly inconclusive in the record rather than written up as a failure, with a note that it deserves one clean retry driven by auto-detected boxes.

**→ Rule.** If the input to an experiment was produced by hand and not verified, the result measures your hand, not the hypothesis. Mark such results inconclusive — recording a bad test as a disproof kills a good idea permanently.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · measurement-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · The chars/2.2 token estimate driving MAX_LENGTH has never been validated against the real tokenizer

**What happened.** Sequence-length totals (including the 44,606 figure that MAX_LENGTH=47104 is sized against, a 5.3% margin) come from a chars/2.2 heuristic inherited from train_t03.py's `_est()`. The visual-token half of the calculation is arithmetically exact; the text half is not, and has never been checked against the actual tokenizer.

**Root cause.** A convenience heuristic was adopted for estimating text tokens and then quietly promoted into a load-bearing input for a hard VRAM limit, without anyone validating it.

**Impact.** The 5.3% safety margin on MAX_LENGTH rests on an unvalidated ratio. Thai text in particular can tokenize very differently from the assumed ratio, and a truncation mid-JSON is the t01 §0.4 bug class.

**Fix.** Not fixed — explicitly recorded as an open limitation in the workflow doc and repeated in the end-of-day pending list.

**→ Rule.** Any heuristic that becomes an input to a hard limit must be validated against ground truth once. Run the real tokenizer over the longest few examples and record the true ratio before trusting a margin under 10%.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · unvalidated-heuristic</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Automatic template harvesting produced overwhelmingly garbage candidates — 45 of 57, then 71 of 79

**What happened.** The harvester's candidate output was mostly not templates at all: in the first round about 45 of 57 candidates were Thai text characters or grid circles; in the second round only 8 of 79 were real, the rest Thai letters, grid bubbles and lines.

**Root cause.** The harvester's criterion is "similarly-sized icons repeating 3 or more times", which Thai characters and grid bubbles satisfy perfectly. The tool has no notion of what a structural symbol is.

**Impact.** Every harvest round requires manual visual review of dozens of candidates; auto-promotion would have poisoned the bank immediately (see the 22px "+" and 31px shaded-template bugs, both of which came from harvest output).

**Fix.** Hard rule that candidates are never auto-promoted — `--promote <filename>` requires a human. Added `--review` to rank candidates by |repeat count − that house's GT count| and build a montage sorted best-first, explicitly to speed up the eye, not to decide for it.

**→ Rule.** When an automatic harvester's precision is under 15%, keep a mandatory human gate and never auto-promote. Ranking to speed up review is fine; ranking that decides is how poison templates get in.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · low-precision-automation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-29 · Turning on xgrammar for all passes confounds every JSON-validity comparison against prior rounds

**What happened.** xgrammar was enabled for every subtask (previously plan_beam only). This means any JSON-validity improvement measured against earlier rounds is partly caused by grammar, not by the model getting better — earlier rounds had no grammar on non-plan_beam subtasks.

**Root cause.** An inference-time configuration changed between measurement rounds. Without noting it, a metric jump would be naturally attributed to the model.

**Impact.** Cross-round JSON-validity numbers are no longer directly comparable. Caught and documented before anyone drew the wrong conclusion.

**Fix.** Warnings added to both RUNBOOK and WORKFLOW that a JSON-valid jump is partly grammar, not model improvement alone. `--no-grammar` retained specifically so an A/B remains possible.

**→ Rule.** Record every inference-time configuration change alongside the metric it affects, and keep a flag to disable it so the confound can be measured rather than argued about.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-29 · k-fold splits distribute the 5 human-reviewed houses unevenly — folds 0 and 3 get none

**What happened.** The new `--folds N` house-level greedy balance produced 5 folds of 8 houses each (203–205 examples, perfect partition summing to 1020), but the 5 human-reviewed houses (01-05) landed unevenly: folds 0 and 3 contain zero reviewed houses.

**Root cause.** The balancing algorithm balances example count per fold, not GT-quality composition. Reviewed vs. op04-only was not a stratification dimension.

**Impact.** Two of five folds validate entirely against unreviewed GT, so their scores measure agreement with possibly-wrong labels. Fold-to-fold variance will be partly GT quality, not model variance.

**Fix.** Not fixed — documented in fold_manifest.json and flagged. Also flagged that k-fold has never actually been run on GPU (infra only, 5x cost/time, awaiting a human decision).

**→ Rule.** Stratify cross-validation folds on GT quality, not just example count. A fold validated against unreviewed labels measures a different thing than one validated against reviewed labels.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · eval-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · The hypothesis that plan_beam failed because the page contained two mixed plans was disproven — t03 genuinely cannot read beam plans

**What happened.** On the rented card, plan_beam scored 0/11 on both the full page and a cropped image containing only the beam plan, confirming the failure is not caused by two plans sharing one page. It matched the earlier house 08 result (0% on all 3 tasks) exactly. plan_footing meanwhile got 2/3 marks (67%).

**Root cause.** The earlier explanation attributed the failure to page layout rather than to a genuine model capability gap on beam plans — a plausible hypothesis that had never been tested by isolating the variable.

**Impact.** Time would have been spent on cropping/preprocessing work that could not have fixed anything. The real conclusion is that beam extraction must be disabled or deferred to t05/pass3.

**Fix.** Ran the controlled comparison (full page vs cropped page) and recorded that beam plans are genuinely unreadable by t03; listed as a pre-presentation decision item — either disable the subtask or wait for t05.

**→ Rule.** Test a failure hypothesis by isolating the single variable it blames (here: crop the page) before building any fix around it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · evaluation-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · Three real data gaps block the t05 dataset build — no pass0 GT anywhere, CV sidecars on only 10 pages, and no cv_mark↔GT matcher

**What happened.** Checking the real files (not old reports) before building the t05 dataset found: ① no house has `pass0.json` GT — structural pages can be derived from rawjson GT but the non-structural majority of 2,990 pages has none; ② CV sidecars (`_cv25.json`) exist for only 10 pages in the entire library; ③ there is no matcher linking `cv_mark` to GT elements at all.

**Root cause.** The plan to include pass0/pass2.5/pass3 in training was formed before verifying that the required ground truth and sidecar artifacts actually exist at scale.
