**Root cause.** Production extraction was started before the artifact had a content-correctness verification (see the weak sanity gate and the shallow Phase 10 test); no staging area separated trial output from accepted output.

**Impact.** Four contaminated result files that must be discarded or re-run; near miss on filling a whole house's folder with unusable data.

**Fix.** Extraction halted pending the LoRA-presence test.

**→ Rule.** Write model output to a staging area until the artifact has passed a content-correctness check; never let an unverified pipeline write directly into the dataset of record.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · process/data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model invented a grid_table giving one length per grid intersection — a quantity that does not exist — poisoning every span downstream

**What happened.** On page 06 the model emitted a grid_table structure with one numeric value per grid intersection. An intersection is a point and has no length; the model took the real dimensions on the sheet (7.0, 9.5, 4.0, 3.5) and scattered them into the wrong cells. Because PROMPT_SHORT states 'Span length comes from the grid table, not your own visual estimate', every span computed from that page is wrong.

**Root cause.** The model produced a structurally plausible but physically meaningless object, and nothing in the pipeline validates that a grid table's cells correspond to spans between adjacent lines rather than to points.

**Impact.** Not just individual wrong numbers — the prompt makes the whole span chain depend on this table, so one invented structure invalidates every downstream quantity on the page, which then feeds BOQ.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as a defect on 2026-07-29; no schema validation of grid_table exists in the extraction path.

**→ Rule.** Validate that emitted structures represent real physical quantities, not just valid JSON — a table indexed by points instead of by spans passes every syntactic check and corrupts everything computed from it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · data-correctness</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-01 · Dummy grid 2'=5.2 added to house 04's grid master but never cascaded into the plan files

**What happened.** A new x-axis dummy grid `2'`(5.2) was inserted into house 04's gridline file between grids 2 and 3, at confidence 1 — but was not propagated into the pattern=plan files (footing/beam plans on pages 31–34 and others) that reference the grid.

**Root cause.** The grid master and the plan files that consume it are edited independently, with no cascade step or checker enforcing that a change to the grid master reaches its dependants.

**Impact.** House 04's grid master and its plan files disagree; any element positioned relative to grid 2 or 3 on those plans is now referenced against a stale grid.

**Fix.** Not fixed — explicitly left pending as a cascade + source-image re-check task.

**→ Rule.** A grid-master edit is not done until every dependent plan file is updated and re-checked against the source image. Add a checker rule: every grid referenced in the master must resolve in the plans, and vice versa.

<sub>`2026-08-01.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · Houses 10/11 stored 65 rebar values as plain strings instead of schema §6 objects

**What happened.** 65 `main_bar`/`stirrup` values across houses 10 and 11 were plain strings (as printed on the drawing) rather than the structured §6 objects the schema requires; they had to be converted.

**Root cause.** No shape enforcement on field values — the schema said 'object' but the checker did not test it, so an extraction could write the printed text verbatim and pass.

**Impact.** 65 rebar specifications were unparseable by anything expecting structured counts/diameters — directly the fields the downstream BBS and BOQ calculations depend on.

**Fix.** Converted all 65 to §6 objects, keeping the original string in `printed_as` on every one so nothing was lost.

**→ Rule.** Enforce field *shape*, not just field presence. And when converting a value, always keep the original in a `printed_as` sibling — conversion is a lossy operation until proven otherwise.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · House 05 put descriptive suffixes on element_id (F1.30x1.30_E1), breaking cross-page joins

**What happened.** House 05 wrote element ids with a suffix appended to the printed mark, so the id no longer matches the mark used on other sheets and cross-page joins fail.

**Root cause.** No rule existed saying `element_id` must be exactly the printed mark and nothing else; descriptive ids look more informative and were written that way.

**Impact.** Elements in house 05 cannot be joined between the plan sheet and the schedule/section sheet — the join is the whole mechanism by which specs reach elements.

**Fix.** 82 element_ids were reduced to the printed mark with the original kept in `element_id_printed_as`; the rule was later locked as §0.3.

**→ Rule.** An identifier's only job is to join. Put descriptive information in its own field, never in the id — a 'more helpful' id is a broken join.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · An array named `column_sections` actually held beam sections — all 17 cut refs name B-marks

**What happened.** An array called `column_sections` was found to contain no columns at all: all 17 of its `cut_ref` values name beam marks (B1, B2A, B3, R1, RB0, B4, B5, B6X).

**Root cause.** The array was named from the sheet's heading or from an assumption rather than from what the entries actually reference; nothing cross-checked the array name against the marks inside it.

**Impact.** 17 beam sections were typed as columns — they would have been costed, scheduled, and reinforced as columns downstream, and would have trained the model to mislabel beams.

**Fix.** Converted all 17 to `element_type: "beam"`, keeping the cut label in `section_ref`.

**→ Rule.** Never trust a container's name to describe its contents. Validate element_type against the mark prefix — a B-mark inside a column array is an automatic failure.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-07 · House 14's beam runs on pages 18/19 were not fully traced — left at confidence ≤0.6

**What happened.** Beam runs on หน้า18 and หน้า19 of house 14 were not fully traced; entries were left at confidence ≤ 0.6 and flagged `needs_zoom_review`, with the house otherwise reported complete.

**Root cause.** Beam tracing across a plan is the hardest and least automatable part of extraction, and the workflow allows a house to be marked done with low-confidence beam entries outstanding — the same class of gap as the houses 01–05 missing-beam problem.

**Impact.** Another house enters the corpus with known-incomplete beam data, adding to the missing-beam debt that is already the dataset's biggest defect.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged `needs_zoom_review` and carried as pending.

**→ Rule.** Beams are the known weak point of this whole pipeline. Treat any beam entry below the confidence threshold as blocking for that house, not as a flag to be carried forward.

<sub>`2026-08-07.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-10 · House 19's structural and architectural sheets label the grid axes oppositely for the same building

**What happened.** In house 19, the structural sheets and the architecture sheets for the same building use opposite axis labelling — a genuine cross-discipline label swap within one drawing set.

**Root cause.** Different design disciplines produced their sheets with their own grid-labelling conventions and the set was published without reconciling them.

**Impact.** Any element joined across a structural and an architectural sheet in this house would be positioned on the wrong axis unless the conflict is detected and resolved.

**Fix.** Resolved via a 'structural wins' precedence rule, and the checker relaxed to accept either assignment.

**→ Rule.** Grid conventions can differ *within* a single drawing set, not just between houses. Detect axis-labelling conflicts per discipline and apply an explicit written precedence rule rather than assuming one grid definition per building.

<sub>`2026-08-10.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · notes is the worst-drifted pattern: 55 files carry the same content under six different container keys

**What happened.** 55 notes files carry the same content under six container keys — notes (22), notes_sections (9), sections (8), spec_notes (3), notes_text (1), raw_text (1) — plus one-offs. The spec names sections[]; only 8 of 55 use it.

**Root cause.** The notes pattern's container key was never enforced by check_format.py and the pattern is the least structured of the 16, so each extraction session invented a plausible key. Same failure class as roof_frame_plan and the discipline spelling split, but larger.

**Impact.** 85% of notes files are unreadable by any consumer keyed on the spec's name. The newly-defined §4a path is empty in practice until they are rewritten.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Migration of the 55 files to sections[] + notes{} recorded as pending.

**→ Rule.** Container/key names must be enforced by the format checker, not merely named in the spec — for any pattern where the checker is silent, expect one key per session and audit key distribution across the dataset periodically.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · plan_column was designed as its own subtask but only 2 files exist across 11 houses

**What happened.** The pass design split plan into plan_footing / plan_column / plan_beam / plan_slab, but counting the real data showed plan_column has only 2 files across 11 houses — columns almost never get their own plan sheet, appearing instead as markers on beam/footing plans and in column schedules. As a standalone subtask it would have zero training data.

**Root cause.** The subtask split was derived from the structural element taxonomy rather than from a count of how many sheets of each type actually exist in the dataset. Designing categories before counting instances.

**Impact.** A subtask with 2 training examples would have been trained and evaluated as if it were real — producing a model branch that cannot work, and a metric nobody could interpret. Caught by counting before training.

**Fix.** Not decided. Recorded as a blocking decision: merge plan_column into plan_beam, or move it to schedule. Also written into the op04 skill as a trap ('plan_column normally does not exist as a sheet — its absence is expected, not a miss').

**→ Rule.** Count the real files per proposed category before creating it as a training subtask — a category with under ~20 examples is a metric generator, not a model; the 13-examples/11%-recall result already proved the floor.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · 11 houses were annotated but t02 was actually trained on only 4 — most of the annotation effort never reached the model

**What happened.** Dataset counting revealed that of the 11 fully annotated houses in `json_แก้ไขแล้ว/` (1,180 files / 4,625 elements), t02's training run used only 4. That is why 35 beam-plan sheets existed on disk but the model only ever saw ~13 of them — the precise reason beam-plan recall came in at 11%.

**Root cause.** The training set was assembled from a subset of available annotated houses and nobody re-checked coverage per page type before or after the run; the shortfall was only discovered by counting weeks later while sizing t03.

**Impact.** Roughly 7 houses' worth of human annotation (the most expensive input in this project) produced zero training value, and the resulting model shipped with 11% recall on the single most important page type.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded in `tune_ai/t03/dataset_sizing.md` with a target of 25-30 houses; the next training run must use everything annotated.

**→ Rule.** Before a training run, count examples per page type actually going into train.jsonl — not houses annotated. Unused annotation is indistinguishable from annotation never done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · training-data-coverage</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · 267 schema violations across 246 GT files had accumulated undetected

**What happened.** A schema-normalize pass across all 11 houses of json_แก้ไขแล้ว found 267 changes needed in 246 files: discipline `architecture`→`architectural` (157 occurrences), 6 off-vocabulary values, container shape errors (element→elements, steel_members/void_bays/stair_details/reinforcement/sheet_index all sitting outside `elements`), stirrup_or_tie→stirrup, rebar_cover_m→cover_mm.

**Root cause.** GT files were produced by many agents/reviewers over time with no schema validator running as a gate. The schema evolved and old files were never re-validated against it, so drift accumulated silently.

**Impact.** Every downstream consumer (training dataset builder, Constistant BOQ) was reading inconsistent field names and container shapes; the training set carried the drift into the model.

**Fix.** Normalized all 246 files, re-validated all 1,180 files with json.loads, logged in json_แก้ไขแล้ว/README.md § 2026-08-24.

**→ Rule.** Run check_format/schema validation as a gate on every GT commit, not as a periodic cleanup campaign. Schema changes must trigger a repo-wide re-validation the same day.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · A truncated JSON file was broken in both data trees at once

**What happened.** `31.../หน้า25_plan_footing.json` was truncated mid-file and unparseable in both `json_แก้ไขแล้ว/` and `rawjson_ยังไม่ได้แก้ไขโดนคน/`.

**Root cause.** A write was interrupted or an output was saved incomplete, and the corruption propagated to both trees because the corrected tree was derived from the raw one without a parse check at the copy boundary.

**Impact.** One footing plan unusable in both trees; the F10 element data in it is permanently lost (no source to recover the missing values from).

**Fix.** Closed the file so it parses, kept the complete F5 record, discarded the partial F10 fragment rather than guessing the missing values, and attached a warning.

**→ Rule.** Parse-check every JSON file at the moment it is written and again at every copy boundary between trees. When a truncated record cannot be recovered, drop it with a warning — never fill the missing fields with a guess.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · data-corruption</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-26 · House 07 footing-spread had wrong rebar counts and depths locally — anything computed from them needs recheck

**What happened.** Merging house 07's footing-spread file revealed the local version had wrong real drawing data: F0.80 main_bar count was 8 when it should be 5; F1.00 and F1.50 `depth_m` were 1.5 when they should be 1.2; F1.00 was missing its `main_bar` block entirely. The teammate's numbers were correct.

**Root cause.** Two people read the same drawing and got different numbers, with no reconciliation step. Nothing flagged the disagreement until git forced it.

**Impact.** Wrong rebar counts and footing depths were live in the GT. Any BOQ/BBS computation done off the old local numbers is wrong and needs re-running.

**Fix.** Merged per Makham's rule — teammate's real drawing numbers win, Makham's JSON shape/schema wins. Flagged that downstream computations need re-checking.

**→ Rule.** When two people transcribe the same drawing, the data-owner's numbers win and the format-owner's schema wins — settle this rule in advance. And when GT numbers change, explicitly list what downstream results are now stale.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-26.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-28 · 16 of 40 grid masters were missing the z-axis entirely

**What happened.** Only 24 of 40 grid masters had z-axis level data. Filling the gap took three different recovery routes: 6 houses reconstructed from existing elements, 2 dug out of prose text, and 8 required opening the original drawing images and reading them by hand. Z-chains were also verified closed on 9 houses.

**Root cause.** z_levels was added to the gridmaster spec after many houses had already been extracted, and no back-fill sweep was run when the spec changed. The data existed in four different ad-hoc storage shapes across houses (Thai-label keys, prose "ระดับ… +X.XX", level_labels_as_printed, levels_m dicts).

**Impact.** 40% of houses had no vertical dimension available to any consumer; recovering it required manual image reading for 8 houses.

**Fix.** All 40/40 gridmasters now carry z_levels, harvested from each house's own reviewed per-page data. Z-chains checked closed on 9 houses.

**→ Rule.** When a schema field is added, immediately run a coverage report across all existing data and schedule the back-fill. A field present in the spec but absent in 40% of records is worse than not having it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-28.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-28 · 382 pages dumped into the catch-all `etc_plan` bucket — 183 were real structural plans

**What happened.** `etc_plan` held 382 entries; 183 of them were actually classifiable structural plans (beam 82, footing 57, roof_frame 44). After the split, zero structural pages remained miscategorized.

**Root cause.** A permissive catch-all bucket existed with no periodic audit. Extraction agents routed anything ambiguous into it, and because nothing failed, the bucket grew unchecked.

**Impact.** 183 structural plan pages were invisible to any consumer filtering on specific plan types — including the training dataset builder, which selects by subtask.

**Fix.** Split `etc_plan` 382 → 199, promoting 183 pages to beam/footing/roof_frame. Structural leftovers now 0.

**→ Rule.** Audit catch-all buckets on a schedule and treat growth as a defect signal. A bucket named "etc" that holds hundreds of items is a classification failure, not a category.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-28.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-29 · Relying on a prompt rule alone to stop the model deleting elements was rejected as untrustworthy

**What happened.** pass 3's prompt states the model must never delete an element from the confirmed inventory. The team explicitly did not trust the prompt to enforce this and wrote tools/merge_guard.py to reinsert any missing element as a flagged stub.

**Root cause.** Prompt instructions are probabilistic requests, not constraints. Any invariant enforced only in natural language will be violated at some rate, and silently.

**Impact.** Prevented — but had merge_guard.py not been written, elements would have disappeared from the inventory with no trace, exactly like the pass 0 roof-beam loss.

**Fix.** tools/merge_guard.py enforces the invariant in code and flags every reinserted stub for human review.

**→ Rule.** Never enforce a data-integrity invariant with a prompt instruction alone. Enforce it in code after the model responds, and flag every violation rather than silently repairing it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอน_t04_Purson_2026-08-29.md` · data-integrity</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-29 · The new scaled_from_grid rule has zero positive examples anywhere in the GT — the model is taught by prompt text alone

**What happened.** Counting the GT to decide how to teach the new span-measurement rule found 113 unresolved cases across 20 files and only 2 pos_m nulls — meaning zero examples of a correctly measured `scaled_from_grid` value exist to train on.

**Root cause.** The rule was invented after the GT was written; no correction pass has gone back to produce examples of it, and the fallback answer (unresolved) is already well represented.

**Impact.** Fine-tuning cannot teach a behaviour it has never seen an example of. The model is being asked to learn a measurement procedure from instructions in a supervised-imitation setup that only rewards copying output shape — the exact weakness the prompt work itself names.

**Fix.** chose prompt-only teaching plus a P/U pixel-number requirement in the flag, with fallbacks recorded (CV code measures instead, or an intern fills 113 cases into GT)

**→ Rule.** Before shipping a new output value, count how many GT examples of it exist. Zero means you are relying on instruction-following from a model trained to imitate, and the GPU round must be treated as a test of that gamble, not of the rule.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · training-data-gap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Supabase service key leaked into the conversation transcript via automatic file diffs

**What happened.** While editing `worker_config.json`, the Supabase service key value appeared in the chat because the system automatically sends file diffs to the assistant.

**Root cause.** A live secret was stored in a file that the tooling automatically diffs and echoes into a conversation transcript — the secret's storage location was chosen without accounting for the tool's automatic diff behaviour.

**Impact.** A full-privilege service key is now present in a transcript. Still usable for testing, but must be revoked.

**Fix.** Not yet done — flagged that the key should be revoked and regenerated after the work is finished.

**→ Rule.** Never place a live secret in a file the agent tooling will read or diff; keep secrets in env vars or an untracked file the agent is told not to open, and rotate immediately if one ever appears in a transcript.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · security</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Measured CV template coverage: only 23 of 44 houses come out exact — 19 under-detect and 2 produce false positives, and beams have no templates at all

**What happened.** A direct survey of the real library (measured, not read off an old report) found 3,149 pages, a bank of only 17 templates (14 footing, 3 column), and harvest_report coverage of 'พอดี 23 / ขาด 19 / เกิน(FP) 2 หลัง'. Beams use no template bank whatsoever — beam detection is synthesised as a pair of lines from BEAM_GAP. So the CV layer that the t05 plan intends to feed the model as production-shaped input is itself wrong on roughly half the houses, and is weakest on exactly the element the model already scores 0% on (plan_beam).

**Root cause.** The bank was grown opportunistically from whatever harvested cleanly rather than driven to coverage per house; beams were handled by a heuristic instead of templates because their shape does not match the icon-template approach. Coverage was never a release gate.

**Impact.** Any pass2.5/pass3 dataset built on this bank inherits 19 under-covered and 2 false-positive houses. Training on it would teach those errors into the model.

**Fix.** Not fixed. `tools/review_staging.py` built to speed the human review of 146 staged candidates, which is the path to more coverage, but the coverage numbers themselves are unimproved and the beam gap is unaddressed.

**→ Rule.** Before a CV layer is promoted to 'production input' for training data, measure per-house coverage and treat under-detection and false positives as blockers — a detector that is wrong on half the corpus will teach that wrongness into whatever is trained on it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Dataset image paths pointed at a flat folder that only existed on the old training machine

**What happened.** pass1 and pass2.4 rows referenced images/<file>.png — a flattened directory that only ever existed on the t04 rental box, not in the repo.

**Root cause.** Paths were baked at dataset-build time relative to a transient machine layout instead of the repo root.

**Impact.** Would have failed to find every image on a fresh rental; caught on free CPU before renting.

**Fix.** Rewrote paths as image/<house>/<file>.png relative to the repo root.

**→ Rule.** All dataset paths must be relative to a stable repo root, never to a rented machine's layout — and must be validated by actually opening every referenced file before renting hardware.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · data-integrity</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Model emitted negative dimensions and corrupted JSON keys that reached the production output

**What happened.** Real outputs contained height_mm:-500, spacing_mm:-200, corrupted keys such as "height_mm:-500,": ":null," and width-mn, and a beam labelled as a column.

**Root cause.** Unconstrained free-form JSON generation with no grammar enforcement on field names or value ranges.

**Impact.** Physically impossible values could flow into quantity takeoff and pricing downstream.

**Fix.** Added sanitize_elements() to worker.py: drops any element with a negative numeric dimension or a key containing ':' or ',', never repairs or guesses, and always records the drop count in warnings. Tested on real files, dropping 2 of 4 correctly.

**→ Rule.** Validate model output against physical plausibility at the production boundary and drop rather than repair — and record every drop so silent data loss is visible.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · guessItemMaterialKey knew only 3 of 7 formwork types, so priced formwork lines matched nothing

**What happened.** `guessItemMaterialKey` recognised only 3 of the 7 formwork types that actually exist in the price table. 'แบบหล่อ ฐานราก' (footing formwork) failed to match even though `formwork.footing` had a real price of ฿250/m² waiting in the table.

**Root cause.** Two lists that must agree — the key-guesser's vocabulary and the price table's keys — were maintained separately and drifted apart.

**Impact.** Formwork cost silently missing from BOQ lines that had a real price available.

**Fix.** Unified onto one table plus a test asserting every key the guesser can return has a real price, so key list and price list can never separate again.

**→ Rule.** When two lists must agree, derive one from the other or add a test that pins their agreement. Never hand-maintain a lookup vocabulary against a separate data table.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · pricing/data-drift</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Only ~10 of 40 houses have pass0/2.4/3 annotations at all — pass0 has just 5 — so the newer passes cannot be evaluated under any split

**What happened.** When the t04 folds were audited, the underlying cause was not only a blind split but a dataset shortfall: only about 10 of the 40 houses carry pass0/2.4/3 data, and pass0 exists for just 5 houses. Every fold shows 204 pass1 eval files against 0 pass0 files.

**Root cause.** Annotation effort tracked pass1 (which was mature) while pass0/2.4/3 were being designed; nobody counted per-pass house coverage before promising fold-level evaluation of those passes. 5 houses cannot be split into 4–5 folds and still leave eval houses anywhere.

**Impact.** Even a perfectly designed split cannot measure whether the model learned pass0 or pass3 — the capability being built is structurally unmeasurable with the current data. Any training run aimed at those passes ends with 'still don't know if it worked'.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the diary records the count and the conclusion ('ถ้าใช้ fold เดิมต่อ = เทรนไปแล้วก็ยังไม่รู้อยู่ดี'), but no annotation backfill is recorded.

**→ Rule.** Before designing an eval split, count examples per capability, not per house. A capability with 5 labelled examples has no eval set at any k; the fix is annotation, not a better splitter.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · data-coverage</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · pass0 could auto-classify only 31 of 72 real pages — its plan-subtask training signal is a handful of examples

**What happened.** The honest house02 simulation (driven from the real pass0_labels.jsonl instead of a derived mapping) showed pass0 resolving only 31/72 pages automatically, feeding just 24 real pass2 jobs. Checking the actual training file explained it: out of 171 rows the whole system has plan_beam 14, plan_footing 7, also_gridline 32.

**Root cause.** pass0's training set was never balanced per subtask — the plan-page classes that matter most for the BOQ have single-digit-to-teens example counts, so more than half of a real house falls into the manual queue.

**Impact.** Over half of every house needs human labelling before extraction can even start; the automation rate quoted from earlier simulations was inflated because those simulations derived pass0 labels from filenames rather than from the model's real capability.

**Fix.** not fixed — measured and recorded; requires more pass0 training data per subtask

**→ Rule.** Measure a classifier's coverage on a whole unseen house, not on the pages it happened to be trained on — and count training examples per class before quoting an automation rate.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-09-01.md` · training-data</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-02 · Pilot comparison documents were explicitly unreviewed drafts but sat alongside real output where they could be mistaken for ground truth

**What happened.** _inventory_pass_pilot.md and _pilot_comparison_summary.md — the first real Claude-vs-Qwen comparison over 4 pages of house 01 — were marked in their own headers as drafts never reviewed and not usable as ground truth directly, yet lived in the normal claude_output_01 output path.

**Root cause.** Draft status was recorded only inside the document header, not in its location or filename, so the only thing preventing misuse was that a reader would open the file and read the header first.

**Impact.** Risk of unreviewed pilot conclusions being treated as verified. This risk persisted for over a month until the 2026-08-04 archival cleanup.

**Fix.** Archived to wait_for_ทิ831/ path alongside the other pilot docs on 2026-08-04; deliberately kept rather than deleted because they are the origin of still-cited lesson #6 (the DB↔RB misread).

**→ Rule.** Encode draft/unreviewed status in the file's location or name, not only in its header. Anything not yet reviewed belongs in a separate directory from output that downstream work is allowed to trust.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-02.md` · data-hygiene</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-05 · Door/window counts on page 06 were taken from the schedule table rather than counted from the actual plan

**What happened.** Among the low-confidence pages flagged, page 06's door/window counts were recorded as 'taken from the schedule, not counted from the actual plan'.

**Root cause.** The schedule table is far easier to read than counting symbols on a plan, so the easier source was substituted for the source the field is defined against — without the substitution being blocked, only noted.

**Impact.** Schedule tables and as-drawn plans disagree routinely (revisions, items shown but not scheduled). The count may be wrong, and because the value looks like a normal extracted number, the substitution is invisible to any downstream consumer.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged as low confidence, needing someone to zoom into the image and re-verify.

**→ Rule.** When a value is taken from a different source than the field's definition intends, record the source in a provenance field (as span_source does for beam spans) rather than only mentioning it in prose. A silent source substitution is indistinguishable from a correct read.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-05.md` · methodology / wrong-data</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · The fresh Gen 3 extraction repeated the DB→RB bar-type error itself, on every element of page 21

**What happened.** The already-known DB↔RB misread was not just a Qwen/Gen-2 problem — the hand-done fresh mk_test extraction of page 21 view1 (section) had recorded every element's main_bar.type as "DB" when the drawing's Ø symbol means RB. It was only caught by comparing against claude_output_03 (Gen 2) the next day, and had to be corrected element-by-element with confidence_flags added explaining the source of the correction. The underlying wrong rule was inferring bar type from the printed diameter instead of from the symbol.

**Root cause.** Bar type was being inferred from diameter size (a plausible-looking heuristic) rather than read from the Ø symbol; no extraction rule existed at the time saying the symbol is authoritative, so a fresh human-supervised read reproduced exactly the failure the pilot had already documented on 2026-07-02.

**Impact.** A whole page of section-spec ground truth carried the wrong steel type until manually corrected; since this same page 21 spec was later joined into the beam plan pages (Gen 3.3), a late catch would have propagated the wrong bar type into every beam element on pages 19 and 20.

**Fix.** Rewrote main_bar.type DB→RB for every element in _หน้า21_view1_section.json, updated confidence_score/confidence_flags/warnings, and recorded the rule as Generation 3.1 point 4: "the Ø (circle) symbol always = RB — never infer DB from the diameter size alone."

**→ Rule.** A documented model-failure mode is not only a model failure — write the correct rule into the extraction spec, because a human/agent reading fresh will reproduce the same wrong inference. Encode the symbol→type mapping as a rule, never let diameter imply bar type.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-07 · A 0-byte stub file sat in the Training repo for a day pretending to be the schema doc

**What happened.** On July 6 an IDE auto-created an empty file at Training/No_touch_box/Makham's patter of rawjson20260705.md during a move. The real 53,167-byte Gen 3.3 document stayed behind in Constistant. The empty file was only replaced on July 7, as a side effect of an unrelated move task.

**Root cause.** The July 6 move was done as a manual copy that never verified the destination file size, and the IDE's auto-created placeholder made the destination look populated.

**Impact.** For a full day, anyone opening the canonical path in the Training repo would have read an empty schema document.

**Fix.** The real file was copied over the stub during the July 7 cross-repo move, and the 'empty 0-byte file' item was struck from the pending list in SESSION_HANDOFF_2026-07-06.md.

**→ Rule.** After any cross-repo file move, assert the destination file's byte size is non-zero and matches the source before deleting the original.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · data-integrity/file-ops</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-08 · The original BOQ drawings contain real numbering errors that two independent reads both reproduced

**What happened.** Both t3 and the independent t4 re-read of pages 38-47 found the same anomalies: category numbers 2.8/2.9 swapped, dimensions for items n2/n3 duplicated, and item numbering jumping from 3.2.x to 3.5.x. Roughly 150 rows otherwise matched exactly.

**Root cause.** The source drawings themselves are inconsistent; the extraction process had no explicit channel to distinguish 'the drawing is wrong here' from 'the extraction is wrong here'.

**Impact.** Anomalies that would look like extraction errors to anyone downstream, requiring the same investigation again on every future pass.

**Fix.** Re-confirmed by an independent read and recorded as flags on the data rather than silently corrected.

**→ Rule.** Record source-document errors explicitly as flags on the row so the next reader does not re-investigate them — an anomaly confirmed twice is data about the drawing, not a bug in the reader.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-08.md` · source-data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-10 · House #2's drawings contain multiple genuine errors that agents flagged rather than silently fixed

**What happened.** Agents flagged, in house #2, a dimension mismatch across sheets (1.30 vs 1.00 at elevation 3), a sanitary fixture labelled WC.2 where it should be WC.1, a doorbell symbol not matching the legend, a duplicate BOQ item code, and an anomalous price for house design #6 (spread footing costing more than pile foundation).

**Root cause.** The source drawing set is internally inconsistent; the extraction process's only defence is the confidence_flags/warnings channel, which depends entirely on each agent remembering to use it.

**Impact.** Several values in the dataset are known-suspect and require human review before being used as ground truth; none is resolved.

**Fix.** Recorded in each file's confidence_flags/warnings rather than guessed or corrected.

**→ Rule.** Flagging a contradiction is always correct and silently reconciling it is always wrong — but the flags must be aggregated into one review queue, or they stay buried in 100 JSON files.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · source-data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-11 · The raw_json_data_log row for house #2 was forgotten and had to be added retroactively

**What happened.** raw_json_data_log.md, required by rule_of_tune.md rule 3, was not updated when house #2 was created on July 10 — the entry explicitly deferred it 'until the work is fully complete'. It was added retroactively on July 11 alongside house #3's row.

**Root cause.** The logging step was made conditional on the house being finished, and the house was not finished (10 pages missing), so the log silently skipped a whole day's work.

**Impact.** A day where a 88-file production dataset existed with no provenance record, in a system whose own rules require one.

**Fix.** Added the house #2 row retroactively together with house #3's.

**→ Rule.** Log provenance when the data is created, not when it is finished — an incomplete dataset needs a log row more than a complete one does, marked incomplete.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-11.md` · process/provenance</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-11 · House #3's drawings contain a mislabelled staircase, a mislabelled floor, a riser mismatch and a missing AC spec

**What happened.** Agents flagged four genuine problems in the source set: the staircase labelled ST.3 on the 2nd-floor plan but ST.2 on the section header, a one-step (~0.175 m) mismatch between riser count and landing level, SN-04 labelling the +3.75 upper floor as 'ground floor' (confirmed against SN-06 as a real drawing error), and the 2nd-floor 24,000 BTU air conditioner having no breaker or wiring spec anywhere in the electrical set.

**Root cause.** The source drawing set is internally inconsistent and in one case incomplete; the extraction can only detect this when an agent cross-checks against another sheet.

**Impact.** Four suspect or missing values in house #3's ground truth, all requiring human review; the AC spec gap is data that does not exist and cannot be extracted at all.

**Fix.** All four flagged for review rather than guessed; the SN-04 error was cross-checked against SN-06 to prove it is the drawing's mistake, not a misread.

**→ Rule.** Cross-check any label or dimension against a second sheet before flagging it, so the flag distinguishes 'the drawing is wrong' from 'I read it wrong' — and record a missing spec as an explicit gap, never as an inferred value.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-11.md` · source-data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-12 · Mislabeled floor levels in the sanitary vertical riser diagram recur house after house and are still only flagged, never resolved

**What happened.** House 3, house 4 and house 5 all had a floor mislabeled in the sanitary vertical riser diagram (house 5's case explicitly: level +3.75 printed as 'ground floor'). Each was flagged for review and carried forward as pending; none was resolved during these sessions.

**Root cause.** The source drawings themselves carry the mislabel, and the workflow has no decision rule for 'the drawing is internally wrong' — so each occurrence gets re-flagged rather than resolved once with a project-wide ruling.

**Impact.** The same review item accumulates on every house's pending list and consumes review attention repeatedly with no resolution; downstream consumers get level data that is known-suspect.

**Fix.** not fixed — flagged in confidence_flags/warnings on each house, still open in the pending lists.

**→ Rule.** A defect that appears in the source of three consecutive houses needs one project-wide ruling recorded in the spec, not a per-house flag.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-12.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-13 · House 5's dummy grid A' had three conflicting overhang values across three structural sheets and sat at 0.65 confidence

**What happened.** The grid master put dummy grid A' at -2.05m from the 1st-floor beam plan (S-04), but the 2nd-floor beam plan (S-05) and the tie-beam plan (S-06) printed different overhang values (0.40m and 0.70+0.50m). All three were flagged rather than guessed, leaving the grid master at confidence 0.65.

**Root cause.** Structural sheets of the same house disagree, and no structural sheet alone resolves it — the deciding evidence was in a completely different section (the mechanical sheet).

**Impact.** The whole house's grid master was blocked at low confidence, which blocks every beam span derived from it; resolution needed a separate discipline's sheet to be read first.

**Fix.** Resolved later the same day: page 65 (M-01, the AC/fan plan) showed the area is a single-storey carport separate from the main house, raising confidence 0.65→0.78 and changing the flags to 'confirmed'.

**→ Rule.** When structural sheets disagree about an extent, the answer is often on an architectural or MEP sheet — widen the search outside the discipline before flagging it unresolved.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-13.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-19 · House 2's beam and tie-beam plans were missing beams that only surfaced during the dummy-grid cascade

**What happened.** During the dummy-grid cascade into house 2's structural sheets, beam B1 at B2-B3 (span 3.2) was missing entirely and was spotted by the human, not the extraction or the earlier review pass; page26 was missing six RB1 beams that mirror page25; RB1A A3-A4 had a null span that had to be filled in (3.2).

**Root cause.** The original extraction and the first review pass both worked from labels present on the sheet rather than from geometric completeness — a beam with no printed mark near it is simply never noticed until something forces a full-sheet reconstruction.

**Impact.** Elements missing from the structural model of a house that is part of the training set; the omissions were found by chance during unrelated work rather than by any check.

**Fix.** Added with confidence 1 during the 07-19 cascade session.

**→ Rule.** A beam plan needs a completeness pass (every grid intersection accounted for), not just a label-reading pass. The dummy-grid cascade accidentally functioned as that pass — make it a deliberate step.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-19.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-19 · Warnings left in files after their issues were resolved, and one warning that was itself factually wrong

**What happened.** House 4's page00 carried warnings about S-04/S-05/architecture that had already been checked and resolved on July 16 and needed refreshing. House 3's page31 carried a warning stating 'nothing at B'', which was wrong — there is a horizontal line at y=10.07, just with no readable label.

**Root cause.** Warnings are written at extraction time and never revisited when the underlying question is answered; nothing links a warning to the finding that closes it.

**Impact.** False flags waste review attention and, worse, a wrong warning can be taken as evidence in a later reasoning chain — the same failure mode as the circular-reference bug.

**Fix.** House 4's page00 warnings refreshed on 07-19; page31's wrong warning corrected on 07-20.

**→ Rule.** A warning is data that goes stale. Every fix must close the warnings it resolves, and a warning asserting a negative ('nothing here') needs the same evidence standard as a positive claim.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-19.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · A beam recorded with a distance guessed from a box edge rather than a printed dimension

**What happened.** `B1_landing D1'-D1''` on page32 carried a span of 3.06 measured from the staircase box edge — not an actually printed dimension. It was deleted on instruction.

**Root cause.** A measured-off-the-drawing estimate was stored in the same field as printed dimensions with nothing distinguishing the two.

**Impact.** A fabricated dimension in the dataset; deleted, along with two other elements (page31's `B2 E1'-E1` and `B2 E3-E3'`) that were also not supportable.

**Fix.** Deleted the element; element counts dropped to 27 (page31) and 31 (page32).

**→ Rule.** Only printed dimensions go into a dimension field. A value measured off the image must carry an explicit source flag, or it must not be recorded at all.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · Beams that do not exist were recorded and had to be deleted on instruction — in house 3 and again in house 5

**What happened.** House 3's page31 carried two row-E extension beams (B2 E1'-E1 at 1.1 and B2 E3-E3' at 0.5) that were deleted on instruction, and page32 carried a landing beam whose span was guessed from a staircase box edge. House 5's pages 32/33 needed three more lines deleted (line39, line44, A'1-A'2).

**Root cause.** The extraction adds an element wherever a line appears in the drawing, including construction lines, slab edges and box outlines that are not beams. There is no negative check for 'this line is not a structural member'.

**Impact.** Fabricated structural members inflate element counts and quantities; six known instances across two houses, and the deletions were driven by human instruction rather than by any automated check.

**Fix.** Deleted per instruction across houses 3 and 5 (page31 down to 27 elements, page32 down to 31).

**→ Rule.** Over-prediction is a real failure mode in the human-corrected data too, not just in the fine-tuned model. A line without a mark and without a printed dimension is not a beam by default.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-20.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · House 2's beam plan carried specs that disagreed with the section sheet they were supposed to come from

**What happened.** Checking house 2's pages 25/26 revealed that page25's specs{} did not match page28 (the beam-section sheet that is the authoritative spec source) and had to be re-synced.

**Root cause.** specs{} was extracted into the plan sheet independently rather than being derived from the single spec-source sheet, so the two copies drifted — the same duplication problem the specs{} refactor was meant to eliminate, just at file scope instead of element scope.

**Impact.** Two conflicting spec values for the same beam mark inside one house; whichever a consumer reads first wins.

**Fix.** page25's specs corrected to match page28 on 2026-07-20.

**→ Rule.** Splitting duplicated specs into specs{} solves duplication within a file but creates it across files. The section sheet must be the single spec source, with plan sheets referencing it, not copying it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-20.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Two rooms given identical corner points but different names

**What happened.** On page 06, F6 = ["C-2","C-3","D-3","D-2"] labelled 'เตรียมอาหาร' and F7 = ["C-3","C-2","D-2","D-3"] labelled 'นอน 2' — the exact same four points, declared to be two different rooms.

**Root cause.** Nothing in the extraction or validation step checks that geometry is unique across elements, so the model can emit duplicated footprints with different labels and nothing objects.

**Impact.** Duplicated area in any downstream quantity takeoff; two rooms counted where one exists.

**Fix.** not fixed

**→ Rule.** Add a cheap post-extraction invariant: no two elements may share an identical point set. Self-contradiction is the easiest class of error to detect mechanically and the hardest to spot by reading.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Real Thai room names dumped into notes while element_id was invented as F1–F11

**What happened.** Gold element_ids are the real room names (นอน1, จอดรถ). The model invented F1–F11 as ids and pushed the actual room names into the notes field instead.

**Root cause.** The model had read the correct information but placed it in the wrong field — a schema-mapping failure, not a reading failure, consistent with the untuned-model hypothesis.

**Impact.** Elements cannot be joined to anything by id; the correct data is present but unreachable by any consumer that reads the contract.

**Fix.** not fixed

**→ Rule.** When output is wrong, check whether the right value is present in the wrong field before concluding the model cannot read it. Misplacement and misreading need completely different fixes.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · '1 of 15' in the title block read as page number 15 — on two different pages

**What happened.** Pages 03 and 06 (gold doc_page 1 and 4) were both reported as page_number: 15, because the model read the '1 of 15' sheet counter in the title block and took the total as the page number.

**Root cause.** No rule distinguishes 'current page' from 'total pages' in an X-of-Y string, and no uniqueness constraint exists on page numbers across a document.

**Impact.** Two different pages carry the same page number; page-level provenance for the whole extraction is unreliable.

**Fix.** not fixed

**→ Rule.** Parse X-of-Y counters explicitly rather than grabbing a nearby number, and assert page numbers are unique and within [1, total] across a document — a duplicate page number is a free, deterministic error signal.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Site plan extracted with not a single dimension — content-free output that still looked valid

**What happened.** Gold for page 05 gives every element a dimension_m (11.70 / 14.60 / setback ≥2.0 / ≥3.0). The model returned no dimensions at all; the diary notes a site plan with no distances is a site plan with no content.

**Root cause.** No required-field check per page pattern, so a structurally valid but semantically empty result passes as a successful extraction.

**Impact.** A page counted as extracted while carrying zero usable information — the worst kind of failure because the run log says success.

**Fix.** not fixed

**→ Rule.** Define per-pattern required fields (a site plan must carry dimensions; a schedule must carry rows) and fail the page if they are absent. 'Valid JSON' and 'contains an answer' are different acceptance criteria.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Thai construction terms mis-spelled into non-words

**What happened.** เฉลียง → เจี๊ยง, บันได → บ้านได้, ยิปซั่มบอร์ด → อีปซั่มบอร์ด across the output.

**Root cause.** Character-level degradation consistent with the resolution mismatch (training at ~266 visual tokens vs 3,796 at inference) plus quantization damage — the model reads shapes it never practised at this density.

**Impact.** Terms will not match any material/element lookup table; silent join failures downstream rather than loud errors.

**Fix.** not fixed

**→ Rule.** Validate extracted domain terms against a controlled vocabulary and flag near-misses. Spelling corruption on domain nouns is an early, cheap signal of a visual-input problem — treat it as a symptom worth tracing, not cosmetic noise.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-30 · Extraction manifest guessed the site-plan page range wrong (3 pages instead of 1)

**What happened.** The pre-built manifest for house 08 claimed the site-plan criteria section spanned 3 pages. On actually opening them, only 1 page was criteria; the other 2 were team credits and the series price-comparison table (misc).

**Root cause.** The manifest's page ranges were inferred from position/adjacency rather than confirmed against each page's own content, so contiguous-looking pages were assumed to belong to the same section.

**Impact.** Two pages would have been extracted under the wrong pattern, injecting mislabelled training data; caught mid-run and re-scoped, costing rework on the manifest.

**Fix.** Corrected the manifest after opening each page and reading its actual content; the two pages were reclassified as credits + misc.

**→ Rule.** Never trust a manifest's page ranges — open every page and classify from its own content before extracting. A section boundary is proven by what is printed on the page, not by page adjacency.

<sub>`2026-07-30.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-30 · BOQ tables read by hand at 0.35–0.65 confidence because the table is rotated 90° with tiny type

**What happened.** House 08's BOQ sheets are rotated 90° with small type, dropping read confidence to 0.35–0.65 — far below the normal band. An existing purpose-built tool (`run_pipeline.py`'s `extract_boq()`) was proposed but the order was to keep hand-reading anyway.

**Root cause.** No pre-flight image-quality/orientation gate exists before extraction starts, so a page that is objectively hard to read is processed by the same route as a clean one; and an existing tool built for exactly this case was not in the standard workflow.

**Impact.** A whole BOQ set entered the corpus at roughly half the usual confidence, with needs_zoom_review scattered through it — data that later training rounds will inherit as noisy labels.

**Fix.** Extraction proceeded by hand with per-row confidence recorded and needs_zoom_review flagged, rather than silently accepting the numbers.

**→ Rule.** Check page orientation and type size before extraction; rotate/upscale first, or route to the purpose-built extractor. Low confidence must always be recorded per-row, never averaged away.

<sub>`2026-07-30.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-30 · House 10's price table says pile foundations are cheaper than spread footings — reverse of every other house

**What happened.** The series price table on house 10 lists pile foundations as cheaper than spread footings, the opposite of every pair in houses 08 and 09. Recorded as an oddity and deliberately not 'corrected'.

**Root cause.** Either a genuine printing error in the published drawing set, or a real price difference for this seismic sub-series — undecidable from the sheet alone.

**Impact.** An unexplained cost figure sits in the corpus; any downstream cost model that ingests it will inherit an inverted relationship without warning.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as an anomaly for a human to rule on, rather than silently normalised to match the other houses.

**→ Rule.** When a value contradicts a strong cross-house pattern, flag and escalate — never quietly 'fix' it to match the majority. Overwriting a real outlier is worse than carrying a flagged one.

<sub>`2026-07-30.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-30 · The 'BOQ items 2-5 are identical between foundation systems' rule turned out to have a real exception — caught only because the sheets were still being read

**What happened.** House 08 established that BOQ items 2/3/4/5 are byte-for-byte identical between the two foundation systems and only item 1 (structure) differs. House 09 mostly repeated that, but a genuine difference appeared at sheet 10/19 (fascia work 305 vs 262) plus values on sheets 12/18. House 10 was then clean again, and house 11's plan explicitly proposed skipping re-reads of sets 2-6 on the strength of the same expectation.

**Root cause.** A pattern observed on one house was being promoted to a rule about the series before enough houses had been checked, and it was about to be used as the justification for not reading 172 sheets.

**Impact.** Had the rule been applied as planned, at least one real cost difference would have been copied over with the wrong number and shipped into the dataset silently. The differing sheets were flagged needs_zoom_review instead of being forced to match.

**Fix.** Flagged the differing sheets needs_zoom_review rather than forcing them to match; the diff-instead-of-reread strategy for house 11 was recorded as still needing verification per set

**→ Rule.** 'These sheets are always identical' is a hypothesis to test per set, not a licence to skip reading. Diff the files by content; never assume identity from a pattern seen on one or two houses.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-30.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-31 · House 11's ปร.4 BOQ tables read at 0.45–0.55 — worse than the rotated tables they replaced

**What happened.** House 11's BOQ was expected to be easier (standard ปร.4 tables, not rotated 90°), but the scan's type is smaller and denser, so confidence landed at 0.45–0.55, below houses 08–10's 0.6–0.8, with needs_zoom_review on nearly every row of categories 2.3–2.6.

**Root cause.** 'Not rotated' was assumed to mean 'readable'; the real driver of read quality is scan resolution and type density, not orientation.

**Impact.** An entire 29-sheet BOQ set entered the corpus below the usual confidence band, with most rows flagged for review — review debt that has to be paid later or the data can't be trusted.

**Fix.** Recorded per-row confidence and flagged needs_zoom_review rather than reporting clean numbers.

**→ Rule.** Judge page readability by measured confidence on a sample, not by orientation or format. Sample 2–3 sheets and check confidence before committing to a 29-sheet set.

<sub>`2026-07-31.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-31 · Dummy grids A'/D' paired with footing C0 have no supporting structure anywhere in the sheet set

**What happened.** House 11's grid master contains dummy grids A' and D' tied to a footing C0, separate from the main grid. S-05 and S-06 were checked and no supporting structure for them was found.

**Root cause.** Either the structure exists on a sheet not yet extracted, or the published drawing set genuinely omits it — unresolvable from the sheets examined.

**Impact.** Orphan grid lines and an orphan footing sit in the grid master; anything joining elements to grids will find a grid with nothing on it.

**Fix.** Not resolved — flagged in the grid master rather than deleted or invented.

**→ Rule.** An unexplained grid or mark stays flagged, never deleted. Deleting it destroys evidence that the source is incomplete; inventing its structure fabricates data.

<sub>`2026-07-31.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · House 07 used 3 pattern values that do not exist in the schema (detail/elevation/diagram)

**What happened.** 21 files in house 07 carried `pattern` values (`detail`, `elevation`, `diagram`) outside the schema's 14-value list, and had to be remapped to the vocabulary the other 10 houses use.

**Root cause.** Nothing enforced the pattern vocabulary at write time — the schema listed the legal values but no checker rejected an illegal one, so an extraction run could invent a plausible-sounding pattern with no failure.

**Impact.** 21 files were unroutable by pattern; anything grouping by pattern silently skipped them.

**Fix.** Remapped all 21 to the canonical vocabulary; later locked by §0.9/§0.4 and enforced by `check_format.py`.

**→ Rule.** Any closed vocabulary must be machine-enforced at write time. A rule that exists only in prose will be violated by the first plausible-sounding alternative.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · Multi-level column schedules stored two incompatible ways — nested levels[] vs flat rows

**What happened.** Houses 04/05 stored multi-level column schedules as nested `levels[]`; houses 01/02/03 used flat rows with a `level` field. §8 says flat is correct, so 04/05 were wrong.

**Root cause.** The spec's preference for flat rows was written but never enforced, and nested arrays are the more natural-looking representation of the printed table.

**Impact.** 20 rows in house 05 (and house 04's equivalents) were in a shape no consumer could read alongside the other houses.

**Fix.** House 05's 20 rows split into one row per (mark, level) and `tie` renamed to `stirrup`.

**→ Rule.** Where the spec expresses a preference between two valid-looking shapes, the checker must reject the non-preferred one. A preference with no enforcement produces both shapes.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · The identical series price table was stored 5 different ways in 5 houses

**What happened.** The same series price table — byte-identical content across houses — was stored in 5 completely different structures in 5 different houses. Credits pages were similarly split across 4 different patterns.

**Root cause.** Each house's extraction independently decided how to represent shared back-matter, with no rule and no cross-house consistency check for pages that are known to be identical.

**Impact.** Five representations of one table, none joinable to the others; and house 01's copy was still raw text.

**Fix.** Unified to `series_price_table[]` (the majority form from houses 08–10); house 01's copy left as raw text and flagged PENDING rather than guessed at.

**→ Rule.** Content that repeats across houses must have one canonical representation decided once. Detect identical pages by hash and reuse the existing extraction rather than re-representing them.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · The schema's specs{} block is populated in only 24 of 1,183 files — two houses have none at all

**What happened.** Across all 11 houses, specs{} — the block that carries the specification data elements join against — appears in 24 files out of 1,183. Houses 07 and 11 contain none whatsoever. The item is listed as pending on 08-02 rounds 1, 2, 3 and 4 and again on 08-04, never worked.

**Root cause.** specs{} was defined in the spec but never made a required field or a checker rule, so extraction runs could omit it without failing anything.

**Impact.** The spec-join step of the production merge has almost nothing to join against in this dataset; two whole houses cannot participate in it at all. Any training round that assumes spec data is present will be trained mostly on its absence.

**Fix.** not fixed — carried as a pending item across at least five sessions

**→ Rule.** A field that matters to a downstream join needs a coverage number in the checker output, otherwise 2% coverage looks exactly like 100% coverage from the pass/fail line.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · Rebar printed with a 'หยุดที่ L/8' / mid-span qualifier in houses 10-11 is still not merged into a bar face

**What happened.** Houses 10 and 11 print some bars with a stop-at-L/8 or mid-span qualifier. Those bars were never merged into a top/middle/bottom face as §7 requires, because doing so needs the leader lines checked against the drawing image. Listed as pending on 08-02 rounds 2, 3, 4, at session close, and again on 08-04.

**Root cause.** The format work was done without the drawings open, and this particular case cannot be resolved from the JSON alone — it needs the source image, which put it outside every format-only session.

**Impact.** Those bars sit in the dataset unassigned to a face, so any rebar-face training signal from houses 10-11 is incomplete, and a downstream consumer reading main_bar{top,middle,bottom} sees them as missing rather than as unresolved.

**Fix.** not fixed — requires a §7 leader-line check against the source drawings

**→ Rule.** Items that need the drawing open should be queued into a drawing-open session with an owner, not re-listed as pending at the end of every format session where they can never be done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · House 04's 10 BOQ files were stored as pattern=unknown with elements[] instead of a material list

**What happened.** The independent round-5 audit found all 10 of house 04's BOQ files carrying pattern=unknown and an elements[] array, when a BOQ is material_list with categories[].items[]. They had passed every earlier check.

**Root cause.** 'unknown' is a legal value in the pattern vocabulary, so a mis-typed page passes the pattern check by definition; nothing cross-checked that a file whose content is a priced table was classified as one.

**Impact.** Ten BOQ pages were invisible as BOQ data to anything selecting by pattern, and their table structure was stored in the wrong container shape.

**Fix.** Converted to material_list + categories[].items[] during the round-5 audit

**→ Rule.** 'unknown' passing the pattern check is a hole, not a pass. The checker should flag any file whose content looks like a known pattern while being labelled unknown, at minimum as a NOTE.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · Numeric fields were stored as strings and arrays across the corpus — ~170 level_m values alone

**What happened.** The type-purity audit found house 01's steel_section stored as strings, main_bar/rebar stored as arrays, count values written as "4+4", dia_mm as "16+12", roughly 170 level_m values as strings instead of numbers, 30 grid_ref values as arrays, and span_m as arrays. All of it had survived every prior format pass.

**Root cause.** The spec constrained which fields must exist and what they mean, but not their JSON type, so a value written the way it was printed on the drawing was never wrong by any written rule.

**Impact.** Any consumer doing arithmetic on level_m or span_m would have hit a string, and "4+4" or "16+12" would have silently failed a numeric parse rather than summing. This is the same root cause as the format-lock finding, but it survived the format lock itself.

**Fix.** Converted to §6a objects / bar_layers[] / summed counts / mixed_dia_mm / numbers, originals kept in *_printed_as; the checker gained type-purity checks (14 → 19)

**→ Rule.** Lock the type of every field, not only its name and meaning — a spec that says what a field means but not what shape it is will collect five encodings of the same value.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · Two new schema patterns were added with zero examples anywhere in the corpus

**What happened.** `bbs_schedule` and `soil_boring_log` were added to the pattern taxonomy (14 → 16) but a cross-check against real file counts (12 houses, 1,240 files) found zero examples of either anywhere in the corpus. Both are marked `(draft)` with no field set confirmed by a real extraction. A further three patterns (`gridline`/`site_plan`/`title`) are structurally thin at 13/12/5 files.

**Root cause.** The taxonomy was extended from anticipated need (borrowing field sets from Constistant's existing prompts) rather than from an encountered sheet.

**Impact.** Two pattern definitions exist that nothing validates, so the first real sheet of either type may not match the assumed shape. And the thin patterns give any training round almost no examples to learn from.

**Fix.** Both marked `(draft)`; the decision was to fix the zero/thin patterns by growing the dataset for real, not by dropping them from the plan. `check_format.py` had to be updated in the same commit or any file using a new pattern would FAIL instantly.

**→ Rule.** Mark a schema entry added without a real example as draft, and let the first real instance settle its shape. Also: a spec change and its checker change must land in the same commit, or the checker rejects the new spec.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-07 · House 14 has no sheet codes or index page at all — sheet_code null throughout

**What happened.** House 14, the first from the BMA 'แบบบ้านยิ้ม...เพื่อประชาชน' series rather than the กรมโยธาธิการ series, has no sheet codes and no index page, so `sheet_code` is null across every file.

**Root cause.** The extraction workflow and schema assumed every drawing set has title-block sheet codes — an assumption formed from 13 houses that all came from one publisher.

**Impact.** An entire house's files carry a null identifier that other houses use for routing and cross-referencing; any consumer keying on sheet_code degrades for this house.

**Fix.** Recorded `sheet_code: null` honestly and documented the reason in the grid master's warnings, rather than inventing codes.

**→ Rule.** An invariant confirmed across N houses from one publisher is a publisher convention, not a universal rule. When a new source series appears, re-validate every structural assumption — and record a genuine absence as null with a warning, never as an invented value.

<sub>`2026-08-07.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-09 · Houses 14–18 had the grid-master png/doc_page convention swapped versus houses 01–13

**What happened.** The grid-master file convention (`png:"00"`, `doc_page:null`) was implemented the other way round in houses 14–18 compared with houses 01–13. It had to be locked into the schema §2 after five houses had already been extracted with the swap.

**Root cause.** The convention was informal — followed by imitation of earlier houses rather than written into the spec — so when the extraction workflow changed hands or context, the two fields were transposed with nothing detecting it.

**Impact.** Five houses' grid masters disagree with thirteen others on a field that identifies where the grid came from; joins or lookups keying on these fields break for one group or the other.

**Fix.** Locked the convention explicitly in `primary_rawjson_schema.md` §2 and logged the edit.

**→ Rule.** Any convention followed by imitation rather than by written rule will invert eventually. Write it into the spec and add a checker rule the moment you notice two houses doing it differently.

<sub>`2026-08-09.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-09 · Three fields had been in use since houses 06/11 but were never in the spec

**What happened.** Per-line `confidence_score`/`confidence_flags` on grid lines, `dummy_grid_rule_check`, and `non_grid_dimensions_do_not_confuse` had all been written into real files since houses 06 and 11 but were never specified anywhere. They were documented into §4 only now.

**Root cause.** Fields can be invented at extraction time with no gate rejecting unknown keys, so useful-but-undocumented fields accumulate silently.

**Impact.** Three fields carrying real quality information existed in the corpus with no defined meaning — inconsistently populated and invisible to any consumer written from the spec.

**Fix.** Documented all three in `primary_rawjson_schema.md` §4 and logged the edit.

**→ Rule.** Add an unknown-key report to the checker. A field that appears in real data but not in the spec is either a missing spec entry or a typo — both need surfacing immediately, not three houses later.

<sub>`2026-08-09.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-18 · หน้า26.json wrote spec.rebar as an array of strings, violating schema §0.6

**What happened.** During house 24 extraction, หน้า26.json emitted spec.rebar as an array of strings when §0.6 requires a single object per spec. check_format.py caught it and it was changed to spec.note.

**Root cause.** Free-text rebar notes on the sheet did not fit the structured rebar object shape, and the extractor defaulted to dumping them into an array rather than recognizing that unstructured text belongs in spec.note.

**Impact.** One file would have shipped a shape the downstream adapter cannot read; caught before commit so zero downstream impact.

**Fix.** Changed spec.rebar array to spec.note in หน้า26.json.

**→ Rule.** When drawing content does not fit a structured schema field, route it to the designated free-text field rather than loosening the structured field's type — and keep check_format.py in the loop on every house before logging it as done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-18.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-18 · Eight BOQ pages shipped as reference stubs instead of real transcriptions

**What happened.** House 24's pile-footing-system BOQ pages หน้า47-54 were not individually re-transcribed. The first/last sheet of both foundation-system BOQs were spot-checked, categories 2-4 confirmed identical (matching house 22's precedent), and reference stubs written instead of reading eight near-duplicate pages.

**Root cause.** A deliberate time-saving shortcut under the 90-minute op3 ceiling, based on a two-page sample generalized to eight pages. Sound in this instance, but it means eight files in the dataset are not real extraction ground truth.

**Impact.** Eight of 70 files in house 24 are stubs, not annotations. If used as training or eval ground truth without reading the warnings[], they would look like real data. Flagged, not hidden.

**Fix.** Every stub file states the shortcut explicitly in its own warnings[] array.

**→ Rule.** A shortcut is acceptable only if it self-declares in machine-readable form — write the reason into warnings[] in the file itself, never only into a diary entry a training script will never read.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-18.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Slab markers (SO/SI/ST) carry no grid_ref at all, so slabs can never be positioned or overlaid

**What happened.** During the house 01 หน้า19 overlay proof, every beam segment resolved (24/24) but the SO/SI/ST slab markers drew nothing — they carry no grid_ref in the schema, so the overlay had no position to draw. Recorded as 'exactly as expected' rather than as a gap.

**Root cause.** The schema's position model is grid-ref based and slab markers were never given one; a slab is an area, not a point or a line between two grid refs, and no field was defined for it.

**Impact.** Slabs are structurally invisible to any grid-based tooling: no overlay, no QC click-to-accept, and downstream no floor area — the same blind spot that later shows up as slab BOQ quantities of zero.

**Fix.** Not fixed — noted as expected behaviour.

**→ Rule.** 'Expected' and 'acceptable' are different. An element class that no positioning mechanism can ever locate deserves a recorded gap, not a shrug, because every consumer downstream inherits the hole.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · data-gap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · discipline field carries two spellings of one value: architectural (182 files) vs architecture (157)

**What happened.** Counting across all 11 annotated houses found the discipline field written as "architectural" in 182 files and "architecture" in 157. Nothing consumes discipline today, so nothing is broken yet — but any future filter would silently drop roughly half the files.

**Root cause.** discipline was never given a closed vocabulary in the schema, so annotators (and prompts) used whichever English form came to mind. No validator enforced membership in a value set.

**Impact.** 339 files split near 50/50 across two spellings. A latent data-loss bug that would look like a 46% recall drop the moment anyone filters on discipline.

**Fix.** Added a closed discipline vocabulary of 11 values to §2 of primary_rawjson_schema.md, pinning architectural as canonical. Migrating the 157 existing files was left pending.

**→ Rule.** Every enum-like string field needs a closed vocabulary in the spec and a check_format.py membership assertion from day one — an unenforced free-text taxonomy field will always split, and it will split silently because no consumer exists yet to complain.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · Four files record rebar_cover_m in metres, violating §0.5's mm rule for member dimensions

**What happened.** While defining §4a's cover fields, four existing files were found carrying rebar_cover_m in metres. §0.5 pins cover to mm because it is a member dimension.

**Root cause.** The unit convention exists in §0.5 but no validator enforces unit-per-field, and a field name ending in _m does not trigger any check. A 0.025 value and a 25 value are both valid numbers.

**Impact.** Four files carry cover values 1000x off from what any consumer expects. Silent — a cover of 0.025 would be treated as 0.025 mm, effectively zero, in any calculation.

**Fix.** cover pinned to mm in §4a; the four offending files recorded as still needing correction (pending).

**→ Rule.** Enforce unit conventions in check_format.py with per-field plausibility ranges, not just in prose — unit errors are silent by nature because both values are valid numbers, and a 1000x error in cover is a structural safety number.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · data-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · Filename drift (beam_plan / beam_plan_floor1 / beam_floor_plan / beam_plan_สุขา) rules out filename-based routing entirely

**What happened.** The same job appears under at least four filename forms: beam_plan, beam_plan_floor1, beam_floor_plan, beam_plan_สุขา. Floor level and building were deliberately kept as fields (floor_level, building) rather than becoming subtasks, and filename-based routing was ruled out as unreliable.

**Root cause.** Filenames were never governed by a naming convention, so annotators encoded floor, building and language variation into the filename ad hoc. Semantics that belong in fields leaked into filenames.

**Impact.** The cheapest possible routing mechanism (parse the filename) is permanently unavailable, forcing every page through an AI classification pass. Also means any filename-based analysis across the dataset undercounts.
