**What happened.** Phase 0.5's binary-level check read the model's real config and found the default image token budget is 16,384 tokens/image, described as '3.2x too long if not overridden'. The same config read also proved vision_config has no image_size key (the direct evidence for bug 2). Both traps sat in the model's own defaults, invisible to any amount of script reading.

**Root cause.** Model-side defaults were never enumerated; the team's checks compared their own scripts to each other rather than to the model's actual configuration.

**Impact.** Left unoverridden this alone would blow the 24,576-token sequence budget on a single image. Caught before the paid run, but only because someone opened the real config rather than trusting documentation.

**Fix.** max_pixels/resolution overridden in the training config; the number was recorded in Phase 5 so the observed value would not read as a failure.

**→ Rule.** For every new model family, dump the real preprocessor/vision config on the actual machine and compare its defaults against your budget — vendor defaults are variables you did not set.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-24 · Page 22 stalled 45+ minutes on a rented GPU under pure greedy decoding

**What happened.** During the t01 house-11 batch run, page 22 hung for over 45 minutes generating under plain greedy decoding, burning rental time before anyone intervened.

**Root cause.** The batch runner was launched with no repetition penalty and no grammar constraint, so the model entered an unbounded repetition loop with no stopping mechanism. The known t02 fix existed but had not been carried into the t01 runner.

**Impact.** 45+ minutes of paid GPU time on a single page that produced nothing, on a ~$1.1/hr instance.

**Fix.** Added xgrammar + repetition_penalty (the proven t02 fix) — page 22 then completed in 321s.

**→ Rule.** Carry proven decoding fixes forward into every new runner script at creation time. A new runner must never ship without repetition_penalty and a stall guard.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Advisor's tuning suggestion pointed at max_frames=768, a video-only setting the project never uses

**What happened.** The advisor asked to increase max_frames from 768. The value exists in processor_config.json but sits under `video_processor` — it caps frames extracted from a video. The project only ever feeds still images (`{"type": "image"}`); no video path is ever exercised.

**Root cause.** A configuration value was read out of a JSON file without reading its parent key. Adjacent, plausible-looking numbers in a config are easy to mistake for the live knob.

**Impact.** Would have consumed a tuning cycle and possibly a paid training run to change a setting with literally zero effect. Cost was limited to investigation time because the value was traced before being changed.

**Fix.** Traced the key to `video_processor` and confirmed the codebase never emits a `"video"` message type. Identified the real knobs as MAX_PIXELS and MAX_LENGTH in train_t03.py.

**→ Rule.** Before changing any config value, grep the codebase to prove the code path that reads it actually executes in your workload. A knob that is never read is not a knob.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · A second resolution-bound magic number (100px minimum beam run) is hardcoded with no CLI override, unlike the 21px gap beside it

**What happened.** Beam detection discards any joined run shorter than 100 pixels to avoid matching text. Like gap=21, 100 is tied to this scan resolution (3309×2339, scale 1:75) — but only the gap was given a `--beam-gap` option and a written warning. The length threshold got neither.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · BEAM_GAP=21px is calibrated to one scan batch's DPI and drawing scale

**What happened.** The beam template's line gap is hardcoded at 21px, measured off บ้าน17 หน้า16 (faces at y=758-760/777-779). It is valid only for this scan batch's DPI at 1:75 scale; a different DPI or drawing scale would break beam detection entirely.

**Root cause.** A pixel measurement from one document was baked in as a constant with no derivation from DPI and drawing scale.

**Impact.** Beam detection will silently fail on any drawing set scanned at a different resolution or drawn at a different scale — and it will fail as zero detections, not as an error.

**Fix.** Not fixed — a `--beam-gap` knob was exposed and the limitation recorded, with auto-scaling deferred until a house actually needs it.

**→ Rule.** Any pixel-space constant must record the DPI and scale it was measured at, and be exposed as a knob. Silent zero-detection is the worst failure mode — add a sanity check that warns when a detector finds nothing on a page that should have something.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-26 · Adding the Thai glossary to every subtask pushed sequence length past MAX_LENGTH and would have forced a VRAM increase

**What happened.** Injecting the Thai→field glossary into all subtasks pushed the longest sequence from 44,606 to 45,592, which would have required raising MAX_LENGTH from 47,104 to 48,128 and increasing VRAM — with only ~4GB margin left. Measurement showed the 8 longest examples were all `gridline`.

**Root cause.** A prompt addition was applied uniformly without measuring its effect on the length distribution first. `gridline` prompts were already the longest and the glossary adds nothing there — gridline only finds grid lines and never touches element_type or rebar.

**Impact.** Would have forced a VRAM/MAX_LENGTH increase for zero benefit on the affected subtask, on a card already close to its ceiling.

**Fix.** Marked the glossary with an HTML comment delimiter and stripped it for `gridline` only → longest sequence back to 44,607, MAX_LENGTH and VRAM untouched. Verified: gridline 0/49 have glossary, other 1,059/1,059 have it, no `{{GLOSSARY}}` placeholder leaked.

**→ Rule.** Measure the sequence-length distribution before and after any prompt change, and exclude the subtasks a change cannot help. Apply prompt additions selectively, not uniformly.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-29 · gridline prompt grew ~1.5k chars cumulatively in one day, creeping toward the MAX_LENGTH ceiling

**What happened.** Successive prompt improvements (span-scaling rule, worked examples) added ~1.2k then ~1.5k cumulative characters to the gridline prompt, which was already the longest at ~45.6k against a 47,104 ceiling.

**Root cause.** Each prompt edit was evaluated for correctness in isolation, with no running length budget. The subtask already known to be longest kept receiving additions.

**Impact.** Margin against MAX_LENGTH shrinking with no explicit budget; an overflow would mean truncated training examples or an OOM mid-run.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged twice in the same day to watch MAX_LENGTH at training time.

**→ Rule.** Keep a hard character/token budget per subtask prompt and check it on every edit. Improvements accumulate silently; the ceiling does not move.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · Epoch count changed three times (3→5→4→3) on non-technical reasoning, forcing two training restarts and wiping outputs twice

**What happened.** num_train_epochs went 3.0 → 5.0 (to 'match the k-fold=5 idea', explicitly noted in the yaml as technically unrelated to epochs), then 5.0 → 4.0 for the stated reason 'ถูกชะตากับเลข 4' (t04 + Sicilian44 + epochs4), then 4 → 3 to fit the k-fold budget. Each change required killing the tmux `train` session, wiping `outputs_t04`, and restarting.

**Root cause.** A cost-driving hyperparameter was set from analogy and preference rather than from a measured convergence signal, and was allowed to change after training had already started.

**Impact.** The 5-epoch setting alone raised projected training time/cost ~1.67× (8-26h → ~13-43h). Two full restarts and two output wipes; luckily each restart happened within minutes so little GPU time was actually lost.

**Fix.** Every change was documented honestly in the yaml comments as a non-technical decision, and the final value (3) was chosen to fit the k-fold budget. A note was added to watch the loss curve for overfitting after epoch 3-4.

**→ Rule.** Freeze cost-driving hyperparameters before launching a paid run, and set them from a measured signal (loss curve / dry-run) — if one must change after launch, do it before any meaningful GPU time is spent, and record that it was not a technical decision.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · model-training-config</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · cutoff_len / image_max_pixels / lora_rank were left at defaults carried over from a different model family without verification

**What happened.** The InternVL3 training yaml was written with `cutoff_len`, `image_max_pixels` and `lora_rank` still at unverified defaults, explicitly flagged at the time as not transferable from the Qwen configs because InternVL3 uses a different tokenizer and a different resize mechanism.

**Root cause.** Image/sequence parameters were treated as generic knobs rather than as model-family-specific ones; the flag was raised but the verification (dry-run measurement) never covered the image-token path.

**Impact.** This is the same blind spot that produced the `crop_to_patches` disaster — the image pipeline was never measured on the new model family before a full paid run.

**Fix.** Flagged in the yaml with a ⚠️ and a requirement to dry-run and measure before full training. The dry-run was performed but only measured VRAM/loss, never tokens-per-image.

**→ Rule.** When a flagged 'must verify before full run' item exists, define exactly what measurement satisfies it — a dry-run that checks VRAM and loss does not discharge a warning about image resolution parameters.

**Fix.** Recorded as an open question with no answer; not resolved.

**→ Rule.** Measure the token-length distribution of the dataset against the tokenizer's model_max_length and the configured cutoff_len before training, and assert no example silently overflows.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Only the new PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF name was set; torch's own OOM message still names the old variable

**What happened.** Dry-run OOM'd at step 2 (1.18 GB short of 94.97). The script set only the new PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF, while torch 2.11 still prints the legacy PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF name in its own OOM message.

**Root cause.** An environment variable rename where both names are still honoured in different places, and only one was set.

**Impact.** Allocator configuration was not fully applied, contributing to an OOM one step into training.

**Fix.** Set PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF as well.

**→ Rule.** When a library renames an environment variable, set both the old and new names until the old one disappears from the library's own messages.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-01 · Client sends temperature 0.7 instead of 0 — harmless today only because the server overrides it, catastrophic if the server ever changes

**What happened.** `call_purson` sends `temperature 0.7 / top_p 0.8 / top_k 20` rather than `temperature 0`. This is currently masked because `serve_purson.py` forces the correct values server-side. If the stack ever moved to vLLM (which trusts client values), it would silently regress to 0% recall.

**Root cause.** Two places define sampling parameters and they disagree. The correct behaviour depends entirely on which side happens to win — a latent landmine, not a working design.

**Impact.** Zero today; a silent 0% recall regression the moment the serving layer is swapped, with no error to point at it.

**Fix.** Documented as a known latent hazard.

**→ Rule.** Never leave two components disagreeing about a critical parameter on the assumption that one currently overrides the other. Make both sides agree, so swapping either is safe.

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-06 · Label Studio XML paste failed because the copy started at line 2, dropping the opening <View> root tag

**What happened.** Pasting label-studio-makham-elements.xml into Label Studio produced 'Extra content at the end of the document, line 7, column 1'. The copy had started from line 2, omitting the first line `<View>`, so the parser treated the sticky-header View as a complete closed root and everything after it as extra content.

**Root cause.** A manual select-and-copy from an editor that made line 1 easy to miss, combined with an XML parser error message that names the position of the symptom (line 7) rather than the missing root at line 1.

**Impact.** Failed paste and a diagnosis round. It also recurred as a standing risk every time the config changed, which happened four more times the same day.

**Fix.** Diagnosed the cause and supplied the exact expected line counts for all three files (elements=96, material_list=70, single=46) as a checksum to verify a complete copy.

**→ Rule.** For any hand-pasted config, publish the expected line count alongside it and check it after pasting. An XML 'extra content' error almost always means a missing or duplicated root tag, not a problem at the line the parser names.

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-06 · Spec document header still claimed 2026-07-05 while it had been continuously edited through 2026-07-06

**What happened.** Makham asked for the date in the header of Makham's patter of rawjson20260705.md to be corrected, because the document had been continuously edited through July 6 (Generations 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 all added that day) while its header and filename still said 2026-07-05.

**Root cause.** The document was named and dated after its creation date, and three substantial revisions were appended without touching the header. Nothing prompts a date update when content is appended.

**Impact.** Anyone reading the header would believe they were looking at a one-day-old snapshot rather than a document three schema generations further along, and might act on a stale mental model of what had been decided.

**Fix.** Changed the first line to '# Makham's Pattern of Raw JSON — 2026-07-05 (last edited 2026-07-06)' and expanded the opening paragraph to note the ongoing updates. The filename was deliberately not renamed, since it is referenced elsewhere.

**→ Rule.** Put a 'last edited' line in every living spec and update it in the same edit that changes content. Never encode a date in a filename for a document that will keep evolving — the filename becomes a lie that cannot safely be corrected once it is referenced.

**Root cause.** Five config files evolved by hand, one at a time, with no shared base or check that a change applied to all of them.

**Impact.** Inconsistent annotator experience across three projects, and a standing note that making them consistent later 'would require more effort'.

**Fix.** Converted material_list to sticky-left; the header inconsistency was accepted as a deliberate decision.

**→ Rule.** When N config files must behave alike, change them as a set and diff them against each other afterwards — hand-maintained siblings drift, and the drift is only visible side by side.

**What happened.** All 5 configs put the header block (house/page/Sheet/sheet name/Pattern/View) inside `.stickycol` — the column whose entire purpose is to keep the drawing image visible while the annotator scrolls the data. Makham asked for 'the left side to have only the image', and the header was moved to the top of the data column in all 5 files, with the image's maxHeight expanded to a full 94vh.

**Root cause.** The header was grouped with the image because both are page-level context, without checking what that costs the pinned column — the one piece of screen real estate an annotator cannot do without when reading a construction drawing.

**Impact.** Every annotation session before this fix showed the drawing at a reduced height with metadata stealing the top of the pinned column. Compounded the scroll bug fixed the same day (content taller than the column was cut off entirely).

**Fix.** Header moved out of `.stickycol` and onto the data side in all 5 XML configs; image column left with `<Image>` alone at 94vh.

**→ Rule.** In a two-pane labeling UI, the pinned pane holds exactly one thing — the artifact being read. Anything else goes on the scrolling side.

The stale warning was caught only later, incidentally, during the pass that translated the README into English.

**Fix.** The stale warning was corrected while translating the README to English.

**→ Rule.** When a session's code change invalidates a doc written earlier in that same session, fix the doc in the same commit. Do not rely on a later unrelated pass to catch it.

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-25 · Beam template gap of 21 px is hardcoded to one scan resolution and scale

**What happened.** The synthetic beam template uses gap=21 px, measured from real images at 3309×2339 and 1:75 scale. Any house scanned at a different resolution or drawn at a different scale will not match.

**Root cause.** A pixel-space constant derived from one document set was baked into the template generator; the underlying physical quantity (beam width in mm) was not carried through as the parameter.

**Impact.** Beam detection will silently return nothing on differently-scanned drawings, with no error message to explain why.

**Fix.** Mitigated rather than solved: the constraint is documented in the code and a `--beam-gap` CLI override was added.

**→ Rule.** When a constant is measured in pixels from one scan, either derive it at runtime from the drawing scale or make it a required, documented parameter — never leave it as an invisible default that fails silently elsewhere.

## T07 — Infrastructure, GPU Rental & Cost

*Rented machines, quotas, capacity, network, and money burned.*

**124 entries** · 7 critical · 54 high

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-15 · additional_bars recorded on the wrong face of the beam — the same bug found in all five houses

**What happened.** Reinforcement recorded as being on the wrong face repeatedly: house 2's B2 'stops at L/8' recorded as top but actually bottom (2→4); B2X's lap splice recorded as mid-span but actually top (2→3); house 3's B3X and B4; house 4's B4, B4A, B4X, B5; house 5's B2X, B3X, B4, B5. Found only by zooming into the section and counting rebar points instead of trusting the printed label.

**Root cause.** Extraction trusted the printed label text and the leader-line's apparent target instead of counting actual rebar points in the section. The label's position on the drawing does not reliably indicate which face the bar is on.

**Impact.** Wrong rebar distribution on major beams in every house reviewed — a direct structural-quantity error, in some cases nearly doubling or halving a face's bar count.

**Fix.** Zoomed into the beam-section images and counted rebar points, then merged additional_bars into the correct face of main_bar and cascaded into the beam plans' `specs{}`. Recorded as a standing convention: always check `additional_bars[].position` against the real leader line, never trust the printed label.

**→ Rule.** For rebar face assignment, count points in the zoomed section image — never trust a printed label or a leader line's apparent target. When a bug appears in two houses, sweep every house immediately rather than finding it again per house.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-19 · A cross-house price-table 'fix' was itself a misread and corrupted four files before being reverted

**What happened.** On 2026-07-16 a cross-house check concluded house 3's reading (2,945,000/2,034,000) was correct and 'fixed' house 2's file (2,145,000/2,035,000) to match. On 2026-07-19, zooming 8x and comparing against reference glyphs on the same sheet showed all four copies agree on 2,145,000/2,035,000 — house 2 had been right all along; ๑ had been misread as ๙ while zoomed in.

**Root cause.** A glyph was judged in isolation at high zoom rather than compared against known instances of the same digit elsewhere on the same sheet. High zoom degrades the glyph and removes the surrounding context that disambiguates it.

**Impact.** A correct value was overwritten with a wrong one across multiple houses' files, then had to be reverted across five files; two days of confidence in a wrong number. The same sweep also found genuinely wrong values (#1, #2, #4, #8, and house design 3/8 size) that the earlier pass had missed.

**Fix.** Reverted the July 16 fix, corrected #1=1,020,000, #2=1,460,000, #4 spread=1,824,000, #8 spread 1,662,000→1,622,000, #10 spread 2,235,000→2,035,000, and confirmed the table now matches across all five houses.

**→ Rule.** Never judge a Thai numeral in isolation — always compare it against a reference instance of the same glyph on the same sheet at the same zoom. And when a cross-source check disagrees, re-verify both sides before rewriting either one.

<sub>`2026-07-19.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · A HuggingFace write token was pasted into chat and was still not revoked at end of day

**What happened.** The constistant-tune_t02 HuggingFace token, carrying repo.write permission, was pasted into the chat transcript. It was noted for revocation after Phase 8, and at the close of the diary it was still listed as not done.

**Root cause.** No secure secret-passing channel existed for the rented-machine workflow, so a write-scoped credential travelled through a logged conversation. Revocation was tracked as a to-do rather than executed at the moment the token stopped being needed.

**Impact.** A write-capable credential to the account holding the only backups of both rounds' adapters is exposed in a transcript and still live at the end of the session.

**Fix.** Not fixed — still listed under Pending: 'Revoke the HF token pasted in chat today'.

**→ Rule.** Never paste a write-scoped credential into a transcript; pass secrets via the machine's own environment or a secret store. If one is exposed anyway, revoke it the moment its task completes, not at the end of the day.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · security</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · Phase 8 export failed: merging the LoRA adapter into the MoE base produced a model outputting the wrong schema entirely

**What happened.** export_gguf.py loaded base + adapter and merged with no errors, but the sanity check caught that the merged output emits page_number/title/project instead of the real schema (png/doc_page/discipline/sheet_code/views). Four diagnostic scripts proved the adapter itself is fine (100% schema match before merge), delta_weight shape and orientation correct, scaling factor correct at 2.0, but the merged tensor values changed by only 0.67% in magnitude across 201 million values. Unsloth's own _merge_lora() does not support MoE ParamWrapper at all.

**Root cause.** A genuine defect in peft/Unsloth's merge path for target_parameters-style LoRA on MoE experts — the merge silently applies a near-null delta rather than failing. Not a training or dataset problem. Compounded by no upstream check that the merge implementation supports the architecture in use before committing to the export path.

**Impact.** No GGUF exists for t02, so the round produced no runnable local model. Diagnosis consumed significant paid machine time across four separate diagnostic script sets.

**Fix.** The script's own sanity check stopped it before quantizing and uploading a garbage model. Makham's decision: stop, after three main hypotheses were tested. The LoRA adapter was backed up separately and remains proven working.

**→ Rule.** Always place a schema/output sanity check immediately after any merge, quantize, or convert step so a silently-corrupt artefact can never be published. And verify that a merge/export toolchain supports your model architecture before choosing it as the delivery path.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · tooling/vendor-bug</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-02 · The 2026-07-21 'Mark of Shame' — a machine shut down while work only looked done, costing a 7.5GB LoRA and a 21GB GGUF

**What happened.** Cited as the reason `op3`'s shutdown gate exists: a machine went down while work only *looked* finished and nothing had actually been saved, destroying a 7.5 GB LoRA and a 21 GB GGUF.

**Root cause.** 'Looks done' was treated as 'is done' — there was no verified save/commit checkpoint between finishing work and powering off, and no requirement that a summary be printed before the screen goes dark.

**Impact.** A 7.5GB trained LoRA and a 21GB GGUF export were lost outright — GPU hours and a full training round burned.

**Fix.** Designed `op3` around a six-condition gate before shutdown: files written and parsing → `check_format.py` ALL PASS → row in the data log → `git commit` → summary printed to the user first → only then `shutdown /s /t 120`. `/t 0` is banned, and any failed step means no shutdown at all.

**→ Rule.** Never power off on 'looks done'. Automate the ending with a hard gate — verified output, passing checks, logged, committed, and reported — and always leave a cancellable delay, never `/t 0`.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · Pass 2 is dead code that still costs money — N API calls per run, result never used, errors swallowed

**What happened.** Pass 2 collects `layoutIds` and then never uses them (Pass 3 loops over Pass 1's ids instead), with its errors swallowed by an empty `catch`. It costs N API calls on every production run and produces nothing.

**Root cause.** A pipeline stage was superseded but never removed, and its empty `catch` block hid the fact that it was failing/idle — nothing measured whether its output was consumed.

**Impact.** Money burned on every single production run for zero benefit, silently. Worse, Pass 2 is possibly a real recall lever if wired up — it would catch marks present in plans but absent from section sheets — so the cost was paid without the benefit.

**Fix.** Identified and documented; the recommendation is to either wire it up (it may improve recall) or delete it.

**→ Rule.** Never leave an empty `catch`. And audit every paid API call for whether its result is actually consumed — a pipeline stage whose output nothing reads is either a bug or a bill.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · cost</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · requeue_stale() used claim time as heartbeat, so every real job qualified as dead while still running

**What happened.** `requeue_stale()` filtered on `claimed_at`, which is written once when a worker grabs a job and never refreshed. Real jobs run 75–80 minutes while `STALE_PROCESSING_MIN = 45`, so every genuine job entered the 'stale' condition mid-flight. If a second worker started (Makham double-clicking GO.bat, or opening a new window because the job looked stuck), it would flip the running job back to `pending` and re-claim it.

**Root cause.** Confusing 'when work started' with 'when work was last alive'. There was no heartbeat concept at all — the liveness check read a timestamp that by definition never updates, so the timeout threshold could never be satisfied by a healthy job.

**Impact.** Double GPU billing for the same house, plus two workers writing over each other's results. Never observed in the wild only because a second worker had not yet been started concurrently.

**Fix.** Switched the filter to `updated_at`, which the `purson_jobs_touch_updated_at` trigger refreshes on every `set_progress` write — so a job still reporting progress can never be considered dead.

**→ Rule.** A staleness check must read a field that a healthy process actively refreshes. Before shipping any timeout, ask 'what updates this timestamp while the job is alive?' — if the answer is 'nothing', the check is wrong by construction.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · concurrency/job-queue</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-09 · A day of config fixes lived only on disk; the live Label Studio projects still ran the old broken config

**What happened.** All of the day's fixes (scroll fix, header move, 50/50 split, hdrbar redesign) were made to XML files on disk, but the already-created Elements and Single projects (271482, 271493) on Label Studio Cloud were never re-pasted, so the live projects still had the invisible-overflow bug.

**Root cause.** Label Studio config is deployed by manual copy-paste into a web UI, and nothing in the workflow ties a file edit to a deploy step.

**Impact.** The scroll bug that prompted the whole session remained live for annotators despite being 'fixed'; carried into the next day's pending list.

**Fix.** Not fixed in this session — recorded as pending item 1: re-paste the latest config into the already-created projects.

**→ Rule.** For any manually-deployed config, treat 'edited the file' and 'the running system changed' as two separate facts, and never report a fix as done until the second one is verified in the live tool.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-09.md` · deployment/ops</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-10 · Highest-risk rebar data on houses 2 and 3 carries unresolved low-confidence flags that nobody has zoomed in on

**What happened.** On house 2, parts read without full confidence were flagged rather than guessed: the southward extension beyond grid C in the beam/tie-beam plans, the position of RB2 not sitting on the main grid, and roof/tie-beam rows in the column schedule that looked like blanks or arrows. House 3 repeated the same pattern: the bay-window extension area position, RB2 again off the main grid, and a dowel-bar count where a '+' appeared twice. All were given low confidence_score plus needs_human_review_zoom_required.

**Root cause.** Image resolution and drawing conventions (arrows meaning 'continues from the floor below', blank-looking schedule rows) exceed what can be read reliably at the page zoom used, and no zoom-and-verify pass has been scheduled for the flagged items.

**Impact.** This is the structural section — the data explicitly described as highest-risk and read personally rather than by agent for exactly that reason. Flagged-but-unverified rebar positions and counts sit in the production folders for houses 2 and 3, and are candidates for fine-tuning ground truth.

**Fix.** not fixed — flags recorded, review listed as pending; only the house-2 BOQ low-confidence items are named in the July 11 pending list, the structural ones are not.

**→ Rule.** Flagging instead of guessing is correct, but a flag with no scheduled review is just a deferred guess. Structural flags need a named review pass before that house is called complete — and the pending list must actually list them.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-11 · The Claude account session limit killed both BOQ agents mid-task on house #3

**What happened.** Both the spread-footing BOQ agent (pages 64-74) and the pile-foundation BOQ + site-plan agent (pages 75-89) were terminated by the account's session limit, which resets at 2am Thai time. The first was missing one file (page74_2), the second was missing all of Part B (pages 86-89).

**Root cause.** Five agents were dispatched simultaneously against a shared per-account session budget, with no check of remaining capacity before launching and no per-agent retry budget.

**Impact.** A second consecutive house left incomplete by an agent kill; manual repair required, and re-dispatching would have hit the same limit since it had not reset.

**Fix.** Repaired by reading the missing pages personally rather than re-dispatching, and the lesson was written into the entry: check how far the agent got, then read the missing part by hand.

**→ Rule.** Treat the account session limit as a shared resource: check remaining capacity before fanning out parallel agents, and when one is killed, measure what it produced before deciding to repair by hand or retry.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-11.md` · agent-orchestration/quota</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-12 · Dispatching 5 background agents at once repeatedly hits the account session limit mid-task

**What happened.** Five background agents were dispatched in parallel for the remaining document sections. Three of the five (architectural, spread-footing BOQ, pile-foundation BOQ) were terminated mid-task by the account's session limit. The same thing had already happened on houses 2 and 3.

**Root cause.** The parallel-agent fan-out pattern consumes the shared account session budget faster than a single house's work can finish; the workflow was designed without any budget accounting for how many agents the account can actually sustain.

**Impact.** Roughly 55 pages of extraction work had to be redone by hand across three sections; the same loss recurred on every house since house 2.

**Fix.** Rather than re-dispatching (which would burn the budget again), the missing pages were read personally. The reliable recovery method: inspect the files actually written to disk, not the agent's last reported message.

**→ Rule.** Never trust a cut-off agent's final message as a checkpoint — always diff files-on-disk against the expected page list. And size parallel agent fan-out against the real session budget rather than dispatching the maximum every time.

<sub>`2026-07-12.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-16 · The dash-stripping regex silently corrupted every sheet_code it touched

**What happened.** The regex used to strip dashes from point-type grid refs was also matching `sheet_code` values, turning 'S-04' into 'S04' in every file it ran over in house 3.

**Root cause.** The regex matched a letter-dash-digit pattern anywhere in the file rather than being scoped to the specific grid_ref fields it was meant to change.

**Impact.** Collateral corruption of a field across an entire house's files; had to be found and reverted file by file. A later run on house 5 was done with perl normalization specifically checked to confirm 'sheet_code survived'.

**Fix.** Checked and fixed sheet_code back in every affected file; subsequent bulk normalizations explicitly verified sheet_code integrity afterwards.

**→ Rule.** Scope a bulk regex to the exact JSON field it targets, never to raw file text — and always diff a sample of the output for collateral matches before running it over a whole house.

<sub>`2026-07-16.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-19 · B2X read as four vertical beams when it is actually a section of horizontal beams

**What happened.** On house 2's `หน้า25_beam_plan.json`, B2X had been recorded as 4 vertical beams. Zooming 3x showed it is the middle of horizontal beams on rows E/D, in the extension span reaching 1.00m to `1'`/`4'`.

**Root cause.** Beam orientation was inferred from the mark's position in the drawing rather than traced along the actual member line; the surrounding horizontal E/D-row beams were entirely missing, which removed the context that would have made the orientation obvious.

**Impact.** Wrong orientation on four members plus six entirely missing horizontal beams (E1-E2, E2-E3, E3-E4, D1-D2, D2-D3, D3-D4) and a grid2/3 label wrong (B2→B1).

**Fix.** Re-extracted at 3x zoom, added all missing horizontal beams and the vertical beams at 1'/1''/3'/4'/F'', and corrected the mark label.

**→ Rule.** Trace every beam along its member line before recording orientation, and check that a row's beam run is continuous — a gap in a row is a missing-element signal, not an empty span.

<sub>`2026-07-19.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-20 · onstart.sh crash-looped the first rented instance because pip upgrade collided with the apt pip

**What happened.** `pip install --upgrade pip` in `onstart.sh` collided with the apt-installed pip and errored; `set -euo pipefail` then killed the entire script, sending the first rented instance into a crash-loop.

**Root cause.** A non-essential convenience command was placed inside a strict-mode script with no failure tolerance, on a machine whose base image installs pip via apt.

**Impact.** A rented GPU instance burned in a crash-loop, requiring a second instance (id 45406175) to be launched.

**Fix.** Appended `|| true` to the pip upgrade; the second instance ran through completely, confirmed from the logs.

**→ Rule.** In a `set -euo pipefail` provisioning script, every non-essential command must be `|| true`. On a rented instance, a startup script failure costs money, so dry-run it on a cheap machine before the expensive one.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Rented the expensive GPU first and debugged the scripts live on it

**What happened.** The RTX PRO 6000 96GB at $1.056/hr was rented before any of the training/eval scripts had been proven to run; four separate code bugs and four OOM rounds were then debugged while the meter was running.

**Root cause.** No cheap-rehearsal step existed in the process — script correctness was assumed rather than verified, so the first real execution environment was also the most expensive one.

**Impact.** Hours of $1.056/hr rental spent on debugging instead of training; Makham called it out directly as obvious waste ('even this chatbot knows it's a waste of money'); he had to top up another $10 (total ~$19).

**Fix.** Recorded to persistent memory as a standing rule: rent a cheap machine to smoke-test scripts first, then rent the expensive one; also added a TEST_STEPS=5 rehearsal toggle to train_qwen36.py.

**→ Rule.** Never debug on a premium GPU. Prove every script end-to-end on the cheapest instance (or a tiny local dry-run) first; the expensive card is only for the run you already know works.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · cost-management</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Repeated disk-full failures during merge/GGUF; hit exactly 100% mid-conversion

**What happened.** The 150GB instance disk filled repeatedly during merge→f16→quantize; 44GB of old checkpoints, a 67GB HF cache, 5.4GB pip cache and intermediate q8_0/f16 files had to be deleted mid-flight, and at one point the disk hit exactly 100% just as the f16 conversion finished, forcing an emergency deletion of `merged/`.

**Root cause.** No disk budget was computed before starting a pipeline whose intermediates (70GB model + 66GB f16 + 21GB quantized + caches) obviously exceed 150GB; verify_env.py checked GPU/VRAM/libraries but not free disk.

**Impact.** Multiple stalls and emergency deletions under time pressure — and the panic deletion of `merged/` is what later made mmproj extraction impossible.

**Fix.** Deleted caches/checkpoints/intermediates as space ran out and continued the conversion.

**→ Rule.** Compute peak disk requirement for the whole conversion pipeline before renting, choose an instance with headroom, and add a free-disk check to verify_env.py — never free space by deleting artifacts you have not finished using.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · capacity-planning</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Instance rented with 150GB disk for a pipeline that needs well over 200GB of intermediates

**What happened.** The rented machine had only 150GB of storage, but the merge/GGUF chain needs the 70GB source model + checkpoints (44GB) + merged model (66GB) + f16 GGUF (~70GB) + the Q4_K_M output (21GB) at overlapping times. The whole conversion was run as a series of emergency deletions: old checkpoints (44GB), the HF cache (67GB), the pip cache (5.4GB), intermediate q8_0/f16 files — and the disk still hit exactly 100% mid-conversion.

**Root cause.** Disk size was never sized against the downstream pipeline when choosing the instance — only GPU/VRAM was checked (verify_env.py checks VRAM, not free disk). The whole merge/quantize chain was planned only after the machine was already rented.

**Impact.** Hours of firefighting during the conversion; forced the emergency deletion of `merged/`, which is the direct reason the vision component (mmproj) could no longer be extracted.

**Fix.** Deleted files reactively at each failure until the conversion squeezed through.

**→ Rule.** Size the instance's disk against the *largest simultaneous footprint* of the whole pipeline (source + merged + f16 + quantized), not just the model size, and pick disk at rent time — it cannot be grown later. Add a free-disk assertion to verify_env.py.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · infra/capacity-planning</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Rented instance disk filled up repeatedly during GGUF export (150GB was too small)

**What happened.** During merge and GGUF conversion the instance ran out of disk multiple times, forcing manual deletion of old checkpoints, cached base-model files and intermediate conversion artifacts mid-process.

**Root cause.** Disk was sized for training only. Nobody added up the peak simultaneous footprint of base model + merged model + f16 GGUF + quantized GGUF before renting.

**Impact.** Repeated interruptions and manual cleanup during a paid session; risk of deleting something still needed.

**Fix.** Deleted unused artifacts as the run progressed; on the next rental the required disk was pre-computed at 300GB.

**→ Rule.** Size instance disk from the peak concurrent artifact footprint of the whole pipeline (train + merge + export + quantize), not just the training step.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · infra-planning</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Debugging done on a rented GPU while the hourly meter was running, instead of on free local hardware

**What happened.** During the 2026-07-21 round, problems were hit after renting and were then fixed live on the paid instance at ~30 baht/hour, rather than having been caught beforehand for free on the local machine.

**Root cause.** No separation between checks that require the rented GPU and checks that don't. Every verifiable-for-free item (API token validity, account balance, disk defaults, script correctness, model-runs-locally) was deferred until after the expensive resource was already ticking.

**Impact.** Rental hours burned on diagnosis rather than training; unquantified but sufficient that the team built an entire Phase 0 regime to stop it.

**Fix.** Phase 0 created: token test, balance check, local dry run, script re-read, machine selection — all completed before the Rent button is pressed.

**→ Rule.** Sort every pre-flight check into 'needs the paid resource' vs 'doesn't'. Everything in the second bucket must be green before the first satang is spent.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24(teach mk).md` · cost/process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Training script hangs at its epilogue holding 83GB of VRAM, causing the next run to fail OOM

**What happened.** After the short test (`TEST_STEPS=5`) finished, the process refused to exit and hung holding 83GB of VRAM. It had to be killed by hand. Because it wasn't, the first Phase 6 run died with an OOM-adjacent meta-tensor error — not enough VRAM was free at restart. The hang recurred on every subsequent run, at the demo-generate epilogue after saving.

**Root cause.** The demo-generate epilogue after saving hangs (later traced to the same reasoning-mode template problem that broke evaluation), and the process holds its CUDA context until killed.

**Impact.** One wasted full training start that died OOM; every subsequent run needed a manual kill, on billed GPU time.

**Fix.** Kill the process by hand after the adapter is saved — it does not affect the training result. The underlying cause is the `enable_thinking` template mismatch fixed later.

**→ Rule.** Always verify VRAM is actually released before starting the next run on a rented GPU — a held context makes the next run's OOM look like a model-size problem when it is a cleanup problem. And treat a script that will not exit as a bug to root-cause, not a quirk to work around.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Deleting vision_config to skip mmproj conversion broke the main model save with triple-nested tensor names

**What happened.** Unsloth auto-detects the model as a VLM and tries to convert mmproj even though that was deliberately skipped; the conversion fails on the too-new architecture and brings the whole export down. The first fix attempt — temporarily deleting `model.config.vision_config` — broke something different instead, producing tensor names nested three levels deep (`language_model.language_model.language_model...`).

**Root cause.** The fix targeted a config field that affects how the main model is saved, not only mmproj conversion. The blast radius of the config change was not traced before making it.

**Impact.** A broken export requiring another cycle of debugging and re-running on billed GPU time; each re-run added to the disk-full problem.

**Fix.** Monkey-patched `unsloth.save.convert_to_gguf` to force `supported_vision_archs=set()` (forced, not defaulted, since the kwarg is always present), triggering Unsloth's own built-in `is_vlm=False` fallback — which does not touch the main model save at all.

**→ Rule.** Before mutating a shared config object to disable one code path, trace every consumer of that field. Prefer patching the specific function whose behaviour you want over removing state that many paths read.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Export failed with 'No space left on device' from 147GB of stale artifacts left by repeated re-runs

**What happened.** The export hit `No space left on device`. Cleanup recovered 147GB: old checkpoints duplicating the real LoRA adapter (33+11GB), pip cache (3GB), and a stale `outputs_qwen36/gguf/` directory (66GB).

**Root cause.** Every failed export re-run wrote a fresh full-size artifact set without cleaning up the previous one, and there was no disk-space check between attempts.

**Impact.** A failed export on billed GPU time, plus the whole cleanup cycle; on a 150GB default disk this would have hit far sooner.

**Fix.** Deleted stale checkpoints, pip cache, and the stale gguf directory, recovering 147GB.

**→ Rule.** Any script that writes multi-GB artifacts must clean the previous run's output before starting, and check free space against the expected output size first. On a rented machine, disk exhaustion mid-export is money spent for nothing.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Running llama-cli without --ctx-size reserved a 262k-token KV cache and left 0.1GB of RAM free

**What happened.** The first local test used `llama-cli --n-gpu-layers 999` with no `--ctx-size`. RAM dropped to 0.1GB free out of 31.4GB; `llama-cli` had committed 34.96GB of virtual memory — more than all installed RAM — because the model supports a 262,144-token maximum context and reserved a KV cache for it. The user spotted it first.

**Root cause.** `--ctx-size` defaults to the model's declared maximum, and this model's maximum is enormous. The KV cache scales with context, so the default reserves far more than any single-page task needs.

**Impact.** The workstation was pushed to the edge of freezing while in use. The identical mistake recurred the next day at ctx-size 12288 (0.45GB free), requiring another emergency kill.

**Fix.** Killed the process (21GB of RAM returned), re-ran with `--ctx-size 8192` (sufficient for one page plus the answer), using ~20GB and stable.

**→ Rule.** Always pass an explicit `--ctx-size` sized to the actual task — never let it default to the model's maximum. On a shared workstation, check free RAM during the first run of any new inference command.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-25 · Rented GPU instance left possibly running with destroy unconfirmed

**What happened.** Backups were verified in two independent places and the green light was given to destroy the rented instance, but it was never confirmed that the destroy actually happened. Phase 11 stayed unticked and the instance had to be assumed still running at ~$0.111/hr.

**Root cause.** The teardown handoff had no confirmation step — 'green light given' and 'instance destroyed' were treated as the same event by everyone except the diary.

**Impact.** Ongoing GPU charges of unknown duration; the entry explicitly ties this to a prior 'DAY OF SHAME' incident on the 21st when backups had not been done before teardown.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded honestly as unconfirmed, with the instance assumed running until the user confirms.

**→ Rule.** Teardown is not done until the provider confirms it — check the instance list, do not accept 'I gave the green light' as completion. Money keeps burning on the gap between approval and action.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · cost-money</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · House 07 EE-03/04: switches (solid dots) systematically counted in with light fixtures; one whole group missing and one row assigned to the wrong room

**What happened.** Across the electrical sheets, solid-dot switches were being counted as light fixtures — systematically, not once. Recounting gave floor 1 = 29 fixtures (group b had been missing entirely) and floor 2 = 19 (row d had been assigned to the wrong room).

**Root cause.** Symbol classification was done by visual similarity rather than against the sheet's own legend, and the error was systematic because the same wrong rule was applied everywhere. The missing group and the misassigned row show the count was never reconciled per room against the legend.

**Impact.** Fixture counts wrong on both floors in both directions — inflated by counted switches, deflated by a missing group — feeding electrical quantities and costs.

**Fix.** Full recount by symbol type against the legend; correct totals recorded as 29 and 19.

**→ Rule.** Count each symbol type separately against the sheet's legend and reconcile per room, never by lumping visually similar marks. A systematic classification error corrupts every sheet it touches, so fix the rule and recount everything, not just the instance found.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · House 07 M-02/03: plan adjacency read as physical stacking — CU pair, CEF-3's room, and CU-2/01's roof all placed wrong

**What happened.** Three mechanical placement errors from the same cause: the CU pair was recorded as stacked when it is lined up along the wall, CEF-3 was placed in the stair hall instead of the bathroom, and CU-2/01 was placed on the tiled wing of S-05 instead of the metal-sheet roof of the S-04 frame.

**Root cause.** A 2D plan projects 3D arrangement onto one surface; two symbols drawn close together were interpreted as physically stacked, and room/roof assignment was inferred from proximity in plan rather than traced to the enclosing boundary or the structural frame beneath.

**Impact.** Three equipment items located wrongly — affecting which structure carries them (a metal-sheet roof and a tiled wing are different load cases entirely) and which room's services they belong to.

**Fix.** Corrected by re-reading against the room boundaries and the S-04/S-05 frame layout; logged as one of three recurring error classes.

**→ Rule.** Never infer 3D arrangement or containment from 2D proximity. Trace equipment to its enclosing room boundary and to the structural frame drawn beneath it, on the structural sheet, before recording a location.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · Vast.ai's listed RAM of 76GB was misleading — the delivered machine had 188GB — and RAM had never been a selection criterion at all

**What happened.** The candidate machine's listing showed 76GB RAM, below the new ≥80GB criterion, forcing three layers of mitigation to be designed (verify_env warning, adapter-to-HF before GGUF, a 64GB swap plan). The machine actually delivered had 188GB. Separately, t01 had never had a RAM criterion at all — that round's machine simply happened to have enough.

**Root cause.** Two failures at once: the vendor's advertised RAM figure does not reflect what is delivered, and the resource that actually kills the bf16 30B merge (host RAM, ~60GB, and it dies with a silent Killed) had never been part of machine selection because it had never yet been the binding constraint.

**Impact.** Planning and mitigation work done against a false number; and a latent gap — any earlier round could have been silently killed by RAM with no criterion in place to prevent it.

**Fix.** RAM ≥80GB set as a criterion; verify_env.py extended to read RAM from /proc/meminfo; guarded in three layers including a documented swap remedy that avoids retraining.

**→ Rule.** Verify advertised specs on the delivered machine before relying on them, and derive selection criteria from every resource that can kill the job — including the ones a previous round survived only by luck. A silent 'Killed' means host RAM, not GPU.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · infra/vendor</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · The rented GPU machine was left running at the end of the session, still billing at $1.161/hour

**What happened.** At the close of the day the machine had not been shut down. It is blocked behind a Phase 11 hard block requiring an explicit instruction from Makham, so it continues to bill until that instruction arrives.

**Root cause.** The shutdown gate correctly requires human authorisation (to prevent destroying unbacked-up work), but there is no mechanism ensuring that authorisation is actually requested and obtained before the session ends — so the safety rule converts directly into open-ended spend.

**Impact.** Continuous billing at $1.161/hour on an idle machine for an unbounded period after all useful work finished and all data was confirmed safe.

**Fix.** Not fixed — listed under Pending, with the note that all data is already safe whenever shutdown does happen.

**→ Rule.** A human-authorisation gate on shutdown must be paired with a deadline or dead-man's switch. Once backups are verified, an idle metered machine is pure loss — request the authorisation explicitly before ending the session, never leave it as a to-do.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · Option B (retraining t01 at resize='max') was declined, leaving the round's original question permanently unanswered

**What happened.** Faced with the invalidated comparison, two options were offered: accept with warnings, or retrain t01 at matched resolution for ~$0.60-1.80 more. Option A was chosen. The A/B question the whole round existed to answer therefore remains open, and answering it later requires redoing t01's training first.

**Root cause.** The decision was made after the fact, when the sunk cost of the day was already visible and the incremental cost looked separate from it — rather than the far larger cost of the round having produced no answer.

**Impact.** A full paid tuning round plus a day of analysis produced no answer to its own research question; the outstanding work is now larger than the $0.60-1.80 it would have cost to close it on the spot.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded under Pending: to answer 'which family is genuinely better' fairly, t01 must first be retrained with resize='max'.

**→ Rule.** When an experiment is found invalid, weigh the remediation cost against the entire cost already sunk, not against zero. A round that answers nothing has already spent far more than the fix.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · decision/cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · 21GB model on an 8GB card — CPU offload made local inference ~20 hrs/house

**What happened.** Q4_K_M was chosen specifically so the model would run on the laptop, but 21GB still exceeds 8GB VRAM. llama.cpp aborts fitting ('failed to fit params to free device memory ... abort'), roughly two-thirds of the model runs on the CPU, generation drops to 3.46 t/s, and a full page takes 13-21 minutes → ~20 hrs/house × 5 houses.

**Root cause.** The quantization target was picked to shrink the file, not to satisfy a measured VRAM budget. Nobody computed 'does 21GB fit in 8GB' before committing to the local-inference plan.

**Impact.** The entire local extraction plan is economically unworkable at this speed, and the quantization quality hit was accepted for a fit that never actually happened.

**Fix.** not fixed — GPU rental proposed but correctly deferred until the LoRA question is settled

**→ Rule.** Before choosing a quantization level, write the arithmetic down: model size vs available VRAM, with headroom for context. If it does not fit, quantizing further or renting is a decision to make up front — not something to discover from an abort message mid-run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Almost rented a GPU to fix 'slow' when the real problem was 'wrong'

**What happened.** A GPU rental (≥24GB, $0.2-0.5/hr) was proposed to speed up the extraction run. It was caught in time that renting only addresses speed, and if the LoRA is genuinely absent from the GGUF, the rented machine produces identical garbage 10× faster.

**Root cause.** Reflex to treat the visible symptom (slowness) before the diagnosis of the invisible one (quality) had completed.

**Impact.** Money not burned — this one was caught before spending. Cost would have been rental fees plus a second round of unusable output.

**Fix.** fixed — rental explicitly blocked until the base-model comparison test is run

**→ Rule.** Never buy capacity to fix a quality problem. Order the work by 'what changes the decision': a free 20-minute diagnostic always precedes any paid step, because a wrong diagnosis just makes the failure faster and more expensive.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Rented Vast.ai instance from the 28th still not shut down

**What happened.** Shutting down the rented Vast.ai instance was a hard block on the 28th (Phase 11) and is still listed as carried over and not done on the 29th.

**Root cause.** Teardown lives in a prose checklist at the end of a work session, so it is the first thing lost when a session ends abruptly or attention moves to the next problem.

**Impact.** Continuous hourly billing for a machine doing no work, for more than a day.

**Fix.** not fixed — still listed as carried over from the 28th

**→ Rule.** Instance teardown is not a checklist item, it is an automated deadline: set a self-destruct/auto-stop on the instance at rental time so forgetting costs nothing. Never let 'shut it down' depend on a human remembering after the interesting work is over.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Renting a GPU was on the table as a response to bad output quality, which would have burned money for nothing

**What happened.** With extraction slow and bad, renting a GPU was a natural next move. It was explicitly blocked: renting fixes speed, not correctness, and if the LoRA is genuinely absent from the GGUF the rented run produces the same garbage, faster.

**Root cause.** Two distinct symptoms (slow, wrong) tempt one expensive remedy. Without root-causing 'wrong' first, spend gets allocated against the symptom that is easiest to price.

**Impact.** Avoided — the free 20-minute base-model comparison was ordered first. Had it been skipped, GPU rental money would have produced identical bad output.

**Fix.** Priority order set: (1) free base-model comparison to confirm LoRA presence, (2) free fix of the export sanity gate, (3) only then decide anything costing money. Explicitly forbade continuing house 01 extraction meanwhile.

**→ Rule.** Never spend money on a symptom you have not root-caused. Run every free diagnostic first, and stop producing output into the dataset while the pipeline is under suspicion.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · process/cost-control</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-01 · 5 commits with ~2.8GB of drawing PNGs sat unpushed for a long time because GitHub caps a push at 2GB

**What happened.** The Training repo had 5 old commits totalling ~2.8GB of house-drawing PNGs that would not push. The cause was GitHub's 2GB per-push cap. They had to be split into ~500MB batches and pushed one chunk at a time.

**Root cause.** Large binary assets were committed straight into git with no size awareness, and the push failure was not diagnosed when it first happened — it was simply left stuck for weeks.

**Impact.** ~2.8GB of work existed only on one laptop for an extended period with no remote backup; then a whole session spent splitting and pushing chunks.

**Fix.** Split the history into ~500MB pushes and pushed sequentially until complete; verified the diff against the source matched 100% afterwards.

**→ Rule.** Diagnose a failing push the day it fails — an unpushed commit is unbacked-up work. Keep pushes under 2GB and keep bulk binary assets out of git (or in LFS) from the start.

<sub>`2026-08-01.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-01 · ku_project_jop cannot be pushed at all — a 2.1GB zip is baked into commit history

**What happened.** The `ku_project_jop` repo cannot be pushed. A 2.1GB zip ('data from รุ่นพี่') was committed, then deleted in a later commit — but the blob remains in history, so every push still carries it. History has to be rewritten to strip it.

**Root cause.** A large archive was committed without checking its size, and the 'fix' was `rm` + commit, which does not remove the blob from history — a very common misunderstanding of how git stores data.

**Impact.** An entire repo has been unpushable and unbacked-up; the fix (history rewrite) is destructive and was still pending a decision at the time of writing.

**Fix.** Not fixed — waiting on confirmation to rewrite history and strip the blob.

**→ Rule.** Deleting a large file in a later commit does NOT shrink the repo. Never commit multi-GB archives; if one lands, rewrite history immediately (filter-repo/BFG) before more commits pile on top of it.

<sub>`2026-08-01.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · op3's shutdown only knows about its own house — it will kill any other job on the machine

**What happened.** Documented as a limitation when op3 was created: op3 must not be used when anything else is running on the machine (a training job, an upload, another agent), because its gate only checks its own house's completion.

**Root cause.** The completion gate is scoped to one unit of work, but the action it triggers (machine shutdown) is global.

**Impact.** A latent hazard: running op3 while a training job or upload is in flight would destroy that work exactly the way the original Mark of Shame incident did.

**Fix.** Documented as a standing restriction in the op3 definition rather than being enforced in code.

**→ Rule.** When a local completion check triggers a global destructive action, either scope the action or check the global state. A documented restriction is weaker than a check for running jobs before shutdown.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-20 · Rented a Vast.ai instance with only 78GB disk because the default slider was left low — third time this trap has bitten

**What happened.** The first rented instance for the t02 inference run had only 78GB disk, too small for the job, because Vast.ai's disk-size slider defaults low and was not raised. The diary notes this is the third time the same trap has been hit.

**Root cause.** Vast.ai's rental form defaults the disk slider to a value below what a 30B-class VLM workload needs, and there is no pre-rent checklist enforcing the override — so the same manual step is forgotten every time under time pressure.

**Impact.** One wasted rental plus the time to detect the problem, destroy, and re-rent. Cumulatively three occurrences of the same avoidable cost.

**Fix.** Instance abandoned; a third instance (158GB disk) was eventually rented and used.

**→ Rule.** Write the minimum disk/VRAM/RAM figures into the pre-flight workflow doc as a checklist that must be ticked before clicking rent — a trap that has bitten three times is a missing checklist item, not carelessness.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-20 · GPU hourly price misread as $0.058/hr when it was $1.792/hr — a 30x error caught only after an ~11hr run was planned

**What happened.** The working instance's price was recorded as $0.058/hr; the real rate was $1.792/hr. The 30x error was noticed only after estimating the run at roughly 11 hours / $20 — i.e. after the plan was already built around a wrong cost basis.

**Root cause.** The price figure was read off the Vast.ai listing without cross-checking against the running instance's actual billing rate, and no sanity check ('is $0.058/hr plausible for a 96GB RTX PRO 6000?') was applied to an implausibly cheap number.

**Impact.** Cost planning for the entire session was wrong by 30x. The error was caught before it caused an overrun, but every scope decision made before the catch was made on false economics.

**Fix.** Corrected to $1.792/hr; scope was subsequently cut repeatedly as real cost and timing became clear.

**→ Rule.** Read the hourly rate off the running instance, not the listing, and apply a plausibility check — a flagship 96GB card at under $0.10/hr is a misread, not a bargain; write the confirmed rate into the workflow doc before starting the job.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-20 · SSH dropped mid-nohup after a restart, so the old job was killed and the new one never started

**What happened.** After a mid-run reorder, the old batch process was killed and a new one launched via nohup — but the SSH session dropped during the launch, so the new process never actually started. Nothing was running. Caught by checking pgrep afterwards rather than trusting the launch command's exit code.

**Root cause.** nohup over a fragile SSH session gives no reliable confirmation that the process survived the disconnect; the command's exit code reports the shell's success at forking, not the job's continued existence. The kill-then-relaunch ordering left a window where zero jobs were running.

**Impact.** Silent dead time on a $1.792/hr instance under a slipping 1am deadline — caught only because it was verified, not assumed.

**Fix.** Detected via pgrep and the process relaunched. No tooling change recorded.

**→ Rule.** Never trust a launch command's exit code on a remote box — always confirm with pgrep/ps after launching, and prefer tmux/screen over nohup so a dropped SSH cannot orphan the launch; start the new job before killing the old where possible.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · The real cause of the post-grammar failures: lm-format-enforcer emits trailing commas that Python's json rejects

**What happened.** After grammar-constrained decoding was added, the first run still produced unparseable JSON. The actual root cause (found only after reading the code layer by layer) was that `lm-format-enforcer` treats `{"a":1,}` — a trailing comma before the closing brace — as valid, while Python's json parser rejects it. Two components disagreed on the definition of 'valid JSON'. Proven in one line: deleting the extra comma from a 'broken' file made it parse immediately.

**Root cause.** A grammar backend was adopted without checking that its notion of valid JSON matches the consumer's (Python json.loads). The grammar was working correctly the whole time; the two specs of 'correct' simply differed.

**Impact.** Wasted a debugging cycle on rented GPU time, produced a confidently wrong entry in SUMMARY.md blaming Unsloth, and nearly caused the entire grammar approach to be abandoned as non-functional.

**Fix.** Switched the default backend to `xgrammar` (which cannot emit a trailing comma at source) with `lmfe` demoted to fallback; recorded as rule_of_tune lesson 13.

**→ Rule.** When a constraint layer and a parser disagree, verify both definitions of 'valid' against each other before blaming either — and prefer the backend whose grammar makes the invalid output physically impossible rather than merely unlikely.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21(teach mk).md` · vendor-tool-mismatch</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · Vast.ai price misread by ~20x for the second time — web display shows storage rate, not GPU rate

**What happened.** The Vast.ai web page showed $0.056/hr; DLPerf/$ math implied ~$1.16/hr. The real bill for the morning instance was $5.43 with the GPU at $1.1067/hr. The $0.056 figure is the *storage* rate. This was flagged as "same class as the 30x misread on 2026-08-20" — the same mistake had already been made four days earlier.

**Root cause.** The web UI puts a storage rate in a position that reads as the instance price, and the team kept sourcing price from the UI instead of the API. The 2026-08-20 occurrence produced no rule, so it repeated.

**Impact.** Budget planning was wrong by ~20x across at least two rental decisions; the bill went unchecked for most of a day while decisions were made on a false price.

**Fix.** Checked the real bill via vastai CLI (GPU $1.1067/hr, storage 0.24, DL 0.48, total $5.43). New standing rule: read price only from `vastai search offers` (`dph_total`), never the web display.

**→ Rule.** Never source a rental price from a vendor web UI. Read it from the API/CLI field that bills you (`dph_total`), and when a pricing surprise happens once, write the rule down the same day or it will repeat.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · cost-control</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · Training survived but per-epoch eval OOM'd — accelerate upcasts the whole logits tensor

**What happened.** TEST_STEPS=5 passed cleanly (3,778 visual tokens/image, seq 21,445 < 32,768, ~55s/step, loss 1.86) and then the run died at eval time on the rented GPU.

**Root cause.** `evaluate → convert_to_fp32`: accelerate wraps forward and upcasts the entire output, materializing logits at seq 21k × vocab 152k × 4 bytes ≈ 13GB on top of 6.5GB bf16, asking for 24.72GB. Training never hits this because Unsloth uses a fused loss that never materializes logits. t01 escaped it (512px images, short seqs) and t02 escaped it (30B left headroom); t03 was the first run combining a 35B model with full-resolution images.

**Impact.** A full training run died on paid GPU time after passing every pre-flight check, requiring a restart.

**Fix.** Set `eval_strategy="no"`, kept `save_strategy="epoch"` so three checkpoints remain for retrospective measurement.

**→ Rule.** A training smoke test that skips the eval step is not a smoke test. Peak memory at eval can exceed training peak by 2-3x because eval materializes logits; size VRAM for the eval path, not the train path.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · infra-bug</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · A widely-quoted $0.67/hr GPU price was a misread of the interruptible min_bid column — the second time this exact trap was hit

**What happened.** A "$0.67/hr RTX PRO 6000" figure in circulation was checked against vast.ai's live API and refuted — the cheapest real offer is $1.01/hr. The $0.67 was likely a misread of the `min_bid` (interruptible) column. The diary notes this is the same trap as an earlier `$0.056` storage-vs-GPU price misread.

**Root cause.** Marketplace listings show several price columns (on-demand, interruptible min_bid, storage) and the cheapest visible number gets quoted without checking which column it belongs to. The same misread had already happened once and no rule was written to prevent it.

**Impact.** Budget planning against a price 40% below reality. Repeating a known trap means the first occurrence produced no durable lesson.

**Fix.** Queried `vastai search offers` directly (not web-scraped, not an aggregator) and recorded the real on-demand rates: RTX PRO 6000 96GB $1.01–1.11/hr, ×2 $2.00–2.19/hr, H200 141GB $3.29/hr.

**→ Rule.** Always read GPU prices from the vendor's own live API and name which column the number came from (on-demand vs interruptible vs storage). When a trap repeats, write it into the rules file, not just the diary.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · cost-misread</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Documented framework support did not match reality — GLM-4.6V has an open LoRA-blocking bug, InternVL3-78B fails to load in Unsloth

**What happened.** Checking framework support against real GitHub issues rather than documentation claims found that GLM-4.6V has an open, unresolved LoRA-blocking bug (hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory#9635, `NotImplementedError: get_input_embeddings`), InternVL3-78B does not load in Unsloth (two open issues #3401, #2341), and Pixtral-Large / Molmo-72B / NVLM-D-72B have no mainstream framework confirmed working at all.

**Root cause.** Framework documentation lists models as supported based on intent or partial support, not on a verified working fine-tune run. Trusting the docs would have produced a false candidate list.

**Impact.** Would have committed GPU rental to a model that cannot be LoRA-fine-tuned at all. Two of the surviving finalists still require either a different framework (LLaMA-Factory, not Unsloth) or a different training mode (4-bit QLoRA, not bf16 LoRA) — a real pipeline change, not a drop-in swap.

**Fix.** Verified support against open GitHub issues and confirmed third-party runs (e.g. Llama-4-Scout via a Fixstars blog report on 8×H100) before shortlisting.

**→ Rule.** Never accept a framework's model-support table as proof. Search its open issue tracker for the exact model plus your training mode, and require evidence of a real completed run before committing rental money.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · vendor-doc-mismatch</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-29 · A wrong --cv-dir path silently degrades arm 2.4a into arm 2, invalidating the experiment and burning GPU time

**What happened.** apply_arm() looks for a sidecar hint file; if it cannot find one it returns the original prompt with hint_used: false rather than erroring. A mistyped --cv-dir therefore produces a full run where the treatment arm is silently identical to the control arm.

**Root cause.** The no-hint-found path is intentionally non-fatal (correct for houses genuinely lacking CV data) but there is no distinction between 'legitimately absent' and 'path is wrong'. The failure surfaces only as a flag buried in the results.

**Impact.** An entire experimental run can produce results that cannot answer the question it was run for, consuming GPU rental for nothing.

**Fix.** Documented as a mandatory pre-flight check: verify hint_used is true for pages that have sidecars before continuing the run.

**→ Rule.** Before any paid run, assert that the experimental treatment is actually being applied — check the flag on a sample row first. Silent degradation to control is worse than a crash because you pay full price for a null result.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอน_t04_Purson_2026-08-29.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · `hf upload <repo> <folder> --exclude 'pattern'` silently uploaded zero files while logging success-looking output

**What happened.** Uploading the fold2 adapter with `--exclude 'checkpoint-*/*'` produced logs reading 'Start hashing 19 files / Processing Files (0/0) / New Data Upload 0.00B/0.00B' even though all files existed. Not a token or permission problem — `whoami` was fine and a single-file upload test succeeded.

**Root cause.** Not fully determined; suspected interaction between `--exclude` and the large-folder incremental sync logic in the HF CLI. Vendor tool reports apparent success while transferring nothing.

**Impact.** A backup that appeared to have happened had not. If not caught, an adapter would have been believed safe on HF and the GPU destroyed, losing the weights.

**Fix.** Workaround that works 100%: copy only the top-level files (excluding `checkpoint-*/`) into a separate staging folder and upload that folder without using `--exclude` at all. 842MB uploaded successfully. Recorded so the same trap is not hit on fold3/fold4.

**→ Rule.** Never trust an upload tool's exit status — verify the uploaded byte count / file list on the remote side (and sha256 after pulling back) before deleting or destroying the source.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · vendor-tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Image tarball uploaded only half (514MB/1005MB), tar extract failed silently, and the training data ended up with 0 images

**What happened.** On the fold1 instance, the images tarball transferred only 514MB of 1005MB. `tar` extraction then failed silently, leaving 0 image files, even though the logs of the preceding step looked normal.

**Root cause.** No integrity check between upload and extraction — the pipeline assumed a transfer that returned without an error had transferred the whole file, and tar's failure on a truncated archive was not surfaced.

**Impact.** A fold would have trained on a dataset with no images at all if not caught. Required re-uploading and restarting that fold's setup.

**Fix.** Re-uploaded, and added a mandatory `stat` size comparison between local and remote before every extract. The pattern was applied to fold2/fold3 from the start and both passed first try.

**→ Rule.** Always compare file size (or checksum) local vs remote before extracting or consuming a transferred archive; a transfer command exiting 0 is not evidence the bytes arrived.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · Scaled to 4 parallel GPUs with $49.75 credit against a $63 job — instances would have been stopped mid-training

**What happened.** After expanding from 2 to 4 folds and renting 2 more cards, total projected cost was ~$63 while the account held $49.75. The four instances burned $4.29/hr, leaving roughly 10 hours before the credit ran out mid-run.

**Root cause.** The rental scale-up decision was executed before checking that the credit balance covered the full projected runtime; cost was computed after committing rather than as a gate.

**Impact.** Risk of all four training runs being killed partway through, losing up to ~14 hours of GPU work across 4 cards. Averted only because Makham topped up ($76.63) in time.

**Fix.** Reported to Makham immediately with the deadline; credit topped up manually and auto top-up enabled as a second layer.

**→ Rule.** Before starting any long unattended GPU run, compute total_hours × hourly_burn and refuse to start unless credit covers it plus a buffer — treat the balance check as a hard gate, not a follow-up.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · fold1 still OOM'd at step 68/252 even at the reduced MAX_PIXELS that the other three folds survived
