**What happened.** After the uniform reduction to 6912, three folds completed but fold1 died at step 68 of 252, leaving only checkpoint-50 on HuggingFace.

**Root cause.** Per-fold sample composition differs, so a globally-set memory ceiling is not equally safe on every fold — the margin left was still too thin for fold1's longest sequences.

**Impact.** Only 3 of 4 folds available; the model soup had to be merged at k=3 instead of k=4.

**Fix.** Decided not to rerun (same settings would likely OOM again, and lowering only fold1 would break cross-fold parity); merged k=3 with equal 1/3 weights, noting all 40 houses are still covered.

**→ Rule.** Size memory headroom against the worst fold, not the average, and if one fold must differ, accept losing it rather than breaking cross-fold parity.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Hours of inference were run on gpu1, which was ~20x slower than needed because its torch build did not match the image's CUDA

**What happened.** smoke_destrier and the whole pure-power queue ran on gpu1 at ~20 minutes per page, forcing a 25-minute timeout rule, an xgrammar retry system, and cutting the test from 65 pages to 8. Only when GPU-B was rented later did it become clear that a machine with torch 2.11+cu128 matching CUDA 12.8 runs about 20x faster.

**Root cause.** gpu1 carried torch cu13.0 on a CUDA 12.8 image (the same mismatch that blocked flash-linear-attention), so everything fell back to slow torch paths — and nobody compared its throughput against a known-good machine before committing a long queue to it.

**Impact.** Most of a day of inference at 20x cost in wall-clock time, a whole timeout/retry subsystem written to work around it, and the pure-power test reduced from 65 pages to 8.

**Fix.** GPU-B's working config (torch 2.11+cu128 on CUDA 12.8) saved to results/gpuB_working_config/ as the rental recipe for next time

**→ Rule.** Benchmark one page on a new rental against a known-good baseline before queueing hours of work onto it; a 20x slowdown reads as "the model is slow" instead of "this box is misconfigured".

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Eight real bugs sat undetected in the Constistant app until a whole-house run was simulated without a GPU

**What happened.** On 1 Sep the team simulated running a whole house through the Constistant application without renting a GPU, and immediately found 8 real bugs, all of which were then fixed.

**Root cause.** The application side had never been exercised end-to-end on a full house — testing had been per-module, so integration-level defects accumulated invisibly until the first whole-pipeline dry run.

**Impact.** Eight latent bugs would have surfaced during an expensive live GPU run instead, wasting rental time on debugging application code rather than on model work.

**Fix.** All 8 fixed the same day; details recorded in that day's diary.

**→ Rule.** Run the full pipeline end-to-end in cheap simulation mode (no GPU, no rental) before every expensive live run. Integration bugs are invisible to per-module tests and are far cheaper to find on a laptop than on a rented card.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · testing</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Job sat pending 7+ minutes with zero GPU activity because the SSH tunnel was never actually started

**What happened.** A job submitted from the web stayed in `pending` for over 7 minutes with no GPU activity and no error message at all. Investigation showed `presentation.py up` had never actually opened the SSH tunnel, so `localhost:8000` was unreachable and `worker.py` had nowhere to send requests.

**Root cause.** `presentation.py up` reported success without verifying the tunnel was actually listening. A silent partial-startup: the orchestration command returned OK while its most critical side effect (the tunnel) had not happened, and nothing downstream checked reachability before accepting jobs.

**Impact.** 7+ minutes of a paid GPU rental burned on a job doing nothing, plus debugging time during a live demo session; the job had to be manually reset to `pending` and `worker.py` restarted.

**Fix.** Tunnel started manually, orphaned job reset to `pending`, `worker.py` restarted; GPU activity then confirmed. Later hardened with `ServerAliveCountMax=6` and `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` on the tunnel.

**→ Rule.** A startup command must verify its critical side effect before reporting success — `presentation.py up` should probe `localhost:8000` and fail loudly if the tunnel is not listening. Never let a job enter `pending` when its transport is unproven.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · infra/orchestration</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · pass3 shipped with only a synthetic self-check whose answers were known in advance

**What happened.** pass3 (`pass3_measure.py`) was written with a self-check using a fabricated 50 px/m grid whose correct answer was already known. No real drawing had ever been run through it — real px/m and residual figures were completely unseen. The entry itself flagged this as the top pending item.

**Root cause.** The self-check validated the arithmetic against data the test itself constructed, so it could only prove 'the fit function fits a perfect fit'. It could not detect whether real drawings even produce enough valid anchors — which turned out to be the actual failure mode (see the cv_mark and count>1 bugs).

**Impact.** A whole measurement stage was believed working while its dominant real-world failure modes (0 anchors, wrong scale, multi-ref elements) were entirely untested — and three separate real bugs were later found in it.

**Fix.** Closed later the same day with `validate_pass3_real.py` using real human-verified pairs and a leave-one-out methodology: 191/191 correct, fit succeeding on 15/18 pages, error 0.004–0.093 m.

**→ Rule.** A self-check on synthetic data you generated proves the code runs, not that it works. Before claiming a measurement stage is done, run it on real artifacts already sitting on disk — here the real data was available locally and required no GPU at all.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · worker.py had no retry anywhere, so a momentary network blip killed operations mid-job

**What happened.** `update_job`, `download_image` and `call_purson` all had no retry logic. Any transient network failure during a 75–80 minute GPU job broke the operation outright.

**Root cause.** The code was written assuming a stable local network, but it runs against a rented remote GPU over an SSH tunnel — an inherently flaky path, as the HuggingFace stalls the next day proved.

**Impact.** Any network hiccup wasted the remaining GPU time on a job that could no longer report or fetch.

**Fix.** Added `_retry()` with 5/15/30/60s backoff wrapping `update_job`, `download_image` and `call_purson`.

**→ Rule.** Every network call that crosses a rented-machine boundary needs backoff retry from the first version. The cost of a dropped call is measured in GPU-minutes, not milliseconds.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · resilience</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Naively retrying on ReadTimeout would have made the GPU run two generations at once

**What happened.** Adding retry to `call_purson` created a new hazard: retrying on `ReadTimeout` means the model is still generating while a second identical request is sent, so the GPU does two jobs simultaneously.

**Root cause.** 'Retry on failure' is not safe for non-idempotent long-running operations. A read timeout says nothing about whether the server is still working — it only says the client stopped waiting.

**Impact.** Would have halved effective GPU throughput and doubled cost per page. Caught during design of the retry itself.

**Fix.** ReadTimeout is explicitly not retried; only connection failures and 5xx are.

**→ Rule.** Classify each error before retrying: connection-refused and 5xx are safe to retry, read-timeout on a long generation is not. Never apply a blanket retry to a non-idempotent expensive call.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · resilience</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · No automatic tunnel reconnection — a fully dead tunnel requires a human to retype a command

**What happened.** If the tunnel dies completely, nothing restarts it; a person must run `python presentation.py tunnel` by hand. The worker will retry and wait, but the job stalls until a human notices.

**Root cause.** Retry was added to the client calls but not to the transport itself, so the resilience layer stops one level short of the actual failure point.

**Impact.** An unattended overnight run can stall indefinitely on a dead tunnel while GPU billing continues.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as pending.

**→ Rule.** Resilience must extend to the transport, not just the calls over it. If a run can be unattended, every layer it depends on needs self-recovery — otherwise the GPU bills while nothing happens.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · resilience</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · The full pass0→pass3 pipeline had never once been run end-to-end against a real GPU

**What happened.** After a full day of simulation work proving every stage, the entry states plainly that the whole belt has never been run with a real GPU — everything proven was 'all stages except the model itself'.

**Root cause.** GPU cost pressure pushed all verification into CPU simulation. Valuable, but it structurally cannot catch model-interaction faults (timeouts, truncation, malformed JSON) — which is exactly what broke on the very next day.

**Impact.** The first real GPU run the next day immediately hit three broken pages from server-side timeouts — a failure class no simulation could have surfaced.

**Fix.** Not fixed that day; the real run happened 2026-09-02 and immediately found new bugs.

**→ Rule.** Simulation proves your code, never the model interaction. Budget at least one cheap full end-to-end GPU run per major pipeline change — the failures unique to that boundary (timeouts, truncation, malformed output) are invisible to every mock.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · No checkpointing meant any failure forced restarting an 80-minute GPU job from zero

**What happened.** Until this change, a job that failed part-way had to be restarted from the beginning — re-running every model call already completed. This is what made the page-12 failure cost a full house re-run.

**Root cause.** Results were written only at job completion, so all intermediate work was discarded on any failure. On a 75–90 minute paid job this makes any single-page failure catastrophic.

**Impact.** Full house re-runs on paid GPUs for single-page failures (directly caused the job 43323920 re-run).

**Fix.** `save_checkpoint()` writes `result` after pass0/gridline/each page of pass2/pass2.5; `claim_next_job()` also fetches `result` so `run_house_extract` skips any pass already checkpointed — real resume, not just saving. Web side remembers the last job id per project and offers a '🔁 ทำต่อ' button that PATCHes the existing job back to pending rather than creating a new one.

**→ Rule.** Any paid long-running job must checkpoint after every expensive unit of work, and resume must actually skip completed units — 'we save results' is not resume.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · resilience/cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · Renting a GPU took 7 attempts — 2 stuck loading, 3 SSH key propagation lag

**What happened.** Getting a working rented GPU for the house09 run required 7 attempts: 2 instances stuck loading, 3 rejected the SSH key with 'Permission denied (publickey)' despite the key being correct (propagation lag).

**Root cause.** vast.ai provisions the instance before the SSH key has propagated, so the first connection attempt fails on a perfectly good host. The team's script connected immediately and treated the failure as terminal, so every lag event was misdiagnosed as a bad host and answered with destroy-and-re-rent.

**Impact.** Five wasted rentals and a large amount of setup time; each destroy/re-rent cycle costs both money and minutes. This was a repeat of the same symptom seen on 2026-09-01.

**Fix.** Root-caused as propagation lag and fixed in `presentation.py` with 6 retries over 60s before the first mkdir/scp, instead of destroying and re-renting every time.

**→ Rule.** Distinguish 'host is bad' from 'host is not ready yet'. Give a freshly provisioned instance a bounded retry window (60s) before destroying it — destroy-and-re-rent as a first response to a publickey error burns money on healthy hosts.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · vendor/infra</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · HuggingFace download stalled with 4 repeated timeouts while pulling a 70GB model onto a $2.05/hr rental

**What happened.** On a successfully started $2.05/hr instance, the HuggingFace network stalled badly — 4 repeated timeouts on different files while downloading the 70GB model. Makham stopped mid-way rather than continue paying for a bad connection and asked to pick the machine himself.

**Root cause.** Model weights are pulled from HuggingFace onto every fresh rental, so the whole setup depends on a third-party CDN's throughput to that specific datacenter. No local cache, mirror, or pre-baked image exists.

**Impact.** Paid rental time burned entirely on a failed download; the rental was abandoned with no work done.

**Fix.** Rental abandoned. The incident directly produced the 'attach to a card you rented yourself' feature (GO.bat menu item 7 / `presentation.py attach <id>`).

**→ Rule.** Downloading 70GB from a third party on every rental makes cost hostage to their CDN. Bake the weights into a snapshot/image or mirror them to storage in the same region — and abandon a rental early once the download is clearly degraded, rather than paying while retrying.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · vendor/cost</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · Job reported 'success 9/9' while three of its output pages contained invalid JSON

**What happened.** Job f63bc71e finished and reported จบสำเร็จ 9/9, but three pages (page_03_notes, page_12_plan_footing, page_13_notes) had corrupt/truncated JSON. Nothing between generation and the 'done' status validated that each page's output actually parsed.

**Root cause.** The worker's completion status counts pages generated, not pages that produced valid parseable JSON — the server-side generation timeout cuts mid-token and the worker still marks the page done.

**Impact.** A green 9/9 status that a user would trust; the corruption was only found by opening raw text by hand, and three pages of an ~87-minute paid GPU run were silently unusable.

**Fix.** Found by manual inspection, then recovered with a purpose-written `salvage_json.py` bracket-depth walker; no validity gate was added to the worker itself

**→ Rule.** A pipeline that emits JSON must json.loads() every page before it may report success — 'the model returned bytes' is not the same as 'the page is usable', and a false green is worse than a loud failure.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-09-02.md` · observability</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-07 · Reference-only -all.json and an .xml config were uploaded into Label Studio's Data Import tab

**What happened.** During the first real Label Studio Cloud test, the combined reference file label-studio-tasks-makham-all.json (explicitly never meant for import) was uploaded into Data Import, and a freezeR .xml (which belongs in Labeling Setup) was uploaded into the same tab, producing 'label config has more than one data key'.

**Root cause.** The never-import reference file is generated into the same directory with the same filename prefix as the three importable files, so nothing but memory distinguishes them; and the two-tab setup order (Labeling Setup before Data Import) was not written down anywhere at that point.

**Impact.** A blocked import session and live troubleshooting time on an error whose message pointed at the config, not at the wrong file choice.

**Fix.** Told to upload label-studio-tasks-makham-elements.json instead and to move the .xml to the Labeling Setup tab; the setup-order rule was documented the following day.

**→ Rule.** A file that must never be imported must not share a naming prefix or directory with importable ones — name it *-REFERENCE-DO-NOT-IMPORT or put it in its own folder.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · tooling/ops</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-09 · Merging the 3 Label Studio projects into one via visibleWhen would have failed on a known vendor bug

**What happened.** The idea of collapsing the Elements/Material List/Single projects into one config with an if/else on pattern was investigated by actually searching, and found that visibleWhen only conditions on annotator actions, not task data; that Label Studio's own GitHub Issue #3313 documents visibleWhen showing/hiding incorrectly; and that the official docs admit XML config may not handle complex data-type combinations.

**Root cause.** The three data shapes are genuinely different (element_id/grid_ref_start vs item_no/quantity vs no items at all) and the config language has no data-driven branching — an assumption that it did would have gone undetected until annotators saw wrong fields.

**Impact.** Avoided; had it been implemented on the assumption, annotators would have labelled against silently wrong field sets.

**Fix.** Kept the three projects separate, on the explicit basis of the vendor bug and the documented limitation.

**→ Rule.** Search the vendor's issue tracker before designing on top of a conditional-display feature — and prefer three honest configs over one clever config that can display the wrong fields.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-09.md` · tooling/vendor-limitation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-12 · 90-degree rotated micro-text on BOQ pages extracted at low confidence and shipped needing review

**What happened.** Pages 75 (house 4) and 76 (house 5) contain BOQ text rotated 90 degrees at very small size. Extraction produced item-to-quantity pairings that were flagged as low confidence and never confirmed.

**Root cause.** The extraction workflow has no dedicated handling (rotation + zoom pass) for rotated small text; it was read at normal orientation and scale and the reader could not resolve the item-quantity pairing reliably.

**Impact.** Unverified BOQ quantity data sits in the dataset flagged for human review; if used for training or costing it could produce wrong numbers.

**Fix.** Flagged in `confidence_flags`/`warnings` for human review; not resolved as of the entries.

**→ Rule.** When a page has rotated or micro-scale text, rotate and zoom it as a dedicated pass before extraction — do not accept a low-confidence pairing and defer it, because deferred flags accumulate and never get cleared.

<sub>`2026-07-12.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-12 · Label Studio task script silently drops files whose JSON shape it does not support

**What happened.** Running `label-studio-tasks-makham.js` on house 4 produced 141 tasks from 144 valid files — page36 (roof_frame_plan, empty `elements:[]`) and page58 (hanger_spacing_schedule, uses `columns`/`rows` instead of `items`) were not picked up. The same two shapes recurred on house 5 (page35 used `steel_members`).

**Root cause.** The script assumes every file exposes a populated `elements[]`/`items[]` array; the schema legitimately allows other shapes for roof-frame and schedule-table patterns, and the script has no branch for them and no warning when it skips a file.

**Impact.** Pages silently missing from the Label Studio annotation set on every house; the count mismatch was only noticed by manual comparison. Unfixed across houses 4 and 5.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the decision on whether to change the schema or the script was still pending across multiple diary entries.

**→ Rule.** A converter that skips input must log what it skipped and why; a silent count mismatch is a data-loss bug. Decide schema-vs-script the first time it appears rather than carrying the gap forward house after house.

<sub>`2026-07-12.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · Git push rejected with 403 because the account lacked collaborator access on the org repo

**What happened.** A git push failed with 403; the cause was that the `chaichanaju-dot` account does not have push access on the organisation repo.

**Root cause.** Repository access was never granted for the account being used to push — an unverified prerequisite for the whole 'commit the work' task that had been pending for weeks.

**Impact.** Blocked committing the accumulated work at exactly the moment it was finally being attempted, compounding the already-large uncommitted-work risk.

**Fix.** Diagnosed as a permissions issue; resolution is to add the account as a collaborator via the GitHub website.

**→ Rule.** Verify push access on day one of a repo, not at the first push. A permissions gap turns 'commit the work' from a five-minute task into a blocked one.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · Repeated 'Jupyter connection refused' failures chasing an access method the setup never supported

**What happened.** Repeated 'Jupyter connection refused' errors were hit when trying to reach the rented instance. The root cause is that `onstart.sh` does not start a Jupyter server at all, and direct HTTPS access would require installing a certificate.

**Root cause.** An access method was assumed to be available on the rented machine without verifying that the provisioning script actually provides it.

**Impact.** Time lost on connection debugging before the access method was abandoned entirely.

**Fix.** Switched the standard access method to SSH + scp + tmux, dropping Jupyter completely.

**→ Rule.** Verify the access path is actually provisioned before debugging connection failures — and prefer SSH/scp/tmux, the method that works everywhere, over a notebook server that has to be stood up.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Days lost fighting Jupyter web UI 'connection refused' before switching to SSH

**What happened.** The team tried to drive the rented Vast.ai GPU through the Jupyter web UI and hit repeated 'connection refused' errors across multiple days (since 2026-07-20) before finally reading Vast.ai's docs and switching to SSH + scp + tmux.

**Root cause.** Tool choice was made by convenience (a web page looks easier) instead of by checking what the standard professional workflow for the platform actually is; nobody read the vendor docs until after the failures piled up.

**Impact.** At least a full day of wall-clock time lost across two dates, plus rental hours burned on a machine that could not be driven reliably.

**Fix.** Abandoned Jupyter entirely; created an SSH key, registered it at vast.ai/manage-keys, and standardised on ssh + scp + tmux.

**→ Rule.** Before renting infrastructure, read the vendor's own docs and adopt the workflow that serious practitioners use (SSH/tmux for GPU rental); do not burn hours proving a convenience UI unusable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · infra-tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Baseline eval re-launched itself and burned GPU time unnoticed

**What happened.** After `eval_fields.py --base --limit 20` finished and printed its summary, the same command started running again on its own; it had to be killed with pkill/kill -9.

**Root cause.** Stray terminal control codes were interpreted by bash as an up-arrow (history recall) plus an Enter, re-submitting the previous command — an input-hygiene failure, not a script bug.

**Impact.** Paid GPU time and wall-clock time spent re-running a job whose result was already in hand.

**Fix.** Killed the duplicate process as soon as it was noticed; added the habit of checking for accidental restarts after any long job.

**→ Rule.** After any long/expensive job reports completion, check `ps`/`nvidia-smi` that it has not restarted itself before walking away.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · cost-management</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · Vast.ai's rent form defaults disk to 150GB — the exact value that caused disk-full failures

**What happened.** While checking the account balance screenshot before the second rental, the Vast.ai container disk slider was noticed still sitting at its 150GB default, the same size that caused repeated disk-full failures on 07-21. 300GB was required.

**Root cause.** Vendor UI default is unrelated to the workload; renting on defaults silently reproduces the previous failure. The value is easy to miss because it is set once, at rent time, and cannot be changed afterwards.

**Impact.** Caught for free before renting — had it been missed, the disk-full failures would have repeated on paid time.

**Fix.** Explicit instruction recorded to drag disk from 150 to 300 before pressing Rent.

**→ Rule.** Every provider default on a rent/provision form is a decision you are making by omission — write the required non-default values into the pre-rental checklist and verify them on the confirmation screen.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · infra-planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · Vast.ai's disk slider silently defaults to 150GB and must be dragged to 300 by hand

**What happened.** During Phase 0.2 it was found that the Vast.ai rental page's disk slider defaults to 150GB and has to be dragged to 300GB manually for this workload.

**Root cause.** Vendor UI default is well below what this training and export pipeline needs; nothing in the rental flow warns about it.

**Impact.** Caught before rental. Undersized disk is exactly what caused the later 'No space left on device' failure during export — with 150GB it would have hit far sooner.

**Fix.** Documented in the Phase 0 checklist; disk confirmed at 300GB on the actual rental.

**→ Rule.** Record vendor UI defaults that must be overridden into the pre-rental checklist. A default that silently undersizes the machine costs a re-rent, not just a resize.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · Export sanity check raised its token limit three times before the check itself was recognised as wrong

**What happened.** The export sanity check failed with `max_new_tokens=500`. It was raised to 3000 (still failed), then to 4096 (still failed — the model genuinely over-predicts, it was not truncation). The real fix was to change what the check asserts.

**Root cause.** The failure was diagnosed as a limit that was too small and the limit was raised repeatedly, instead of asking what the check needed to prove. Full-JSON-parse is the wrong assertion for a sanity check on a model known to over-predict.

**Impact.** Three failed attempts on billed GPU time before the correct fix; each attempt also generated artifacts that contributed to the later disk-full failure.

**Fix.** Changed the check from 'does the full JSON parse' to 'does it start with the real JSON schema' (1200 tokens of generation suffices) and switched to a shorter test page.

**→ Rule.** After the second time raising a limit fails, stop raising it and question the assertion instead. A sanity check should prove the smallest sufficient thing, not reproduce a full production output.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · Export reported 'file not found' although conversion and quantization had genuinely succeeded

**What happened.** The script checked `outputs_qwen36/gguf/` for the output files, but Unsloth actually saves them to `outputs_qwen36/gguf_gguf/` (duplicated suffix). The script reported failure even though the conversion and quantization had succeeded.

**Root cause.** The output path was assumed rather than read back from the library's own return value or verified by listing the output directory.

**Impact.** A successful expensive step reported as a failure — nearly triggering a full re-run of merge and quantize on billed GPU time.

**Fix.** Fixed the path without re-running merge/quantize, and wrote a separate `resume_upload.py` to upload straight from the files already on disk.

**→ Rule.** Never assume a library's output path — list the directory or use the returned path. And when an expensive step reports failure, check whether the artifact exists before re-running it.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · The GPU selected in the Phase 0.5 pre-flight was not the one rented, and the first machine actually rented was switched away from

**What happened.** Phase 0.5 concluded by picking a specific listing (m:67820, RTX PRO 6000 96GB, $0.975/hr, Japan). What was actually rented was m:130161, and then that was switched to a different RTX PRO 6000 WS in Hong Kong at ~$0.111/hr.

**Root cause.** The pre-flight machine selection is done at planning time against a live marketplace whose listings and prices move; by rental time the chosen listing is stale, so the selection step produces nothing reusable.

**Impact.** The Phase 0.5 selection work was wasted, and one instance was rented and abandoned before the working one was found. Positively, the machine finally used was ~9x cheaper per hour than the one selected — meaning the pre-flight pick was also a bad price.

**Fix.** not fixed as a process — the correct machine was found ad hoc at rental time and the disk-300GB check was carried over from Phase 0.3.

**→ Rule.** Pre-flight should fix the machine *criteria* (VRAM, disk, reliability, max $/hr), not a specific listing id. Selecting an id hours in advance guarantees it is stale and hides better prices.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-25 · The exact RAM-exhaustion mistake from Phase 10 was repeated the next day at a higher ctx-size

**What happened.** A smoke test on page10 was launched with `ctx-size 12288` (chosen larger to avoid truncation) and immediately reproduced the previous day's danger: 0.45GB free out of 31.4GB (PrivateMem 20.08GB). It had to be killed at once because the machine was in use.

**Root cause.** The previous day's fix (ctx-size 8192 is safe) was known but the new run raised it to solve a different problem (truncation) without re-checking the RAM headroom the larger value implies.

**Impact.** A second emergency kill, plus the run producing no output; the machine was again pushed to the edge while the user was working on it.

**Fix.** Re-ran at ctx-size 8192 (the value already proven safe), leaving 11.84GB free.

**→ Rule.** When raising a resource parameter to fix a different problem, re-check the constraint that parameter was originally tuned against. Handle truncation by re-running the one affected page at higher ctx, not by raising it globally.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · House 07 SN-04: inspection chambers counted as 8 when there are 11

**What happened.** The sanitary sheet's inspection chambers had been extracted as 8; the recount found 11 — three missing.

**Root cause.** Same class as the other count errors: symbols enumerated at reading zoom without an exhaustive per-region sweep, so items in dense or peripheral areas were skipped.

**Impact.** Three inspection chambers missing from the sanitary takeoff — a 27% undercount on that item.

**Fix.** Full recount at zoom; corrected to 11 with the reversal logged.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Running the 21GB model locally made the working machine unusable for anything else, forcing the run to be stopped after 2 of 61 pages

**What happened.** Inference on the tuned model consumed so much VRAM on the local RTX 5060 (8GB) that the machine could not be used for anything else. The run was stopped on Makham's instruction after 2 pages, with 61 planned. Real speed was 273s and 409s/page, projecting 5.5-6.5 hours.

**Root cause.** A long-running heavy GPU job was started on the same machine being used for interactive work, with no estimate of duration or resource impact computed beforehand.

**Impact.** 59 of 61 pages left unprocessed; the work must be resumed later. Became rule_of_tune.md Lesson 11.

**Fix.** Script made resumable (skips pages already done); recorded as Lesson 11 — never stack a GPU load on top of a real job that's running.

**→ Rule.** Estimate duration and resource footprint before starting a long GPU job, and never run one on a machine someone needs interactively. Make every long batch job resumable from the start.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · process/resource</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Bug 5: the training script's epilogue hangs while still holding VRAM

**What happened.** After training completes, the script's demo epilogue hangs and does not release VRAM, blocking any subsequent step on a machine that is billed by the hour.

**Root cause.** A convenience demo block ran unconditionally at the end of training with no way to skip it, on a script intended for unattended paid runs.

**Impact.** Paid GPU time consumed by a hung post-training demo, and the GPU held against the next phase.

**Fix.** Added SKIP_DEMO=1.

**→ Rule.** Any script that runs on metered hardware must have every optional convenience step behind an off switch, and must release resources before it can possibly hang.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · cost/tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · A GPU load was stacked on top of a job already running — recorded the same day as permanent Lesson 11

**What happened.** A new permanent rule (Lesson 11) was added to rule_of_tune.md: 'never stack a GPU load on top of a real job that's running'. The diary records the rule in the Files line but never narrates the incident that produced it, so the cost is undocumented.

**Root cause.** Ad-hoc diagnostic/inference work started on a machine whose GPU was already committed to a real job, with no rule or check preventing it.

**Impact.** Unknown from the diary — but the rule was judged serious enough to become one of only twelve permanent lessons. An undocumented incident cannot be sized or learned from properly.

**Fix.** rule_of_tune.md Lesson 11 added.

**→ Rule.** Two things: never start a second GPU workload against a card already running a real job; and when a failure is serious enough to become a permanent rule, write down the incident, not only the rule.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · resource contention / undocumented incident</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · GPU showed 100% utilisation while drawing only 33.7W — the card was waiting, not working

**What happened.** nvidia-smi reported 100% utilisation, which reads as 'the GPU is the bottleneck'. Power draw of 33.7W on a card capable of far more revealed the truth: the GPU was stalled waiting on the CPU, which held the offloaded layers.

**Root cause.** GPU 'utilisation' counts time with a kernel resident, not useful work done, so a stalled-on-host pipeline pins at 100% while doing almost nothing.

**Impact.** Would have driven the wrong optimisation (a bigger/faster GPU) when the actual constraint is that a 21GB model does not fit in 8GB VRAM and offloads to the CPU.

**Fix.** fixed as a diagnostic practice — read power draw alongside utilisation

**→ Rule.** Never diagnose a bottleneck from utilisation percentage alone. Cross-check power draw and memory residency; 100% util at low wattage means the device is starved, and the fix is upstream of it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · HuggingFace token constistant-tune_t02 still live after the job it was issued for ended

**What happened.** Revoking the HF token used for the t02 tuning run was on the 28th's list and is still outstanding on the 29th.

**Root cause.** The token was created for a job with a natural end but had no expiry attached, so revocation became a manual task competing with active work.

**Impact.** A write-capable credential remains valid on a rented machine that is also still running, expanding the blast radius of both oversights.

**Fix.** not fixed — still listed as carried over

**→ Rule.** Issue job-scoped credentials with an expiry that outlives the job by hours, not with unlimited life plus an intention to revoke. If the platform supports no expiry, revocation goes in the same automation that tears down the instance.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · security</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Second rented Vast.ai instance had a dead SSH connection outright

**What happened.** The second instance rented from the same listing could not be reached over SSH at all — dead connection. A third instance had to be rented before work could begin.

**Root cause.** Vendor-side instance health is not guaranteed and Vast.ai does not validate SSH reachability before billing starts; the same listing that produced the disk problem also produced an unreachable box.

**Impact.** A second wasted rental and further delay before the run started, contributing to the deadline slip that later forced cutting scope from 4 houses to 19 pages of one.

**Fix.** Abandoned; third instance (154.59.156.33, RTX PRO 6000 96GB) was used.

**→ Rule.** Budget for one or two dead rentals per session and validate SSH plus nvidia-smi within the first two minutes of any rental; if a listing produces two bad instances in a row, change listing rather than retrying it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · t02 has no working GGUF because export failed, forcing raw transformers/PEFT inference on rented GPUs

**What happened.** t02's GGUF export failed (noted in the t02_workflow.md header), so testing t02 outside the eval harness required running the LoRA adapter as raw transformers/PEFT inference on a rented Vast.ai GPU instead of a lighter local/quantized path.

**Root cause.** The GGUF conversion step was never made to work for this adapter, and the failure was recorded but not resolved — leaving the model permanently dependent on renting a large GPU for every test.

**Impact.** Every ad-hoc test of t02 costs a GPU rental at ~$1.79/hr plus setup time, instead of running locally. Directly contributed to the scope pressure that shrank the generalization test.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Worked around by renting a GPU and running transformers/PEFT directly.

**→ Rule.** A failed export path is not a footnote — it changes the cost of every subsequent experiment; fix the export or explicitly budget every future test as a paid GPU rental in the plan.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · A previous run OOM'd with 470 MB of VRAM headroom left

**What happened.** An earlier training round ran out of GPU memory when only about 470 MB of headroom remained. The new MAX_PIXELS=7,680 setting narrows headroom from 7.5 GB to 4.0 GB, re-entering the same risk zone.

**Root cause.** VRAM headroom was calculated on paper from static estimates; activation memory spikes at real peak were not verified with a short live run before committing to a full multi-hour training job.

**Impact.** A crashed training run wastes the whole rental period up to that point — the GPU is billed by the hour whether or not the job finishes.

**Fix.** Standing rule adopted: run a short 5-step test to confirm peak VRAM before every full run. Not yet re-verified at the new 7,680 setting.

**→ Rule.** Always run a 5-step smoke run and read actual peak VRAM before starting a paid full-length training job, especially after changing any memory-affecting parameter.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · infra/cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · LoRA size had to be halved mid-plan to fit MAX_LENGTH 32,768 on the 95GB card, and it still barely fit

**What happened.** To fit a 32,768 context on the 95GB GPU in the previous round, the LoRA rank had to be cut in half — and even then it only just fit.

**Root cause.** The context length was chosen before checking whether it and the intended LoRA capacity could coexist in the available VRAM; the memory budget was not planned as a whole.

**Impact.** Reduced model adaptation capacity (smaller LoRA) was forced by a memory constraint rather than chosen for quality reasons — a silent degradation of the training setup.

**Fix.** VRAM was subsequently decomposed into its three parts (weights 74.0 GB static, LoRA+gradient+optimizer 5.7 GB static, activation 7.8 GB scaling with image size), giving a real budget to plan against.

**→ Rule.** Budget VRAM by component (static weights vs. trainable state vs. activation) before choosing context length and LoRA rank together — not by shrinking whatever is easiest once the run refuses to start.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · infra/planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Only $8.91 credit remaining — not enough to finish even one round on the H200 upgrade path

**What happened.** The zero-downscaling option requires an H200 140GB at $3.29/hr = $17.45 per round. Available credit was $8.91, which cannot complete a single round.

**Root cause.** Credit balance was not tracked against the planned upgrade path; the option was priced only after the technical case for it was made.

**Impact.** The full-resolution training path is blocked pending a top-up; if the run had been started blind it would have died mid-training and burned the credit for nothing.

**Fix.** Price checked live before committing; balance verified; the cheaper 7,680 compromise on the existing card was chosen instead (30% images downscaled, $0 extra).

**→ Rule.** Check the credit balance against the full projected cost of a run BEFORE starting it. A run that dies at 60% for lack of credit costs the same as one that never started, minus the money.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · cost/planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Pixtral-Large evaluated in depth for capability, then disqualified on licence in one line

**What happened.** Pixtral-Large (~124B, Mistral) was assessed as strong at document/table/chart reading with a Qwen-like dynamic pixel-budget design — then ruled out entirely because the Mistral Research License forbids commercial use without a separate paid licence.

**Root cause.** Licence screening was performed after technical evaluation rather than as the first filter, so the technical work on a disqualified candidate was wasted.

**Impact.** Evaluation effort spent on a model that could never be used for STECON work regardless of how good it is.

**Fix.** Recorded as disqualified. The same pattern recurred with NVLM-D-72B (CC-BY-NC) and MiniMax M3 (fine-tuning for production counts as commercial).

**→ Rule.** Screen model licences BEFORE evaluating capability. Licence is a binary gate; capability is a ranking. Never rank candidates that have not passed the gate.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · vendor/licensing</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · MiniMax M3 carries the same hidden commercial-use licence trap as Pixtral-Large, and it was left unresolved

**What happened.** MiniMax M3 is free for non-commercial use, but fine-tuning it for real use counts as commercial and requires a separate licence — explicitly identified as 'คล้ายดักของ Pixtral-Large'. The diary records it as still not conclusively ruled out, pending a closer read of the terms.

**Root cause.** Licence pages state a headline ('free') that does not survive contact with the actual use case (fine-tune + deploy for STECON). The trap had already been hit once with Pixtral-Large in the same session and was recognised but not closed out.

**Impact.** An unresolved candidate can pull a future session back into the same evaluation, or worse, be adopted on the headline and hit the licence wall after training money is spent.

**Fix.** not fixed — flagged as needing a detailed terms read

**→ Rule.** After a licence trap bites once, close every candidate carrying the same shape of trap in the same session — leaving one 'to read later' is how the same hour gets spent twice.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · vendor-licence</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · The PRINTED_ID classifier is a regex heuristic that misclassifies genuinely-printed Thai labels

**What happened.** `measure_id_ceiling.py` classifies GT ids as printed-vs-invented by regex. `ห้องนอน` is classed as "invented" although it is physically printed on the drawing — it is a room label, not an element mark. So the reported ceilings are conservative estimates, not proven values.

**Root cause.** A regex cannot distinguish "text present on the page" from "text that is an element mark"; the two concepts were collapsed into one pattern.

**Impact.** All published ceiling figures carry unquantified error, and the same regex now drives a GT batch edit — long ids that are genuinely printed (e.g. `เหล็ก WF 150x150x7x10`) got nulled and will train as null.

**Fix.** Documented as a conservative estimate in the workflow doc rather than presented as a proven value; the batch edit preserves original names in `element_name_assigned` so the nulling is reversible per field.

**→ Rule.** When a heuristic drives a published number or a data edit, state its error direction in the same sentence as the number, and make the edit reversible per record so the heuristic's misses can be recovered.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · heuristic-limitation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · The cheapest big-VRAM offer (8× RTX 4090, 384GB at $2.99/hr) would have been a bad buy for an MoE model — no NVLink

**What happened.** Live vast.ai pricing showed 8× RTX 4090 at 384GB total for $2.99/hr — cheaper than a single H200 at $3.29/hr and with far more VRAM. On inspection the cards have no NVLink and only 18.9 GB/s PCIe interconnect, which MoE expert routing depends on; it was flagged as risky rather than recommended.

**Root cause.** GPU offers are ranked by $/hr and total VRAM, neither of which reflects interconnect bandwidth — the property that actually decides whether a MoE model trains usefully across cards.

**Impact.** Caught before renting; had it been taken on the headline numbers, an 8-GPU rental would likely have delivered poor throughput on a MoE model and burned credit that is already short ($8.91 on record).

**Fix.** Flagged as risky in the research write-up; not rented.

**→ Rule.** For MoE, read interconnect bandwidth before $/hr and total VRAM — the cheapest big-VRAM offer is often the one whose cards cannot talk to each other.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · Vast.ai auto top-up trigger set at `< $0.00` — it refills AFTER the balance runs out, not before

**What happened.** Auto top-up was enabled as a safety layer, but the trigger threshold was set to `< $0.00`, meaning the refill only fires once the balance is already exhausted.

**Root cause.** A threshold-based safety mechanism was configured at the boundary value rather than above it, misreading 'trigger' as 'floor'. There is a real gap between hitting zero and the refill landing, during which instances can be stopped.

**Impact.** The safety net would not have prevented mid-run instance termination; the run was only safe because the manual top-up made the balance sufficient anyway.

**Fix.** Flagged and documented; not changed, deemed acceptable because credit was already sufficient.

**→ Rule.** Set auto top-up thresholds above zero by at least a few hours of burn rate (e.g. burn_rate × 4h), and never treat a zero-threshold refill as protection for an unattended run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · Rented a host that showed an abnormal signal at provision; it dropped offline 26 minutes later

**What happened.** Instance 49172551 (Virginia US) went `actual_status: offline` while `intended_status: running` after 26 minutes — the host dropped off vast.ai's control plane, confirmed by 4 polls in 1 minute. The instance had shown a warning sign from the start: `direct_port_start: -1`, forcing proxy SSH instead of a direct port.

**Root cause.** An abnormal provisioning signal (no direct port) was treated as an inconvenience to work around rather than as evidence of an unhealthy host, so the run proceeded on a flaky machine.

**Impact.** ~26 minutes and ~$0.50 lost on model loading; the HF token copied onto it could not be verified before it died and had to be redone on the replacement. Had it failed at hour 10 the loss would have been ~$16 plus the elapsed time.

**Fix.** Destroyed immediately and re-rented 49175439 (Czechia, $1.134/hr, reliability 0.997, net_down 8496Mbps) chosen for highest reliability and 10× network speed (156GB model load ~5 min instead of 30).

**→ Rule.** If a rented host shows any abnormality at provision time (no direct port, slow network, low reliability score), destroy and re-rent immediately — the cost of a fresh rental is trivial compared to a host failing 10 hours into a run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · `vastai destroy instance` prompts y/N interactively and aborts silently in a script — a card can be left running while you believe it was returned

**What happened.** Running `vastai destroy instance` non-interactively aborts quietly because it waits for a y/N confirmation that never comes; it must be invoked as `echo "y" | vastai destroy ...`.

**Root cause.** A destructive CLI command defaults to interactive confirmation, and its silent abort path is indistinguishable from success when scripted.

**Impact.** A GPU believed destroyed keeps burning money. At the day's peak burn of $4.29/hr that is $103/day for a single forgotten card.

**Fix.** Documented in `t04_workflow.md` item 13 with the full command including instance IDs, plus three traps written out: (1) must pipe `echo "y"`, (2) destroy ≠ stop, (3) must run `vastai show instances` and confirm 0 afterwards — not just trust that the command ran.

**→ Rule.** After any destroy/teardown command, re-query the provider for the actual instance count and require it to be zero; never accept 'the command ran without error' as proof a resource was released.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · vendor-tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · Full evaluation would have taken 7-8 hours per fold — as long as training itself, unbudgeted

**What happened.** Measured inference speed was ~2-2.5 minutes per sample, so a full 205-sample eval per fold would have taken ~7-8 hours per fold, comparable to the training time itself.

**Root cause.** Eval cost was never estimated during planning; only training time and cost were budgeted.

**Impact.** Would have roughly doubled the round's GPU cost and delivery time if run as originally planned across 4 folds.

**Fix.** Makham decided on 20-30 random samples per fold instead (~1-1.5h/fold), implemented via `make_eval_samples.py` producing 24 samples/fold.

**→ Rule.** Budget evaluation GPU-hours in the same estimate as training — measure seconds-per-sample during the smoke test and multiply before committing to a full eval.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · vLLM's MoE LoRA support exists but `is_3d_lora_weight` can be declared wrong, producing silent garbage with no error

**What happened.** Research found vLLM now supports MoE LoRA via `--enable-mixed-moe-lora-format`, but that if `is_3d_lora_weight` is declared incorrectly the result is garbage output with no error raised.

**Root cause.** A vendor feature validates format declarations weakly — a wrong declaration is accepted and silently produces wrong numerics instead of failing.

**Impact.** Would have appeared to work in a demo while producing nonsense. Directly changed the serving decision.

**Fix.** Rule adopted: always fire a page whose correct answer is known and compare before trusting the serving stack. Ultimately vLLM was dropped entirely for this adapter.

**→ Rule.** For any inference stack change, run a known-answer regression page and diff against the reference output before trusting it — 'no error' is not evidence of correctness in ML serving.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · vendor-tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · The vast.ai image had no `/workspace` (onstart log redirect failed silently) and torch lived in `/venv/main`, not system python3

**What happened.** The onstart script redirected its log to `/workspace`, a directory the vast.ai image does not create, so the redirect failed silently. Separately, torch was installed in `/venv/main` rather than being importable from the system python3.

**Root cause.** The onstart script assumed a directory layout and python environment from a previous image without verifying them on the new one; a failed shell redirect at script start produces no visible output by definition.

**Impact.** Onstart failures were invisible — the log that would have shown the problem was the thing that failed to be written.

**Fix.** onstart now creates the directory (mkdir), uses the venv python path directly, and sets `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.0` for Blackwell.

**→ Rule.** Never redirect a bootstrap log into a directory you have not created in the same script, and always resolve the interpreter path explicitly (`which python`, venv path) rather than assuming `python3` has the deps.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · vastai/pytorch image created authorized_keys with wrong permissions, making SSH impossible

**What happened.** Two instances rented with vastai/pytorch:cuda-12.8.1-auto had /root/.ssh/authorized_keys created with wrong ownership/modes, so sshd refused a correct key ('Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes'). It could not be fixed from outside — vastai execute only works on stopped instances and reboot did not clear it.

**Root cause.** Vendor image defect; no way to repair a running instance's sshd from outside.

**Impact.** Two instances had to be destroyed and re-rented, contributing to ~$0.3-0.5 wasted.

**Fix.** Re-rented with pytorch/pytorch:2.8.0-cuda12.8-cudnn9-devel, the image already proven to accept SSH on the other arm.

**→ Rule.** Standardise on one image that has been proven to accept SSH, read vastai logs for the real sshd error instead of guessing, and treat an unreachable fresh instance as destroy-and-re-rent rather than a repair project.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · vendor-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · 27 steps of fold1 training had to be thrown away when MAX_PIXELS changed mid-round

**What happened.** fold1 already had checkpoint-25 (3.78 GB adapter, 27 steps) trained at MAX_PIXELS 7680. Continuing from it at 6912 would have mixed two image resolutions inside one fold's training.

**Root cause.** The resolution parameter had to change after training had already started because capacity was never validated in advance.

**Impact.** 27 steps of paid GPU time discarded and all four folds restarted from scratch.

**Fix.** Discarded the checkpoint and restarted all four folds clean at the new setting.

**→ Rule.** Validate resolution and memory settings before the first real step — any mid-run change to a data-shaping parameter invalidates everything trained before it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · money-burned</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · flash-linear-attention could not be installed because CUDA toolkit 12.8 clashed with torch cu13.0

**What happened.** The smoke test ran on a slow torch fallback path because flash-linear-attention would not install — the box had CUDA toolkit 12.8 against a torch cu13.0 build.

**Root cause.** The same torch/CUDA build mismatch from the dry-run round 4 also blocked optional accelerated kernels.

**Impact.** Inference was very slow (~20 minutes per page later), making page-level testing expensive in GPU time.

**Fix.** Gave up on installing it as not worth the time; later a different machine with torch 2.11+cu128 matching CUDA 12.8 proved ~20x faster and was recorded as the rental recipe.

**→ Rule.** Match the torch CUDA build to the image's CUDA toolkit at rental time — a mismatched pairing silently costs an order of magnitude in speed, not just optional features.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · A watcher process lost its SSH connection mid-operation, leaving the old queue running work that had been cancelled

**What happened.** A watcher was set to wait for plan_beam to finish, then kill and relaunch the queue. Its SSH dropped (exit 255) before completing the kill+relaunch, so the old queue proceeded to start `notes` — a task that had been cancelled — and overwrote the log. The GPU also sat idle for a short period.

**Root cause.** A multi-step control operation was run over a single fragile SSH session with no idempotency or state re-check.

**Impact.** A cancelled task started and overwrote a log; brief paid GPU idle time. No output files were lost.

**Fix.** Recovered by checking real machine state before trusting the log, then relaunching one command at a time rather than chaining.

**→ Rule.** Never run a multi-step kill-and-relaunch over a single SSH session; issue one command at a time, and re-check real machine state (ps) before believing any log.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · A GPU was rented after Makham had said to stop

**What happened.** Instance 49408084 was rented accidentally at a point when the instruction was to stop; it is listed in the day's card summary as such.

**Root cause.** An action proceeded past a stop instruction, likely from a queued or already-in-flight step.

**Impact.** Additional rental cost within the day's ~$10-11 total across 6 cards.

**Fix.** Card returned; all 6 confirmed destroyed with 0 instances remaining.

**→ Rule.** On a stop instruction, cancel queued and in-flight provisioning steps explicitly and confirm zero instances, rather than assuming nothing further will start.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · money-burned</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-01 · Rented vast.ai instance rejected a correct SSH key for minutes, forcing destroy-and-re-rent

**What happened.** Instance 49421807 (ssh3.vast.ai) refused the SSH key for several minutes even though the key matched the registered vast.ai account key exactly (fingerprint verified). This matched an already-documented lesson about misbehaving hosts.

**Root cause.** Vendor-side SSH key propagation lag / a bad host — not a local misconfiguration. The team's own key was verified correct before destroying, so the fault sat entirely with vast.ai's provisioning.

**Impact.** Several minutes of paid instance time plus destroy/re-rent cycle time during a demo-day session, contributing to the demo not finishing that day.

**Fix.** Destroyed the instance and rented a new one, per the pre-existing rule 'host มีอาการ = destroy แล้วเช่าใหม่'.

**→ Rule.** When a freshly rented host misbehaves and your own config verifies clean, destroy and re-rent immediately — do not spend more than a couple of minutes debugging someone else's provisioning. Verify the fingerprint first so you know it is theirs, not yours.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · vendor/infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-01 · A single failed status poll aborted the whole web flow while the job was still running fine

**What happened.** `pursonVision.js` threw an error and killed the entire flow if one poll request failed, even though the underlying job was still executing normally on the GPU.

**Root cause.** No distinction between 'the job failed' and 'one status request failed'. A transient polling error was treated as terminal job state.

**Impact.** Users lost visibility (and the flow) on a healthy job because of one dropped HTTP request.

**Fix.** Now tolerates 180 consecutive poll failures (~15 minutes) before giving up.

**→ Rule.** Polling errors and job errors are different things. A status-check failure must never terminate the work it is observing.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · resilience</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-01 · SSH tunnel had no keepalive or forward-failure detection, so it could die silently

**What happened.** The tunnel in `presentation.py` lacked `ServerAliveCountMax` and `ExitOnForwardFailure`, so it could go quiet or fail to establish forwarding without anyone noticing.

**Root cause.** Default SSH settings tolerate silence indefinitely and do not exit when port forwarding fails — so a broken tunnel looks identical to an idle one. This is the same underlying condition as the first bug of the day (job pending, tunnel not up).

**Impact.** Silent transport failures presenting as 'the job is just slow' — directly linked to the 7-minute zero-activity incident.

**Fix.** Added `ServerAliveCountMax=6` (tolerates 3 minutes of silence) and `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes`.

**→ Rule.** Any SSH tunnel that a pipeline depends on must run with keepalive and `ExitOnForwardFailure=yes` — a tunnel that fails silently is worse than one that never started.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · infra</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-01 · All network-resilience work was verified only by simulated tests, never against a real network drop on a live GPU run

**What happened.** The entire retry/timeout/keepalive hardening round was proven only with simulated tests. No real network outage during a real GPU run had ever been exercised.

**Root cause.** Live failure injection was skipped because it requires a running rental — the same cost pressure that makes the resilience matter in the first place.

**Impact.** Unknown whether the hardening actually holds under real conditions; false confidence in an untested safety net.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as pending.

**→ Rule.** Resilience code proven only by mocks is a hypothesis. Schedule one deliberate failure-injection run (pull the network for 60s mid-job) on a cheap rental before relying on it.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-02 · Checkpoint/resume shipped with unit tests only, never exercised against a real failed GPU job

**What happened.** The resume feature was covered by unit tests for `save_checkpoint` and the `claim_next_job` select, but had never been tried against a real job that failed on a real GPU.

**Root cause.** The realistic test requires a paid GPU and a real failure, so it was deferred to 'the next run will find out'.

**Impact.** An untested recovery path in exactly the situation it exists for — the moment you most need it working.

**Fix.** Not fixed at write time; the entry notes the house09 run would be the first real test.

**→ Rule.** A recovery path proven only by unit tests is unproven. Deliberately kill a job mid-run once on a cheap instance and verify resume actually skips the completed passes.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-09-02 · A self-selected vast.ai offer accepted the rental then reported resources unavailable and queued the state change

**What happened.** Makham rented a Switzerland offer at $1.23/hr from the vast.ai web page, then `vastai start instance` returned 'Required resources are currently unavailable, state change queued' — the host was not actually free. Diagnosed as a genuine vendor condition, not a script bug, and the machine was abandoned rather than waited on.

**Root cause.** vast.ai lists and accepts rentals for hosts that cannot actually start, and reports it only at the start step. Cheap offers are disproportionately likely to be in this state.

**Impact.** A wasted rental attempt and setup time; correctly abandoned instead of waiting.

**Fix.** Decision to drop that machine and not wait.

**→ Rule.** Treat 'state change queued' as a dead host, not a delay — abandon immediately. A suspiciously cheap offer that will not start is the vendor's problem, and waiting on it costs more than re-renting.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · vendor/infra</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-09 · Drag-resizable columns were requested but Label Studio's config language has no splitter

**What happened.** A request for a drag-resizable left column led to an investigation that found Label Studio provides no splitter tag in a self-authored config; the resize behaviour that does exist belongs to its own built-in Outliner/Details panel, a different part of the app.

**Root cause.** A feature was assumed available because it exists elsewhere in the same product's UI, without checking whether it is exposed to config authors.

**Impact.** Investigation time, and a fallback to a fixed 50/50 split applied across five files.

**Fix.** Implemented a fixed 50/50 layout (flex:1 1 0%; max-width:50%) on both columns in all 5 files.

**→ Rule.** Before promising a UI capability inside a third-party config DSL, confirm the tag exists in that DSL — seeing the behaviour in the vendor's own chrome proves nothing about what your config can do.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-09.md` · tooling/vendor-limitation</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-21 · Initial $9.49 GPU budget (~9 hours) ran out mid-session, needing a $10 top-up

**What happened.** The instance was started on a $9.49 balance sized at roughly 9 hours of runtime; the session ran far longer because of the bug-chasing, OOM rounds and GGUF work, and Makham had to top up another $10 (total ~$19) while the machine was live.

**Root cause.** The budget was sized against the *estimated* job time (~1 hour of training) with no allowance for the debugging that always accompanies a first run on a new machine — and the debugging happened on the meter because the scripts had never been rehearsed on a cheap box.

**Impact.** Roughly double the planned spend, plus the risk of the instance being killed for insufficient balance mid-training, which would have destroyed the run.

**Fix.** Topped up $10 mid-session.

**→ Rule.** Budget a rented GPU at 2–3× the estimated job time for a first run, and set a balance alert — an instance that dies for lack of credit mid-training loses everything on it, the same way a destroy does.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · cost/planning</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-21 · Repeatedly retried Jupyter on the rented GPU before switching to SSH

**What happened.** First attempts to reach the rented Vast.ai box went through Jupyter, which failed to open several times in a row, before the team researched and switched to SSH + tmux.

**Root cause.** Default/most-visible access path was chosen without first checking what practitioners actually use for long-running remote training; Jupyter drops sessions and has no detach story.

**Impact.** Wasted setup time at the start of a paid rental hour, plus repeated retries with no diagnosis.

**Fix.** Switched to SSH with key auth + tmux, which also enabled detaching from long jobs.

**→ Rule.** For any rented-GPU session, connect by SSH + tmux from the first minute; treat notebook UIs as a debugging convenience, never as the control channel for a multi-hour job.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · tooling/infra</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-24 · A HuggingFace 404 was briefly taken as an upload failure when the repo was simply private

**What happened.** Opening the HuggingFace model link in a browser returned 404. Checking via the API showed the repo is genuinely private (`"private":true`) — the browser was not logged into the `Sicilian44` account.

**Root cause.** A browser 404 on a private resource is indistinguishable from a missing resource without checking auth state.

**Impact.** Brief false alarm on a successful upload; correctly resolved by checking the API before concluding anything.

**Fix.** Checked directly through the HF API, then logged into the account in the browser; everything displayed correctly (35B params, qwen35moe, Q4_K_M 21.2GB).

**→ Rule.** Verify remote artifacts through the authenticated API, not an unauthenticated browser tab. A 404 on a private repo means 'not logged in' far more often than 'not uploaded'.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · tooling-infra</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-28 · House 07 A-30/31: headboard placed on the wrong wall and a sofa recorded as a bed in the dressing room

**What happened.** The bedroom headboard was recorded against the wrong wall (it is against the west wall), and an item described as 'bed in the dressing room' is actually the sofa belonging to bedroom 3.

**Root cause.** Furniture symbols were classified by rough outline similarity rather than by the legend and the room they sit in; orientation was assigned without reference to a compass or grid direction.

**Impact.** Wrong room contents and wrong orientation in the architectural record.

**Fix.** Corrected against the real images at zoom, reversals recorded.

**→ Rule.** Resolve every symbol against the legend and its containing room before recording it, and state orientation relative to a named datum (grid line or compass), never 'the wall it looks like it's on'.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-28 · The two diaries disagree on what t01's machine cost — one of the recorded prices must be wrong

**What happened.** 07-24 records the machine selected for t01 as m:67820 at $0.975/hour. 07-28 records the t02 machine at $1.161/hour and calls it '10.5x more expensive than t01', which implies t01 ran at roughly $0.11/hour. Both cannot be true: either t01 was not run on the machine Phase 0.5 selected, or one of the two prices is wrong.

**Root cause.** The machine actually rented was never written back into the record after Phase 0.5's selection, so cost comparisons are made against a selection rather than against what was billed.

**Impact.** Cost history is unreliable, and the '10.5x more expensive but only ~$3 different in practice' judgement that approved the expensive machine cannot be re-checked.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the discrepancy stands in the record.

**→ Rule.** Record the machine ID, hourly rate and final bill of the machine actually rented, not the one selected during planning. Cost comparisons across rounds are worthless otherwise.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · documentation inconsistency / cost tracking</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-28 · Assumed similar model size means similar training time — t02 took 2.9x longer than t01 with identical hyperparameters

**What happened.** With every hyperparameter verified identical, t01 (35B) finished training in 29:23 while t02 (30B) took 84:53 — 2.9x longer on the same class of card. The cause was internal architecture (layer count, image handling), not any misconfiguration.

**Root cause.** Time and cost were implicitly budgeted from the previous round's wall-clock on a similarly-sized model; parameter count was treated as a proxy for throughput.

**Impact.** Roughly an extra hour of paid GPU time on the t02 rental beyond what the t01 run would have predicted, on an account holding only $12.29.

**Fix.** Recorded as a lesson; no change to how future rentals are time-budgeted.

**→ Rule.** Never budget rental hours from parameter count — measure throughput on a short test run of the actual model before committing to a full run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · cost-estimation</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-29 · Phase 11 (destroy the rented instance) still not executed — an open billing exposure

**What happened.** The t01 workflow records Phase 0-10 complete but Phase 11, destroying the rented instance, still not done, held pending an explicit order from Makham.

**Root cause.** An over-correction from the 07-21 data-loss incident: destruction now requires a human order, but no counterpart rule caps how long an idle paid instance may sit waiting for that order.

**Impact.** Rented GPU time potentially billing while idle; the exact cost is not recorded in the diary.

**Fix.** Not fixed — still awaiting the explicit instruction.

**→ Rule.** Pair the 'never destroy without confirmation' rule with a 'confirm backup and decide within N hours' rule — an unbounded hold on a metered resource converts a safety rule into a money leak.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · cost-control</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-20 · Deployed-site login failed with 'Invalid login credentials' — cause could not be distinguished

**What happened.** Constistant login on the deployed site returned Invalid login credentials for Makham's account. Deploy and local point at the same Supabase project so it is not a config split; the most likely cause is that the account was simply never created, because Supabase returns the identical message for 'no such user' and 'wrong password'.

**Root cause.** Supabase deliberately returns an indistinguishable error for both cases (an anti-enumeration security feature), so the failure is unfalsifiable from the client side. Compounded by nobody having confirmed the account was ever created.

**Impact.** Time spent suspecting a deploy/config split that did not exist; the actual state of the account remained unconfirmed at end of session.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recommendation recorded: sign up to resolve it; demo projects need no login at all.

**→ Rule.** When an auth error is deliberately ambiguous by design, do not debug the deployment — verify account existence directly at the provider first, and note that demo paths that need no login are the faster way to unblock a demo.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · infra</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-25 · Vendor-side breakage: GLM-4.6V cannot be LoRA-trained, NVLM-D-72B cannot even run on vLLM

**What happened.** GLM-4.6V has an acceptable licence but an unfixed bug preventing LoRA fine-tuning. NVLM-D-72B is both CC-BY-NC (commercially unusable) and unrunnable on vLLM, which NVIDIA acknowledges on the HuggingFace forum.

**Root cause.** Published model weights do not guarantee a working training or serving path; framework support lags releases and vendors ship models with known unfixed defects.

**Impact.** Two of the very few surviving candidates are unusable for reasons unrelated to model quality, narrowing the viable set to essentially zero.

**Fix.** Both documented as blocked with the specific reason, so they are not re-evaluated from scratch next time.

**→ Rule.** For any candidate model, verify a working train path and a working serve path exist today before counting it as a candidate — and check the vendor's own issue tracker, not just the model card.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · vendor/tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-30 · Used `--max_steps 5` for a LLaMA-Factory CLI override; the parser breaks — it wants `key=value` with no dashes

**What happened.** The dry-run was first attempted with `--max_steps 5`, which crashed with an `HfArgumentParser` unused-keys error. The correct override syntax is `key=value` without the leading `--`.

**Root cause.** Assumed a standard argparse CLI convention for a framework that uses a different override mechanism, without checking its docs/examples first.

**Impact.** A failed dry-run attempt; small time cost on a rented GPU that was already billing.

**Fix.** Corrected to `max_steps=5`; dry-run then passed 5/5 steps.

**→ Rule.** Check a framework's own example invocation for CLI override syntax before running it on a billing machine — one failed launch on a rented GPU is pure waste.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · vendor-tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-30 · Plan assumed two separate rentals (cheap card for dry-run + big card for training); measurement showed one 96GB card covered both

**What happened.** The workflow was written around renting two different cards. The dry-run measured VRAM peak at 54.6GB of 97.9GB (~43GB spare), proving a single 96GB card was sufficient for both dry-run and full training.

**Root cause.** Resource planning was based on an unmeasured worst-case estimate rather than a measured peak.

**Impact.** Would have wasted a second rental's provisioning time and model-download time (~156GB per machine). Caught before the second rental for this purpose.

**Fix.** `t04_workflow.md` items 1 and 13 corrected to reflect a single card.

**→ Rule.** Measure actual peak VRAM in a 5-step dry-run before planning multi-GPU or multi-rental strategies — estimated requirements routinely over-provision.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-30 · Starting the server before onstart's pip install finished would fail the unsloth import and leave a health check that never goes green

**What happened.** `presentation.py` was restructured so onstart only installs dependencies, then `serve_purson.py` is scp'd up and only started after waiting for pip to complete (`while pgrep -f 'pip install'`).

**Root cause.** Race between the provider's onstart script and the operator's own start command — starting the server mid-install produces an import failure while the operator sits waiting on a health endpoint that will never respond.

**Impact.** Averted before it happened, but this is a burn-money-while-waiting failure mode: the GPU bills the whole time the health check never turns green.

**Fix.** Added an explicit wait for pip completion before issuing the run command.

**→ Rule.** Never start a service that depends on a provisioning script until you have positively confirmed provisioning finished — poll for the installer process to exit, don't sleep and hope.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra-cost</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-30 · HF token copied onto the fold3 card was never verified before that host went offline — the whole copy had to be redone on the replacement

**What happened.** To avoid asking Makham to retype a token, the `token` and `stored_tokens` files were copied from the fold0 card to the fold3 card via a local temp file (temp deleted, no token value in chat).
