The host went offline before the copy could be verified, so the work was thrown away and had to be repeated on the replacement card.

**Root cause.** Verification was treated as a separate later step rather than part of the copy operation, on a host that had already shown an abnormal signal at provision (`direct_port_start: -1`, proxy SSH only). Doing setup work on a host not yet trusted meant the work was at the host's mercy.

**Impact.** Small: one setup step repeated, plus the residual uncertainty of not knowing whether the copy had ever been correct.

**Fix.** Redone on the replacement instance (49175439); Makham ran `hf auth login` himself on the new card after provision, and all 4 cards were confirmed logged in later that night.

**→ Rule.** Verify immediately inside the same operation, not as a follow-up — and do not invest setup work in a host that showed an abnormal signal at provision until it has proven stable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · infra/process</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-31 · A rented instance's SSH proxy could not bind its forwarding port

**What happened.** One newly rented instance returned 'remote port forwarding failed for listen port 18712' — a stale port on the vast.ai proxy side, unfixable from inside the machine.

**Root cause.** Provider-side port allocation defect.

**Impact.** Instance destroyed and re-rented; part of the ~$0.3-0.5 wasted (no data lost since nothing had been uploaded yet).

**Fix.** Destroyed and rented a replacement.

**→ Rule.** Rent, connect, and verify SSH end to end before uploading anything — a provider-side networking fault is cheapest to discover while the machine is still empty.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · vendor-failure</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-31 · gpu3 failed to start with CUDA out of memory right after tmux kill-server, despite an empty GPU

**What happened.** On restart, gpu3 crashed with CUDA error: out of memory during unsloth import. nvidia-smi showed 0 MiB used and no lingering processes.

**Root cause.** Race condition — tmux kill-server had terminated the previous process but the driver had not yet released its VRAM when the new process started.

**Impact.** One wasted launch attempt during a time-critical restart.

**Fix.** Relaunched a second time and it started normally.

**→ Rule.** After killing a GPU process, poll nvidia-smi until the memory is actually released before launching the replacement, rather than launching immediately.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · infra</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-09-01 · A 90-minute auto-shutdown was armed at session start and had to be cancelled mid-session; a stale timer from a previous run was already pending

**What happened.** Task 1 of a session was `shutdown //s //t 5400`, and it had to first cancel an already-pending shutdown with `//a` (a leftover from an earlier run). The following session then had to cancel the 90-minute timer mid-work on Makham's order, because real work was still in progress when the machine was due to power off.

**Root cause.** The dead-man's-switch shutdown is armed unconditionally at the start of a run, with no link to whether the run is still producing work — and it is not cleared when a run ends early, so timers survive into the next session.

**Impact.** Near-miss loss of an in-progress session; every subsequent session inherits an unknown pending shutdown state it must defensively cancel first.

**Fix.** Cancelled manually both times (`shutdown //a`); no automatic disarm on job completion or on new-session start

**→ Rule.** An armed auto-shutdown must be disarmed by the thing that finishes the work, not by whoever happens to notice the clock — and a session should verify no stale timer is pending before it starts anything long.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-09-01.md` · ops</sub>

---

## T08 — Tooling Traps & Vendor Behaviour

*A tool or third-party service that behaved differently from what its docs, name, or output implied.*

**58 entries** · 2 critical · 14 high

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-24 · mmproj extraction failed because the tooling did not support the model, and it was only discovered with the job nearly done

**What happened.** During GGUF export on 2026-07-21 the mmproj (image-to-numbers projector) could not be extracted — the model was too new for the tooling. The result was a GGUF that read text only. This was found at the very end of the pipeline.

**Root cause.** Tooling support for a brand-new model architecture was assumed rather than verified, and the check sat at the last stage of a long expensive pipeline instead of at the front where it costs nothing.

**Impact.** An entire tuning round produced an unusable artefact for its stated purpose; the blocker sat unresolved from 07-21 to 07-24.

**Fix.** Established that finetune_vision_layers=False means the vision half is byte-identical to the base model, so the vendor's own published mmproj (899MB) can simply be downloaded and paired with the tuned GGUF — no extraction needed at all.

**→ Rule.** Verify tooling support for a new model architecture before training, not at export time. And when a component is provably untouched by training, take the vendor's published version instead of regenerating it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24(teach mk).md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-02 · The checker's first version would have merged away 4 footing groups carrying different confidence_flags

**What happened.** The first version of the duplicate-footing check judged duplicates by `confidence_score` and `note` alone. It would have merged away 4 groups whose entries each carry a *different* `confidence_flags` reason — including entries flagged `inferred_from_repeating_module`.

**Root cause.** The de-duplication key was built from the fields that came to mind, not from every field that can legitimately distinguish two entries.

**Impact.** Would have destroyed the record of which footing positions were read off the drawing versus inferred — irrecoverable provenance loss, presented as a clean 'fix'.

**Fix.** The checker now counts `confidence_flags` too; the 11 remaining groups are documented in §0.10 as an allowed exception so nobody 'fixes' them later.

**→ Rule.** A de-duplication key must include every field that can legitimately distinguish two entries — provenance fields especially. And document deliberate exceptions in the spec, or a future pass will 'clean them up'.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Lack of a zoom/crop tool made the new extraction rounds less accurate than the older Gen 2 that had real image zooming

**What happened.** Page 19 view2 (beam plan) still had low-confidence segments in round t2 (B1, top B3, B3X/B5X in the extension zone below A). The diary states this is 'better than t1 (structure is clearer) but still not as accurate as Gen 2, which had real image zooming', because there is no real zoom/crop tool available.

**Root cause.** Tooling capability was lost between generations — the Gen 2 workflow could zoom into the image, the Gen 3 hand/agent workflow could not. Nobody rebuilt the zoom/crop capability before starting two full extraction rounds that depend on reading fine detail.

**Impact.** A measurable accuracy regression against a previous generation across two rounds of work, on exactly the pages (beam plans) that carry the most valuable structural data. Multiple pages across both days were listed as needing someone to zoom in and re-verify.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recorded as a known limitation; page 19 view2 confidence improved but remains below Gen 2.

**→ Rule.** Before starting a new extraction generation, inventory the capabilities the previous generation had and confirm each one still exists. A rewrite that quietly loses a tool ships worse data while looking like progress — and a crop/zoom step is a prerequisite for fine-detail drawing reads, not an optimization.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · tooling-regression</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-10 · A background agent was killed mid-task having written zero files, leaving 10 BOQ pages empty for two days

**What happened.** Agent 4 (spread-footing BOQ, pages 49-58 of house #2) was terminated — either stopped manually or by the session closing, cause never confirmed — while still verifying item codes and before writing a single file. House #2 stood at 88 files covering 62 of 72 pages, and stayed incomplete until it was finished by hand on July 11.

**Root cause.** The agent's design buffered all its work until the end instead of writing each page as it finished, so a mid-task kill destroyed everything it had done; and no supervisor checked completion, so the gap was found only during validation.

**Impact.** 10 pages of a house missing for two days, blocking the label-studio run and the data-log entry for that house; the work had to be redone page by page manually.

**Fix.** Re-read pages 49-58 personally, one page at a time, on July 11, bringing house #2 to 107/107 files and 72/72 pages.

**→ Rule.** Long-running extraction agents must write each unit to disk as soon as it is finished, never buffer to the end — and always diff produced files against expected page coverage before declaring a house done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · agent-orchestration</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · Whether Unsloth can export GGUF for this MoE VL model at all was never established — and a known corrupted-GGUF issue existed upstream

**What happened.** At session close it remains unconfirmed whether Unsloth can export GGUF for this MoE VL model, with issue #3899 already reporting corrupted GGUF for Qwen3-VL-2B. Also unconfirmed: the real VRAM requirement of bf16 LoRA 30B-A3B, which was only estimated from t01 at ~74GB and judged from a TEST_STEPS=5 run.

**Root cause.** The delivery path's feasibility was assumed rather than checked against upstream issue trackers before committing a paid round to it, and a critical resource figure was extrapolated from a 5-step test rather than measured on a full run.

**Impact.** The round's headline deliverable (a runnable GGUF) was blocked by a limitation that a pre-flight search of the upstream issue tracker would likely have surfaced.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as unconfirmed, with the note that continuing means waiting for a new peft/unsloth release or writing the merge ourselves.

**→ Rule.** Before committing paid compute to a delivery path, search the toolchain's issue tracker for your exact model family. And never treat a figure extrapolated from a 5-step test as a confirmed resource requirement.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · tooling/planning</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S=1200 killed genuinely-running work at page 03

**What happened.** The timeout was calibrated from pages 01-02, which are the cover and the table of contents — the lightest pages in the book. Page 03 needed 1,256s and was killed at 1,200s. After raising it to 3,600 the page completed normally.

**Root cause.** The threshold sample was the first-encountered case, not the worst case. Pages 01-02 are structurally the cheapest content in any drawing set, so any budget derived from them under-covers everything else.

**Impact.** A restart of the run and lost wall-clock time on a job already running at ~13-21 min/page; briefly created a false impression that the job was hung.

**Fix.** fixed — REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S raised 1200 → 3600, page 03 then completed in 1,256s

**→ Rule.** Calibrate any timeout/threshold against the heaviest plausible case, never against whatever ran first. If the sample size is 2 and both samples are the cheapest items in the set, that is not a sample.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · The new §0.1 rule was too broad — it flagged 106 files and 104 of them were legitimate

**What happened.** The first draft of §0.1 banned any array called `sections` or `columns`. The new checker then flagged 106 files; opening them showed 104 were legitimate — `sections` in an `index` file means document sections, `columns` in a BOQ means table column headers. Only 2 were real violations.

**Root cause.** The rule banned a *name* rather than a *context*, ignoring that the same word means different things in different pattern types.

**Impact.** A 98% false-positive rate on a brand-new gate; had it been trusted, 104 correct files would have been 'fixed' into incorrectness.

**Fix.** Fixed the spec and the checker (not the data) to scope the ban by pattern context. Only the 2 genuine cases were changed.

**→ Rule.** When a new gate flags a large batch, open the hits before fixing anything — the gate is more likely wrong than 104 files. Ban by context, not by name.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-10 · check_format.py hardcoded 'letters = rows, digits = columns' — true for 18 houses, wrong on the 19th

**What happened.** The grid_ref validator in `tools/check_format.py` assumed letters always label rows and digits always label columns. House 19's structural sheets do the opposite — they letter the horizontal axis and number the vertical axis — so valid data failed the checker.

**Root cause.** A convention observed to hold across 18 consecutive houses was hardcoded as a universal rule; 18 samples from a limited set of publishers looked like proof.

**Impact.** The gate would have rejected correct data for house 19, and pressure would have been to 'fix' the house to match the checker — corrupting valid extraction to satisfy a wrong rule.

**Fix.** Changed the validator to accept either axis assignment; re-ran across all 19 houses with no regressions.

**→ Rule.** Do not hardcode an observed convention as a validation rule, no matter how many samples support it. When a gate fails on new data, first ask whether the gate is wrong — 18 houses of agreement is a pattern, not a law.

<sub>`2026-08-10.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · check_format.py has no page-completeness check, so a 38-page partial house passes as legitimately finished

**What happened.** Designing op04's partial-house mode required reading check_house() and confirming that check_format.py skips _-prefixed files and has no page-completeness check at all — so a folder holding 38 of 107 pages passes validation legitimately, indistinguishable from a finished house.

**Root cause.** The format checker validates per-file shape only. Completeness is a property of the folder, which nothing owns — and the extraction log records houses as done without recording scope.

**Impact.** Any partial house in the dataset is silently counted as complete, inflating apparent dataset size and misleading anyone sizing a training run. The house-24 stub pages from 08-18 have a related version of the same problem.

**Fix.** Introduced a required _scope.json marker keeping three separate lists (subtasks_done / subtasks_absent_from_this_house / deliberately_skipped) — the last two kept distinct because collapsing them destroys the only signal saying whether a page is missing or merely unwanted. Log rows for an op04 run must carry op04 / pass2-only.

**→ Rule.** A validator that checks per-item shape must be paired with a completeness marker at the collection level — and never collapse 'absent from source' with 'deliberately skipped', because that distinction is the only thing that tells a later reader whether data is missing or unwanted.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-26 · GLM-4.6V passes every criterion on paper but cannot be LoRA-trained due to an unfixed upstream bug

**What happened.** GLM-4.6V has an MIT licence, the right size, and would have been the second choice — but LLaMA-Factory issue #9635 raises NotImplementedError and nobody has fixed it, so LoRA training is impossible.

**Root cause.** Documented framework support does not mean working framework support. A model can be listed as supported while the actual code path throws.

**Impact.** Would have been discovered only after renting a GPU and attempting the run, had the team not checked the issue tracker during evaluation.

**Fix.** Caught during catalogue research; the criterion 'มีเครื่องมือเทรน LoRA ที่ยืนยันว่าใช้ได้จริง (ไม่ใช่แค่เอกสารอ้าง)' was applied explicitly.

**→ Rule.** Verify training-framework support by finding someone who actually ran it, or by checking the issue tracker for open blockers — never by reading a support matrix. Documentation claims are not evidence.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-28 · CV template scan detected footings well but found ~0 columns and beams — the experiment had to be cut back

**What happened.** Running pass 1.5+2.5 on 25 real plan pages across the 5 val houses showed footings detected reliably (9–20 points/page) but columns and beams at essentially zero. The night's 3-arm experiment had to be narrowed to `plan_footing` only.

**Root cause.** The template bank had exactly 1 column template and a single hardcoded BEAM_GAP value of 21px. One template cannot cover multiple drawing series, and one gap value is blind to any series using a different spacing.

**Impact.** The 3-arm CV-hint experiment could not test the subtask it was built for (plan_beam), on the night it was scheduled.

**Fix.** Same night: expanded the column bank 1→7 templates (hand-picked from a 78-candidate montage) and BEAM_GAP 21 → BEAM_GAPS (16,21) measured across 33 houses. cv_val was rescanned and both plan_footing and plan_beam became runnable.

**→ Rule.** Measure detector coverage across the whole corpus before scheduling an experiment that depends on it. A single hardcoded geometric constant will always be blind to half a heterogeneous dataset.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-28.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · LLaMA-Factory only warns (never errors) when a media file referenced via media_dir is missing

**What happened.** Reading LF source confirmed that the join in converter.py:58 emits a warning, not an error, for a missing image file.

**Root cause.** Vendor library chose a permissive failure mode for missing media, so a broken dataset can train to completion silently on partial input.

**Impact.** A run could complete looking healthy while having trained on missing images; risk mitigated only by a manual smoke check.

**Fix.** Verified all 1,416 path references resolve through media_dir with 0 missing, and made a smoke run mandatory before every training launch.

**→ Rule.** Assume media-loading libraries warn rather than fail; always run an explicit 'open every referenced file' pass before paying for a training run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · The training monitor produced SSHFAIL on every line for 7 hours and never alerted

**What happened.** watch4.sh was set to check every 10 minutes and wake on CRASHED or ALL_4_DONE. It returned SSHFAIL on every single line from the very first round for 7 hours, never obtaining real data, and never exited because SSHFAIL was not classified as CRASHED.

**Root cause.** The monitor was launched without verifying its first output, and its failure mode ('cannot connect') was treated as a pass-through rather than an alert condition.

**Impact.** Seven hours of unmonitored paid training; the two folds that OOM'd were found by manual check, not by the monitor.

**Fix.** Recorded as rule_of_tune Lesson 17: a monitor's first round of output must be eyeballed before walking away, and 'cannot connect' must be an alerting condition.

**→ Rule.** Never trust a monitor you have not watched produce one real reading, and make connection failure an alert, not a silent skip.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-bug</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · pkill -f <script name> over SSH matched and killed the SSH session itself — twice in one day

**What happened.** Because the SSH command line contains the script name being searched for, `pkill -f serve_purson.py` matched its own session and exited 255 before the following commands ran. First occurrence: the GPU-A queue would not die and required finding PIDs 3411/3412 directly. Second occurrence: a chained pkill; mv; nohup left no server running at all, undetected until ps -C python was checked and found empty.

**Root cause.** Pattern-matching process killers search the full command line, which includes the invoking command itself.

**Impact.** An unnoticed window with no inference server running — any job fired at the machine during it would have hit nothing.

**Fix.** New rule: never pkill by script name over SSH; use explicit PIDs or separate commands, and always verify real process state afterwards.

**→ Rule.** Never kill processes by a pattern that appears in your own command line; kill by PID and always confirm the intended process state afterwards rather than trusting the command returned.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · A wait-for-pip loop matched its own command line, so the inference server never started while the GPU billed

**What happened.** The launcher used `while pgrep -f 'pip install' > /dev/null; do sleep 10; done && nohup ... serve_purson.py`. The bash process's own command line contains the string 'pip install', so pgrep always found itself and the condition was permanently true. On instance 49411642, pip finished at about minute 3 but the loop kept spinning for ~17 more minutes with 2 MiB GPU usage and no purson.log line — it looked exactly like a 70GB model load in progress.

**Root cause.** Same self-matching class as the pkill bug: a pattern search over command lines that includes the searcher.

**Impact.** ~17 minutes of paid GPU time doing nothing, disguised as normal startup; the third occurrence of this exact bug class in a single day.

**Fix.** Changed the pattern to '[p]ip install' so the bracket makes the regex not match the literal string in its own command line; proved both patterns against a real regex before committing.

**→ Rule.** Any pgrep/pkill/ps-grep pattern must be written so it cannot match the process issuing it (bracket trick), and a wait loop must be proven to terminate on a real machine before it is trusted.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · The 'command searches its own command line' bug class occurred three times in a single day

**What happened.** pkill -f killing its own SSH session (twice) and pgrep -f matching its own wait loop (once) are the same defect class, hit three times within one day across different scripts.

**Root cause.** No standing rule existed about pattern-matching over process command lines, so each instance was fixed locally without generalizing.

**Impact.** An unnoticed window with no server running, ~17 minutes of idle billed GPU, plus repeated debugging time.

**Fix.** Recorded the class explicitly with two concrete mitigations: use PIDs instead of name patterns, and bracket the first character of any pattern.

**→ Rule.** Treat any pgrep/pkill/ps-grep by name as unsafe by default — use PIDs, or bracket the pattern, and generalize the fix to every script the moment the class is identified.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · IDE auto-created a 0-byte file at the moved document's old path, making it look like 24KB of work had been lost

**What happened.** Makham found the file at its old Training-repo path was empty and asked where the data had gone. Investigation showed the full 24,120 bytes were intact at the new Constistant path, and that a new 0-byte file had appeared on its own at the old path on July 6 at 16:03 — presumed to be the IDE creating an empty file when opening a path that no longer had a file.

**Root cause.** The editor was still holding a tab or bookmark pointing at the pre-move path; opening and saving that phantom path materialized an empty file. The underlying enabler was the previous day's move without updating references or closing stale editor state.

**Impact.** A false data-loss scare and an investigation session. The empty decoy file then sat in the repo as a trap for anyone who found it before the real file, and the decision to delete it remained unanswered through the end of both days.

**Fix.** Confirmed no data was lost, located the intact 24,120-byte file, and recommended deleting the empty decoy. Deletion was never confirmed.

**→ Rule.** After moving a file, close every editor tab pointing at the old path and verify the old path is truly gone before ending the session. A 0-byte file at a known-good path is worse than a missing file — it reads as corruption rather than as a move.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · tooling-trap / false-alarm</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · TextArea with rows>1 silently adds a '+Add' multi-value button, which would corrupt single-value fields

**What happened.** While trying to make the grid_ref box bigger, a documentation search revealed that a Label Studio `TextArea` with `rows > 1` unintentionally shows a '+Add' button allowing extra items — so it must never be used for a field meant to hold exactly one value. The box was widened with CSS instead.

**Root cause.** A visual sizing property in Label Studio carries a hidden semantic side effect (single-value becomes multi-value). This is discoverable only in the docs, not from the attribute name.

**Impact.** Caught before shipping. Had rows been used, human reviewers could have entered multiple values into single-value fields such as grid_ref, silently corrupting reviewed ground truth in a way that would be very hard to trace back.

**Fix.** Widened the grid_ref box with `style="width:100%; min-width:380px; font-size:14px;"` and did not add rows. Recorded as a rule.

**→ Rule.** Read the tool's own docs before styling its widgets — search first, do not guess. In annotation tooling specifically, any property that could turn a single-value field into a multi-value one is a data-integrity risk, not a layout choice.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · Config must be pasted before tasks are imported, or already-failed tasks must be deleted first

**What happened.** After fixing the multi-variable XML bug, the recovery required a specific order: paste the fixed XML into Settings → Labeling Interface → Code → Save first, then import the task JSON. If tasks had already been imported while the config was broken, those failed tasks had to be deleted before retrying.

**Root cause.** Label Studio validates task data against the labeling config at import time and stores the result, so a broken config poisons imports permanently rather than transiently. There is no re-validation when the config is later fixed.

**Impact.** An extra cleanup step on every recovery, and a trap where re-importing over failed tasks appears to do nothing. Compounds with the separate stale-task-data trap found earlier the same day.

**Fix.** Documented the required order explicitly, and noted the task JSON itself did not need regenerating since the fault was in the XML config, not the data.

**→ Rule.** In Label Studio, config changes are not retroactive: always fix and save the labeling config before importing, and delete previously failed or stale tasks rather than importing over them. Write the recovery order down next to the tool, not just in the session log.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · Label Studio's lack of layout switching was worked around by duplicating each config into freeze-L/freeze-R twins, so every later fix had to be applied 4-5 times

**What happened.** Because Label Studio's spec allows no custom JS, the 'freeze image left or right' request was implemented as separate mirrored files (elements.xml + elements-freezeR.xml, single.xml + single-freezeR.xml), with the markup positions physically swapped rather than reordered by CSS. From that point on every subsequent change had to be made in all copies — the $variable import bug alone required fixing 7 spots across 5 XML files, and the <Style>/grid_ref-width change had to be mirrored again.

**Root cause.** A vendor limitation was answered with copy-paste duplication instead of a generator (the task files were already generated by a Node script that could equally have emitted both XML variants from one template), so an N-way fan-out of the same content was accepted with no mechanism keeping the copies in sync.

**Impact.** Every fix carried a 4-5× multiplier and a silent drift risk — the material_list.xml freezeR variant was in fact never made, so that config already diverged from its siblings on day one.

**Fix.** not fixed — copies were kept and hand-mirrored each round; one variant (material_list freezeR) deliberately skipped

**→ Rule.** When a tool forces duplicated config, generate the variants from one source rather than hand-mirroring them — otherwise every later bug fix becomes an N-file chore and the copies drift.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-09 · 'Permission denied' when renaming the folder back looked like data damage; it was another program holding it open

**What happened.** During the undo, mv and Rename-Item both failed with Permission denied on the renamed folder. Writing and deleting files inside it worked normally, which isolated the failure to renaming the folder itself — a Windows lock from another program (File Explorer, another terminal) holding it as its working directory. Once that program was closed, the rename succeeded.

**Root cause.** Windows locks a directory when any process has it as a current working directory, blocking rename/delete of the directory while leaving its contents fully writable — a failure mode whose error message says nothing about the cause.

**Impact.** The undo of a 533 MB folder stalled mid-way with the repo in a half-renamed state, and briefly looked like data corruption.

**Fix.** Tested writing a file inside the folder to prove the contents were fine, reverted the code changes while waiting, then retried the rename after the holding program was closed.

**→ Rule.** On Windows, 'Access denied' on a folder rename means a process holds it open, not that data is damaged — prove it by writing a file inside, close the holder, and retry before escalating.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-09.md` · os/tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-10 · Every extraction round was validated with a throwaway ad-hoc script

**What happened.** Validation (JSON parses, source_image present, page coverage, pattern completeness) was performed by writing a fresh one-off script each round, with no standard reusable checker — and one of those ad-hoc scripts had itself produced a false all-61-files-missing result two days earlier.

**Root cause.** Validation was treated as a per-round chore rather than as part of the pipeline, so nothing accumulated.

**Impact.** Inconsistent checks between rounds, re-written code each time, and at least one false failure caused by the throwaway script rather than the data.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as pending item 4: write a standard validation script.

**→ Rule.** The check that decides whether a dataset is complete must itself be a committed, tested artifact — an ad-hoc validator is one more unverified thing between you and the truth.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · process/tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Built llama.cpp with CUDA three times unsuccessfully — CUDA was never needed

**What happened.** Three consecutive attempts to build llama.cpp with CUDA failed (cmake could not find nvcc; CUDA auto-detected itself even with the flag explicitly OFF; PowerShell's own interpretation mangled $PATH, breaking that window too).

**Root cause.** The requirement was never questioned — GGUF conversion and quantization are pure CPU work, so the whole CUDA build was unnecessary effort chasing an accidental dependency.

**Impact.** Three failed build cycles plus a corrupted shell PATH, all during a paid rental.

**Fix.** Rebuilt CPU-only with `-DGGML_CUDA=OFF` in a fresh clean window; conversion/quantization then worked.

**→ Rule.** Before fighting a build, ask whether that build option is needed at all — convert/quantize steps are CPU-only, so build the minimum configuration the task actually requires.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Converted to q8_0 first to save disk; llama-quantize refuses to requantize from q8_0

**What happened.** To save space the model was converted to q8_0 first, but `llama-quantize` rejected it with 'requantizing from type q8_0 is disabled', forcing a second full conversion from f16 (~70GB).

**Root cause.** An optimisation was applied without checking the tool's supported conversion paths; quantized formats are not valid sources for further quantization.

**Impact.** A wasted full conversion pass plus the disk pressure of producing the much larger f16 file anyway — the exact cost the shortcut was meant to avoid.

**Fix.** Re-converted from f16 and quantized to Q4_K_M (66,152 MiB → 20,176 MiB, 21.2GB file).

**→ Rule.** Always quantize from the full-precision source (f16/bf16); check a tool's supported input formats before inventing a space-saving shortcut.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · PowerShell's own interpretation mangled $PATH and broke the working terminal window

**What happened.** While trying to build llama.cpp with CUDA, cmake couldn't find nvcc; during the attempts to point it at CUDA, `$PATH` was mangled by PowerShell interpreting the variable itself, corrupting that terminal window's PATH so nothing in it worked correctly afterwards. The build only succeeded after moving to a fresh clean window.

**Root cause.** Typing shell commands containing `$PATH`/env-var syntax through PowerShell, which expands `$` differently from bash — the command that was meant to run on the remote/bash side was rewritten by the local shell before it ever got there. Compounded by trying to repair the environment in the same window that was already damaged.

**Impact.** Extra failed build attempts and a dead terminal window; contributed to the three consecutive failed CUDA builds before the CPU-only path was taken.

**Fix.** Built with `-DGGML_CUDA=OFF` in a fresh clean window (new session, uncorrupted PATH).

**→ Rule.** When a shell environment starts behaving wrongly (PATH, env vars), open a brand-new window instead of repairing in place; and never let PowerShell interpret `$VAR` syntax that is meant for the remote bash shell — quote it or write it into a script file.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · tooling/shell</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Training script printed its success line but kept running a ~15-minute sample-generation step, making a busy job look finished

**What happened.** `train_qwen36.py` prints `✓ Saved LoRA adapter` and then runs a bonus step generating 3 sample answers, which takes many minutes. Operators read the success line as "done", typed the next command, and were confused when the new log file never appeared. Investigation via process list showed the original script had been running 885 seconds — far longer than the 5-step test should take.

**Root cause.** The script's most visible completion signal is emitted well before the script actually exits; there is no "ALL DONE" marker at the true end. This same trailing step is also what broke when the environment was clobbered by the parallel pip install.

**Impact.** Wasted investigation time, a queued command that silently didn't run, and a near-miss where an env break during that step could have hit before the adapter was saved.

**Fix.** Diagnosed by checking running processes and which log file the process had open; the queued command started on its own once the first finished.

**→ Rule.** Judge completion by the shell prompt returning or by `ps`, never by a log line; and put the final success banner at the true end of a script, after every optional/bonus step.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21(teach mk).md` · tooling/script-design</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Typed the full-training command into a busy terminal, then panicked that full_train.log did not exist

**What happened.** After the 5-step smoke test appeared finished, the full 3-epoch command was typed into the same terminal. Later the expected full_train.log was missing entirely, causing a confused investigation.

**Root cause.** The smoke-test script had not actually exited — its final bonus step (generating 3 sample answers) was still running for ~885 seconds, so the shell had queued the new command instead of executing it. 'Training finished' on screen was mistaken for 'process exited'.

**Impact.** Time lost to a false alarm and to investigating a missing log file; risk of typing the command a second time and launching a duplicate expensive run.

**Fix.** Checked the running process list and its open log file, confirming the old script was still writing to test_run.log and the new command was merely queued.

**→ Rule.** Never judge a job finished from console text — wait for the shell prompt to return, or verify with a process check. When a log file is missing, check whether the command ever started before assuming it failed.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · process/tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-01 · VSCode auto-commit swept the remaining split files back into one 2.4GB chunk mid-push

**What happened.** Partway through pushing the ~500MB batches, a VSCode auto-commit gathered all the remaining files into a single 2.4GB commit — back over the cap — and the split had to be redone.

**Root cause.** An editor-side auto-commit feature was active while a manual, carefully staged history-splitting operation was in progress; nothing disabled or guarded against it.

**Impact.** The splitting work was partially undone and had to be redone, extending an already long recovery session.

**Fix.** Re-split the 2.4GB chunk and continued pushing batch by batch until complete.

**→ Rule.** Turn off editor auto-commit/auto-stage before any manual git surgery (history rewrite, staged splitting, rebase). An IDE writing to the index behind you will silently undo your staging.

<sub>`2026-08-01.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · First id-warning pass was too broad — flagged 1,059 legitimate ids and polluted 205 files with noise

**What happened.** The first pass at flagging unjoinable element ids flagged 1,059 ids that were legitimately descriptive (dimensions, rooms, windows), adding noise warnings to 205 files. All of it had to be removed and redone narrowly.

**Root cause.** The heuristic tested 'does this id look descriptive?' instead of 'is this a structural element whose id fails to join?' — the wrong question, so it matched everything descriptive.

**Impact.** 205 files polluted with false warnings and a full redo of the pass; worse, a flood of false warnings trains people to ignore warnings.

**Fix.** Removed all the noise warnings; re-scoped to flag only structural elements whose id genuinely cannot be joined.

**→ Rule.** Test a flagging heuristic on a sample and read the hits before running it over the corpus. A warning system that cries wolf gets ignored, which is worse than having no warnings.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · A known footgun: a bulk regex written for grid refs also matches sheet_code values

**What happened.** The sheet_code regex footgun, recorded as items 26/31 in สิ่งที่ต้องแก้.md, was serious enough to be folded into primary_rawjson_schema.md as a standing warning. In the round-3 grid_ref rewrite it was avoided only by restricting the edit to grid_ref/grid_ref_start/grid_ref_end/grid_refs fields — the diary explicitly notes this made it 'impossible by construction, not merely avoided by care'.

**Root cause.** Grid references (C-1, D-E) and sheet codes (S-05, A-16) are the same letter-dash-digit shape, so any pattern-based bulk edit aimed at one hits the other.

**Impact.** Recorded twice as a hazard requiring active defence on every bulk edit touching these values; the original occurrence cost enough to be written into the spec.

**Fix.** Warning folded into primary_rawjson_schema.md; subsequent bulk edits scoped by field name rather than by regex over whole files

**→ Rule.** Scope a bulk edit by field path, never by value pattern, when two different fields share a text shape. Make the safety structural, not a matter of being careful.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-02.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-09 · A bug in the op01/op03 skill wrapper created on 08-05 had to be fixed on 08-09

**What happened.** A bug was found and fixed in `.claude/skills/op01/SKILL.md` and the README — the skill wrapper created on 2026-08-05 to avoid re-reading the full README on every op01/op03 trigger.

**Root cause.** The skill file is a synced *copy* of the canonical README, so the two can drift; a copy created for convenience became a second source of truth with nothing checking it against the original.

**Impact.** Houses extracted between 08-05 and 08-09 ran under a buggy workflow definition.

**Fix.** Fixed both the skill file and the README.

**→ Rule.** A synced copy of a canonical document needs a drift check, or it will diverge. Prefer having the skill reference the canonical file over duplicating its content.

<sub>`2026-08-09.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Overlay prototype hardcoded ELEMENT_TYPES to footing and column, ignoring all beams

**What happened.** ELEMENT_TYPES = ("footing", "column") is hardcoded in the King-try prototype; line elements (beams) are not handled anywhere in diff, render, or calibration.

**Root cause.** The prototype was validated on one page (house 01 หน้า19, a footing/column plan) and the element-type list was frozen to what that one page contained, rather than driven from the schema's element taxonomy.

**Impact.** The overlay cannot display or verify beams — which are the exact elements the whole pipeline struggles with most (11% recall) and the one thing an overlay would be most valuable for.

**Fix.** Not fixed — one of the 3 open King-try gaps.

**→ Rule.** Never freeze a type list to what the single validation sample contained; drive it from the schema, and pick a validation sample that includes the hardest element class, not the easiest.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · reportlab cannot shape Thai text — PDF generation had to be rebuilt on headless Edge

**What happened.** The new tools/md_to_book_pdf.py renders md → PDF via Edge headless rather than reportlab, because Thai requires real text shaping (vowels and tone marks stacking on the base glyph) which a browser performs and reportlab does not.

**Root cause.** reportlab has no complex-script shaping engine; the obvious Python-native choice for PDF generation silently produces broken Thai rather than erroring, so it looks like it works until a Thai reader sees the output.

**Impact.** Would have produced a 7-page Thai chapter with mispositioned vowels and tone marks appended to a 24-page Thai book. Avoided by choosing the browser renderer up front.

**Fix.** tools/md_to_book_pdf.py renders through Edge headless with automatic .bak.pdf before every overwrite. Book verified 24 → 31 pages, with the new pages extracting identically in style to the original 24.

**→ Rule.** For any Thai (or complex-script) document output, use a real shaping engine — a browser renderer — and verify by extracting text back out of the produced PDF; a library that silently drops shaping produces output that only fails on visual inspection.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-24 · An op04 agent hit an API session limit and left a GT file truncated mid-write

**What happened.** `31บ้าน_เล็ก_1ชั้น_11 หน้า25_plan_footing.json` was cut off mid-file because the op04 extraction agent hit an API session limit, as its own `_scope.json` recorded.

**Root cause.** Agents write GT files incrementally with no atomic-write or completion marker per file, so an interrupted agent leaves a syntactically invalid partial file indistinguishable from a corrupt one.

**Impact.** One page of GT lost; the dataset builder had to skip it. If the builder had silently repaired it, fabricated data would have entered training.

**Fix.** The builder skips it and reports the filename by name rather than guessing values to repair it.

**→ Rule.** Write GT files atomically (temp file + rename) and record per-file completion. A dataset builder must skip-and-report a malformed file, never repair it by inference.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Column and beam detection ship on one hand-cropped template and one code-synthesized template respectively — neither ever harvested

**What happened.** While the footing bank grew to 14 harvested templates across many houses, the column bank still holds exactly one template cropped from บ้าน 17, and the beam "template" is not a template at all — it is two parallel dark lines synthesized in code at a gap measured off a single page of บ้าน 17. Neither has been harvested across houses or series.

**Root cause.** Harvesting was built and iterated for footings only (GT filenames identify foundation-plan pages), and the other two classes were left on their bootstrap artifacts while their numbers were still being quoted in verification results.

**Impact.** Every column/beam count reported (14 columns, 17 beam bands, 13 columns, 19 beam bands) rests on a one-house sample; the two classes are far less validated than the footing numbers reported beside them, which reads as equal confidence.

**Fix.** not fixed — "harvest ฝั่ง column/beam ยังไม่เริ่ม" left as next-round work.

**→ Rule.** When one class of a multi-class detector is validated far more than the others, say so beside the numbers — otherwise a single well-tested class lends unearned credibility to the rest.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-26 · Unsloth does not work with InternVL3-78B, and Llama-4-Scout on Unsloth is 4-bit only

**What happened.** The catalogue records that InternVL3-78B can only be LoRA-trained via LLaMA-Factory or ms-swift — Unsloth does not work with it. Separately, Llama-4-Scout on Unsloth is restricted to 4-bit only, with full-precision training requiring LLaMA-Factory on 8×H100.

**Root cause.** Training-framework support is per-model and per-precision, not a general property. Assuming the familiar tool works for a new model architecture is unfounded.

**Impact.** Choosing a model without checking framework compatibility per-model would have wasted setup time; the 4-bit-only restriction on Unsloth is also precisely the constraint that later destroyed t44's vision encoder.

**Fix.** Recorded per-row in the catalogue table with the specific framework and its restriction.

**→ Rule.** Record, for every candidate model, which specific training framework works and at which precision. A framework that only supports 4-bit is a red flag for any vision task — that constraint is what blinds the vision encoder.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · tooling</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-28 · Column template bank still misses 13 houses; sub-gaps and the whole slab class remain uncovered

**What happened.** After the column bank expansion, 16 of 30 houses match GT. The remaining 13 houses have only garbage candidates and need manual cropping. Sub-pixel beam gaps of 8/11/24/39/44px and the entire slab class have no coverage at all.

**Root cause.** Template harvesting depends on automated candidate mining that only succeeds where an existing template already catches something — the same ceiling noted in the self-harvest work. Series never caught cannot bootstrap themselves.

**Impact.** CV hints are unavailable for 13 houses' columns, all sub-gap beam series, and every slab page — silently degrading any arm that depends on them for those pages.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as outstanding work requiring manual crops.

**→ Rule.** A bootstrapping detector cannot discover a series it has never seen. Budget explicit manual seeding for uncovered series, and report coverage per house so "no hint" is visible rather than silent.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-28.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-29 · Subagents hit a spend limit for an entire session — all op04 extraction had to be done by hand

**What happened.** During op04 extraction of two new houses (บ้านไทยพอเพียง 1 and 2), subagents were blocked by a spend limit for the whole session, so all extraction — S sheets (11+12), A-11 doors/windows, A-09/A-06 z_levels and roof form — was done directly instead of in parallel.

**Root cause.** No spend-limit check before dispatching a parallelizable workload, and no fallback plan for when the parallel path is unavailable.

**Impact.** An op04 run designed for 20 parallel agents ran single-threaded for an entire session.

**Fix.** Completed manually; both houses passed check_format ALL CHECKS (22 items) on the first attempt.

**→ Rule.** Check the spend/quota budget before committing to a parallel-agent workload, and have the serial fallback plan and its time cost written down in advance.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-30 · The CV template bank is built from these 40 houses only — a new customer's drafting office may match nothing, and self-harvest cannot bootstrap without a seed

**What happened.** The CV template bank holds 17 templates (14 footing, 3 column) with beams not using the bank at all, and harvest coverage across the library is 23 houses matched / 19 missing / 2 false-positive. Since the bank is derived only from the 40-house library, a new customer using a different drafting office with different icons may get zero detections — and the pass2.5 self-harvest mechanism cannot help because it needs at least one seed template to start from.

**Root cause.** A template-matching approach was scaled on an in-house corpus without a mechanism for bootstrapping onto an unseen drawing convention.

**Impact.** Unresolved production risk: CV assistance may contribute nothing for a real new customer, which undermines the whole 'Python CV helps extract elements' argument for the current architecture.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Proposal recorded but not implemented: have the user click 1-2 examples on their own drawing to create per-project templates, then let self-harvest sweep the rest — converting an unsolvable generalization problem into two clicks.

**→ Rule.** Any pattern/template system trained on an internal corpus needs an explicit cold-start path for unseen conventions; design the bootstrapping UX at the same time as the matcher, not after.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · data-pipeline</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Own inspection script read the wrong field name and concluded the CV boxes had no coordinates

**What happened.** While starting to eyeball beam pages, a self-written checking script reported that bbox had no coordinates. The data actually had cx, cy, w, h all present — the script queried the wrong field name.

**Root cause.** The verification tool itself was unverified; a missing field was interpreted as missing data instead of a possible tool defect.

**Impact.** Nearly steered the whole beam-matching approach toward manual eyeballing on a false premise about the data.

**Fix.** Found the real fields and pivoted to geometric matching using the real pixel coordinates.

**→ Rule.** When a check reports 'the data is missing X', first prove the checker reads the right field on a known-good record — a broken checker looks exactly like broken data.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-bug</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Instance status-polling loop called python3, which on Windows is a broken Store alias, so it spun forever

**What happened.** A loop polling instance status invoked python3 every 15 seconds. On this machine python3 is a Microsoft Store alias stub, so the loop failed silently and never terminated, long after all cards were already running.

**Root cause.** The interpreter name was assumed portable and the loop's first iteration was never checked for real output.

**Impact.** Wasted wall-clock waiting on a loop that had never produced data, while the GPUs were already up and billing.

**Fix.** Use plain python or grep instead; recorded so it does not recur.

**→ Rule.** Verify the very first iteration of any polling loop actually produced real data before walking away from it — and never assume python3 exists on a Windows shell.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-bug</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Two Windows packaging traps: Python-written manifest got CRLF, and tar read D:/ as a remote host

**What happened.** While bundling the 771MB upload, the image manifest written by Python came out with CRLF line endings, and tar interpreted a D:/... path as a remote host specification.

**Root cause.** Default text-mode newline handling on Windows and tar's host:path syntax colliding with drive letters.

**Impact.** Bundle creation would have failed or produced a manifest the Linux side could not read.

**Fix.** Open the manifest with newline='\n' and use /d/... form for tar paths.

**→ Rule.** On Windows, always write cross-platform manifests with explicit newline='\n' and use MSYS-style /d/ paths for tar — never a drive-letter path.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Visual-token warning compared against the global cap, so it fired on every legitimately small image

**What happened.** The 'visual tokens more than 25% below cap' warning compared against the global cap rather than the ceiling that row could actually reach, so it warned every time a source image was naturally smaller than the cap (2339x1654 = 3.87 MP = 3,778 tokens by exact math, measured 3,796 — not downscaled at all).

**Root cause.** The alarm's baseline was a constant instead of a per-row computed expectation.

**Impact.** Constant false warnings that would have masked a real downscaling problem.

**Fix.** Compare against min(actual pixels, MAX_PIXELS)/1024 per row, and print a positive confirmation instead.

**→ Rule.** An alarm's threshold must be computed per item from what that item should legitimately achieve — a global constant baseline turns a detector into noise.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-bug</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · PEFT's add_weighted_adapter cannot merge MoE adapters using target_parameters

**What happened.** The planned merge path via PEFT's add_weighted_adapter turned out to be unusable for MoE with target_parameters (one adapter per model), confirmed against TRL issue #5222.

**Root cause.** Library limitation not checked before designing the merge step.

**Impact.** Merge script had to be rewritten to add tensors manually (soup_safetensors.py) while GPUs were still billing.

**Fix.** Wrote soup_safetensors.py to sum tensors directly.

**→ Rule.** Verify that the intended library API supports your specific architecture before designing the final assembly step of an expensive pipeline.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · Naming the merged adapter 'destrier' would have hidden it in a subfolder with no files at repo root

**What happened.** PEFT saves any adapter not named 'default' into a subfolder, so publishing the merged adapter under the name destrier would have produced a HuggingFace repo with no files at the root. The merge script also would have pushed all four source adapters.

**Root cause.** An assumption that the adapter name is cosmetic, when it determines the on-disk layout.

**Impact.** Would have shipped a repo that consumers could not load; caught before push.

**Fix.** Named the merged adapter 'default' and added delete_adapter for the source folds before pushing.

**→ Rule.** Check how a serialization library maps names to paths before choosing a name, and verify the published artifact's file layout, not just that the upload succeeded.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · New rental template had no /workspace and plain pip installed into the wrong Python

**What happened.** Renting with vastai/pytorch:cuda-12.8.1-auto, scp failed immediately because /workspace does not exist, and plain `pip` installed into the system Python (/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages) rather than /venv/main which actually holds torch — everything installed successfully yet `python -c "import unsloth"` failed with 'python: command not found'.

**Root cause.** Template layout differs between vast.ai images, and the first executable named pip on PATH is not the one belonging to the torch environment.

**Impact.** Lost setup time on a billing machine and produced installs that appeared to succeed but were unusable.

**Fix.** mkdir -p /workspace first and use /venv/main/bin/pip and /venv/main/bin/python explicitly for every command; recorded in op04_gpu_setup.sh.

**→ Rule.** On any new rental template, verify the working directory exists and resolve the absolute path of the Python that owns torch before installing anything — never rely on bare pip/python.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-trap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · presentation_state.json kept a stale instance id after the card was returned

**What happened.** After destroying an instance, the local state file still held its id, so the tooling believed a machine existed that did not.

**Root cause.** Local state was written on create but never reconciled against the provider on read.

**Impact.** Misleading state that could hide a genuinely-running billed instance or point commands at a dead one.

**Fix.** current_instance() now asks vast.ai whether the id actually exists and clears the state if not; if the provider cannot be queried it trusts the state and over-warns rather than letting money run silently.

**→ Rule.** Reconcile any local record of a billed cloud resource against the provider on every read, and bias toward over-warning when the provider cannot be reached.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling-bug</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · The merge script would have uploaded all four source fold adapters alongside the merged one

**What happened.** merge_adapters_soup.py loaded each fold's adapter into the model to average them, and would then have pushed every loaded adapter to the destrier repo, not just the merged result.

**Root cause.** PEFT pushes all adapters currently attached to the model; the script never detached the source adapters before push.

**Impact.** Caught before push — would otherwise have put 4 stray adapters in the destrier repo, making it ambiguous which weights the repo actually serves.

**Fix.** call delete_adapter on each source fold before pushing

**→ Rule.** Before pushing a model, enumerate what is actually attached to it — a push uploads state, not intent.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-06 · Two git config commands pasted back-to-back with no separator produced 'no action specified'

**What happened.** Makham ran `git config --global user.name "makham"git config --global user.email "chaichana.ju@ku.th"` in PowerShell and got 'no action specified'. The two commands had been pasted with no space or newline between them, so PowerShell merged `"makham"` and `git` into the single token `makhamgit`, turning the whole line into one git config call with garbled arguments.

**Root cause.** The source the commands were copied from presented them without a visible line break, and PowerShell tokenized the concatenation into a valid-looking single command instead of erroring on the join point — so the error message pointed at the arguments, not at the real problem.

**Impact.** Small time loss and a confusing error message. Git identity was left unconfigured until Makham ran the corrected commands himself.

**Fix.** Explained the cause and gave the correct syntax (separate lines, or separated by `;`). Deliberately not run by the agent, per the Git Safety Protocol that git config is never modified directly.

**→ Rule.** Hand over multi-command snippets one command per line, or explicitly joined with `;`. And keep the rule that an agent explains git config rather than executing it — the safety protocol held correctly here.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · shell-usage</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-21 · scp -P vs ssh -p port flag case mismatch caused failed upload attempts

**What happened.** The dataset upload with scp failed at first because scp takes an uppercase -P for the port while ssh takes lowercase -p.

**Root cause.** Assumed flag parity between two tools from the same suite instead of checking each command's own syntax.

**Impact.** Minor confusion and retries at the start of the 158MB / 320-file dataset upload.

**Fix.** Used `scp -P 24400 -r data_before_tune/ root@...:/workspace/tune/` and noted the difference in the diary.

**→ Rule.** Write the exact working command (with flags) into the runbook the first time it succeeds; never assume two related CLI tools share flag casing.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-07-24 · Assumed Unsloth could be used to run the model locally for real use — it needs the full 70GB model and a 74GB+ card

**What happened.** As Phase 10 (running the model on the local machine) approached, the question was raised whether Unsloth could be used for inference instead of llama.cpp. It cannot: Unsloth expects the full bf16 model and a 74GB+ card, while the local machine has 8GB of VRAM. Only the GGUF + llama.cpp path works locally.

**Root cause.** The training tool and the inference tool were treated as interchangeable, without noticing they assume completely different hardware.

**Impact.** Caught in discussion before any attempt was made — no time lost. Had it been tried on the 8GB machine it would have failed outright, and the whole GGUF/quantization pipeline (Phase 8) would have looked like unnecessary work.

**Fix.** Documented as its own section (6.5) with a side-by-side table of when each tool is used and what hardware each needs.

**→ Rule.** Training-time tooling and inference-time tooling are different programs with different hardware assumptions. Confirm which tool owns each phase before planning around it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-24(teach mk).md` · misconception / tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-04 · The pattern vocabulary lives in two places — extend the spec without the checker and every new file fails instantly

**What happened.** Adding bbs_schedule and soil_boring_log took the taxonomy from 14 to 16 values, which required editing PATTERNS_14 in tools/check_format.py in the same commit. Splitting them would have made any file using a new pattern fail the gate immediately, since the checker is the actual enforcement. The number 14 was also hardcoded into four separate places in the spec text (§0.9 heading, §0.10 checklist, §1 title, the automation-scope line) that all had to be found and updated.

**Root cause.** The canonical list is duplicated between the spec prose and the checker constant, and the count is written out in prose in several more places.

**Impact.** A same-commit coupling that must be remembered by hand every time the taxonomy changes; the count-in-prose duplication is a standing source of a spec that contradicts itself.

**Fix.** Both changed in one commit and the four hardcoded counts updated; noted explicitly in the entry as a rule for next time

**→ Rule.** Derive the count from the list rather than writing the number in prose, and treat the checker constant as part of the spec — one change, one commit, or the gate fails on correct data.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-04.md` · tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-20 · Overlay click-to-accept toggle only console.logged — nothing was saved

**What happened.** The prototype's click toggle only writes to console.log; no accept/reject decision is persisted anywhere.

**Root cause.** The prototype stopped at proving the visual interaction was possible and never wired the output side, so it demos as a working accept/reject flow while producing no data.

**Impact.** A reviewer could click through an entire sheet and lose every decision — worse than having no toggle, because it looks like it worked.

**Fix.** Not fixed — one of the 3 open King-try gaps.

**→ Rule.** A UI affordance that discards its own output is worse than a missing one; either persist the decision or disable the control until the write path exists.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-20 · The house 01 overlay render — the strongest proof produced all week — was a scratch script never added to the repo

**What happened.** The 24/24 grid-ref overlay proof (HoughCircles calibration + linear per-axis fit, 55.55 vs 55.65 px/m) was produced by a script written to scratch and explicitly not added to the Training repo. Later the same week two more comparison/overlay scripts met the same fate, and by 08-21 an overlay script finally had to be written a third time (`overlay_gt_vs_ai_house09.py`) using 'วิธีเดียวกับ overlay บ้าน01 20/8'.

**Root cause.** Proof-of-concept scripts were treated as disposable even after producing the result the whole argument rests on; no rule required promoting a script the moment its output is cited.

**Impact.** The same calibration+overlay logic was re-derived at least three times across two days, and the artifact backing the 24/24 claim cannot be re-run or audited.

**Fix.** Partially — `overlay_gt_vs_ai_house09.py` was eventually committed on 08-21; the earlier two were not.

**→ Rule.** The moment a script's output is quoted as evidence, the script is a deliverable: commit it. Re-deriving the same calibration three times costs more than a one-line `git add`.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · throwaway-tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-21 · House 09 หน้า28 overlay skipped — grid circles incomplete on the printed sheet, calibration impossible

**What happened.** The GT-vs-AI overlay for house 09 หน้า28 (roof frame) had to be skipped: the printed grid-label circles on that sheet are incomplete, so the OpenCV HoughCircles + linear-fit calibration used on the other pages cannot establish a px/m mapping.

**Root cause.** The overlay calibration method depends entirely on printed grid-label circles being present and detectable on every sheet — a source-data assumption that holds on most sheets but not all, with no fallback path.

**Impact.** One roof-frame page cannot be visually verified — and roof framing is already the element class with the known pattern-misclassification data-loss bug, so it is the page class that most needs verification.

**Fix.** Not fixed — page skipped and recorded as pending.

**→ Rule.** Any calibration method that depends on a printed feature needs a documented fallback (manual two-point calibration, or reuse of a sibling sheet's scale) — otherwise the sheets that most need checking will be exactly the ones that cannot be checked.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · tooling</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-26 · graphify CLI not installed — documented workflow step silently skipped

**What happened.** A session hit `graphify: command not found` and simply skipped the step. The cause was only identified the next day: graphify had not been set up in this repo yet.

**Root cause.** A tool referenced in the workflow had no install check and no repo-level presence. Because the CLI is machine-local (per-user PATH) rather than repo-checked-in, its absence is silent and per-machine.

**Impact.** A documented analysis step was skipped without anyone knowing why, on at least one session.

**Fix.** graphify was set up on 2026-08-27 (graph over tools/ then tune_ai/, wired into CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.json hooks). The 2026-08-27 entry documents the cause for future readers.

**→ Rule.** A workflow that depends on a machine-local CLI must document the install and check for it, not fail with 'command not found' and get skipped. Prefer repo-checked-in tooling over per-user PATH dependencies.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-26.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-29 · PaddleOCR needed two environment workarounds before it would run at all

**What happened.** Installing PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv5, lang=th) locally required fixing two environment problems: the ~/.cache symlink is broken on this machine so PADDLE_PDX_CACHE_HOME + HOME + USERPROFILE had to be set manually, and the CPU hit a oneDNN bug requiring enable_mkldnn=False.

**Root cause.** Machine-specific environment breakage (broken cache symlink) plus a library/CPU incompatibility, neither documented by the vendor.

**Impact.** Setup time before any measurement could begin.

**Fix.** Set the three env vars explicitly and disabled mkldnn.

**→ Rule.** Record vendor-tool environment workarounds in the runbook the moment you find them — the next person on a different machine will hit the same two walls and re-derive them from scratch.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · tooling-failure</sub>

#### ⚪ LOW · 2026-08-31 · measure_capacity.py's --split was locked to a fixed choice list, blocking measurement of the fold files

**What happened.** The sequence-length measurement tool accepted only train/val/test for --split, so it could not be pointed at train_fold0 etc. after the dataset moved to fold-based files.

**Root cause.** A fixed argparse choices list encoded an assumption about file naming that the fold restructure invalidated.

**Impact.** The critical seq-length safety measurement could not run against the real training files until the tool was patched.

**Fix.** changed --split to accept a free string; all 4 fold files then measured (max 45,839 tokens, unchanged)

**→ Rule.** Don't hard-code a choices list for a filename fragment — it turns a data-layout change into a tool outage right when the measurement matters.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · tooling</sub>

---

## T09 — Model Training & ML Methodology

*Training runs, data splits, prompts, merges, and inference that did not do what was intended.*

**75 entries** · 18 critical · 34 high

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-24 · MAX_LENGTH sized from a single-image example would have truncated away the labels of every gridmaster example

**What happened.** `MAX_LENGTH=9216` had been calculated from a single-image example, but the five gridmaster examples (one per house) use 2-4 images and genuinely need ~22,067 tokens. Left unfixed, the trainer would have truncated the label away entirely on those examples.

**Root cause.** A sequence-length budget was computed from the median example rather than from the maximum, and multi-image examples were not considered when it was set.

**Impact.** Caught in the Phase 0.4 re-read before a real GPU rental — had it shipped, five of the most structurally important examples would have trained on truncated (label-less) sequences with no error raised.

**Fix.** Raised `MAX_LENGTH` to 24576, accepting higher OOM risk on those 5 examples rather than reducing image resolution.

**→ Rule.** Size sequence-length budgets from the maximum example, not the median, and measure it per example class (single-image vs multi-image). Silent truncation of labels is the worst kind of training bug — it produces no error and a worse model.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-24 · JSON valid dropped to 0% because the inference chat template enabled reasoning mode that training never used

**What happened.** The first Phase 7 evaluation run scored 0% JSON valid — worse than the untuned baseline. Investigation found the model writes a long reasoning preamble before every answer, consuming the token budget so it never reaches the JSON.

**Root cause.** `apply_chat_template(add_generation_prompt=True)` was called without `enable_thinking=False`. Training uses `add_generation_prompt=False` and never inserts a `<think>` tag, but at inference the default inserts an empty `<think>\n`, putting the model into reasoning mode. The inference template did not match the training template.

**Impact.** A result that looked like the fine-tune had destroyed the model. After the fix the real numbers were JSON valid 90%, view exact match 70% (up from 60%), and element recall 28.2% (up from 9.4%, a 3x improvement) — the fine-tune had actually worked all along.

**Fix.** Passed `enable_thinking=False` in all three files (`eval_fields.py`, `train_qwen36.py`, `export_gguf.py`) and re-ran; it passed immediately.

**→ Rule.** The inference chat template must be byte-identical in behaviour to the training one — diff them explicitly as a checklist item. A catastrophic eval number is more often a harness mismatch than a model failure; check the harness before concluding the training failed.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-25 · Nearly fed 28%-accurate model output back into the folder that is used as training ground truth

**What happened.** The question was raised of using the tuned model to produce raw JSON for `บ้าน_ใหญ่_1ชั้น_01` directly into the folder actually in use. `rawjson_ยังไม่ได้แก้ไขโดนคน/` is the ground truth that feeds training, so unreviewed 28%-accurate output there would be self-poisoning.

**Root cause.** The output folder for AI drafts had not been decided in advance, and the ground-truth folder is the natural default destination for 'raw JSON for a house'.

**Impact.** Caught before it happened. Had it shipped, the training set would have been contaminated with the model's own 28%-accurate errors, creating a feedback loop that degrades every future round.

**Fix.** Agreed the output is a draft for human review, written to a separate folder, never into the ground-truth folder.

**→ Rule.** Model output must never be written into the folder that trains the model. Enforce it with a separate path and, ideally, a write guard — one accidental save contaminates every subsequent training round.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · merge_and_unload() silently fails on MoE ParamWrapper LoRA — tensors changed only 0.67%

**What happened.** When merging the LoRA adapter into the base model before GGUF conversion, the function completed without error, but hand-measurement across a 201-million-value tensor showed only 0.67% of values changed — i.e. the merged model is behaviourally almost the untuned base. This blocked t02's GGUF and is strongly suspected to have silently corrupted t01's GGUF too.

**Root cause.** peft's ParamWrapper mechanism, which is how LoRA attaches to MoE experts, is not correctly handled by merge_and_unload(). The failure is structural-pass/behaviour-fail: no exception, correct shapes, wrong content.

**Impact.** Every downstream decision made from the t01 GGUF is suspect. The bug now blocks both training rounds, not just t02. Potentially the entire deployable artifact contains no fine-tuning at all.

**Fix.** Not fixed. A free ~20-minute test was designed (run page 03 with the untuned base GGUF and compare to t01's output) to confirm, and must be run before spending any more money.

**→ Rule.** After any merge/convert/quantize step, verify by measuring the weights (percentage of values changed) and by behaviour on a held-out example — never accept 'it completed without error' as proof that a transform took effect.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-export</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · 0/6 pages used the trained schema — three different key vocabularies emitted at random

**What happened.** Gold uses png / doc_page / discipline / sheet_code. The model emitted 'page', 'page_number', and 'page_number'+'sheet_id' across the six pages — three shapes alternating, none matching gold — despite pages 03-06 being its own training data seen for 3 epochs.

**Root cause.** Format is the fastest thing a fine-tune learns; failing it on memorised pages while succeeding on hard content is the fingerprint of a model that never received the tuning — i.e. the silent merge failure.

**Impact.** Output is unparseable by any downstream consumer expecting the contract; but more importantly this anomaly is what exposed the root cause.

**Fix.** not fixed — resolves only if the LoRA/merge issue is resolved

**→ Rule.** Watch the shape of the errors, not the error rate. 'Wrong on the easy things, right on the hard things' is diagnostic gold — an aggregate score would have hidden it completely.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · model-training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · Model output matched the trained schema on 0 of 6 pages and used three different key styles

**What happened.** None of the six extracted pages used the ground-truth keys (png / doc_page / discipline / sheet_code). The model used "page", "page_number", and "page_number"+"sheet_id" across different pages, inconsistently.
