**Root cause.** Strong evidence that the fine-tuning is not present in the running artifact: output format is the first thing a fine-tune locks in, within a few hundred steps. An untuned model given a schema-describing prompt behaves exactly this way — it follows the prompt's vocabulary and does not know keys that exist only in the training answers.

**Impact.** Every extracted file is unusable downstream without remapping; the inconsistency across pages makes even a mapping script unreliable.

**Fix.** Not fixed. This observation became the primary clue pointing at the missing-LoRA hypothesis.

**→ Rule.** Output-format compliance is the cheapest and earliest signal that a fine-tune is actually loaded — check it on the first page, and treat format failure with good content as a deployment bug, not a model-quality issue.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · Model hallucinated 59 elements on a page where ground truth has 17

**What happened.** On page 06 the model output 59 elements against a ground truth of 17 — inventing 12 columns, 8 doors and 4 windows that do not appear on that drawing sheet.

**Root cause.** With no fine-tuning active (suspected) the model fills the requested schema with plausible-looking entries rather than restricting itself to what is on the page; the prompt's 'use null, do not guess' rule was not learned, only stated.

**Impact.** Any quantity takeoff built on this output would be wildly overstated; the extracted files for house 01 are contaminated.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Extraction of house 01 was halted until the missing-LoRA question is answered.

**→ Rule.** Add an element-count sanity check against ground truth (or against a second pass) before accepting extraction output — over-generation is as dangerous as omission and is easier to detect than to notice by eye.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-29 · Model reversed the grid letters and invented all interior grid distances; only the total happened to match

**What happened.** Ground truth grid was D=0, C=4.0, B=6.0, A=9.5. The model answered A=0, B=1.5, C=5.0, D=9.5 — letters reversed, every interior spacing wrong, only the 9.5 total correct. It also produced a grid_table giving one value per grid intersection, a quantity that does not physically exist.

**Root cause.** Real numbers from the drawing (7.0, 9.5, 4.0, 3.5) were shuffled into slots rather than read positionally; the model built a plausible-looking table instead of admitting it could not resolve the geometry.

**Impact.** The prompt explicitly requires spans to come from the grid table, so every downstream span computation is wrong — this corrupts the structural quantities the whole project exists to produce.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Flagged as a top-severity output defect.

**→ Rule.** Validate grid output structurally (monotonic coordinates, letters in drawing order, cumulative sum consistency) before any span is derived from it — a correct total is not evidence of correct spacing.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · The entire t02 training round was wasted — Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B cannot export to GGUF and lost to t01 on every metric

**What happened.** t02's workflow was marked ⛔ SUPERSEDED: Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B's GGUF export is impossible (a MoE-merge bug in `ParamWrapper.merge()` for MoE experts) and the resulting model lost to t01 on every measured metric. The line was abandoned and the plan reverted to Qwen3.6.

**Root cause.** A model was chosen and trained before its full deployment path (merge → GGUF export → local inference) had been proven end to end on this machine. The blocker was in the export step, discovered only after training.

**Impact.** A complete fine-tuning round — GPU rental, dataset build, training time — produced a model that cannot be deployed and is worse than its predecessor. Pure loss.

**Fix.** Marked t02 SUPERSEDED with the reason recorded, kept the file as the record of why, and returned to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B whose merge/GGUF path is already proven working on this machine.

**→ Rule.** Prove the full deployment path (merge → export → run locally) on the base model BEFORE spending a training round on it. A model you cannot export is worth zero regardless of its scores.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · Training taught one-shot single-page while production runs 5-pass cross-page — the tuned model can replace at most one pass

**What happened.** An end-to-end trace found that training teaches a one-shot single-page task (1 image → complete JSON for that page) while the production pipeline is 5-pass and cross-page. The tuned model was never taught to cross-reference across pages, so at best it can replace Pass 1 — not the pipeline. This also structurally caps element recall, because ground truth is built from several sheets while the model only ever sees one.

**Root cause.** The training task shape was designed from the data format (one file per page) rather than from the production task it needs to perform; nobody mapped training input/output onto a production pass before training.

**Impact.** Two full fine-tuning rounds (t01, t02) produced models with no clear deployment slot, and the headline recall metric was structurally unachievable — the numbers were misleading, not just low.

**Fix.** Made it a hard rule that any t03 plan must state which pass it replaces before it starts; designed t03 as a 2-pass architecture matching a real production pass 1:1.

**→ Rule.** Before training, state exactly which production step the model replaces and make the training input/output identical to that step's. A round that measures well but cannot be deployed anywhere is a round wasted — and a metric the task shape makes unreachable is a broken metric.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · Production's Pass 3 asks the model to eyeball span lengths — directly against the schema's own §4 rule

**What happened.** Schema §4 states span is 'calculated by code from the grid only — never let the model estimate distance', but `qt_buildCountPrompt` asks the model for elements 'grouped by span length (meters)' — i.e. estimating distance off the image.

**Root cause.** The production prompt and the extraction schema were written by different tracks with no cross-check; the schema's rule was never enforced against the prompts.

**Impact.** Span lengths — which feed directly into concrete volume, rebar length and cost — come from a model eyeballing pixels rather than from the grid table. Wrong quantities flow into every downstream calculation.

**Fix.** Documented as a contradiction; t03's architecture puts span calculation in pure code (merge step) with no AI involvement.

**→ Rule.** Audit prompts against the data spec, not just code against the spec. A prompt is an implementation of a rule — a prompt that asks for a value the spec forbids the model to produce is a spec violation.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · model-pipeline</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · Pass 1's output shape cannot hold top/bottom rebar — even a perfect read gets flattened on write

**What happened.** Production carries one flat `main_bar_count`, while schema §6 requires a `main_bar{top, middle, bottom}` split. Even a perfectly accurate model read is flattened away when written.

**Root cause.** The production data model predates the schema's rebar-face requirement and was never widened; the loss happens at the write boundary, invisible to any accuracy measurement of the model itself.

**Impact.** Rebar face information is destroyed on every extraction regardless of model quality — and it makes tuning Pass 1 pointless until the output shape changes.

**Fix.** Documented as a prerequisite: prompt and output shape must both change before tuning Pass 1 is worth anything.

**→ Rule.** Check that the destination schema can hold what the model produces before tuning for it. Improving a reader whose writer truncates the result is wasted effort — widen the sink first.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · model-pipeline</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-04 · t01 was trained on ~266 visual tokens per image — 14x blurrier than intended — because resize="max" was missing

**What happened.** t01's training run used roughly 266 visual tokens per image, about 14 times fewer than intended, because the `resize="max"` setting was never applied. This is named as one of the two things known to be broken and requiring a fix before any t03 round.

**Root cause.** An image-preprocessing default was accepted without checking the resulting token count per image; nothing in the training setup reported or asserted on visual token count.

**Impact.** A full fine-tuning round was trained on effectively low-resolution inputs — on a task (reading small printed marks and dimensions off construction drawings) where resolution is the whole game. Every t01 metric is depressed by this, and the model's ceiling was set by a config default.

**Fix.** Not yet applied — recommended as one of the two mandatory fixes for t03 (the other being rebuilding the dataset from 11 houses instead of 5).

**→ Rule.** Assert on the actual visual token count per image before starting a training run, and log it. On a fine-detail reading task, an image-preprocessing default can silently cost you the entire round.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-22 · VLM collapsed 48 real beams into 2 JSON entries and nothing caught it mechanically

**What happened.** On house09 page 26 the model produced 2 beams in its JSON where the sheet had 48. The failure was only visible if a human eyeballed the JSON; no automated check compared the output element count against anything.

**Root cause.** Documented VLM counting hallucination — imbalanced cross-modal attention makes the decoder over-trust text priors over visual tokens, and accuracy degrades sharply past ~4 objects. Compounded by having no independent count source to compare against, so the pipeline had no way to notice.

**Impact.** Silently wrong extraction ground truth / model output on the single most important subtask (beam plans), undetectable without manual review of every page.

**Fix.** Proposed (not yet built) a QA cross-check pass: request bbox output alongside grid_ref, convert grid_ref→pixel with the existing gridmaster, and flag bbox-count vs elements[]-count disagreement automatically.

**→ Rule.** Any VLM output that is a count must be cross-checked against a second, independent count source (classical detection, bbox output, or a printed schedule) — never trusted on its own.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-22.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-24 · plan_beam recall stayed at 0% — the entire goal of the t03 round was not achieved

**What happened.** House 08 t03 results: JSON valid 32/33 (97%), overall id-recall 10/81 = 12.3% (up from t02's 3.5%), with schedule 21.9% and plan_slab 20% genuinely improved. But plan_beam scored 0/15 = 0%, identical to t02. On page 20 the model emitted only metadata and closed the JSON with no elements[] at all — and the metadata pointed at the wrong house (`source_image` referenced house 22), i.e. it pasted boilerplate memorized from similar examples.

**Root cause.** 149 plan_beam training examples is still not enough, and the failure is architectural (counting hallucination) rather than a decoding problem. Grammar fixes syntax, not content recall — the model produced valid JSON containing nothing.

**Impact.** The round's headline objective failed. Worse, JSON-validity went up while the target metric stayed at zero, which is exactly the shape of result that can be misread as progress.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recorded plainly; the named paths forward are more data via op04, or the grounding/bbox↔gridmaster approach — explicitly not more decoding tweaks.

**→ Rule.** A valid-JSON metric can rise while the metric that matters stays at zero. Always report the target metric separately, and never let format-level wins substitute for content-level wins in a summary.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · Purson model died because a single missing line (crop_to_patches) shrank every drawing to a 256-token stamp — third occurrence of the same bug class

**What happened.** The Purson model failed because `crop_to_patches` was missing — one line — so an A1-size drawing was downscaled to a stamp at 256 tokens per image. Documented with three layers of evidence, and explicitly noted as the third time this same bug class had occurred.

**Root cause.** Image preprocessing silently degraded rather than erroring: the pipeline accepted a drastically under-resolved image without complaint. There was no assertion on token count or effective resolution per image, so the same class of failure had recurred twice before undetected.

**Impact.** A whole fine-tuned model was worthless. Training compute and rental cost fully burned. Third repeat of the same failure class.

**Fix.** Root-caused and documented in `workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md`.

**→ Rule.** Add a hard assertion on tokens-per-image / effective resolution before any training run starts — a bug class that has now recurred three times needs a guard, not another root-cause writeup.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · ml-training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · Voldemort model was blinded by 4-bit quantisation of the ViT — reported seeing Barbie and BB-8 in construction drawings

**What happened.** Voldemort failed for a different reason than Purson: image tiling was correct, but 4-bit quantisation destroyed the ViT to the point of blindness. It answered that it saw Barbie and BB-8 in a construction drawing.

**Root cause.** Quantisation applied uniformly across the model including the vision tower, where 4-bit precision is not survivable. No per-component precision policy and no visual sanity check after quantising.

**Impact.** A second fine-tuned model rendered useless — more burned training/rental cost.

**Fix.** Root-caused and documented in the teaching document.

**→ Rule.** Never quantise the vision tower to 4-bit. After any quantisation, run a trivial visual sanity probe ('what is in this image?') before spending money on evaluation or training.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · ml-training</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · The house01 simulation was unintentionally cheating in two ways, making its results not representative of Destrier

**What happened.** When Makham asked whether the JSON used for the house01 simulation could really be trusted as Destrier-equivalent, two forms of unintentional cheating were found: (1) it mapped `pattern` → subtask directly (e.g. etc_plan → plan_slab always) whereas real pass0 must inspect element_type; (2) it returned the whole GT file back verbatim, including fields real training strips (`element_name_assigned`) and element types the subtask model was never taught to answer.

**Root cause.** The simulator was built to produce plausible output rather than to replicate the real pass0/dataset-filter code paths. It bypassed `build_dataset_t03.py`'s per-subtask element_type filtering entirely, so it modelled a far more capable system than actually exists.

**Impact.** The impressive house01 numbers (62 files, 153 elements, ฿144,704 BOQ) reflected an idealised system, not the real one. A rebuild (`sim_house_from_labels.py`) showed reality: pass0 only auto-answers 31 of 72 pages, and only 24 real pass2 jobs result.

**Fix.** Built `sim_house_from_labels.py` following real `pass0_labels.jsonl` and mirroring `build_dataset_t03.py::PLAN_SUBTASKS` filtering exactly.

**→ Rule.** A simulator must import or exactly mirror the real code paths, not re-implement 'what it probably does'. Any shortcut in a simulator becomes an overstatement in its results — and someone will quote those numbers.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-20 · Random page-level train/val split would have leaked across the split

**What happened.** The train/val split for fine-tuning was flagged as needing to be by house, not by randomly sampling pages, because pages from the same house share grids, marks and specs.

**Root cause.** The natural unit of a dataset example is a page, so a naive random split is per-page — which puts near-identical sheets from the same house on both sides of the split.

**Impact.** Caught before it shipped; a page-level split would have produced inflated validation metrics that hid the model's real generalisation gap.

**Fix.** Split by house (train = 01+02+04, val = 03) per instruction; recommended 4/1 or 5-fold now, 80/10/10 once 8-10 houses are labelled.

**→ Rule.** Split evaluation data by the largest correlated unit (here: house), never by the example unit. A leaked val set produces a number you will trust and shouldn't.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Tuned model still finds only 9.4% of drawing elements — recall unfixed

**What happened.** Post-tuning evaluation showed a big win on format (JSON valid 0%→90%, view exact match 0%→60%) but element recall of only 16/170 (9.4%), i.e. the model still misses the great majority of rebar/beam/column items.

**Root cause.** The training set is small (226 examples from 3 houses) and the run used a reduced LoRA rank; format is far easier to learn than exhaustive element enumeration, so a headline 90% can mask the metric that actually matters for takeoff.

**Impact.** The tuned model is not yet usable for quantity takeoff; a further tuning round is required — and the artifacts that would have supported it were subsequently lost.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as the target for the next tuning round (more data / more epochs / prompt adjustment).

**→ Rule.** Judge a fine-tune on the metric that carries the business value (element recall), not the easiest-to-move metric (JSON validity); report both together so a headline number never implies readiness.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · GGUF shipped text-only because the vision projector (mmproj) could not be exported

**What happened.** The GGUF conversion succeeded for the language part but the mmproj (image encoder projection) could not be split out — llama.cpp itself warned it only supports certain models. The resulting artifact could not read drawings, which is the entire purpose of the project.

**Root cause.** The export path's support for this very new model family was never verified before the end of the pipeline; the vision half of the deliverable was assumed to follow the text half.

**Impact.** The day's deliverable was unusable for the actual task; discovered only at the very end of the run.

**Fix.** Three days later realized the fix was free: since training froze vision layers (finetune_vision_layers=False), the upstream vendor's mmproj (899MB) is byte-equivalent and can simply be downloaded and paired with the tuned GGUF.

**→ Rule.** Verify the hardest/most novel step of an export pipeline first, on a throwaway model, before spending a full training run on it — and check whether a frozen component can simply be reused from upstream instead of re-derived.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-export</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · Fine-tuned model reaches only 28.2% element recall while over-predicting 78 elements

**What happened.** After the reasoning-mode fix, the measured results on `--limit 20` were JSON valid 90%, view exact match 70%, element recall 28.2%, element_id/count exact 100%, element_type exact 87.5% — with 78 elements over-predicted.

**Root cause.** The training set is small (315 train examples from five small houses) and the element-level task is the hardest part of the schema; the model both misses most elements and hallucinates extras.

**Impact.** The model cannot be trusted to produce production raw JSON — over 70% of elements missing plus fabricated ones. Directly drove the decision that its output is a human-reviewed draft only.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded honestly as the measured state; more labelled houses is the path forward.

**→ Rule.** Report the weakest metric alongside the headline improvement. A 3x recall improvement that lands at 28% is still unusable, and over-prediction must be measured as its own number, not folded into recall.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-25 · Proposed multi-pass call split would have silently discarded the fine-tuning advantage

**What happened.** A proposal to split extraction into five sub-calls like the production Constistant pipeline was analysed and rejected: the model was trained on one call per page, so the sub-tasks (survey ID, counting) were never seen during training and would be handled by base Qwen — implicitly giving up the tuning benefit. It would also cost ~15 minutes per page just re-processing the image five times.

**Root cause.** The inference calling pattern was being designed independently of the training data format; a fine-tuned model only carries its advantage on the task shape it was trained on.

**Impact.** Caught in analysis before implementation — would have spent hours per house to get base-model quality at 5x the image-processing cost.

**Fix.** Concluded: to use the tuned model, one call per page (fix truncation with a right-sized ctx, accept slowness); to go multi-pass, either use the existing cloud pipeline or retrain with multi-pass-formatted data.

**→ Rule.** Training format must match the calling pattern. Changing how a fine-tuned model is invoked silently reverts it to base-model behaviour, with no error to tell you.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · House 07 EE-05/06: four TV outlets missed entirely, despite a 4-way splitter on the same sheet stating the count

**What happened.** Four TV outlet symbols (⊙) had not been extracted at all. The same sheet carries a 4-way splitter diagram whose fan-out matches the four outlets exactly — the evidence was already on the page.

**Root cause.** Extraction read symbols in isolation without using the sheet's own internal consistency checks (a splitter's port count constrains the number of outlets it feeds).

**Impact.** Four fixtures missing from the electrical takeoff, understating quantities and cost.

**Fix.** Outlets recovered and cross-verified against the splitter diagram.

**→ Rule.** Use a sheet's own internal arithmetic as a completeness check — splitter ports, panel schedules, circuit counts all constrain how many downstream items must exist. If the counts disagree, something was missed.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model trained on 512px images (~266 visual tokens) but served 3,796 tokens/image — a 14.3× mismatch

**What happened.** llama-server's log reports 2048 + 1748 = 3,796 visual tokens per image at inference, while the collator bug shrank training images to 512px ≈ 266 tokens. The model was asked at inference to read inputs 14.3× denser than anything it practised on.

**Root cause.** The collator silently used a default image size because the model has no default declared; training resolution was therefore never a deliberate choice, and nobody compared it against what the serving stack would feed in.

**Impact.** A large fraction of tonight's poor extraction quality is plausibly attributable to this alone; knowledge learned at training resolution is largely unusable at serving resolution.

**Fix.** not fixed — mitigation identified (--image-min-tokens 1024, free to try); a retrain with resize="max" is the fallback

**→ Rule.** Log and assert the exact preprocessed input shape at both training and inference, and fail loudly if they differ. Train/inference mismatch is invisible in both logs individually — it only appears when the two numbers are put side by side.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · model-training</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Quantized to Q4_K_M despite the vendor's own warning, then never re-measured

**What happened.** t01_workflow.md records that Unsloth warns this model family 'loses quality abnormally when quantized' — which is precisely why bf16 training was mandated and 4-bit banned. At deployment time the model was compressed 70GB → 21GB Q4_K_M anyway (an 8GB laptop cannot hold 70GB) and accuracy was never re-measured after compression.

**Root cause.** A constraint was enforced rigorously for training and then silently dropped for inference, because nobody treated 'putting it to use' as a stage that could change quality.

**Impact.** An unknown share of tonight's quality collapse may be quantization damage, and there is no measurement to separate it from the merge bug or the resolution mismatch.

**Fix.** not fixed — needs a controlled A/B against the unquantized model

**→ Rule.** A quality constraint applies to the whole pipeline, not the training step. When you knowingly violate one out of necessity, book the re-measurement as a required task in the same breath — an unmeasured deliberate compromise becomes an unknown a week later.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · model-training</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Train/inference mismatch: model trained on ~266 visual tokens/image, used at 3,796

**What happened.** llama-server logs showed 3,796 visual tokens per image at inference, while the collator bug had trained the model at ~266 — a 14.3× difference between what it learned on and what it is shown in production.

**Root cause.** The training-side image pipeline (Unsloth collator default) and the inference-side pipeline (llama.cpp) were configured independently and never compared. The training side was silently downscaling.

**Impact.** Whatever the model learned may not transfer at all at production resolution; a plausible secondary cause of the poor real-world extraction quality on 07-29.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Identified --image-min-tokens 1024 as a free first thing to try; retraining with resize="max" is the fallback.

**→ Rule.** Assert that inference-time preprocessing matches training-time preprocessing exactly — capture the actual token/pixel counts on both sides and compare numbers, not settings.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · train-inference-mismatch</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Quantized to Q4_K_M against the vendor's own warning, and never re-measured accuracy afterwards

**What happened.** Unsloth warns that this model family degrades abnormally when quantized — which is exactly why training was forced to bf16 with 4-bit forbidden. Yet for deployment the model was compressed 70GB → 21GB as Q4_K_M (necessary for an 8GB laptop) and accuracy was never measured again after compression.

**Root cause.** The vendor caveat was applied to the training phase where it was first read, and not carried forward to the deployment phase where it applies just as much. The compression was driven by a hardware constraint, and the constraint was allowed to substitute for a quality decision.

**Impact.** The artifact actually in daily use has unknown accuracy; a plausible contributor to the poor 07-29 output that could not be ruled in or out.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recorded as a secondary cause; re-measuring the quantized artifact remains outstanding.

**→ Rule.** A quality caveat about a model applies to every phase, not the phase you first read it in. Any lossy transform on the shipping artifact requires a re-run of the accuracy eval on that exact artifact.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-export</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model read sheet references (A-05, A-07, A-09) as column marks

**What happened.** The drawing contains cross-references such as 'see detail on sheet A-05'. The model treated A-05 / A-07 / A-09 as the names of columns and emitted them as element marks.

**Root cause.** The model reads Thai text accurately but does not understand the function of the text it reads — a semantic-role failure, not an OCR failure. It reads a pointer as a name.

**Impact.** Fabricated structural elements carrying sheet numbers as marks, which would flow into BBS/BOQ as real items.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Documented as evidence that the problem is comprehension, not vision.

**→ Rule.** Validate extracted marks against the project's real mark vocabulary (and reject anything matching the sheet-code pattern) — the model can read text perfectly and still misclassify what it is.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Output contradicted itself: two rooms assigned the identical four grid points

**What happened.** F6 was given grid points ["C-2","C-3","D-3","D-2"] and named 'เตรียมอาหาร'; F7 was given the same four points in a different order and named 'นอน 2'.

**Root cause.** Nothing in the pipeline cross-checks emitted entries against each other; the model generates each entry locally with no global consistency constraint.

**Impact.** Two mutually exclusive room definitions occupy the same footprint — an error that silently propagates into area and finish takeoffs.

**Fix.** Not fixed.

**→ Rule.** Run cheap internal-consistency assertions on model output (no two areas share an identical point set, no duplicate marks with different attributes) — these catch failures no per-field accuracy metric will.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · confidence_score and confidence_flags were emitted 0 times across all 6 files

**What happened.** The ground-truth schema carries confidence_score and confidence_flags marking passages the reader could not resolve (e.g. 'text too small, needs zoom'). The model produced none across six files.

**Root cause.** Those fields exist only in the training answers, never in the prompt text — so a model without the fine-tune loaded has no way to know they should exist. Their total absence is itself corroborating evidence for the missing-LoRA hypothesis.

**Impact.** There is no way to tell which parts of the extraction to trust and which to re-check, so every value must be treated as unverified — removing the human-review targeting the schema was designed to provide.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Used as evidence in the LoRA-presence diagnosis.

**→ Rule.** Fields that appear only in training answers and never in the prompt are the best available fine-tune-presence detector — check for them explicitly in the artifact sanity gate.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model swapped both work category and material type: wall/clay brick became ceiling/AAC block

**What happened.** On page 04 the ground truth is a wall (ผนัง) built of clay brick (อิฐมอญ). The model output a ceiling (ฝ้าเพดาน) built of autoclaved aerated block (อิฐมวลเบา).

**Root cause.** The model matched surface tokens without binding material to its host element; nothing validates that a material is legal for the work category assigned.

**Impact.** Wrong on two dimensions at once — if used for pricing, both the work category and the unit rate would be wrong, so the BOQ error compounds rather than cancels.

**Fix.** Not fixed.

**→ Rule.** Cross-validate material against work category with a legality table before any extracted line reaches pricing — a two-dimensional error produces a confidently wrong number, not an obviously wrong one.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-output-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-04 · Six incompatible page-type vocabularies answer the same question — and two places lose information today

**What happened.** 'What kind of page is this?' is answered by 6 different vocabularies (schema §1 with 14/16 values, Pass 0's 2, CLASSIFY_SHEET/sheet_type's 5, drawing_type's 3, classifyPageType()'s 7, schema-v2's parked 6). Two places actively lose data today: `wz-step1.js:224` squashes 5 values into 2 (general_notes/schedule_table/unknown all become section_detail) and `drawing-index.js:205-208` hardcodes section_detail over whatever was actually read.

**Root cause.** The same concept was modelled independently in six places over time with no canonical owner; each new consumer defined the vocabulary it needed locally.

**Impact.** Classification information is being destroyed on every run in two known places — a correctly-read page type is overwritten with a hardcoded value. And Constistant structurally cannot store a 16-value result, so a better classifier cannot be deployed.

**Fix.** Not fixed — judged not worth it right now; only the 2 genuinely-missing patterns were added to the schema. `sheet_type`/`drawing_type` widening documented as a prerequisite for any new Pass 0.

**→ Rule.** One concept, one vocabulary, one owner. And never hardcode over a value that was just read — if the read result is discarded, the read should not have been paid for.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · model-pipeline</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · The completed end-to-end loop delivered 21 elements but 0 spans and 0 specs — model quality, not platform code

**What happened.** After both adapter bugs were fixed, the Qwen export of house 09 imported successfully and yielded 21 elements including real structural ones (C1 ×8, C2 ×12, B2 ×18, footings, steel trusses) — but span 0/21 and specs 0. The model never emitted grid_ref_start/grid_ref_end (it packs a whole sheet into one string, "F-F x 1'-2', F-F x 2'-3', …"), and no section or schedule page of the house was ever run through it. Ground truth for the same house through the same adapter gives 87 elements / 55 specs / 18 spans.

**Root cause.** Two compounding causes: the model does not emit per-element grid refs on beam plans (the 11%-recall problem, itself caused by ~13 training examples), and the run scope never covered section/schedule pages, which are the only source of specs.

**Impact.** The 'complete loop' demo produces elements with no geometry and no material specs — the BOQ can count things but cannot price or size them. Honest gap named rather than papered over.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as model quality, not platform code. Recommendation: run this house's section/schedule pages through Qwen to at least populate specs and let the BOQ price steel.

**→ Rule.** When demonstrating an end-to-end loop, state the delta against ground truth through the same code path (21 vs 87 elements, 0 vs 18 spans) — a loop that runs is not a loop that works, and comparing against ground truth through the identical adapter is the only way to separate platform bugs from model quality.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-21 · On beam plans the model collapses a whole sheet into ~2 zone-notation elements instead of per-beam rows

**What happened.** Overlay comparison on house 09 หน้า26 showed the model reducing a sheet of 48 real beams to 2 elements, packing the entire page into one string of zone notation (`"F-F x 1'-2', F-F x 2'-3', …"`) whose boxes float free of any real beam line; หน้า27 could not be placed at all. This is a distinct failure mode from the fence-detail hallucination and from JSON parse failure — the JSON here is valid, the content is structurally wrong.

**Root cause.** Too few beam-plan training examples (~13) to teach one-row-per-segment output, so the model falls back on summarising the sheet in a compressed notation it has seen in captions/schedules.

**Impact.** Even after grammar decoding made 96.8% of pages parse, beam spans remain unusable — the platform import produced span 0/21 against ground truth's 18/87. Beam lengths never reach the BOQ.

**Fix.** Not fixed — deferred to t03's per-pattern subtask split plus more beam-plan training examples.

**→ Rule.** Valid JSON is not correct content. Measure element-level recall with a visual overlay against ground truth, not parse rate, before declaring an extraction run successful.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-24 · t01 found 5 beams / 0 columns on a page with 16 beams in GT

**What happened.** On house 11 page 22, the tuned t01 model reported 5 beams and 0 columns, while the sheet visibly carried 13+ beam labels plus columns and GT records 16 beams. Base and tuned produced the same 6 usable pages, and base was often faster (p21: 121s vs 410s) — likely just less verbose, not smarter.

**Root cause.** The same architectural counting hallucination documented on 2026-08-22, now confirmed on our own model and our own data. Fine-tuning did not cure it.

**Impact.** Confirms the tuned model cannot be trusted for element counts; the tuned-vs-untuned comparison produced no quality win, only a confirmation of the failure mode.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as live confirmation of the 2026-08-22 research; the fix direction (detection-first / GroundCount hint) remains unbuilt.

**→ Rule.** Do not read a speed difference between base and tuned as a quality signal. Always compare element counts against GT, and treat count accuracy as a separate metric from JSON validity.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-24.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Model returned an empty element list with a header copied from a different house

**What happened.** On hard beam-plan pages the model output only header fields and `"elements": []` — no beams at all. Worse, the header pointed to the wrong house (claimed house 22 while reading house 08).

**Root cause.** The model had memorized the output form from training examples and was reproducing it from memory instead of actually looking at the image in front of it — a memorization/hallucination failure, aggravated by the image being downscaled so heavily that the beams were not legibly present.

**Impact.** plan_beam recall pinned at 0%; the wrong house code in the output would silently corrupt downstream data if any pipeline trusted the header field.

**Fix.** Root-caused as a 'cannot see the object' problem rather than a 'reads the number wrong' problem; led to the pattern-recognition tool and the MAX_PIXELS fix. The hallucinated header itself is not yet guarded against.

**→ Rule.** When a model outputs a well-formed but empty/mismatched record, treat it as memorization of the template, not as a parsing bug. Add a validation check that the header identity in the output matches the file actually fed in.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · model-behavior</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-25 · Thai-reading ability was never a screening criterion in the model search — both surviving candidates are untested on Thai

**What happened.** Eight models were screened on size, licence and trainability. Only after the shortlist was down to two (GLM-4.6V, Llama-4-Scout) does the diary note that nobody has tested how well either reads Thai — on a project whose entire input corpus is Thai construction drawings.

**Root cause.** Thai capability is the hardest criterion to check (no leaderboard, needs a real trial run), so it was deferred — and deferring it meant it never filtered anything.

**Impact.** Both survivors could fail on the one requirement that cannot be worked around, making the whole survey's shortlist provisional. Adopting either would risk a full training round spent discovering the model cannot read the language.

**Fix.** not fixed — noted as an open unknown

**→ Rule.** The requirement that would disqualify a candidate outright belongs in the first filter, not the footnote. A shortlist screened on everything except the deal-breaker is not a shortlist.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25(teach mk).md` · research-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-26 · InternVL3-78B and InternVL3.5-241B look like non-Qwen alternatives but use Qwen as their language backbone

**What happened.** The search criterion was explicitly 'not Qwen, by brand and by backbone'. InternVL3-78B and InternVL3.5-241B pass the brand test but were found to use Qwen2.5-72B and Qwen3-235B respectively as their brain, so both were disqualified.

**Root cause.** Model branding does not reveal architecture lineage; a different vendor name can wrap the exact backbone you were trying to avoid. Only reading the model card's architecture section reveals it.

**Impact.** Would have selected an apparent alternative that carries the identical dependency and identical failure modes as the incumbent — defeating the whole purpose of the search.

**Fix.** Both explicitly disqualified in the catalogue with the reason recorded ('ข้างในใช้ Qwen2.5-72B เป็นสมอง').

**→ Rule.** When evaluating a model to avoid a specific dependency, check the actual backbone in the architecture section, never the brand name. Record the backbone in your comparison table as a first-class column.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · model-selection</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-26 · Several shortlisted models carry licences that forbid or ambiguously restrict commercial use

**What happened.** Pixtral-Large ships under the Mistral Research License with no direct commercial use (a separate licence must be bought); MiniMax M3 has nested conditions where fine-tuning and deploying may itself count as commercial; NVLM-D-72B is CC-BY-NC-4.0.

**Root cause.** Open weights are routinely conflated with open licences. Restrictions are in the licence text, not in the availability of the download.

**Impact.** Any of these, if adopted without reading the licence, would have created legal exposure discovered only after the model was embedded in a commercial product.

**Fix.** Each licence read and its restriction recorded per row in the catalogue table, with commercial-use marked ✅/❌/⚠️ explicitly.

**→ Rule.** Read the full licence text for every candidate model before any spend, and record the commercial-use verdict as a mandatory column. 'Downloadable' never implies 'usable commercially'.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · legal</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-26 · Llama-4-Scout was selected as the only surviving candidate without anyone testing whether it can read Thai

**What happened.** Llama-4-Scout passed every catalogue criterion (size, licence, confirmed LoRA training) and was named the sole survivor — but the catalogue records that nobody has tested how well any candidate reads Thai, and recommends a zero-shot Thai-OCR test before renting a GPU.

**Root cause.** The selection criteria covered size, licence and trainability but omitted the single most task-critical capability: reading Thai construction drawings. The criteria were about feasibility, not fitness for purpose.

**Impact.** A GPU-rental decision was about to be made on a model whose core required capability was completely unmeasured — the same class of mistake as training t04 without checking image resolution.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged as a recommendation ('แนะนำ zero-shot Thai-OCR test ก่อนตัดสินใจลงทุนเช่า GPU จริง') rather than executed.

**→ Rule.** Include the task-critical capability in the selection criteria itself, and run a free zero-shot test of it before any rental decision. Feasibility criteria (size/licence/tooling) do not measure whether the model can do the job.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · model-selection</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-29 · CV hint blocks must be barred from containing dimension numbers or they teach the model to violate its own rule

**What happened.** The pass 2.4 hint contract explicitly forbids putting any dimension numbers into the hint appended to the prompt, because doing so would teach the model to break the standing rule 'never guess dimensions from the image' — with the team's own hand.

**Root cause.** An auxiliary channel (the CV hint) can silently contradict a prompt rule if its contents are not constrained. Helper data injected into a prompt is training signal, not neutral context.

**Impact.** Caught at design time as a contract rule rather than after shipping, so no measured damage — but the failure mode would have been model-wide dimension fabrication that is very hard to attribute.

**Fix.** Written into pass2.4_hint/prompt.md as an explicit prohibition on the hint block's contents.

**→ Rule.** When injecting auxiliary/tool-derived data into a prompt, explicitly enumerate what it must NOT contain. Auxiliary context that contradicts a stated rule will override the rule.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอน_t04_Purson_2026-08-29.md` · prompt-engineering</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-30 · The repo's import fixtures used pattern names that appear in zero real files, so the whole test suite stayed green while the real import path produced nothing

**What happened.** `raw-extraction-adapter.js` only recognised the spec's pattern names `plan` and `gridline`. Real data across all 50 houses uses `beam_plan` (85), `footing_plan` (60), `etc_plan` (199), `roof_frame_plan` (46) and `grid_master` (42) — `plan`/`gridline` appear in 0 files. The bug survived indefinitely because the fixtures in the repo were written to the spec names too, so every test passed against a code path no real file ever takes. It surfaced only when a real house was pushed through the pipeline in a simulated-user run.

**Root cause.** Fixtures were authored from the spec document rather than sampled from the real data corpus, so the test suite validated the adapter against its own assumptions. Spec names and produced names had diverged and nothing compared the two.

**Impact.** Pressing the real import button produced 0 elements and no grid, silently, for an unknown length of time — the manual-import button was affected too, not just the new Purson path. 1149 tests were green throughout.

**Fix.** `canonicalPattern()` + `PATTERN_ALIASES` added in the adapter, applied at all 5 comparison sites across 2 files; alias list matched to build_dataset_t03.py; `tests/raw-extraction-pattern-aliases.test.js` (4 tests) added; suite 1153/1153.

**→ Rule.** A fixture invented from a spec tests the spec, not the system. At least one test per ingestion path must use a byte-real sample taken from the actual corpus, or a green suite means nothing.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · testing-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Model emitted training-set filenames when reading a brand-new house — overfit memorization

**What happened.** Output for a completely new house contained house_001_หน้า00_gridline.json and image/house_001/... — filenames memorized from the training corpus. Final training losses of 0.10-0.13 are below Unsloth's stated overfit threshold of 0.2.

**Root cause.** Too many epochs and too little house diversity relative to model capacity, producing memorization rather than generalization.

**Impact.** Output for unseen houses is contaminated with fabricated references to training data, which would corrupt any downstream consumer.

**Fix.** Not fixed this round — flagged as a required change for the next training round (reduce epochs, increase house diversity).

**→ Rule.** Track training loss against the overfit threshold during the run, and test on a genuinely out-of-corpus house before declaring a model usable — memorized filenames in output are a definitive overfit signal.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · training-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · All six SP precast slab panels were missed entirely on the beam plan

**What happened.** On the scored beam page the model produced no SP element at all — all six precast floor panels were absent, alongside other errors (row B all labelled B2 when B3 should appear, B3 in the wrong orientation, B0 classified as slab instead of beam).

**Root cause.** Unknown — flagged as a likely systematic gap rather than noise, since a whole element class disappeared rather than individual instances.

**Impact.** Precast slabs are required for BOQ; a whole element class missing means quantities would be silently short.

**Fix.** Not fixed — listed as the second-highest priority next action, to determine whether it is a systematic gap.

**→ Rule.** When an entire element class is missing rather than individual instances, treat it as a systematic gap and investigate before shipping — silent zero for a BOQ-relevant class is worse than a wrong number.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Model returned zero elements with confidence 1.0 on a page with six clearly drawn footings

**What happened.** In the greedy round, page 26 (pile-cap plan) came back as elements: [] with confidence 1.0 and a flag claiming footing marks were present but no footings were drawn — while six footings were plainly visible.

**Root cause.** Nothing in the schema or serving path ties the confidence field to evidence; the model is free to assert full confidence in an empty result, and downstream code has no rule that empty-plus-confident is suspicious.

**Impact.** A confidently empty page is worse than an unknown one — a downstream consumer would take it as "this plan has no footings" and drop 6 real elements from the takeoff.

**Fix.** not fixed for the confidence field itself; the underlying emptiness was fixed by switching off greedy decoding (page 26 then read 100% correct)

**→ Rule.** Treat high confidence on an empty result as a validation failure, not as data — a model that says "nothing here, certainly" needs a guard.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · model-output</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-31 · Model invented column positions by inferring them from beam intersections, breaking the explicit no-guessing rule

**What happened.** In the page-27 output the model emitted columns with its own comment "Column location inferred from beam intersections" — deriving element positions that were not read from the drawing, which the prompt rules forbid.

**Root cause.** The no-guessing rule exists in the prompt but nothing at generation or ingest time detects or rejects an inferred element; the model even labelled the violation and it still passed through.

**Impact.** Fabricated structural elements would enter the takeoff as if read from the drawing; caught only by reading the raw output by hand.

**Fix.** not fixed — no validator rejects self-declared inferences

**→ Rule.** When the model announces it is guessing, that is a machine-readable signal — build a check for it instead of relying on the prompt rule alone.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · model-output</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · t04 memorised training-set answers instead of learning to read drawings, and this was mistaken for competence

**What happened.** Because the input images were unreadable, the model could only learn the shape of the expected answer and recall the answers of houses it had seen during training. On any unseen house it fabricated output immediately.

**Root cause.** Unreadable inputs plus a loss signal that still rewards producing the right-looking JSON means memorisation is the only learnable strategy. The training setup made cheating the optimal policy.

**Impact.** An entire model whose apparent capability was pure train-set recall — worthless on new houses, which is the only case that matters in production.

**Fix.** Diagnosed by testing on unseen houses and by inspecting actual outputs rather than aggregate scores.

**→ Rule.** Always hold out unseen data and check performance there specifically. If a model scores well on seen data and collapses on unseen data, suspect the inputs are unusable and it is memorising labels, not learning the task.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · training-methodology</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · t04's k-fold split was made blind to per-pass data coverage, leaving zero pass0 eval houses in every fold

**What happened.** The 40 houses were split into folds without checking that only about 10 houses carried pass0/pass2.4/pass3 data (pass0 existed for only 5 houses). The random split pushed almost all of those special houses into the training side. Counting the files showed every fold had 204 pass1 eval houses but 0 pass0 eval houses, and only 0–9 for pass2.4 and 0–2 for pass3.

**Root cause.** The split was stratified on house count only, treating all houses as interchangeable, when in fact the data is sparse and unevenly distributed per pass. Nobody counted per-pass file coverage before splitting.

**Impact.** Even after a successful training run it would have been impossible to measure whether the model learned pass0 or pass3 at all. Reusing these folds would have meant training and still not knowing the answer.

**Fix.** Caught by Makham directly ('อย่าเอา fold ของ t04 ไปใช้') and confirmed by counting the actual files; the t04 fold layout was rejected for reuse.

**→ Rule.** Before splitting data into folds, count coverage per sub-task and stratify on the sparse dimension, not just on the total item count. Verify every fold has non-zero eval examples for every capability you intend to measure.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · data-split</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Model-soup merge nearly done without a shared LoRA A initialisation (same-basin requirement)

**What happened.** The plan to average 4 fold models into one 'model soup' at 0.25 weight each only works if every model starts from the same initialisation. The team came close to merging models that did not share a common LoRA A init — recorded as a near-miss in the 30 Aug diary.

**Root cause.** The same-basin precondition for weight averaging is a silent mathematical requirement, not something any tool enforces. Merging models from different initialisations produces a valid-looking file that is numerically meaningless.

**Impact.** Would have produced a merged model that looked fine but was effectively noise, with no error at any stage to reveal it.

**Fix.** Caught before merging; the shared LoRA A initialisation requirement was documented as a lesson in the 30 Aug diary.

**→ Rule.** Before averaging any set of model weights, verify programmatically that all members share the same initialisation. Weight merging has silent preconditions — assert them, do not assume the training script preserved them.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · model-merge</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · A page containing both footing and beam plans failed generation at both attempts even with a 40-minute ceiling

**What happened.** Even after raising the timeout to 40 minutes, page 12 (footing + beam on one sheet) still failed in both views. Reading the raw text showed two distinct failures: for the footing the model had already produced all 7 elements correctly and then looped repeating the same explanatory sentence endlessly; for the beam it was genuinely still producing real content (64 segments) and got cut 144 characters from the end.

**Root cause.** Content density on a single sheet exceeds what one generation call can complete. Two different failure modes were being lumped together: a degenerate repetition loop (which more time cannot fix) and a genuine length overflow (which more time only barely fixes). No repetition penalty / loop detection existed, and no per-sheet content splitting.

**Impact.** Repeated failures across multiple houses (house09 page 9 hit the same thing), each costing a re-run or manual salvage. Not solvable by timeout tuning.

**Fix.** Recovered with a purpose-written `salvage_json.py` (bracket-depth walker finding a safe cut point and closing the JSON, without inventing values). Both files recovered fully.

**→ Rule.** Distinguish 'ran out of time' from 'stuck in a repetition loop' — they need different fixes (splitting vs a repetition penalty/stop condition). For dense multi-view sheets, crop into separate views before generation rather than raising the timeout again.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · model-generation</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-02 · House09 page 9 (beam plan + roof truss overlaid) truncated again — the same dense-page failure recurring

**What happened.** During the house09 run, page 9 (beam plan plus roof truss, two views overlaid) was cut off mid-generation — the identical failure mode as house2's page 12, on a different house.

**Root cause.** The dense multi-view sheet problem was never fixed at the source (no cropping), only made survivable by salvage. So it recurred on the very next house.

**Impact.** Another manual salvage step in a run that was supposed to be timed as a clean end-to-end benchmark; 22 elements had to be recovered by script.

**Fix.** Recovered with `salvage_json.py` (all 22 elements).

**→ Rule.** A failure that recurs on the next dataset is not an edge case — it is the normal case. Fix dense multi-view sheets at the cropping stage before running more houses through the same trap.

<sub>`2026-09-02.md` · model-generation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Tried to quantize from an already-quantized GGUF; had to redo the conversion from f16

**What happened.** To save disk space the merged model was converted to q8_0 first, then an attempt was made to compress that further. The tool refused to re-quantize an already-quantized file, so the whole conversion had to be redone from the full-precision f16 (~70GB) source.

**Root cause.** Assumed quantization was chainable like generic file compression; it is a lossy one-shot transform from full precision.

**Impact.** Conversion work redone, plus extra disk pressure on an already-tight 150GB instance.

**Fix.** Re-converted from f16 and produced Q4_K_M (21.2GB) directly.

**→ Rule.** Always keep and convert from the full-precision export; never derive one quantization from another.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · model-export</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-25 · Nearly used the production app prompt, which targets a different schema than the model was trained on

**What happened.** During prompt selection the user pushed back twice: do not use the production prompt from `js/ai/prompts.js` (a flat `elements[]` schema, a different thing entirely), and do not stuff the whole 6k-token `primary_rawjson_schema.md` into the prompt. The correct choice is `PROMPT_SHORT`, the prompt the model was actually trained with.

**Root cause.** Two prompt families exist in the project for two different schemas, and nothing labels which prompt corresponds to which trained model.

**Impact.** Caught by the user before the run. Using the flat-schema production prompt would have produced output in the wrong shape and made the tuned model look broken.

**Fix.** Used `PROMPT_SHORT` and saved it explicitly to `tune_ai/t01/ai_output_บ้าน_ใหญ่_1ชั้น_01/_prompt_short.txt`.

**→ Rule.** Pin the exact prompt a model was trained with next to the model artifact. When multiple prompt families exist for different schemas, an unlabelled prompt choice is a silent correctness bug.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-25 · Planned to run the tuned model on a big house, a building type entirely absent from training

**What happened.** The plan was to run the tuned model on `บ้าน_ใหญ่_1ชั้น_01`, a big house, when train and val contain only small houses (1-storey and 2-storey). Accuracy was stated as expected below even the measured 28% because the type is out-of-distribution.

**Root cause.** The dataset was built from whichever houses were available rather than from a plan covering the building types the model must handle.

**Impact.** The first real production attempt targets the hardest possible case; results will understate the model and cost hours of slow local inference.

**Fix.** Stated honestly up front ('technically yes, accuracy not yet') rather than claiming readiness; the run was deferred.

**→ Rule.** State the in-distribution boundary of a model before anyone runs it on new data, and plan dataset coverage against the building types you actually intend to process — not against whatever was labelled first.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-25 · Proposed stuffing the entire 6k-token schema document into the inference prompt

**What happened.** While choosing a prompt for the big-house run, the second thing the human had to push back on was an intent to inject the whole ~6,000-token primary_rawjson_schema.md into the prompt. PROMPT_SHORT — the 50-line prompt the model was actually trained with — was the correct choice.

**Root cause.** Treating the prompt as documentation to be maximally informative rather than as the exact input distribution the model was fine-tuned on. A fine-tuned model needs the training prompt, not a better one.

**Impact.** Would have consumed most of the context budget on a machine already at the edge of RAM (ctx-size had to be capped at 8192), leaving little room for the page image and the answer — on top of shifting the input away from what training saw.

**Fix.** Rejected on the human's push-back; PROMPT_SHORT used and written to _prompt_short.txt.

**→ Rule.** For a fine-tuned model the prompt is part of the trained artifact. Any prompt that differs from the training prompt — richer or poorer — discards part of the fine-tune.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-25.md` · ml-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · Time spent evaluating SAM 3 / Grounding DINO / YOLO-World before realising they are the wrong tool class

**What happened.** Object-detection models (SAM 3, Grounding DINO, YOLO-World) were investigated as candidates before it was pointed out that the task is wrong for them: the elements are connected boxes with context needing ID + length, not dogs-and-cats detection, and real length comes from the grid table, not from box size in pixels.

**Root cause.** Candidate models were shortlisted by popularity in the vision space rather than by whether the task is actually a detection task; the problem statement ('read an ID and join it to a grid-derived length') was never written down before searching.

**Impact.** Research time spent on a whole model family that could never have worked.

**Fix.** Direction changed to comparing VLMs; Qwen3.6-35B-A3B was confirmed as the right line (newer, MMMU 81.7 vs ~70.2, 262K vs 32K context, Apache 2.0, proven GGUF path).

**→ Rule.** Write the task down as an input→output contract before shortlisting models. If the required output is an identifier joined to a table value, it is not a detection problem no matter how visual it looks.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · t02 bug 1: the token budget was computed too early, against numbers that then changed

**What happened.** Cited as a mistake to avoid in t03 planning: t02's 'bug 1' was computing the token budget too early, against numbers that subsequently changed. For t03 the budget was deliberately deferred until the dataset is settled.

**Root cause.** A downstream calculation was performed while its inputs (dataset size and shape) were still in flux, so the result was stale as soon as the dataset moved.

**Impact.** On t02 it produced a budget that did not match reality; the cost is re-planning and potentially a mis-sized run.

**Fix.** Deferred the t03 token-budget calculation until after the dataset is settled, explicitly to avoid repeating this.

**→ Rule.** Do not compute a derived plan number until its inputs are frozen. Sequence planning so budget/sizing comes after dataset finalisation, never before.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · The PDF text-layer optimisation has never actually run — every PDF here is vector-outline with 0 text

**What happened.** Layer 1 (PDF text layer extraction) sits ahead of Pass 0 and could drop whole REBAR_SCHEDULE pages from every VLM pass — but every PDF in this project is vector-outline with zero extractable text, so that branch has never executed.

**Root cause.** An optimisation was built against an assumption about the input format that does not hold for this corpus; the assumption was never validated against a real file.

**Impact.** Dead code carried in the pipeline, and a cost saving that was counted on but never materialised — every page still goes through the VLM.

**Fix.** Documented; not removed.

**→ Rule.** Validate an input-format assumption against real files before building an optimisation on it. Log whether an optimisation branch actually fires — a saving nobody measures is a saving nobody gets.

<sub>`2026-08-04.md` · model-pipeline</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · Three pattern classes have almost no examples in the corpus — 13, 12 and 5 files across 12 houses

**What happened.** Cross-checking the 16-pattern taxonomy against real file counts over 12 houses and 1,240 files showed gridline at 13 files, site_plan at 12 and title at 5 — structurally thin, on top of bbs_schedule and soil_boring_log at zero.

**Root cause.** The taxonomy was designed from what a drawing set contains, not from how many examples each class would yield; gridline is one file per house by definition, so its count can never grow faster than the house count.

**Impact.** A per-pattern training plan has five of sixteen classes with too few examples to learn from, which caps what a per-pattern prompt round can achieve regardless of how well the other eleven do.

**Fix.** not fixed — the decision was to grow the dataset in houses rather than drop the thin patterns from the plan

**→ Rule.** Count the examples per class before committing to a per-class training architecture. A class that is one file per house needs a house count, not a page count, to become trainable.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-04 · Pass 3 cannot be tuned — the schema stores beams atomic per segment while Pass 3 wants them grouped by length

**What happened.** Deciding whether t03 should also tune Pass 3 (counting) stalled on a shape mismatch: the schema stores beams atomically, one entry per segment, while Pass 3's job is to return them grouped by span length. No dataset in that shape exists anywhere.

**Root cause.** The schema and the production pipeline were designed against different units of a beam, and nobody checked the two shapes against each other until a tuning round needed to bridge them.

**Impact.** One of the five production passes has no path to being tuned at all without first building a new dataset shape; this compounds the already-recorded finding that the tuned model can replace at most one pass.

**Fix.** not fixed — left as an undecided item

**→ Rule.** Before scoping a tuning round for a pass, check that a dataset in that pass's own output shape can actually be produced from what is stored. A mismatch here is a dataset project, not a training project.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-04.md` · training</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Model systematically drops the letter prefix from element_id on schedule pages (D1 → 1)

**What happened.** Comparing 19 pages against ground truth revealed the model consistently emits element_id without its letter prefix on schedule-type pages — ground truth "D1" becomes AI "1". The comparison script had to key matches on (element_type, trailing digit) instead of exact id string.

**Root cause.** Likely a training-data artifact in how t02's schedule elements were structured — the letter prefix may have been carried in a separate field or column in the training examples, teaching the model to emit only the numeric part. Not yet confirmed for t01.

**Impact.** Every schedule-page element id is wrong in a way that breaks exact-match evaluation and would break any downstream join on element id. The eval had to be loosened, which weakens what the recall number actually proves.

**Fix.** Worked around in the comparison script by matching on (element_type, trailing digit). Root cause not fixed.

**→ Rule.** When an eval needs a looser match key to score at all, that looseness is itself a finding — record it as a model defect and check whether the training data taught it, rather than silently normalizing it away.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Model hallucinated fence details on pages 16/17 as column, footing and ground-beam elements

**What happened.** In the house 08 comparison, pages 16 and 17 (fence details) were read by the model as structural column, footing and ground-beam elements — real misreads that dragged element recall down alongside the JSON parse failures.

**Root cause.** The model has no reliable page-type gate; presented with a detail sheet whose geometry superficially resembles structural sections, it produced plausible structural elements. This is precisely the failure a Pass 0 classify step is designed to prevent.

**Impact.** False structural elements injected into the output; if imported unreviewed, they would have created phantom columns/footings in the BOQ. Contributed to the 11% recall figure.

**Fix.** Not fixed at model level. It is part of the motivation for t03's Pass 0 page-classification design.

**→ Rule.** Single-shot extraction with no page-type gate will invent structure on any sheet that looks structural — classify the page before extracting, and treat hallucinated elements as more dangerous than missed ones because they price into the BOQ.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-20.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · One page still failed after grammar-constrained decoding: the model looped inside a string literal

**What happened.** House 08 หน้า07 still hit the token cap after xgrammar was enabled, emitting "description": "ct_igh_igh_igh_ide_igh_igh_igh_ida_igh_igh_igh_ife_igh...". Grammar cannot catch it because inside a JSON string every character is grammatically valid, and no_repeat_ngram_size=8 was evaded because the rotating separators (_ide, _ida, _ife) meant no 8-token sequence repeated exactly.

**Root cause.** Grammar constraints enforce syntax, not semantics — inside a string literal the grammar imposes no restriction at all, so a repetition loop can run freely there. The n-gram guard has a structural blind spot: any loop that varies one token per cycle slips under an exact-repeat rule.

**Impact.** 1 of 31 pages still invalid after the fix. Bounded, but proves grammar is not a complete answer to repetition.

**Fix.** Detect parse failure and regenerate that single page — judged not worth more complex machinery for 1 in 31.

**→ Rule.** Grammar-constrained decoding closes structural failures only; keep a parse-check-and-regenerate retry for the remainder, and do not expect no_repeat_ngram to catch loops that rotate a token each cycle.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21(teach mk).md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-25 · Three pattern-recognition approaches on section sheets all failed; one looked perfect on the first house tested

**What happened.** HoughCircles on circled marks scored 5/5 with zero false positives on house 17, then 3/20 on house 12 and 0/18 on house 01. Auto-detecting cross-section boxes got 7 of ~14 because grid/extension lines cross the boxes and break the clean 4-gon contour. Cause: section sheets have no shared layout across design offices — house 17 circles its marks, house 01 prints underlined text `B1 1:20` with no circle at all.

**Root cause.** A geometric assumption (marks are circled) was validated on a single house and treated as a property of the drawing type, when it is actually a per-design-office styling choice.

**Impact.** Three dead-end experiments. Would have been repeated by the next person had they not been written down.

**Fix.** All three attempts recorded in the workflow doc and the teaching PDF explicitly so nobody repeats them; the rebar-dot attempt was left marked inconclusive rather than written up as a failure.

**→ Rule.** A CV heuristic that works perfectly on the first sample proves nothing — test cross-source before believing it, and write failed experiments down with their numbers so the next person does not spend the same day.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · overfit-to-one-sample</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-26 · NVLM-D-72B cannot be run at all — even vLLM cannot serve it, as NVIDIA itself admits

**What happened.** NVLM-D-72B was evaluated and found doubly unusable: a CC-BY-NC-4.0 licence forbidding commercial use, and no working inference path — vLLM cannot run it and NVIDIA acknowledges this.

**Root cause.** A published model release does not imply a working serving stack. Weights on HuggingFace are not the same as a runnable model.

**Impact.** Avoided at evaluation time; would otherwise have burned rental time discovering the model cannot even be loaded.

**Fix.** Disqualified in the catalogue on both licence and runnability grounds.

**→ Rule.** Confirm both a permissive licence AND a working inference path before shortlisting any model. Published weights prove neither.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/แคตตาล็อก_AI_ทางเลือก_2026-08-26.md` · model-selection</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-26 · The Thai→English glossary could teach the model to translate labels it is forbidden to translate — mitigated only by where it sits in the prompt

**What happened.** Adding a Thai→field glossary directly conflicts with rule §0.7 ('never translate a label printed on the drawing'). The mitigation was to place the glossary adjacent to that rule so the model reads both together.

**Root cause.** A glossary is a translation table; the task forbids translating printed labels. The two instructions are semantically opposed and the fix is positional, not structural.

**Impact.** If the model starts translating drawing labels, GT-vs-output comparison breaks on verbatim fields and the failure will look like a recall problem, not a prompt-conflict problem. Never measured whether the placement mitigation actually works.

**Fix.** placed the glossary adjacent to rule §0.7 in _common.md — mitigation only, effectiveness unverified

**→ Rule.** When a new prompt block contradicts an existing rule, prompt adjacency is a hope, not a guard. Add an explicit check on the next eval: do verbatim label fields still match GT character-for-character?

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-26.md` · prompt-conflict</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-29 · Markdown punctuation left inside prompts was causing the model to hallucinate

**What happened.** All seven pass 2 prompts contained markdown characters (. _ * # : ; \ | —) outside of JSON and filenames. These were stripped out on 2026-08-29 specifically to stop the model hallucinating.

**Root cause.** Prompts were authored as human-readable markdown documents rather than as model input, so formatting syntax intended for a renderer was fed to the model as content and interpreted as signal.

**Impact.** Degraded extraction quality across all seven pass 2 subtasks for as long as the formatting was present; the effect was diffuse hallucination rather than a discrete failure, so it went unnoticed.

**Fix.** Stripped every markdown character outside JSON and filenames from all seven prompts on Makham's instruction.

**→ Rule.** Prompts are model input, not documents. Strip presentation-layer formatting characters before sending, and keep the human-readable version separate from the shipped prompt text.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอน_t04_Purson_2026-08-29.md` · prompt-engineering</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · pass3 prompt rule 4 wrongly forbade sharing a cv_mark for horizontal beams

**What happened.** Rule 4 required unique cv_mark per element, but a beam_h detection box is a row-level detection — a printed beam line runs continuously across several bays — so several elements legitimately share one box.

**Root cause.** The rule was written from the point-element case (footing/column) and generalized to line elements without checking how the detector actually boxes them.

**Impact.** Correct multi-element rows would have been treated as duplicates and rejected.

**Fix.** Added an explicit exception for beam_h while keeping the no-duplicate rule for beam_v/footing/column; confirmed merge_guard.py already keeps both plus a warning rather than deleting.

**→ Rule.** Write detector-facing rules per element geometry class (point vs line), and verify how the detector actually boxes each class before writing a uniqueness constraint.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · prompt-bug</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · The pass system misclassified beams B1/B2/B2A/B4 as columns where the raw-power run got it right

**What happened.** In the head-to-head comparison on page 12, the pass system labelled beams as columns while the raw-power prompt classified them correctly as beams (though with no rebar detail and one empty element).

**Root cause.** The pass0 subtask hint that generally helps by telling the model what to look for can also bias classification toward the expected element type on a page.

**Impact.** Wrong element type flows into downstream quantity takeoff for that page.

**Fix.** Not fixed — recorded as a known trade-off in the comparison; the pass system still won decisively overall.

**→ Rule.** A subtask hint that improves recall can also bias classification — check element-type accuracy separately from recall when evaluating a guided pipeline.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · model-quality</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-31 · enable_thinking=False did not stop chain-of-thought from leaking into the JSON answer

**What happened.** Around character 1,800 of the page-27 greedy output, the model's reasoning appeared inline in the middle of the JSON in English ("Self-correction based strictly on visible text: Only grids A,B,C shown... Remove hypothetical D references entirely"), despite thinking being disabled.
