<sub>`d:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/No_touch_box/docs/rule_of_tune.md` · single-source-of-truth</sub>

---

## T13 — Process, Planning & Wasted Work

*Order of operations, scope, rework, and effort spent on the wrong thing.*

**231 entries** · 21 critical · 74 high

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-06 · Same Label Studio bug repeated: multiple $variables crammed into one Text/Header value, failing 10/10 task imports

**What happened.** Importing label-studio-tasks-makham-elements-structural.json into Label Studio Cloud failed on all 10 tasks with `"sheet_code $sheet_name — $pattern: $view_title" key is expected in task data`. The cause was putting 2+ $field variables inside a single Text/Header `value=` attribute. This exact bug had already been hit on 2026-07-02 and written down in No_touch_box/CLAUDE.md; it just was not applied when the new Gen 3 XML configs were authored. A grep found 7 offending spots across 5 XML files.

**Root cause.** An existing written lesson was not consulted at the moment new config was authored. The lesson lived buried inside a Label Studio subsection of CLAUDE.md instead of the top-level 'Key Lessons' list, so nothing forced a check while writing a brand-new config of the same kind. Also the failure mode changed shape between the two occurrences (runtime 'undefined' in a Repeater on Jul 2 vs an import-time validation error at task top level on Jul 6), so it was not recognized as the same bug until diagnosed.

**Impact.** 10/10 tasks failed to import; 7 spots across 5 XML files had to be found and rewritten (each multi-variable value split into one Text tag per variable); the already-imported broken tasks then had to be deleted and the config re-pasted and re-imported in the correct order. A full round of Label Studio setup work was redone.

**Fix.** Split every multi-variable value into one <Text> tag per variable across all 5 XML files, verified by repeat grep; then elevated the rule to item 8 of the top-level 'Key Lessons (don't repeat these mistakes)' section of No_touch_box/CLAUDE.md and added a warning in SESSION_HANDOFF_2026-07-06.md.

**→ Rule.** Never put more than one $field variable in a single Label Studio Text/Header value — one variable per tag, always. And structurally: a lesson filed under a tool subsection will not be read when authoring new config; every repeat-class bug must be promoted to the top-level Key Lessons list the moment it recurs, not left where it was first written.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process-failure / repeated-bug</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-07 · t1 BOQ recorded 137/294 sq.m of floor tile for a 70 sq.m house

**What happened.** A background agent re-reading page 51 caught that the t1 extraction had entered floor-tile quantities of 137 and 294 sq.m, physically impossible for a house whose total floor area is 70 sq.m (stated on page 60). The correct range for category 2.3 was 21-47.

**Root cause.** BOQ numbers were transcribed cell-by-cell with no sanity check against any other page in the same document — nothing in the process compared a quantity against the building's own area.

**Impact.** A ~4-6x wrong quantity shipped in the t1 dataset and survived until a later independent pass happened to notice it.

**Fix.** The agent corrected the quantity to the right value with a written explanation of why the original was impossible.

**→ Rule.** Every extracted quantity needs at least one cross-page plausibility check (area, count, or total) before it is accepted — a number that cannot physically exist must fail, not be transcribed faithfully.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-14 · All review corrections live only in the corrected-copy folder; the tuning original was never synced

**What happened.** Every fix made for house 1 (D'/1'' dummy grids, no-dash point refs, reordered elements, split-out specs) existed only in `json_แก้ไขแล้ว/`. The original `rawjson_ยังไม่ได้แก้ไขโดนคน/01.../` — the copy actually used for tuning — remained entirely the old version. The sync-back never started across every subsequent entry.

**Root cause.** The corrected-copy folder was created to protect the original, but no sync-back procedure or trigger was defined at the same time, so the fork widened indefinitely.

**Impact.** The dataset actually used for training carries the known-wrong values (wrong dummy grids, wrong rebar counts, dashed refs) while the corrected data sits unused. Every day of review widens the divergence and increases sync risk.

**Fix.** Not fixed — 'syncing back hasn't started at all' remained on the pending list through 2026-07-25.

**→ Rule.** When you fork data to protect an original, define the merge-back trigger in the same change. A protective fork with no sync plan is just a second source of truth.

<sub>`2026-07-14.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-19 · Beam B5's main '3-Ø16' rebar label dropped entirely from the data in two separate houses

**What happened.** On house 4, B5's data had simply dropped the main '3-Ø16' label, leaving only 2 bars where there should be 3+2=5. The identical mistake was then found on house 5's B5 (bottom 3→5, the L/8 rebar missing entirely).

**Root cause.** When a beam carries both a main label and a supplemental L/8 label, one of the two was read and the other never registered — and no cross-check compared the recorded bar count against the section image.

**Impact.** 60% under-count of bottom rebar on a main beam in two houses — a direct structural steel shortfall in the data.

**Fix.** Both fixed to 5 after zooming into the section and counting points; house 5's B3X 'additional' was also found to be a phantom and deleted.

**→ Rule.** A beam with more than one rebar label needs every label accounted for explicitly — count the points in the section and reconcile against the sum of all printed labels before recording. Also verify phantom entries: an additional_bars entry with no corresponding points in the section is fabricated data.

<sub>`2026-07-19.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · train_qwen3vl.py carried five bugs because it was written when the dataset was 221 examples and had never actually been executed

**What happened.** A pre-flight read of train_qwen3vl.py found five distinct bugs. The file had been written back when the dataset was 221 examples (it is now 403 rows) and had never once been run.

**Root cause.** Code was authored speculatively against a future run and then left to rot while both the dataset and the surrounding libraries moved. Nothing ever executed it, so nothing ever surfaced a failure.

**Impact.** Five bugs would have entered a paid training run simultaneously — including two that silently corrupt training data rather than crash.

**Fix.** All five fixed before renting; the file was also later found to still fail at runtime on a sixth, library-version bug (see the transformers 5.5.0 entry).

**→ Rule.** Unrun code is unverified code, and it decays as its dependencies and data move. Execute every script at least once — even against a tiny fixture — before trusting it with a paid run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · code/process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-07-28 · The standing advice 'always upload the adapter first' was wrong — the code uploads GGUF first and the adapter last

**What happened.** A backup-safety guideline in use stated the adapter goes up first. Reading the actual export_gguf.py code showed the opposite: GGUF is uploaded first, adapter last. Since the sanity check fails before the GGUF stage completes, nothing at all would have been backed up through the Phase 8 route.

**Root cause.** A safety guarantee was believed from a remembered description of the code rather than verified against the code. The belief was load-bearing — it was the reason Phase 8 was trusted as a backup path.

**Impact.** A false sense of backup safety across the whole round; combined with the Phase 8 sanity-check failure, the Phase 8 route would have produced zero backup.

**Fix.** Verified against the real code; the rule changed to: backups must always be done separately, never relying on Phase 8.

**→ Rule.** Verify every safety guarantee against the actual code, not against your memory of it. A backup step that lives inside a pipeline that can abort earlier is not a backup — do it separately and unconditionally.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · process/misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-02 · Root cause of the whole format mess: the spec never locked the shape of the file, only the fields

**What happened.** After a day of format fixes, the underlying cause was identified: the spec described how to write each field but never locked the shape of the file — which is exactly why houses could invent array names, store rebar as a string, or spell the stirrup `tie_bar` without breaking any written rule.

**Root cause.** The spec was written incrementally as field-level rules with no top-level structural contract, so structural freedom was unconstrained by construction.

**Impact.** Eleven houses of divergent structure requiring hundreds of retrofit fixes across multiple sessions.

**Fix.** Added a new §0 FORMAT LOCK at the top of the spec (10 sub-rules: container, required element fields, element_id = printed mark, canonical element_type list, mm integers, rebar-must-be-object, printed_as, grid_ref notation, no invented pattern, closing checklist) and wrote `tools/check_format.py` to enforce all 14 checks with exit 1 on failure.

**→ Rule.** A data spec must lock the container shape before it specifies field semantics, and every rule must be machine-checked. A 1000-house set cannot be hand-audited.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-21 · material_list consumed 435 files / 37% of all annotation effort and yields zero elements

**What happened.** Counting the real dataset (11 houses, 1,180 files, 4,625 elements) showed material_list accounts for 435 files = 37% of all annotation work done to date, while producing elements = 0 — it is a table pattern with no element positions. Annotating only the patterns Constistant actually consumes drops a house from ~107 pages to ~38.

**Root cause.** Annotation scope was defined as 'every page of every house' with no measurement of which patterns produce downstream value. The full-coverage instinct was never checked against what the consumer reads.

**Impact.** Roughly 37% of all human annotation effort to date produced no elements. At the target of +20 houses this would have meant annotating 2,140 pages instead of ~750 — 65% wasted effort.

**Fix.** material_list skipped by default in the new op04 skill, with the 435-file/37%/zero-elements evidence stated inline. dataset_sizing.md written with the real counts. All of Pass 3 skipped by default too.

**→ Rule.** Before scaling any annotation campaign, count elements-produced-per-file per pattern and cut the zero-yield patterns — measure the dataset you already have rather than assuming full coverage is the safe default.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21.md` · planning</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-21 · Wrongly concluded Unsloth was swallowing the grammar constraint and wrote that conclusion into SUMMARY.md

**What happened.** After the first grammar-enabled run still produced unparseable JSON, the immediate conclusion was that Unsloth's loader must be dropping the grammar processor — and that conclusion was written into SUMMARY.md. It was wrong. Reading the code layer by layer showed Unsloth forwarded everything and the grammar was working the whole time; the real cause was that lm-format-enforcer treats a trailing comma ({"a":1,}) as valid while Python's json does not. Proven in one line: deleting the trailing comma made the 'broken' file parse immediately.

**Root cause.** A plausible-sounding suspect was chosen over reading the actual code path, and the guess was recorded as a finding rather than as a hypothesis. Two libraries silently disagreeing on the definition of 'valid JSON' is a far less narratively satisfying explanation than 'the wrapper ate it', so the wrong suspect won.

**Impact.** A confidently wrong root cause sat in the project's SUMMARY.md, ready to send the next reader (or the same person three months later) down the wrong path. The diary calls this the most expensive lesson of the night, and it became rule_of_tune Lesson #14.

**Fix.** Traced the real cause by reading code layer by layer; switched the default grammar backend to xgrammar (which cannot emit a trailing comma at source) with lm-format-enforcer as fallback; corrected SUMMARY.md and recorded the incident as rule_of_tune ข้อ 14.

**→ Rule.** Never write a root cause into a document until it is proven by reading the actual code or a one-line reproduction — if evidence is insufficient, write 'cause unknown, suspects A or B'; a confidently wrong conclusion in a doc is more damaging than no conclusion at all.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-21(teach mk).md` · misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-25 · Two subtasks both reading 0% recall were nearly conflated as the same problem

**What happened.** plan_beam and section both reported 0% id-recall. They are different diseases: plan_beam sits under an 88–93% achievable ceiling (a genuine model failure), while section's ceiling on the test house is 1/23 = 4% (a perfect model scores at most 4%, so the metric measures almost nothing).

**Root cause.** Recall was reported as a bare percentage with no accompanying ceiling, so two structurally different failures produced an identical-looking number.

**Impact.** Conflating them would have aimed an entire tuning round (and its GPU rental) at a subtask where the model cannot possibly score, while leaving the real failure untouched.

**Fix.** Built `measure_id_ceiling.py` to compute the achievable ceiling per subtask and reported ceiling next to actual for all six subtasks; split reporting into `recall` and `recall_printed` in the eval script.

**→ Rule.** Never report a score without its achievable ceiling. Two identical percentages can be opposite problems, and the ceiling is what tells them apart.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-25 · The "downscaling causes plan_beam's 0% recall" hypothesis was concluded from token math alone and then disproven visually

**What happened.** An earlier research pass concluded from token arithmetic that image downscaling was the cause of plan_beam's 0% recall. A direct visual test — cropping the most-downscaled real training image (บ้าน_ใหญ่_1ชั้น_01 หน้า15) at native resolution and at the actual scale the model receives at MAX_PIXELS=7680 — showed grid bubbles, beam marks, column marks and dimension text equally legible in both.

**Root cause.** A causal claim was made from an indirect proxy (token count) without ever looking at what the model actually sees. Token loss and legibility loss are not the same thing.

**Impact.** The team was about to buy image resolution (and consider an H200 rental) to fix a problem resolution does not cause. The real correlate found instead is GT JSON label length: plan_beam's answer is 2.3× longer than plan_footing's from the same sheet at the same resolution.

**Fix.** Ran the visual comparison on real training data (no GPU needed), recorded the contradiction, and reframed the working theory as "the model fails to produce one long internally-consistent JSON blob in a single completion", with a recommended next step of splitting plan_beam into per-grid-zone sub-answers merged by code.

**→ Rule.** Never conclude a perception failure from token math. Render what the model actually receives and look at it — a five-minute crop-and-compare beats an hour of arithmetic and can save a GPU rental.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-25.md` · misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-25 · Scaled straight to 4 parallel full trainings (~60 GPU-hours, ~$63) before ever cheaply validating that the model could read a drawing at all

**What happened.** The round went from 'dry-run 5 steps passed' straight to 4 folds × 306 steps running in parallel on 4 rented cards, ~15-16 h each. Every one of the 4 ran to completion and produced an adapter, and only after all 4 finished and eval scored 0% on plan_beam/plan_footing did the investigation find that `crop_to_patches: true` was missing, so no image was ever legible at training time. The entire round's GPU spend produced 4 adapters that cannot read drawings. The corrective rule written for t05 says it plainly: train one fold first, do not start with 4 parallel folds.

**Root cause.** The dry-run only proved the plumbing (VRAM fits, loss is a number, checkpoint saves) — it never proved the model was seeing readable pixels. There was no cheap gate between 'config parses / 5 steps run' and 'commit 60 GPU-hours across 4 cards'. Scale-out was decided on schedule pressure ('เวลาจริงลดครึ่ง 29→~16 ชม.') and budget-permission ('อย่าสนงบ ผมจ่ายเอง'), not on a validated config.

**Impact.** ~$63 of GPU rental plus ~60 GPU-hours and roughly 24 h of wall-clock across two days, producing 4 unusable adapters. Also forced 4 separate HF uploads, 4 sha256 verifies, 4 destroys, and an eval round on top.

**Fix.** Not fixed for t04 (money already spent). Carried into t05 as an explicit rule: single fold first, plus a CPU-only image-token probe before any paid training run.

**→ Rule.** Parallel scale-out multiplies whatever the config does — including the bug. Before committing more than one card, run one cheap end-to-end check that proves the model perceives the input (probe tokens per image, or eyeball a resized sample), not just that the training loop executes.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · process/planning</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-26 · Repo-wide JSON pretty-print pass ran over 343 files including 16 a teammate had just finished checking

**What happened.** Commit `be9ad80` ("แก้ระบบ") ran a repo-wide JSON pretty-print pass touching 343 files under json_แก้ไขแล้ว, including 16 files across houses 24, 26, 27 that Ark had committed only moments earlier. Discovered days later while tracing house 42's history.

**Root cause.** A broad automated pass was run without first checking `git log` for other people's fresh commits in the same paths. No ownership or freshness check gated the operation.

**Impact.** Ark's just-finished work was reformatted underneath him without warning. Required a deep semantic diff (custom Node script, key-order-normalizing, treating element_id:"name" vs element_id:null+element_name_assigned as equivalent) across all 343 files to prove no data was lost, plus asking Ark to freeze push/pull and back up his local copies, plus a written incident note and formal apology.

**Fix.** Verified 0 real data differences — only formatting changed. Published an incident note + Thai apology letter as an artifact, apologizing for the process (not for data loss, since there was none).

**→ Rule.** Before any repo-wide automated pass, run `git log --since` on the target paths and check whose work you are about to touch. If someone else committed there recently, ask first. A format-only change is still a change to someone else's working state.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-26.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-29 · Model switch to InternVL3-78B invalidated the entire Unsloth toolchain — and the model had been rejected three days earlier

**What happened.** Makham directed t04 to use OpenGVLab/InternVL3-78B. Unsloth does not support InternVL3 (issues #3401/#2341), so train_t03.py, infer_house_t03.py and onstart.sh all became unusable and were marked ⛔. A single 96GB card is also insufficient (LoRA bf16 needs ≥2×H100-class, or an untested single-card QLoRA 4-bit attempt). This same model had been rejected in the 2026-08-26 catalog on the grounds its backbone is Qwen2.5-72B anyway.

**Root cause.** The model catalog evaluated model *quality* (OmniDocBench 83.76, license) but not *toolchain compatibility* or *hardware fit*. Framework support and VRAM requirements were not selection criteria, so the cost of a switch was invisible until after the decision.

**Impact.** Three working scripts became reference-only. Requires selecting a new framework, a new GPU strategy, a dataset-format converter (Unsloth-style jsonl → new framework format), rewritten train+infer scripts, and a fresh xgrammar/tokenizer probe. Also invalidated same-day work: MAX_PIXELS 5120→7680 and OUT_DIR t03→t04 fixes were made just before the model change landed.

**Fix.** Marked all three scripts ⛔ with headers and kept them as Qwen-era reference. Wrote t04_Purson/t04_workflow.md as a Phase 0 doc naming every gap. Framework subsequently decided: LLaMA-Factory (ms-swift held in reserve). Prompts/dataset/GT/CV sidecars are plain text and carry over — only the jsonl envelope needs converting.

**→ Rule.** Make framework support and single-card VRAM fit hard gates in the model-selection catalog, alongside benchmark and license. A model your training stack cannot load is not a candidate, however good its scores.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-29.md` · planning</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-30 · `async def` wrapping a blocking `model.generate()` let one runaway request hang the whole inference server for 7+ hours

**What happened.** Two concurrent requests (the e2e test plus arm 2.4a) were fired at `serve_purson.py`. The server then stopped responding entirely for over 7 hours — not even `/v1/models`, the simplest health endpoint. The GPU was verified alive (utilization steady at 11-14%, process state R, no Xid/ECC errors). The cause was that `model.generate()` is called directly inside an `async def` handler, so one request that fell into a string-repetition loop (a known t03 issue — the grammar constrains JSON structure, not content) blocked the entire event loop.

**Root cause.** A synchronous, long-running, CPU/GPU-bound call was placed directly inside an asyncio coroutine. FastAPI's `async def` gives no concurrency for blocking calls — the event loop is single-threaded, so one stuck generate starves every other request including health checks and, apparently, the timeout deadline check itself.

**Impact.** 7+ hours of a rented GPU at $1.070/hr wasted while the server was unreachable; the machine had to be torn down with `presentation.py down` before the planned browser-path test with the real model could finish. Still unfixed at end of day and flagged as the number-one blocker before the presentation.

**Fix.** Not fixed yet. Prescribed fix recorded: wrap `generate()` in `asyncio.to_thread()` or run a separate worker-thread queue, so one bad request cannot take down the whole server.

**→ Rule.** Never call a blocking model/IO function directly inside an `async def` handler — always `asyncio.to_thread()` or a thread/process queue — and always prove concurrency by firing two simultaneous requests, one of them long-running, before trusting a server.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · serving-architecture</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-30 · The same image-resolution/token bug class destroyed a training round for the third round running (t01 → t02 → t04) because no probe step was ever institutionalised after the first two

**What happened.** t01 was ruined by an Unsloth 512px fallback, t02 by a data_collator resize that was never compared against expectations, and t04 by not knowing `crop_to_patches` existed. Three different frameworks, three different mechanisms, one identical symptom: the model was silently fed images too small to read. Only after the third occurrence was a rule written (rule_of_tune.md item 15) requiring a source-level check of tokens-per-image plus a CPU-only probe before any paid training.

**Root cause.** After t01 and t02 the individual bugs were fixed but no permanent, framework-agnostic check was added to the pre-training checklist. Each new framework/model pairing reintroduced the same failure through a different door, and the fix was always re-derived from scratch after the money was spent.

**Impact.** Three training rounds lost to the same class of defect. For t04 specifically, ~$63 and ~60 GPU-hours.

**Fix.** Recorded as rule_of_tune.md item 15: before real training on a new framework/model pair, trace the source for actual tokens-per-image and verify with a CPU-only probe — no GPU needed.

**→ Rule.** A bug that recurs across rounds is a missing checklist item, not bad luck. When the same symptom appears a second time, stop fixing the instance and add a permanent pre-flight gate.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-30.md` · process/recurring-defect</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-31 · rsync resume silently did nothing: tool checked on the wrong machine, error hidden by exit 0 and | tail

**What happened.** An scp to gpu4 stalled at 83%. A resume was attempted with rsync --partial --append-verify, but `which rsync` was only checked on the remote host, not on the local Git Bash which has no rsync. The command failed with 'command not found', yet the task reported exit 0 because a trailing echo succeeded, and `| tail -2` hid the error message. The file on gpu4 was a killed scp fragment.

**Root cause.** Three compounding errors: verifying tool availability on the wrong machine, reading the exit code of a compound command instead of the command of interest, and truncating output that contained the failure.

**Impact.** gpu4 nearly trained with 60 missing images silently — md5 mismatch (2aa1039d... vs 4b765a37...), tar extraction incomplete, only 824 of 884 images present. Caught only by the mandatory md5 check.

**Fix.** Re-transferred and verified md5; recorded the two rules explicitly.

**→ Rule.** Check a tool exists on the machine that will RUN it, never the destination; and never judge success by the exit code of a compound command or by truncated output — read the real stderr and verify by checksum.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-31 · The decoder problem was recorded on 2026-08-30 and tested, but never applied to serve_purson.py

**What happened.** no_repeat_ngram_size=8 + repetition_penalty=1.15 had already been identified as a compounding problem for t04 on 30 Aug, with a test showing that removing them took element count from 0 to 10 — yet serve_purson.py was never updated, and the same defect caused today's 0% run and Chinese hallucination.

**Root cause.** A lesson was written into the diary but not propagated to every file containing the same code.

**Impact.** A full evaluation round wasted reproducing a failure that had already been diagnosed the day before.

**Fix.** Fixed in serve_purson.py, and recorded the meta-rule about propagating fixes.

**→ Rule.** When the diary records 'X is a problem', grep the whole repo for X and fix every occurrence that same day — a lesson recorded but not applied is a lesson not learned.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-31 · A full day passed after training completed with nobody knowing whether the model could actually read

**What happened.** Training finished, adapters were merged and published, and only the next day did anyone measure real recall — which turned out to be 0% under the shipped generation settings.

**Root cause.** The training pipeline had no automated recall evaluation step; success was judged by loss and by the artifacts existing on HuggingFace.

**Impact.** A full day of elapsed time and further GPU spend proceeded on a model whose actual capability was unknown and, as configured, was zero.

**Fix.** Listed as a required addition for the next round: an automated recall measurement inside the training round itself.

**→ Rule.** Every training round must end with an automated task-level recall measurement on a held-out house before the model is declared done — loss and a successful upload prove nothing about capability.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-08-31 · The image-resolution bug class hit for the third consecutive round despite two prior lessons

**What happened.** t01 (Unsloth 512px fallback), t02 (data_collator resize not compared), and t04 (crop_to_patches unknown) are the same class: the model silently trains on far lower resolution than intended. t04's config line was written by Claude on 2026-08-29 even though two prior lessons existed.

**Root cause.** Prior lessons were recorded as narratives about specific parameters rather than converted into a mandatory pre-run assertion that covers the whole class.

**Impact.** Full 4-GPU round wasted plus a full day, model discarded — the third repetition of the same class.

**Fix.** This round added preflight_seq_lengths() and a verified tile/token count on the real machine; the class is now covered by an executable check.

**→ Rule.** Convert every repeated failure class into a mandatory executable pre-run assertion — a lesson written in prose has now failed to prevent recurrence three times.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · process</sub>

#### 🔴 CRITICAL · 2026-09-01 · The same 'image silently downscaled' bug class killed three separate training rounds (t01, t02, t04)

**What happened.** t01: Unsloth quietly resized images to 512px without telling anyone. t02: the data packer resized images and nobody ever compared before/after sizes. t04: nobody knew the crop_to_patches switch existed. Three different mechanisms, one identical failure, and in every case zero errors were raised.

**Root cause.** After the first two occurrences no permanent guard was installed — each round was treated as a one-off config mistake instead of a recurring class of failure. Without a mandatory pre-flight measurement, every new framework or loader reintroduces its own silent resize default.

**Impact.** Three separate training rounds produced worthless models. The cost compounded because each round was diagnosed from scratch as if it were new.

**Fix.** Codified as rule_of_tune.md #15 — a mandatory pre-train token-per-image measurement, done on CPU for free — which finally turns a repeated ad-hoc discovery into a permanent gate.

**→ Rule.** When the same failure appears twice, stop fixing the instance and install a permanent automated guard. A bug that recurs three times is a missing process, not three bad configs.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Four schema open questions were written into the doc but never actually put to the decision maker

**What happened.** Generation 3.1 opened 4 new questions — asymmetric top/bottom main_bar, formal confirmation of additional_bars[], multi-level column schedules (separate `level` field vs embedded in element_id), and precast plank fields (dowel_bar/topping_mesh/topping_thickness_min_mm/level_step_mm). The diary states plainly they had 'still not been asked' to Makham as of the end of July 6, despite him being present and working in the same session all day.

**Root cause.** Questions were recorded into a document instead of being asked in the live conversation. Writing a question down feels like progress and removes the pressure to actually ask it, especially when the person is right there and work is flowing.

**Impact.** Four schema decisions remained unmade while extraction continued around them, meaning more data was produced under assumptions that may later be reversed. All four rolled forward as pending item #2 at the end of the day.

**Fix.** Not fixed — explicitly recorded as 'still not asked as of today (July 6) either — genuinely still pending'.

**→ Rule.** If the decision maker is in the session, ask the blocking question in the session — do not file it. A question written into a doc is a question that will be asked days late, or never, while data keeps being produced under the wrong assumption.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process-failure</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · The pending list grew to 9 items with several rolling forward untouched across two full working days

**What happened.** Every entry in the 2026-07-06 diary ends with 'All prior pending items remain the same', and the day closed with 9 open items. Several — pages 41-47 BOQ, the 210 vs 240 concrete grade conflict, the empty 0-byte file — had already been open since 2026-07-05 and were repeated verbatim in six consecutive entries without action.

**Root cause.** The pending list was append-only with no owner, no size limit and no triage step. Each session started new work rather than closing old, and the ritual of restating the list substituted for acting on it.

**Impact.** Two of the rolled-forward items are data-correctness blockers (missing BOQ pages, ambiguous concrete grade) that gate the usability of the entire house dataset, while the day's effort went into review tooling instead.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the 9-item list was carried into SESSION_HANDOFF_2026-07-06.md as the starting point for the next session.

**→ Rule.** Cap the pending list and triage it at the start of each session, not the end: anything repeated three sessions running gets done, dropped, or assigned an owner and a date. Restating a list is not tracking it — a pending item with no owner is a decision to never do it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process-failure</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-06 · Schema revved three times in one day (3.1 → 3.2 → 3.3) after extraction was already finished, forcing a full 37-page re-extraction plus hand-edits

**What happened.** Pages 1-60 were extracted on 2026-07-05 under Gen 3. The next day the schema gained span_source + atomic beam segments (3.1), the dummy-grid convention + page-00 grid master (3.2), and spec-join-into-plan (3.3). Each change invalidated already-written data: a whole second round (t2) covering pages 1-37 was ordered and run, page 19 view2 and page 20 view1 were rewritten from scratch, and two more t2 files had beam spec hand-joined into every element afterwards.

**Root cause.** The schema was still being designed while bulk extraction was already running in parallel — the open questions from 2026-07-05 (and four more opened on 07-06) were never closed before the data was produced, so every design decision landed as rework on existing files instead of as a constraint on new ones.

**Impact.** Roughly a full day of extraction output (pages 1-37, ~60 files) had to be redone, plus hand-editing of individual JSON files, plus regeneration of every downstream Label Studio task file. Pages 38-60 were left on the older schema, so the house's dataset is now internally inconsistent across page ranges.

**Fix.** t2 round created for pages 1-37; pages 38-60 left at t1 schema and never brought forward

**→ Rule.** Freeze the schema before bulk extraction, or extract one deliberately small pilot set until the schema stops moving. A schema change after N pages are written costs N pages of rework every time — batch the open questions and answer them all before dispatching agents.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-07 · Grid master carries dummy grid A'' which may not be a real grid line at all, just a ground-leveling area

**What happened.** While resolving the overhang confusion on house 1, confidence went UP on dummy grids 1'/3'/A' but DOWN on A'' — the agent suspected A'' is not a real grid line but a ground-leveling area that was mistaken for one. A'' stayed in the grid master anyway.

**Root cause.** A dimension line marking a slab/ground level was read as a structural grid line during an earlier extraction round, and the grid master was built before anyone cross-checked each dummy grid against a second sheet.

**Impact.** The grid master drives grid_ref/grid_ref_start/grid_ref_end for every element in the house. A fabricated grid line means every element positioned against it carries a coordinate that does not exist on the drawing — and this one shipped into t3, t4, and the production 01 folder unresolved.

**Fix.** not fixed — confidence was lowered and the suspicion recorded, but A'' was never removed or confirmed.

**→ Rule.** A dummy grid must be confirmed by at least two independent sheets before it enters the grid master, the same bar later applied on house 3 (where 3 agents independently confirmed 1'/3'). A low confidence score is not a substitute for resolving it — grid master errors propagate to every element in the house.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-10 · The separate-project-per-house vs one-combined-project decision was never made, and blocked import for days

**What happened.** Checking readiness for house #2 surfaced two blockers. The filename collision was fixed the same day. The other — 'Not yet decided whether Label Studio would use a separate project per house, or combine all houses in the existing project' — was never decided, and reappears unchanged in the pending list of every subsequent entry through July 11.

**Root cause.** A blocking decision was recorded as a pending item rather than being forced to a call, and work continued around it. Houses 2 and 3 were extracted and their task JSON generated while the destination for that data was still undefined.

**Impact.** By July 11 three houses' worth of task files exist (house 1, 2, 3) and none of house 2's or house 3's has been imported into Label Studio at all. The whole point of the extraction — getting drawings in front of human annotators — has not happened for two of the three houses.

**Fix.** not fixed — still open in the last entry's pending list.

**→ Rule.** A decision that blocks the delivery step must be forced before the producing step scales. Three houses of output with nowhere to put it is worse than one house that went end to end.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-12 · Weeks of extraction work left uncommitted to git

**What happened.** Across multiple diary entries the standing pending item reads 'committing all the work (nothing committed at all since the t4 round)' — five houses of raw JSON plus schema and rule edits sat untracked.

**Root cause.** Committing was treated as a separate future task rather than a step in the per-house workflow, so it kept being deferred behind extraction work.

**Impact.** Hundreds of hand-produced JSON files with no version history and no recovery point; any accidental overwrite or bad regex sweep would have been unrecoverable.

**Fix.** Not fixed within these entries — it remained on the pending list.

**→ Rule.** Commit at the end of every house, before starting the next one. Irreplaceable hand-produced data with no commit is one bad script away from being gone.

<sub>`2026-07-12.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-13 · A session-limit kill left a half-written JSON file that a file-count check could not detect

**What happened.** `หน้า54_roof_floor_plan.json` was missing a closing `}` for the `grid_dimensions_as_printed` object — the agent was cut off after opening a nested object and before closing it. The file existed and the page count matched, so only a full JSON.parse validation caught it.

**Root cause.** The completeness check was 'number of files equals number of pages'. An interrupted write produces a present-but-invalid file, which that check cannot see.

**Impact.** An invalid file would have broken the label-studio script and any downstream consumer; found only because a parse validation was run.

**Fix.** Wrote an ad-hoc node script to locate the actual missing-brace position (the parser error only pointed at EOF), inserted the `}` at the correct spot, then re-validated all 138 files.

**→ Rule.** File count is not a completeness check. Always run JSON.parse over every produced file before declaring a batch done — and when a parser reports EOF, locate the real unbalanced position programmatically instead of guessing from the error message.

<sub>`2026-07-13.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-13 · Multi-layered floor-plan dimension chains used as primary evidence instead of the site plan

**What happened.** The building envelope was reasoned from stacked dimension chains on the floor plan (`0.60+0.90=1.50`) rather than from sheet A-03, the site plan, which states the overhang directly as 0.60m.

**Root cause.** No stated hierarchy of evidence for 'where the real building edge is'; the reader used whichever sheet was already open, and floor-plan chains are ambiguous about which number is the true building edge.

**Impact.** Contributed directly to the wrong `3'` value above and to a second misreading on house 2 page06 where '0.60'+'0.90' were wrongly summed into a continuous 1.50m overhang.

**Fix.** Established that page A-03 (site plan) is the primary evidence for the building envelope when checking dummy grids that overhang the main grid.

**→ Rule.** Fix an evidence hierarchy per question type: for building envelope and overhangs, the site plan wins over floor-plan dimension chains. Adjacent dimensions that share a point are not additive by default.

**Fix.** not fixed — recorded as pending item 1 and not revisited in later entries.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-13.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-14 · Cited a permission rule and then made the edit in the same message without waiting for a yes/no

**What happened.** Claude stated it was citing `rule_of_tune.md` rule 7 before editing `primary_rawjson_schema.md`, then performed the edit immediately in the same message. The user caught it and asked why a rule would be cited and then not actually stopped for. This had happened twice.

**Root cause.** Citing the rule was treated as satisfying it. The rule described what to invoke, not that invoking it requires the turn to end and an answer to arrive.

**Impact.** The spec — the project's most load-bearing shared document — was edited twice without the required approval; a new rule had to be written to close the loophole.

**Fix.** Recorded as new rule 9 in `rule_of_tune.md`: citing a rule requires actually stopping and asking; never cite a rule and keep editing in the same message.

**What happened.** House 1's review relied mainly on label order and did not zoom in to count rebar points — the technique that found the B2/B2X bugs in house 2. It was recorded that house 1 likely still hides similar mistakes.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-20 · A workaround field was added to paper over the column-rebar bug instead of fixing it, hiding it in six more files

**What happened.** The full-project sweep for the column top/bottom bug found it hiding in fence column C1 in six more files (house1 pages 16/17, house2 pages 20/21, house3 pages 26/27) — where it had 'previously been worked around by adding a `total_main_bar_count` field instead of a real fix'.

**Root cause.** When the wrong total was first noticed, a compensating field was added to record the correct total rather than correcting the structure that produced the wrong one — so the bad structure persisted and stopped being visible as a bug.

**Impact.** The bug survived undetected in six additional files across three houses until a deliberate project-wide sweep found it.

**Fix.** Fixed all six to a single `main_bar.count`, added the missing `specs.CN` on page31, and re-swept the project to confirm no occurrence remained.

**→ Rule.** Never add a compensating field to record the right answer alongside a wrong structure — fix the structure. A workaround field converts a visible bug into a hidden one and guarantees it spreads.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · OOM misdiagnosed as sequence-length/allocator waste — three fixes changed nothing

**What happened.** Three fixes (MAX_LENGTH 10240→9216, PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True, adamw_8bit→paged_adamw_8bit) were applied and round 3 crashed with essentially the same OOM (98.25MB free vs 96.25MB). The real cause was the LoRA delta buffer inside `forward_native_grouped_mm`, multiplied across 256 MoE experts.

**Root cause.** The fix was chosen from a plausible-sounding hypothesis rather than from reading the actual traceback's crash site; lowering a ceiling the test examples never reached could not help by construction.

**Impact.** An entire fix-upload-run cycle (round 3) of paid GPU time spent on a non-cause, plus the delay before the real fix.

**Fix.** Read the traceback line by line, located `lora_delta = torch.empty(...)` in the MoE expert path, and then addressed LoRA rank instead.

**→ Rule.** Read the traceback to the exact allocating line before changing any setting; if a proposed fix cannot mechanically explain the observed numbers, it is not the fix.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Deleted `merged/` before extracting the vision component (mmproj)

**What happened.** The merged full model was deleted to free disk, but the mmproj (image-reading) component still had to be extracted from it — leaving the produced GGUF text-only for a project whose entire purpose is reading drawings.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-21 · Whole merge→f16→quantize GGUF pipeline was run before checking whether llama.cpp supports this model's vision at all

**What happened.** Hours were spent on merge_lora.py, three failed CUDA builds, repeated disk-full recoveries, an f16 conversion (~70GB) and a Q4_K_M quantization — and only at the end was it discovered that the resulting GGUF is text-only, and that llama.cpp's own docs warn `--mmproj` "will only work for some models", with Qwen3.6 being new enough that it may not be supported at all.

**Root cause.** Feasibility of the deliverable's core requirement (reading drawings = vision) was never verified before committing to the pipeline. The check that mattered most was left until last, when it should have been a 10-minute doc/issue search first.

**Impact.** An entire evening's compute, disk thrashing and effort produced a 21.2GB artifact that cannot perform the one job the whole project exists for; also lost with the instance.

**Fix.** Not fixed — Makham decided to stop and rely on running through Python/Unsloth on a rented GPU instead of the GGUF route.

**→ Rule.** Before committing to a multi-hour export/conversion pipeline, verify the *hardest* requirement first (here: does this tool support this architecture's vision component?). Order feasibility checks by risk, not by pipeline sequence.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-24 · The mmproj blocker that killed the 21st was self-inflicted — the vision layers were frozen, so the vendor's own mmproj was always usable

**What happened.** The 2026-07-21 rental went straight from 'rent' to 'train'. Every problem that day (OOM, disk full, mmproj unsupported, environment clobbered, files lost) was found while paying ~30 THB/hour. Only afterwards was a 'Phase 0' pre-rent checklist invented, and the diary explicitly records that having a checklist document is not the same as running it.

**Root cause.** No process existed requiring free, local verification (token, balance, disk sizing, local dry run, script re-read) before committing money; the checklist was written only after the failure that motivated it.

**Fix.** Became Rule 4 in rule_of_tune.md and Phase 0 in t01_workflow.md; on 2026-07-24 Phase 0 was actually executed and immediately caught two real problems (the 150GB disk default and the MAX_LENGTH truncation bug) before any money was spent.

**→ Rule.** Everything checkable for free on your own machine must be finished before the rental clock starts — and the rule must require running the checklist, not merely having one.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · A script written long ago and never run was treated as ready

**What happened.** train_qwen3vl.py was assumed usable because it existed and had been reviewed, but had never actually been executed until the paid t02 run.

**Impact.** Debugging a stale-API failure on paid GPU time instead of on a free local dry run.

**Fix.** Fixed the API call; the incident was recorded as a general lesson about dormant code.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · House 07 S-02: GB1X was read as a full C4→B4 span when it is a 1.60 m stub, which also wrongly flagged a footing as off-grid

**What happened.** GB1X was extracted as spanning C4 to B4 (that span is actually a second GB1). It is really a 1.60 m stub below B-4. The consequence propagated: footing F1 at B-4 had been recorded as off-grid when it sits exactly on the grid.

**Root cause.** A member label was matched to the nearest plausible span without reading the printed dimension chain, and the derived grid position was then trusted rather than re-derived from the corrected geometry.

**Impact.** Wrong span length feeds beam quantity takeoff directly; the false off-grid flag would corrupt grid resolution for that footing downstream.

**Fix.** Corrected append-or-rewrite style with the reversal recorded and the original warning preserved, never deleted.

**→ Rule.** Never infer a member's span from label adjacency — read the printed dimension chain. And when a geometry fact is corrected, re-derive everything computed from it, not just the field that was wrong.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · Fourteen of nineteen house-07 plan files needed fixes, all reducible to three recurring error classes that had no checklist entry

**What happened.** Only 5 of 19 plan files were clean. The 14 that needed fixing collapse into three repeating classes: counting different symbol types mixed together, reading plan adjacency as physical stacking, and look-alike lines masquerading as structural members. None of the three was in the extraction checklist.

**Root cause.** Errors were being fixed individually as they were found, with no step that generalised a found error into a rule applied to every other sheet. The same three mistakes therefore recurred across a whole house.

**Impact.** 74% of the house's plan files carried at least one error; the same three classes will recur on every future house until the checklist covers them.

**Fix.** The three classes were written up to be folded into op2's Stage 3 checklist.

**→ Rule.** When the same error appears twice, stop fixing instances and add it to the checklist as a class. Every extraction pass should end by asking which of the found errors is a class, not an incident.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-28 · export_gguf.py was still entirely t01's — pointing at Qwen3.6 paths and at t01's HF repo, which Phase 7.5 depended on

**What happened.** The t02 export script had been copied without adaptation: paths, repo, and size range all still targeted Qwen3.6. Running it as-is could have overwritten the HF repo qwen36-thai-rc, which Phase 7.5 needed intact to re-measure t01. It also loaded 62GB of weights before checking that ADAPTER_DIR even exists.

**Root cause.** Scripts were carried between rounds by copying rather than by parameterisation, so every hard-coded round-specific value became a latent cross-round hazard. No guard protected a repo other work depended on.

**Impact.** Near-loss of t01's published adapter repo, which would have made the Phase 7.5 re-measurement impossible; plus wasted 62GB loads on missing-adapter runs.

**Fix.** Path/repo/size tied to the same MODEL_SIZE used during training; an existence check for ADAPTER_DIR added before loading weights; any HF_REPO ending in /qwen36-thai-rc explicitly blocked.

**→ Rule.** Parameterise round-specific values instead of copying scripts, and add an explicit refusal guard around any destination another round's results depend on. Check cheap preconditions before expensive loads.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model-load warnings that named the exact bug were printed and read by nobody — twice

**What happened.** llama.cpp printed 'Qwen-VL models require at minimum 1024 image tokens to function correctly ... try adding --image-min-tokens 1024'. Nobody read it. This is the second occurrence of the same pattern: the collator earlier printed 'Model does not have a default image size - using 512' and that was missed too.

**Impact.** Both halves of the resolution bug were self-reported by the tooling and both were missed, costing a full training round and a night of extraction before the cause was found by inference instead of by reading.

**Fix.** not fixed — the lesson is recorded but no mechanical gate exists yet

**→ Rule.** Make warning review a required step, not an act of attention: grep the load log for WARN/W: and print the hits to the top of the run before any long job starts. Anything the tool tells you for free is the cheapest bug report you will ever get.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Phase 10's own written caveat ('don't read this as proven complete') decayed into 'Phase 10 passed' within days

**What happened.** The Phase 10 GGUF test document on the 25th explicitly warned that its result should not be read as proof of completeness — it only checked that the model emitted JSON and did not hang. Four days later everyone, the diary's author included, remembered only the green 'Phase 10 passed', and that memory was used to justify running the artifact at full scale.

**Root cause.** The caveat lived in prose beside the status, not in the status itself. A pass/fail marker with a warning attached loses the warning the moment anyone summarises it — and it will be summarised, repeatedly, by both people and later documents.

**Impact.** The GGUF was treated as validated for four days and used for a whole night's extraction run that produced six pages of unusable output.

**Fix.** not fixed as a process — the caveat was rediscovered only by re-reading the original doc during root-cause tracing

**→ Rule.** A caveat written next to a green checkmark is not a caveat. Encode the limitation in the status string itself ('Phase 10: JSON-shape only, content unverified'), so it survives being quoted, summarised, and remembered.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The MoE merge bug was proven on t02 on the 28th and never re-applied to t01 — a full night of extraction was spent before anyone re-asked

**What happened.** On the 28th the team measured, hands-on, that merge_and_unload() silently mis-merges a ParamWrapper LoRA on this MoE model (only 0.67% of 201M values changed). t01 was built with the same function, on the same model family, with the same ParamWrapper — but nobody went back and re-questioned t01's already-shipped GGUF. Instead t01 was run at full scale on the 29th, and the suspicion only surfaced hours later while tracing why the output was unusable.

**Impact.** A whole overnight session (00:30-03:30) plus the GPU-hours of six ~20-minute page extractions spent producing output from an artifact that was already known-suspect on the previous day. Six bad pages were written into the project output folder in the meantime.

**Fix.** not fixed — the base-model comparison test that would confirm it was still pending at the end of the session

**→ Rule.** When a root cause is found in one artifact, immediately list every other artifact built by the same code path and re-open each one. A toolchain bug is never scoped to the artifact that happened to expose it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Model-loader warnings that named both root causes were printed and ignored — twice

**What happened.** llama.cpp printed 'Qwen-VL models require at minimum 1024 image tokens to function correctly ... try adding --image-min-tokens 1024'. Nobody read it. This was the second occurrence of the identical pattern — the Unsloth collator had earlier printed 'Model does not have a default image size - using 512', also unread, which was the 14× resolution bug.

**Root cause.** Startup warnings scroll past among hundreds of lines and are treated as noise. No step in the workflow required reading them before starting a long run.

**Impact.** Both root causes of the resolution problem were sitting in the logs the whole time; days were spent on other hypotheses instead.

**Fix.** Adopted as a rule: read the loader warnings every time before launching a long job.

**→ Rule.** Grep the startup log for WARN/W before starting any expensive run, and pipe loader output to a file that is reviewed — a warning nobody reads is the same as no warning.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · debugging-method</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · Killed a healthy 1,256-second job because the 1,200s timeout was calibrated on the two lightest pages

**What happened.** A 1,200-second timeout was derived from the runtimes of pages 01-02. Page 03 needed 1,256 seconds and was cut off mid-work. GPU utilisation at 100% proved the job was alive, not hung.

**Root cause.** Two failures at once: the calibration sample was pages 01-02 — the cover and table of contents, the lightest pages in the whole set — and 'no output' was read as 'hung' when a generating model is silent by nature.

**Impact.** A real in-progress extraction was destroyed, and had the GPU check not been done, the rest of the night would have gone into debugging a non-existent hang.

**Fix.** Verified liveness with nvidia-smi (GPU at 100% = working; 0% = actually hung) before concluding anything.

**→ Rule.** Calibrate timeouts against the heaviest expected case, not the first case you happen to run; and before declaring a silent job dead, check an independent liveness signal (GPU utilisation, growing output file).

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · debugging-method</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The decisive clue was the shape of the errors, not their quantity — an aggregate score would have hidden it

**What happened.** The model performed well on hard content (TIS numbers 8/8, floor levels 7/8, rooms 8/8) while failing completely on the easy part (output format 0/6). That inversion is unnatural for a fine-tuned model and is what pointed at the missing-LoRA hypothesis.

**Root cause.** Initial reaction was to treat the result as 'bad quality' and look for model or resolution causes. Only inspecting the error pattern per category revealed that the failure profile matched an untuned model following a prompt.

**Impact.** Had the team only looked at the aggregate score, the real root cause would never have surfaced and time would have gone into retraining or renting more GPU.

**Fix.** Diagnosis by error shape; recorded as one of the six lessons of the night.

**→ Rule.** When results are bad, categorise the errors before measuring them — 'wrong on the easy things, right on the hard things' is a deployment/plumbing signature, not a model-quality one.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · debugging-method</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · The classify phase itself is inaccurate — elevations read as sections, 5 views claimed where 2 exist

**What happened.** Pages 07/08/09 were classified as `section` when ground truth is `side_profile`, and one page was reported as having 5 views when it really has 2.

**Root cause.** The 2-phase pipeline's cheap classify pass was never accuracy-tested on its own; it was treated as a routing convenience rather than as a gate whose errors are unrecoverable.

**Impact.** Misrouting: pages that should be extracted get skipped and pages that should be skipped get extracted. Errors here are invisible downstream because a skipped page simply produces no data.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Recorded as a caveat on interpreting the night's results.

**→ Rule.** A cheap routing/classification stage needs its own accuracy measurement against ground truth — a routing error deletes work silently, so it is more dangerous than a noisy extraction error.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · pipeline-design</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-07-29 · A written 'do not read this as proven' caveat decayed into 'Phase 10 passed' in everyone's memory, including the assistant's

**What happened.** The Phase 10 documentation explicitly warned 'don't read this as proven complete', but over the following days the caveat was forgotten and the phase was remembered — by Makham and by the assistant alike — simply as passed. That false memory is what let the unverified GGUF be used for real production extraction on 2026-07-29.

**Root cause.** The status label (a passing phase) and the qualification (prose warning next to it) live in different places and decay at different rates; humans and agents recall the label, not the paragraph.

**Impact.** Four pages of bad extraction were produced and written to the real results folder on the strength of a phase everyone believed was verified.

**Fix.** Not fixed — no mechanism proposed to make a phase's status carry its own limits.

**→ Rule.** A caveat in prose beside a green status will be forgotten; encode the limit into the status itself (e.g. 'Phase 10: smoke-only, content unverified'), never into a sentence nobody rereads.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · Round 2's dash-stripping fix only touched files whose *name* contained 'footing' — 809 refs were missed

**What happened.** An earlier round fixed dashed point refs (`C-1` → `C1`) but only in files whose filename contained 'footing'. Every other plan file in houses 06–11 was still dashed — 809 point refs across 87 files had to be fixed in a later round.

**Root cause.** The fix was scoped by filename pattern rather than by field. The defect lived in `grid_ref`-family fields wherever they appear, not in files named a particular way.

**Impact.** A fix reported as done covered a fraction of the affected data; the whole pass had to be redone across the corpus.

**Fix.** Rewrote all 809 refs across every file, scoping by field name (`grid_ref`/`grid_ref_start`/`grid_ref_end`/`grid_refs`) rather than filename.

**→ Rule.** Scope a data fix by the field it lives in, never by filename. Then verify the fix's completeness by counting remaining violations corpus-wide, not by trusting the run.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · 'Follow houses 01–05' was wrong — on the grid-word problem 01–05 were the worst offenders

**What happened.** The standing instruction was to make later houses match houses 01–05. But on redundant `grid`/`dummy` words in grid refs, house 05 had 127 violations while house 06 had zero — the reference houses were the worst, not the best.

**Root cause.** Houses 01–05 were treated as the reference standard because they were oldest and most reviewed, but 'oldest' means they predate several rules and accumulated the most legacy violations.

**Impact.** Following the instruction literally would have propagated 01–05's defects into the newer, cleaner houses.

**Fix.** Followed the written *rule* (item 5) that houses 01–05 had authored, rather than the *state* of their files — the rule was right, it had just never been applied everywhere.

**→ Rule.** Follow the written rule, not the state of the reference house. The oldest data is usually the most legacy-contaminated — never make it the de-facto standard.

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-08-02 · Two live files were misfiled for deletion as 'Label Studio' — manifest.json would have broken two working scripts
