<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-31.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · t04 was trained to completion with no cheap pre-flight check, so the failure was only found after paying

**What happened.** t04's fatal defect was detected only after the full training run finished and cost several thousand baht. The equivalent defect in t44 was caught for about $2 because a go/no-go gate had by then been introduced.

**Root cause.** No pre-spend validation step existed in the process at the time of t04. Verification was implicitly scheduled after the expensive step rather than before it.

**Impact.** Several thousand baht of GPU spend lost on t04 that a ~$2 check would have prevented.

**Fix.** Introduced a go/no-go gate: load the model and have it read 3 real drawing pages before committing to a full run. Pass → train; fail → stop.

**→ Rule.** Put the cheapest possible correctness gate immediately before every expensive step. A $2 check that can save $70 must run every time, without exception, even when the setup 'looks obviously fine'.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_ทำไม_Purson_กับ_Voldemort_พัง_2026-09-01.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟠 HIGH · 2026-09-01 · Live demo day consumed entirely by host failures and teardown/retry cycles, demo never completed

**What happened.** The whole session was spent on infrastructure problems: a dead tunnel, a bad host requiring destroy-and-re-rent, and two full teardown cycles (`presentation.py down`, verified 0 billed instances both times, one of them just to redo the demo with screen recording on). The live demo itself was never completed and got pushed to the next day.

**Root cause.** No pre-demo smoke test. The demo attempt itself was the first end-to-end check, so every latent infra fault (tunnel, host, key) surfaced during the demo window instead of before it.

**Impact.** An entire working session lost with no demo delivered; GPU rental costs incurred across multiple instances for zero demo output.

**Fix.** None on the day — Makham's own call was to retry the next day.

**→ Rule.** Run a full dry-run of the demo path (rent → tunnel → submit → one page) hours before the actual demo slot, on a cheap instance. Never let the demo be the first time the stack is exercised end-to-end.

<sub>`2026-09-01.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-01 · No work log existed before 2026-07-05 and the early git history was never ported into diary format

**What happened.** The diary only started on 2026-07-05. The 2026-07-01 and 2026-07-02 files were created retroactively on 2026-08-04 purely to hold archival notes, and the file states explicitly that none of the actual git history from that early period was ported into the diary format.

**Root cause.** The logging practice was adopted after the project was already underway, and no backfill pass was ever run against the git history that did exist for the pre-diary period.

**Impact.** The reasoning behind the earliest pipeline and schema decisions is unrecoverable except from commit messages. Two files had to be created a month later just to have somewhere to file archival records, and the earliest lessons survive only because they happened to be cited elsewhere.

**Fix.** Partially mitigated — retroactive stub files were created on 2026-08-04 to hold archival records, filed against each document's own creation date rather than the archiving date.

**→ Rule.** Start the work log on day one of a project. If it starts late, do a single backfill pass over the existing git history immediately — commit messages record what changed but never why, and the why is the only part that cannot be reconstructed later.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-01.md` · process-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-05 · A document was moved across repos without checking what still linked to its old path

**What happened.** Makham's patter of rawjson20260705.md was moved from the Training repo (No_touch_box/) to the Constistant repo (mk's stuff/). The diary explicitly records that if any other document in the Training repo referenced the old path — a session handoff doc, other notes — that link would break, and that this was not checked.

**Root cause.** The move was executed as a file operation without a preceding grep for inbound references. There was no rule requiring a reference sweep before relocating a document that other docs cite.

**Impact.** Unknown number of broken references left in the Training repo. It also directly set up the next day's confusion, where a 0-byte file appeared at the old path and Makham believed the data had been lost.

**Fix.** Not fixed on the day — recorded as a known unchecked risk.

**→ Rule.** Before moving or renaming any file that other documents cite, grep the whole workspace for its old path and fix every hit in the same change. A move is not done until the inbound links are done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-05.md` · process-failure</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-05 · Schema had five undecided points at the start of extraction, one of which only surfaced mid-work and blocked progress

**What happened.** Before starting the fresh extraction, four points the schema had not nailed down had to be put to Makham (multi-pattern pages, footings with multiple locations, four new pattern types, whether to keep Gen 1/2 legacy fields). A fifth arose mid-work — pages fitting none of the 9 pattern types, such as cover pages, legends and pure legal text — requiring a new `unknown` pattern to be invented on the spot.

**Root cause.** The schema was designed from a sample of pages rather than from an inventory of every page in the set, so page types outside the sample were only discovered when extraction reached them. There was no pre-pass cataloguing what page types actually exist.

**Impact.** Extraction was interrupted for a decision round, and the `unknown` pattern was created under time pressure mid-run rather than designed. Every page type outside the original 9 landed in a catch-all bucket storing raw_text plus a description.

**Fix.** All five points were decided in-session; pattern type `unknown` was created for pages fitting none of the 9 types.

**→ Rule.** Run a cheap page-type inventory over the entire document set before designing the schema, not a sample. Discovering a whole page class mid-extraction forces a schema decision under time pressure, which is exactly how catch-all buckets get created and never cleaned up.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-05.md` · planning-gap</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-05 · localStorage key strings were hand-declared in 14 separate feature modules with a hand-maintained scoped-key list — the actual root cause of the deleteProject orphan bug

**What happened.** Before Phase A there was no key registry: 14 feature modules each declared their own localStorage key strings, and the list of project-scoped keys used by deleteProject() was hand-maintained. Adding a new project-scoped key (Site, Foundation, manpower) therefore did not automatically make it deletable, which is why deleteProject() was leaving orphaned data.

**Root cause.** Same string of truth duplicated across 14 files with no single source, plus a manually-curated derived list — so 'add a key' and 'remember to also add it to the deletion list' were two separate steps and the second was silently skippable.

**Impact.** Silent per-project data orphaning on every delete (the surfaced symptom), plus an open-ended risk that any future key would be forgotten the same way; 14 modules had to be edited in the cleanup.

**Fix.** Created js/shared/storage-keys.js as the single registry, with PROJECT_SCOPED_KEYS derived automatically instead of hand-maintained, pipeline.js re-exporting STORAGE_KEYS for backward compat, and all 14 modules changed to stop declaring key strings.

**→ Rule.** A derived list that is maintained by hand will go stale — derive it from the registry. When a bug is 'someone forgot to add X to list Y', fix the mechanism that allowed the list to be separate, not just the missing entry.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-05.md` · architecture</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-06 · Label Studio config was written without ever opening it, so Makham had to re-paste it four times in one evening as each defect surfaced from his screenshots

**What happened.** Across four consecutive entries (~19:00, ~19:15, ~19:50, ~20:20) the XML config was changed and handed back to Makham to paste over the previous version each time: sticky-header→2-column freeze layout, then overflow-wrap + grid_ref_display, then a <Style> block + widened grid_ref box, then splitting the $variable header tags. Every defect (image too small at 380/420px, text overflowing its box, grid_ref box too narrow, import validation failure) was discovered by Makham using the real UI and sending a screenshot, not by anyone testing the config before shipping it.

**Root cause.** The config was authored purely from documentation and never loaded into Label Studio Cloud before being handed over — one entry states outright that the new sticky layout 'has not yet been tested in real Label Studio Cloud', including the known risk that Label Studio's own container scroll could conflict with position:sticky.

**Impact.** Four full paste-and-retest cycles for Makham in one evening, each requiring re-copying five XML files and (twice) re-importing the task JSON; the day ended with the review project still not working. Time cost was paid by the person least able to absorb it.

**Fix.** Each defect fixed reactively in its own round; no pre-ship test loop was ever established.

**→ Rule.** Never hand a UI config to someone else as the first test of it. Load it yourself once — even against a single dummy task — before saying it's ready; one self-test would have collapsed four re-paste cycles into one.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-06.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-07 · BOQ pages 41-47 sat unextracted for two days after an earlier run was stopped mid-way

**What happened.** An extraction run started July 5 got through pages 38-40 and was stopped. Pages 41-47 were left with no data at all until the t3 round on July 7 finally completed them.

**Root cause.** A stopped run left no explicit record of the exact page boundary it reached, so the gap was carried forward as an informal 'pending' item across two days instead of being immediately re-queued.

**Impact.** Two days with an incomplete house; the gap had to be re-discovered and re-scoped each session.

**Fix.** The t3 round dispatched an agent specifically for pages 38-47 and closed the gap.

**→ Rule.** When a run is stopped, write the exact last-completed unit into the pending list immediately — a range gap that lives only in conversation gets re-litigated every session.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-07.md` · process/work-tracking</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-08 · 'Issue loading URL from $image value' was suspected to be CORS/GitHub push; the URL was fine all along

**What happened.** Label Studio failed to load a raw.githubusercontent.com image. The July 7 entry hypothesised an unpushed repo, a URL-encoding error, or GitHub's raw CORS policy. Testing with curl (with and without an Origin header) returned 200 OK, the right Content-Type, and Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.

**Root cause.** The failure was diagnosed from the error string and prior beliefs about GitHub raw hosting rather than by making the request directly; the actual cause was browser-side (CDN rate-limiting, an extension, or a stale cache).

**Impact.** An overnight blocker carried across sessions and a round of speculative theories before a two-minute curl settled it.

**Fix.** Verified the URL directly with curl, ruled out server and CORS, and advised retrying plus checking the DevTools Network tab.

**→ Rule.** For any 'cannot load URL' error, hit the URL yourself first (curl, with and without Origin) before theorising — server-side and client-side failures look identical in the app's error message.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-08.md` · debugging-methodology</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-08 · A whole token-saving migration path was built, run, then deleted minutes later

**What happened.** To 'save tokens', a migrate_t3_to_t4.js script was written and successfully run, converting t3 data into a first t4 batch. The order then came to delete all t4 content immediately, and the entire folder was removed; the round was redone as a genuine fresh re-read of all 61 images.

**Root cause.** The approach (convert existing data vs. re-read the images) was chosen for cost before the quality requirement was settled — and a fresh read was in fact needed, since the whole point of t4 was to catch mistakes t3 had baked in.

**Impact.** An entire build-and-run cycle discarded; the real work then had to be done from scratch anyway.

**Fix.** Deleted t4 and re-extracted all 61 pages fresh, which immediately paid off by catching t3's wrong roof slope.

**→ Rule.** Decide whether a round's purpose is re-shaping or re-verifying before optimising its cost — a migration can never find the errors in the data it is migrating.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-08.md` · process/planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-08 · About 13 of t3's pages carried the wrong pattern type; found only because t4 re-read every image

**What happened.** The t4 fresh re-extraction reclassified a long list of pages against t3: page01→title, page03→symbol, page06→roof_plan, pages 07/08/09→side_profile, page11→symbol, pages 12/14→side_profile, pages 26/33→symbol, pages 59/60 index→title. Page 09 in particular had been typed `section` when the tightened definition restricts `section` to structures with actual rebar.

**Root cause.** t3 was extracted against a 10-type taxonomy with no per-type description; every extractor (Claude plus 5 agents) applied its own reading of what each type meant. The taxonomy was only given written definitions during the Gen4→t4 revision.

**Impact.** A whole extraction round's pattern labels were unreliable. Pattern type decides which of the 3 Label Studio projects a page lands in and which field-set applies, so a wrong type puts a page in the wrong basket with the wrong fields. Detecting it cost a complete 101-file re-extraction.

**Fix.** The taxonomy was rewritten to 13 types with a description for each, and t4 reclassified every affected page during the fresh re-read.

**→ Rule.** A closed vocabulary without a written definition per value is not a vocabulary — it is a suggestion. Define each type before the first extraction round, not after the second.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-08.md` · extraction-accuracy</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-10 · The op1 shorthand command was documented as a full 7-step workflow before it had ever been run

**What happened.** An 'op1 <house_name>' section was written into the README defining a 7-step end-to-end workflow for an agent to execute, while it had never been invoked once. It was first genuinely run about an hour later on house #2, where an agent was killed mid-task and 10 pages were left empty.

**Root cause.** A workflow was specified from reasoning about the steps rather than from a run, so its failure modes (agent kill, partial completion, no completion check) were not part of the design.

**Impact.** The first real invocation ended with an incomplete house that took two days to close.

**Fix.** Ran it for real on house #2 and discovered the gaps in practice; the completion-check gap was addressed by hand rather than in the workflow.

**→ Rule.** Do not document a workflow as canonical before running it end to end once — the first real run is what tells you which failure modes the spec has to handle.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-10.md` · process/planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-12 · A session-limit-killed agent's final message reports an older checkpoint than what it actually wrote to disk

**What happened.** When background agents were terminated mid-task, their last reported message did not match the files actually on disk — the message could describe an earlier point than the work genuinely completed. Recovery required listing real files rather than reading the agent's own report.

**Root cause.** An agent's progress narration and its file writes are not transactional; a kill lands between them. Trusting the narration means either redoing work already written or missing work never written.

**Impact.** Every house (2/3/4/5) needed a manual disk reconciliation step before repair could start; guessing from the agent's report would have caused duplicated or skipped pages.

**Fix.** Established the standing method: check how far the agent actually got by inspecting files on disk, then personally read only the genuinely missing pages.

**→ Rule.** After any agent kill, the filesystem is the only source of truth about progress. Never resume from the agent's own last message.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-12.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-13 · Edited tuning-relevant files without the warning step rule 2 requires

**What happened.** Files in the new `json_แก้ไขแล้ว/` folder were edited on the reasoning that rule 1 only protects `rawjson_ยังไม่ได้แก้ไขโดนคน/`. The user then asked 'did you read rule of tune', and the skipped rule-2 warning step was acknowledged.

**Root cause.** Rule scope was read narrowly by path instead of by intent — rule 2 covers 'any action that affects tuning', which the corrected-JSON folder does, since it feeds back into the protected original.

**Impact.** No data damage (git status on the original was clean), but a governance rule was bypassed on the first day the new folder existed.

**Fix.** Confirmed with `git status`/`git diff` that the protected original was untouched; the user waived a retroactive fix.

**→ Rule.** When a rule is scoped by path, check whether a new folder falls under the rule's intent before assuming it is exempt. A new working folder needs its rule scope decided before the first edit, not after.

<sub>`2026-07-13.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-13 · Label Studio task files were generated for houses 2-5 but never actually imported

**What happened.** The label-studio task generator was run successfully for houses 2, 3, 4 and 5, producing hundreds of tasks — but the manual import into Label Studio was carried on the pending list unchanged across multiple days and never performed.

**Root cause.** The generation step is scripted and the import step is manual, so the manual half silently fell off the end of every session; nothing failed loudly to signal it.

**Impact.** Weeks of extraction produced task files that no annotator ever saw; the annotation loop the whole pipeline exists to feed was never actually closed for these houses.

**Fix.** not fixed — carried forward as pending in every subsequent entry.

**→ Rule.** A pipeline whose last step is manual will stop at the last automated step. Either script the import or treat 'imported' — not 'generated' — as the definition of done.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-13.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-14 · Architecture-level finishing-material and door/window data extracted for five houses is used nowhere in the app

**What happened.** A check (run twice, with file:line citations) confirmed that the extracted floor/wall/ceiling/roof material lists with item_no codes and the D1-D3/W1-W4 door-window schedule are not consumed anywhere in the Constistant app — no schema, pricing, or BOQ engine supports the concept.

**Root cause.** Extraction scope was set by 'what is on the drawing' rather than by 'what a downstream consumer actually reads', so effort went into fields with no destination.

**Impact.** Extraction and review effort across multiple houses spent on data with no consumer; also inflates every page's token cost during training.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the finding was recorded, the data was left in place.

**→ Rule.** Before adding a field class to the extraction scope, name the downstream consumer that will read it. Extract-because-it-is-printed is how a dataset grows cost without growing value.

<sub>`2026-07-14.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-15 · Beam B2 endpoints mistyped as D'2/D'3 instead of D2/D3

**What happened.** During the reordering pass, beam B2's grid refs were found written as `D'2/D'3` when they should have been `D2/D3`.

**Root cause.** Hand-editing grid refs adjacent to a newly-added dummy grid (D') with no validation that every referenced grid label is one the beam actually touches.

**Impact.** A beam attached to the wrong grid line — would produce a wrong span and wrong position in any downstream geometry.

**Fix.** Corrected back to D2/D3 during the same pass.

**→ Rule.** After adding a dummy grid, run a check that every grid_ref in the file resolves to a grid the element genuinely touches — hand edits near a newly added label are where transcription slips happen.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-15 · An external AI recommended a rebar grade change that would have corrupted correct data

**What happened.** Another AI analysed page22 and advised changing F2's main bar from RB/SR24 to DB/SD30, reasoning that 12mm is usually DB. The drawing actually prints Ø for both F1(Ø9) and F2(Ø12), differing only in size, and the project rule is 'Ø always = RB, never infer from size'.

**Root cause.** The external model reasoned from a general industry prior instead of the symbol printed on the sheet, and had no access to the project's established symbol convention.

**Impact.** None — the advice was rejected after checking the image directly. Had it been applied it would have changed a steel grade on correct data.

**Fix.** Checked the original image first, confirmed the existing data was already right, and made no edit.

**→ Rule.** Treat external AI advice as a hypothesis, never as a finding. Verify against the source image and the project's own convention rules before editing anything on its say-so.

<sub>`2026-07-15.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-16 · A page12 dimension claims a 2.70m E-D span while the grid master says 2.0m

**What happened.** While fixing page12, `dimension_m` was found claiming '2.70 (E-D span)' although the grid master has E=4.0 and D=6.0, i.e. a 2.0m span.

**Root cause.** Per-file dimension values are written independently of the grid master and nothing validates them against it, so a contradiction can sit undetected.

**Impact.** A contradictory dimension left in the dataset; flagged but not fixed, still pending a decision.

**Fix.** Flagged for someone to check rather than being interpreted and fixed unilaterally (correct, since it was outside the ordered scope).

**→ Rule.** Add a validation pass that checks every per-file `dimension_m` against the grid master's computed span. Contradictions between a file and the master should be a hard error, not a note.

<sub>`2026-07-16.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-16 · House 4's dummy grid E' has three conflicting values across three structural sheets of the same house

**What happened.** Confirming dummy grid E' on house 4 turned up a three-way discrepancy (1.90 / 2.00 / 1.10) between three structural sheets of the same house.

**Root cause.** Either the source drawings genuinely disagree or the three sheets were read at different scales/reference points; no adjudication was possible from the sheets alone.

**Impact.** An unresolved grid value that blocks reliable span computation for anything referencing E'; still open as of 2026-07-19.

**Fix.** Flagged rather than guessed; refreshed the stale warnings on 2026-07-19 leaving only the E' discrepancy as the open issue.

**→ Rule.** Leaving a three-way conflict flagged rather than averaged is correct — but a grid-master value in conflict should block cascading into dependent files, not just carry a warning.

<sub>`2026-07-16.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-16 · The conclusion 'the 1.30 eave is unrelated to 1'/4'' was half wrong and had to be revisited

**What happened.** House 2's page07 had concluded that the 1.30m eave is unrelated to dummy grids 1'/4'. Revisiting found that while the steel eave genuinely is unrelated, the RC canopy at +3.75 on rows E-D does extend exactly to 1'/4' (1.30 = 1.00 to the slab edge + 0.30 roof overhang).

**Root cause.** Two distinct features (steel eave and RC canopy) sharing a similar dimension were collapsed into one conclusion; ruling out one was taken as ruling out the whole sheet.

**Impact.** Correct grid relationships were left unrecorded on page07, plus a leftover '0.60+0.90' sub-split from the earlier misreading remained in the file.

**Fix.** Fixed to 'E-D x 1-1'' / 'E-D x 4-4'' and removed the leftover sub-split.

**→ Rule.** A negative conclusion about one feature does not generalise to the sheet — enumerate the distinct features on a sheet before ruling out a relationship, and delete the artefacts of any superseded reading in the same edit.

<sub>`2026-07-16.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-19 · Grid refs were extracted with 'grid'/'dummy' prefixes and spelled-out primes, forcing a bulk normalization pass in every house

**What happened.** House 5's 30 plan files had to be perl-normalized (grid2-gridF→F2, gridAprime→A'), house 2 needed the grid/dummy prefix stripped across 12 files, and house 5's grid master needed Aprime→A' plus lowercase e'/f'→E'/F'. Each house required its own regex sweep.

**Root cause.** No canonical grid_ref format was fixed in the schema before extraction started, so each extraction run invented a variant; and the same regex family that fixed this previously corrupted sheet_code, so these sweeps are themselves risky.

**Impact.** Repeated per-house rework on dozens of files, using exactly the kind of regex sweep that had already silently corrupted data once.

**Fix.** Normalized per house via perl/regex, with parse-validation after (house 5: 138 files parse-passed, sheet_code survived).

**→ Rule.** Fix the canonical string format in the schema before extraction, not after — retrofitting formats across houses costs a regex sweep per house and each sweep is a chance to corrupt an adjacent field.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-19.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · An uncalibrated pixel measurement produced a false discrepancy flag against a correct grid value

**What happened.** A note recorded that dummy grid `2'` measured 4.9-5.0 on the image and differed from the master's 4.6 by 0.3-0.4m. Re-measuring with a calibrated scale gave floor1=4.69 and floor2=4.59 — `2'=4.6` had been correct all along.

**Root cause.** Distances were read off the image in raw pixels without first establishing a px/m scale from two known grid centrelines.

**Impact.** A false flag on a correct grid value, plus wasted investigation; had it been 'fixed' instead of flagged it would have corrupted a correct master value the way the price-table 'fix' did.

**Fix.** Set a calibrated scale before measuring, re-measured, retracted the note and removed the flag.

**→ Rule.** Never record a measurement-based discrepancy without first calibrating px/m against two known grid centrelines on that same sheet. An uncalibrated measurement is not evidence.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-20 · A grid_ref written as 'A-B'' contradicting the file's own description

**What happened.** House 3's page07 had grid_ref `"A-B'"` even though its own description says the feature is below row A (the A-to-A' span). B' is located elsewhere, above row A.

**Root cause.** The grid_ref was written without cross-checking against the file's own description field, and the similar-looking prime labels (A' vs B') were confused.

**Impact.** An element attached to a grid line on the wrong side of the building.

**Fix.** Fixed to `"A-A'"`.

**→ Rule.** Validate every grid_ref against its own file's description text — a file that contradicts itself is a detectable class of bug that a script can catch, and prime labels are easy to confuse.

<sub>`2026-07-20.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Multi-line paste silently dropped commands (a `cd` never ran)

**What happened.** Pasting several command lines in quick succession let progress-bar control codes interleave, so some lines (including a `cd`) vanished and were never executed — while appearing to have been typed.

**Root cause.** Pasting into a terminal that was still emitting escape sequences; the shell's input buffer mixed the pasted text with the incoming control codes.

**Impact.** Commands ran from the wrong directory / did not run at all, producing confusing downstream failures on a paid machine.

**Fix.** Switched to typing/pasting one line at a time and waiting for the prompt to settle between lines.

**→ Rule.** One command per paste, and wait for the prompt to return before the next one — never bulk-paste a command block into a live terminal.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Full training believed started, but the command was only queued behind the still-running test job

**What happened.** The full 3-epoch training command was typed into the same terminal right after the 5-step test appeared to finish, but `full_train.log` never appeared — the test script was still executing its final 3-sample generation step (885s / ~15 minutes) and the new command was sitting in the input buffer.

**Root cause.** Job completion was judged from on-screen output rather than from the shell prompt returning; the script had a slow post-save generation step that made it look finished long before it was.

**Impact.** Confusion plus a detective investigation, and a period where everyone believed the expensive full training was underway when nothing was running.

**Fix.** Checked running processes and the open log file handle, confirmed the old job was still writing to test_run.log, and waited for the prompt before issuing the command.

**→ Rule.** A command has started only when the prompt returns; verify with a process/log check before assuming a long job is running — never type ahead into a busy terminal.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-21(teach mk).md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-21 · Burned day-21 effort trying to export mmproj when the stock vendor file was already valid

**What happened.** On 2026-07-21 the team spent effort trying to export the vision projector (mmproj) out of the tuned model, failed because llama.cpp did not support the new architecture, and shipped a text-only GGUF. Three days later they realised the export never needed to happen at all: their own training script set finetune_vision_layers=False, so the tuned model's vision tower is byte-identical to the base model's and the vendor's published 899MB mmproj could simply be downloaded and paired with it.

**Root cause.** Nobody read their own training config when diagnosing the export failure. The answer ('we never touched the vision layers, so the stock projector is still correct') was sitting in train_qwen36.py the entire time; the team instead attacked the tooling limitation.

**Impact.** Wasted export attempts on paid GPU time on 2026-07-21, and the whole day ended with a GGUF that could not read images — the single stated goal of the project — when a free 899MB download would have closed the gap the same night.

**Fix.** Fixed 2026-07-24 (Phase 0.3): downloaded the vendor mmproj (899MB) and dry-ran it against a real drawing page on Makham's own PC; it read Thai text, grid 1/2/3 x A/B/C/D and footing labels correctly.

**→ Rule.** Before fighting a tool limitation, check whether your own config makes the problem moot — a frozen component does not need re-exporting, the upstream artifact is still valid.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · wasted-work-misdiagnosis</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-24 · House 5's dummy grid B' recorded as 12.5 before checking the source sheet corrected it to 12.2

**What happened.** Dummy grid B' was added at 12.5 so that beam B2 B'1-B'2 could land, then corrected to 12.2 after checking against the real A-04 sheet.

**Root cause.** The dummy grid was placed at a value derived to make a beam fit rather than measured from the source sheet — the beam drove the grid instead of the grid being measured independently.

**Impact.** A wrong grid value, plus a wrong beam span, until the source sheet was consulted.

**Fix.** Corrected to 12.2 after checking A-04.

**→ Rule.** Never place a dummy grid at whatever value makes a beam land — measure it from the source sheet first, then check whether the beam fits. Reverse-fitting a grid to an element hides the real discrepancy.

<sub>`2026-07-24.md` · data-extraction</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-25 · Both attempts at the big-house extraction run were killed, producing no output at all

**What happened.** Two llama-cli runs on the big house were started and both killed — the first for RAM exhaustion, the second when the task was paused for something more important. No page produced an extraction result; the big house still has no draft.

**Root cause.** A multi-hour job (25 pages at ~3 tokens/sec) was started interactively on a workstation in active use, with no per-page checkpointing so that a kill loses everything up to that point.

**Impact.** Setup, prompt preparation and two run attempts spent with zero output retained.

**Fix.** Not fixed — the run was deferred to the next day, still needing to be started from scratch.

**→ Rule.** A multi-hour inference job needs per-page output checkpointing and should run detached (tmux/nohup) rather than in an interactive foreground session, so a kill costs one page and not the whole run.

<sub>`2026-07-25.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Assumed comparable model size implies comparable training time — Qwen3-VL ran 2.9x slower than Qwen3.6 with identical settings

**What happened.** t01 finished training in 29:23; t02 took 84:53 with every hyperparameter verified identical. The 30B vs 35B headline sizes and identical 3B active parameters had been the basis for treating the two as equivalent for planning purposes.

**Root cause.** Model selection reasoned from headline parameter counts, which say nothing about internal architecture — layer count, how images are handled — which is what actually determines step time.

**Impact.** Training took nearly three times the planned duration on hourly-billed hardware, tripling that phase's cost against the estimate.

**Fix.** Recorded as a lesson; no remedy applied since the run completed.

**→ Rule.** Never estimate runtime or cost from parameter count. Measure step time on a short test run (TEST_STEPS) and extrapolate from the measurement before committing to the full run.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-28(teach mk).md` · estimation</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-28 · Re-verifying t01 on the same machine was not planned into the rental, forcing a second ~70GB base-model download on the clock

**What happened.** Doubt about the t01 numbers only arose after the library-drift bug proved that library versions matter. The re-measurement (Phase 7.5) was then added mid-rental, but the machine had only ever loaded Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B for t02 — so the full ~70GB Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base had to be downloaded from scratch while paying, prompting Makham's 'ทำไมโหลดนาน'.

**Root cause.** The A/B experiment plan treated the two arms as independent runs on separate machines instead of requiring both to be measured on one machine in one session; the need for a same-machine control was recognised only after a version-drift bug surfaced.

**Impact.** An unbudgeted ~70GB download plus load time on a paid instance, purely to answer a question the original plan should have designed out.

**Fix.** Phase 7.5 was executed (t01 adapter re-measured on the t02 machine), but the plan itself was not changed to require same-machine A/B by default.

**→ Rule.** In a controlled A/B, both arms must be measured on the same machine in the same session — otherwise the control run becomes an expensive, unplanned add-on the moment anyone doubts the numbers.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/สอนมะขาม_รวม.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Near-misdiagnosis: a silent model was almost declared hung

**What happened.** When page 03 produced no output for 20 minutes, the natural read was 'the process has hung'. Checking nvidia-smi showed the GPU at 100% — the model was mid-generation. Had the silence been believed, the whole night would have gone into debugging a non-existent hang.

**Root cause.** A generating model and a dead process are indistinguishable on stdout; the only difference is visible in side-channel signals (GPU utilisation, a growing output file).

**Impact.** Near-miss — a whole night could have been spent fixing the wrong thing. Cost was limited to one killed page.

**Fix.** fixed as a practice — verify with nvidia-smi / growing output before declaring a hang

**→ Rule.** 'No output' is never evidence of 'stopped'. Before killing or debugging a silent long-running job, confirm death on a second channel: GPU utilisation, file size growth, or a heartbeat log line the job emits on its own.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29(teach mk).md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · The extraction script written on the 28th lived in the scratchpad and was gone by the 29th

**What happened.** The script that ran house 01 extraction on the 28th was written into the scratchpad rather than the repo, and had to be rewritten from scratch on the 29th as a permanent file (tune_ai/t01/extract_house01_local.py).

**Root cause.** Working code was created in a location with no persistence guarantee, treated as throwaway because the run was 'just a test'.

**Impact.** The same script written twice; a night's worth of accumulated flags and details had to be reconstructed from memory.

**Fix.** fixed — rewritten as a permanent, resumable script at tune_ai/t01/extract_house01_local.py

**→ Rule.** Anything you ran successfully once is a work product: move it out of the scratchpad and commit it before the session ends. Scratchpad is for output you will never want again, not for the script that produced it.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-29 · Original plan was a full extract of every page — ~16 hrs/house before anyone did the arithmetic

**What happened.** The run started as a full extraction of all pages. Partway through it became clear that ~18 min/page × 55 pages ≈ 16 hours per house, which is unacceptable, and the plan was changed mid-run to two phases: cheap classify on every page, full extract only on kept patterns.

**Root cause.** The per-page cost was known from the first pages but never multiplied out against page count before committing to the run.

**Impact.** A run was started on an unworkable plan and had to be redirected mid-flight; the pages already extracted were mostly patterns the new plan filters out anyway.

**Fix.** fixed — switched to a 2-phase classify-then-extract plan (KEEP_PATTERNS: plan / section / roof_plan / side_profile / gridline)

**→ Rule.** Multiply unit cost by unit count before starting any batch job, and compare against the time you are actually willing to spend. A five-second calculation prevents starting a sixteen-hour job you would have cancelled.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-07-29.md` · planning</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-30 · Same page-scoping mistake repeated on house 09 — 4 'criteria' pages, only 1 real

**What happened.** House 09's pages 70–73 were listed as 4 criteria pages; checking showed only page 70 is criteria, the other 3 are credits + price table + back cover, and all 4 are byte-identical to the same pages in house 08.

**Root cause.** The same defect as house 08 (page ranges inferred, not verified) was carried straight into house 09 because the house-08 correction was never fed back into the manifest-building step.

**Impact.** The identical mis-scoping cost a second round of investigation on a house whose pages were already known byte-for-byte from house 08.

**Fix.** Re-classified the 3 pages; confirmed byte-identity with house 08's pages, so no independent reading was needed.

**→ Rule.** When a defect is found and fixed in one house, patch the process that generated it before starting the next house. Also: hash back-matter pages across houses in a series — byte-identical pages should be recognised, not re-read.

<sub>`2026-07-30.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-07-31 · Six near-identical BOQ sets (174 sheets) were being re-read sheet by sheet instead of diffed

**What happened.** House 11 has 6 BOQ sets differing only by foundation type and seismic zone. Set 1 was read sheet by sheet (29 sheets). Only afterwards was it recognised that sets 2–6 should be handled by file comparison — items 2/3/4 are expected byte-identical, with only item 1 (structure) genuinely differing.

**Root cause.** The extraction workflow has one mode — read every sheet — with no branch for 'this document is a near-duplicate of one already extracted'.

**Impact.** 29 sheets read the slow way, and 145 more were queued to be read the same way; a diff-first approach would have cut most of that work.

**Fix.** Strategy changed before starting set 2: compare files against set 1, read in full only where a genuine difference appears.

**→ Rule.** Before extracting a near-duplicate document set, diff it against the extracted one first and read only the differing sheets. Prove byte-identity, then reuse.

<sub>`2026-07-31.md` · efficiency</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · Item-55 lesson applied: don't trust the fix-log, verify against the real data before editing the spec

**What happened.** Before rewriting the spec, the actual JSON was scanned to confirm the claimed state (no dashed point-refs in houses 01–05, zero column elements still carrying `main_bar.top`) rather than trusting the log's claim that the fixes had landed.

**Root cause.** A prior incident (item 55) established that the fix-log records intent and can diverge from what is actually on disk.

**Impact.** None this time — the verification is exactly what prevented a repeat. It is recorded here because the underlying failure mode (log-says-fixed) recurred later the same day.

**Fix.** Verified by scanning the real files; the spec edit proceeded from measured state, not logged state.

**→ Rule.** 'The log says it's fixed' is a hypothesis, not a fact. Grep the actual data before making any decision that depends on a past fix having landed.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · 5 files still carried `phase_note`, which by the schema's own rule means they are unfinished

**What happened.** Five files in houses 09 and 10 still carried a `phase_note` field, which §2a defines as marking an unfinished file — so by the project's own rule those files were never completed.

**Root cause.** An in-progress marker was written but nothing scanned for it, so the marker did its job (recording incompleteness) while nobody ever read it.

**Impact.** Five incomplete files sat in the corpus indistinguishable from finished ones to every consumer.

**Fix.** Folded the `phase_note` content into `warnings[]` and removed the field per §2a — deliberately preserving the unanswered questions verbatim rather than resolving them.

**→ Rule.** Any 'this is unfinished' marker needs a checker that fails on it. A TODO nobody scans for is the same as no TODO.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-02 · A folder rename required editing 454 JSON files because full paths were embedded in data fields

**What happened.** Renaming `raw_json_ตัวที่ใช้งานจริง/` to `rawjson_ยังไม่ได้แก้ไขโดนคน/` required updating 20 .md files, 4 code files, and 454 JSON files whose `grid_source`/`spec_source` fields carry full paths beginning with the folder name.

**Root cause.** Cross-file references were stored as absolute-ish paths including the top-level folder name, rather than as paths relative to a configured root.

**Impact.** A cosmetic rename became a 478-file edit with a real risk of dangling references; extra care and verification was needed to confirm zero live references to the old name remained.

**Fix.** Pure prefix replace across all 454 files, logged in the data log; verified afterwards that `check_format.py` passes on the new path and 2,366/2,366 files parse.

**→ Rule.** Never embed a top-level folder name in a data field. Store references relative to a configured root so the root can be renamed without touching data.

<sub>`2026-08-02.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-05 · Seven straight sessions were never logged live and had to be reconstructed from git log afterwards

**What happened.** Every diary file from 2026-08-05 onward (08-05, 08-07, 08-08, 08-09, 08-10, 08-14, 08-16) opens with the same note: the entry was rebuilt after the fact from git log and the schema edit log, not written during the session. Dates 08-03, 08-06, 08-11, 08-12, 08-13 and 08-15 have no file at all. On 2026-08-04 two diary files (2026-07-01, 2026-07-02) had to be created retroactively because the diary did not exist that early, and three more existing files had retroactive notes appended.

The reconstruction then only recovers what a commit message happened to record.

Reasoning, near-misses and rejected options from those sessions are unrecorded. Backfilling seven days from git log is itself rework.

**Fix.** not fixed — the backfill note is repeated on each affected file rather than the gap being closed

**→ Rule.** Add 'diary entry appended' to op03's pre-shutdown gate alongside the commit. A git log is a record of what changed, never of what was decided or almost went wrong.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-05.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-08 · House 15 was committed with the message 'บ้านต่อมา' and no check_format.py status recorded

**What happened.** House 15's 35 JSON files were committed with a message that said only 'บ้านต่อมา' (the next house). Unlike the `op03:`-prefixed commits which report ALL CHECKS PASS directly, no pass/fail status was recorded, so whether the house passes the format checker is unknown.

**Root cause.** The op03 workflow requires reporting the checker result, but nothing enforces it at commit time — a manual/ad-hoc commit bypasses the reporting step entirely.

**Impact.** A whole house's extraction state is unverifiable from the record; someone has to re-run the checker to find out, and until then house 15 cannot be treated as final.

**Fix.** Not fixed — flagged as pending: confirm house 15 actually passes `tools/check_format.py`.

**→ Rule.** Make the checker result part of the commit itself (a pre-commit hook or a required commit-message field). A quality gate whose result is not recorded did not happen.

<sub>`2026-08-08.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-18 · Seven days of house-extraction work never logged live, reconstructed from git log afterwards

**What happened.** The 00:09 entry is explicitly backfilled from git history, and the afternoon entry records backfilling seven more missing days (08-05, 07, 08, 09, 10, 14, 16) covering op01/op03 house extractions 13-21 that were never written down when they happened.

**Root cause.** Diary writing was treated as an optional end-of-session nicety rather than part of the definition of done for an op-run, so when a run finished late or the session was cut, the entry was silently skipped. Git log only preserves commit messages, not why a decision was made — exactly the gap the diary exists to fill.

**Impact.** Nine work sessions' worth of context (judgment calls, traps hit, near-misses) lost or reconstructed approximately. Later sessions had to spend time re-deriving state instead of reading it.

**Fix.** Backfilled 2026-08-05/07/08/09/10/14/16 entries from git log during the 08-18 afternoon session.

**→ Rule.** An op-run is not finished until its diary entry is written; write the entry in the same session as the work, before destroying any rented instance or closing the session — reconstruction from git log recovers what changed but never why.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-18.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-18 · The 90-minute op3 ceiling systematically leaves the largest houses permanently undone

**What happened.** When asked for 'a house, any house', the smallest not-yet-done house (59 pages) was picked specifically to fit the 90-minute op3 ceiling. Several houses at 130-133 pages (บ้าน_เล็ก_1ชั้น_07/13/14) were skipped as too large for a single run and remained undone.

**Root cause.** op3's dead-man's-switch shutdown ceiling is a fixed wall-clock budget, while house size varies 2x+. With no resume-across-runs path for a large house, the selection heuristic 'pick what fits' biases the dataset toward small houses forever.

**Impact.** Dataset composition is skewed to small houses; the largest, most element-dense houses — likely the most valuable training signal for beam plans — accumulate as permanent backlog.

**Fix.** Not fixed. Small house picked; large houses recorded as still undone.

**→ Rule.** When a time-boxed job cannot fit the largest work item, add a resumable/split mode rather than letting selection quietly bias toward the easy items — otherwise the hard cases never enter the dataset at all.

<sub>`D:/00mk/steel project/training/Training/workmen's_diary/2026-08-18.md` · process</sub>

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-20 · Comparison and overlay scripts written to session scratchpad, never committed

**What happened.** compare_house08.py and overlay_page10.py — the scripts that produced the session's headline numbers (57.9% valid, 11% recall, 88.9% dimension-correct) — were written to the session scratchpad and not committed to the repo.

**Root cause.** They were treated as throwaway analysis code, but they are the measurement instrument for the project's key metrics; nothing distinguished 'scratch' from 'the tool that produced the number we now quote'.

**Impact.** The published numbers cannot be reproduced or audited without rewriting the scripts; the next comparison run pays the same authoring cost again. A near-identical script (overlay_gt_vs_ai_house09.py) was indeed written again the following day.

#### 🟡 MEDIUM · 2026-08-21 · Repetition-penalty fix committed without ever being run on a GPU

**What happened.** repetition_penalty=1.15 and no_repeat_ngram_size=8 were added to run_house_batch.py and infer_t02.py and the diary explicitly notes 'Not yet tested on GPU.' It remained on the pending list at end of session — the beam-plan page had not been re-run to confirm it now closes valid JSON.
